AE's design philosophy heavily relies on weekly updates (of rather varying quality) which unfortunately contradict their long-time goal of creating a truly cross-platform game in an utterly fatal way in their latest endevour, AQ3D. As it stands the game is something like 52mB, and remains an uncomfortable to control, unpleasant to look at, mess, and if AE continuously has to scale down the size and quality of game assets to pander to their mobile platform the PC version simply won't exist as an ejoyable title.
That being said, as someone who's casually followed AE for something like a decade, the game is still very much in development, and will more than likely see a number of performance and UI improvements in the coming months (if AE doesn't decide to arbitrarily cease all development resources on it like they have with so many other titles). I genuinely look forward to the coming improvements because as much as I believe the goal of catering to some incredibly nieche cross-platform MMO market is a terrible idea that relies on a feature that doesn't have nearly enough hardware or consumer support to be feasible, entering the town of Battleon in 3d was a gigantic nostalgia trip that legitimately makes me think they might be able to pull this off.
That is, if they drop mobile support for the main game, and focus on optimizing the pc experience. While it's true that there is a sizable market on cell phones for small, artistic, indie arcade games, the consumer looking to drop $5 on an app for their train ride to work or whatever isn't looking for a vast world to grind in for hours (something AE is notorious for). Even consumers who *do* enjoy grinding for hours every week in games like WoW aren't looking to do so on their mobile phone, they're looking for smaller, lightweight apps that can help them manage their character or access guild chat whilst they are away from the game. They aren't looking to engage in content in the same way shown in the trailer because, simply stated, current PC hardware is more well equipped for the MMO genre than mobile devices. The potential that this game has may be great, but it seems squandered on a philosophy that takes resources away from the actual quality of the title.
**TL;DR**
The art style of AQW clearly shines through in this title, and the humor and accessibility that AE prides themselves on is extremely evident. This game is clearly a passion project, and I applaud the development team for how far they've come since the flash tech demo, but I hate to see them holding themselves back from making a legitamitely **fun** game because of a conviction that a mobile market will supplement the already dying MMO genre.
P.S: Shadowfall in this art style sounds awesome! I really hope you guys pull through!

Chronology doesn't seem to know what it wants to be, or how to go about expressing whatever it eventually decides on.
It's a puzzle platformer in appearance, but more akin to a point and click adventure game in structure. Time manipulation is introduced as the driving mechanic but then barely used in any interesting way, or completely forgotten for more tired adventure and platforming standards. There's this setup to an involving time travel narrative that's rather quickly exchanged for the dull relationship building between your character and a talking snail that does little but demonstrate that you're kind of a jerk.
All of Chronology's best ideas are left on the wayside for an experience that feels painfully typical. Puzzles are bland and extremely simple in construction, only ever becoming difficult do to the finicky interaction icon that makes it hard to discern what exactly you need to interact with, or the backgrounds which while beautiful tend to be hard to make out from objects in the foreground. Progression always felt tedious, puzzles slowing me down but providing no satisfaction to solve beyond the knowledge I'd never have to sluggishly make my way through them again.
There was a point when Chronology seemed promising, but it flounders around with its direction so long as to never feel cohesive or engaging. Its mechanics are disorganized, poorly implemented and rudimentary, and its narrative may as well not exist for as little substance as it has. The artwork is wonderful, but animations are choppy and the lack of vsync made for omnipresent screen tearing. It feels like a game formed in a puzzle platformer mold, with a handful of modifications having been made to differentiate it from the pack that probably did more harm than good in the long run.

I think it took me an evening to complete it (dunno why it shows I only played it only for 2 hours).. The artwork is good, music too, the puzzles are interesting. As with most puzzle games, after the game is completed, there is nothing to come back to - so well, no replay value, but for the small price it's fine.

For something I initially thought to be a laid back game, this game is extremely intense for a puzzle game. It seems to be a combination of Puyo Puyo and Tetris, more so Puyo Puyo as the game's single player really wants you to go fast, so if you have poor reflexes like I do, your not gonna enjoy this. This game's single player isn't really that great for that reason, for the game values speed over skill, as the game itself is about building the tallest and most sturdiest tower. Or so I initially thought at first.
Tricky Towers seems to have multiple modes to it, and by multiple, I mean three. There is Race, which is accurately named due to speed being the name of the game, Survival, where if you lose 3 pieces of your tower, you lose, but if you use up all of your pieces before your opponents, you win (so again, speed is the key here) and Puzzle, which is probably the mode I like the most because it actually takes real strategy to win.
Now for my biggest problem with the game, and it's one that really makes playing this frustrating. The game has 2 ways to move pieces. There is the normal way, which moves each piece half a block and then there is nudging, which moves it a full block, but it's slower and really only used for primarily puzzle mode. My response to that is why would you make it so the conventional movement speed is half a block?! This can make tower building painful as one mistake and you could have a leaning tower that is unsalvagable. Not to mention create a frustrating experience rather than a fun experience.
Another problem I have with the game is that it doesn't like both controller and keyboard being connected at the same time and can sometimes lock you into using one of them and not being able to switch back unless you close out of the game. I found this out playing multiplayer with friends, but I wanted to use the keyboard not the controller, so I unplugged my controller and the game locked me into using my controller anyways. Not to much of an issue, but c'mon!
It may sound like I'm railing on the game alot, and I kinda am, but that's not to say it's a bad game. The multiplayer is exactly as I expected it to be, a competitive tower building game with light powers making the game easier for you and dark powers making the game harder for your opponents to spice up the competition even further. Not to mention, I also got this game on Humble Bundle for a dollar and even for the on sale price of $7, I'd say it's still worth it, however the price I'm told it's normally sold for, which is $15, definitely doesn't seem worth it! Sorry Weirdbeard Games, with friends it can be fun, but other than that, this game just isn't for me.

Visually? The game is gorgeous! I love the style selected, the color selection, the storybook idea for the plot points fit perfectly.
Edit:
I have some feedback on the game that I should have put in originally with my review. Hopefully the dev team can use this.
I recently re-watched the episodes of Extra Credits talking about difficulty and the part about difficulty spikes is what reminded me to come back and reread my review.
This is long-winded so, fair warning!
It's the entire section dealing with the Red Reapers is why I'm not recommending the game. From when you first enter the darkness below the Maw all the way till you come back out after getting the quest item. I have yet to play a game where the difficulty spike made any sense.
It's not a "test of the players skill" when you haven't provided opportunities for the players to build up their skill to "that" point. Now the fact that I didn't see any training doesn't mean that it's not there. I know one of the challenges is to try and make them barely noticeable at worst. However, a hidden tutorial that doesn't work is just wasted dev time and money.
Was this Game Mechanic Test needed? Was it tacked on after the last sections of the play-through were put in?
Darkness:
When you first encounter the darkness it gives you a written warning on the screen to not use your Searchlights. "Ok, but how do I counter the Reapers?" Not being able to see doesn't encourage me to experiment with my equipment to see if anything works on them. You can't aim your torpedoes when you can't see which way you are facing. You also can't see if anything you try had an effect until you re-spawn. Even then, you don't know if what you used hit it's intended target. I still don't know if anything works on them.
As for using the sonar. I ended up getting through that section creeping along the left wall. Only moving a short bit before hitting the sonar again. The recharge time on the sonar doesn't give much time to react if you end up in the patrol route of a Reaper. It's a good thing they can see in the dark. But then how do they navigate around the rocks without hitting them? I don't think it has a store line answer. The answer is simple,  game-play. The devs were making a specific challenge and had to throw the story aside. Fair enough!
I was in flight mode going through there and trying to spam the sonar. I got through, but my heart was pounding in my chest. That leaves me with a rhetorical question. Why did the dev team decide to put in a moment of dis-empowerment?
Chase scene:
I should have recognized that I was going into an obstacle course as I was working my way around to the quest item. The crushing walls that only went half way, the three gates that require you to switch back and forth between torpedoes. The signs were there. So I should have stopped and prepared myself before I triggered the "trap". Maybe calmed my heart rate after the dark section and practiced the course a few times. Now note that I went through this before they issued out patches for it. Though I didn't encounter any problems with the Reapers hitting me unfairly.
When I started the chase I went through the save point while I was using the boost. Each time I re-spawned it felt like I had less of a boost charge to work with. It was impossible to test that given the situation.
I found the Reaper's movements to be inconsistent. I couldn't tell if they were starting to navigate the course better each time because of my movements or not. I have no way to tell anyway. Each time I failed it felt like they were catching up sooner and due to being in a panic you can't really tell how.
I never knew until this point that you could shoot a gate twice to make it break faster. That might be something to point out in text to players earlier in the game.
Final thoughts on the chase scene. Perhaps the dev team could consider turning on the light beams at the "end" of the course automatically. I turned them on by habit and was glad I did. A Reaper was nearly on to me when I reached the end.
Also one of the Reapers did not follow me around and stayed at the location of the quest item for some reason. It was trying to swim to me while I was at the save point outside the obstacle course and was just stuck against the bone wall.

It's entertaining, there's some problems though, like all goods at any given location scale at the same time, so if the price of say food goes up so does everything else, making large swaths of your tripp useless since you'll come across MANY succesive towns with high prices. This makes things very linear, also you generally only start out with enough money to make a trip and usually due to the crumby scaling don't have much of a market to work with, and usually you'll get hit by bandits immediately so on average a game lasts only a couple of turns based straight on luck.
There really isn't much tactic, because the prices can change so rapidly, there's no point in noting them: You'll leave a town that is buying high, you find a place selling low and buy that commodity up (any of them since they all scale equally), return to the town that was buying high to find the market has dropped out. Where you can't even stock a couple commodities to make up lost time and money cause,... everything scales together.
There's no point in plotting a course since it's generally just luck wether or not you find a place to sell, not actually knowing what things go for in different places. Also going back to how every commodity scales up or down at a location together, there isn't even a way to salvage your wasted trip by buying up something at the location you've just revisited (using the example situation still).
So you now have a full load, have to spend probably what money you have left to make a trip to somewhere worth a damn, and will undoubtably get robbed, even if you buy mercenaries to protect you (do they actually do anything?). I'm not saying this game is impossible, but the deck is stacked and in peculiar ways that don't make sense.

16bit Trader is a game that is flawed from the word go. Although the idea of the game is a decent one, 16bit Trader fails to execute on what little potential it has. The first problem arises when one attempts to play the game along its intended methods: the prices of the goods being trade barely fluctuate between locations. One can buy goods for one price in any given city only to find out that every other city sells the same goods for the same prices, and that the price that you can sell the goods for is lower than any of the perchase prices anyware. In moving between cities, one will discover the next problem: the cost for movement between cities can and will exceed one's profits for trading, making actually making a profit to be next to impossible outside of fulfilling the sidequests that are at least quite plentiful, or to find diamonds at any of the dungeon locations strewn thoughout the game world.
The only positive thing I can possibly say about this game is that the art style is bright, colorful, and quite nice.
Pros:
- Wonderful art style.
- It only costs $3
- the game is competantly coded, and doesn't seem to glitch or crash with any regularity.
Cons:
- The intended gameplay features of the game are functionally impossible to use
- The is frustratingly designed.
- The developers have the audacity to charge money for a game that has inferior design to a game you can play for free on Newgrounds.
- Any time you spend playing this game brings you that much closer to the inescapable reality of death, time which can never be gotten back.

16bit Trader is not a game about trading. Buy/sell prices for goods seem to be random and travel is so expensive that you'll always make an overall loss from trading. Taking randomly-appearing quests and gathering once-per-day diamonds are the only reliable way to make money.
It's a lazy port of a mobile game. It's designed around a-few-minutes-a-day casual play, but it doesn't hold up well when you sit down to seriously play it. Don't bother.

The game isn't scary, it's scarcity of ammunition is to the point where you're better off just running past all enemies, the camera control is bulky, the atmosphere is not creepy (Simply covering a wall in blood does not make a game scary), and lots of other nuances that make this game look stupid compared to others in the genre.  If you want an ammo scarce game that makes you think about your moves, go play the original Bioshock.  You want a survival horror game that makes you have precise shooting to actually do anything to the enemies, play Dead Space.  You want a game that has good atmospheric music and sounds that creep you out, go play The Hat Man.  You want a game that has excessive amounts of gore, play the SAW games.  You want a game that has a confusing story that won't make any sense till 3/4ths of the way through it, has no suspense, enough gore that you won't be grossed out by anything ever again, a pointless crafting system, pretty bad voice acting, environments that have been used before, an upgrade system that makes no sense (How does injecting myself with green goo give my Revolver the ability to hold 24 bullets?), and worthless ally AI, then you've come to the right game.

The father of survival horror. I am quite sure that by now, this has pretty much become Shinji Mikami's official title. For a reason, though. Mikami has created Resident Evil, and arguably made the 2 best entries in the series: RE1 and 4 (and the remake of the first one, which to this day remains to be the best remaster of all time). He also had large creative input in the series' general direction. Also, Dino Crisis. Oh, and next to that, he also created some excellent action games such as God Hand or Vanquish.
So, it's clear that Mikami is one of the greatest game directors of all time.  He pretty much invented an entire genre on his own, and then once again revolutionized it. Inspired lots of other great games such as Gears of War series or Uncharted, but at the same time also proved that he knows more than just survival horror by making great fast paced games too.
And this time, he gave us The Evil Within. TEW is unique, even for him, because it's a game made by his own studio, Tango Gameworks. So, it's fair to say he had full creative freedom so he could create the ultimate Shinji Mikami experience.
Starting the game, I quickly felt right at home - yes, this does indeed have Mikami's name written everywhere on it. The game right off the bat feels a lot like Resident Evil 4 on steroids.
You play as Sebastian Castellanos, a detective that's dispatched to a murder scene in a mental hospital along with your partners. The game is quick to get going  - after a little walking and talking and cutscene, you already find yourself in the belly of the beast.
The game reveals it's cards right away. You are in a room with a massive, butcher type enemy. You are right behind him - you have a choice. Either perform a stealth kill, or just take the door key you need to get out.
Most players will definately choose to kill here - only to realize that this enemy is, in fact, unkillable at this point. So while the game does offer you to choice to attempting a kill, and the animation of grabbing him, stabbing him et cetera does actually go through, nothing happens. He grabs you, and you die.
This is something quite unique. Most games make a conscious choice wether to be a game where you can fight back and defeat your foes, or simply not. But TEW seems to want best of both worlds.
Sadly, a seemingly creative design decision isn't always clever. The game ends up feeling like trial & error a lot of times because of this. Because there's no objective indicator in the game, you're never really sure wether you should fight or not. Whenever a larger-than-standard enemy appears, I usually tend to try and flee at first to conserve my ammo, since the resources are scarce. If that doesn't work, then I know I need to kill him.
Sure, as you progress, you get the hang of it - you start to understand the game more, so you will know when to fight and when to flee. But it should've been handled better. Quite frankly, normally I wouldn't make a big deal out of this but when a game tries so hard to be cinematic, having sudden deaths and trial & error based gameplay really does take you out of the immersion.
Speaking of which: the game runs in a forced widescreen mode, and 30 fps. Both of which you can unlock through PC wizardry, but by default, that's just how it's meant to be played. So I did just that, putting faith in Mikami and his team to know what's best for the game.
Sadly, while I understood what they were trying to achieve... it just didn't quite work. The classic Resident Evil games had a strange perspective and the difficulty of navigating. This helplessness made the game way scarier and unsettling than if it was easy to control. RE4 adopted the over the shoulder view, but Leon still moved like a tank, and you couldn't move while shooting - amping up the factor of fear once again. These design decisions were really clever, beacuse, normally, a game would be torn to shreds if it was hard to control. But Mikami balanced the fine line between a clever and a stupid design decision really well.
In TEW, it's quite clear that having super widescreen forced isn't just there for the cinematic experience, but to create tension. Whenever you enter shooting mode, due to the FoV, the camera almost zooms in to your gun, making fighting really quite difficult until you get the hang of it.
Sadly, this ends up being irritating, rather than adding to the atmosphere like in RE4.
That being said, the game's strongest point is definately it's atmosphere. Every chapter is very different from the previous one - which is all very well reasoned in the story.
It's just a great adventure, and gives you the constant feeling of wanting to push on "just one more chapter"! Sadly, the game does not satisfy with it's ending. It's way too heavy handed. Not enough things are laid out for you to gain proper understanding. And again - Mikami claims this is on purpose. But sadly, this is yet another gamble he failed this time. Mystery is great, but there needs to be some sort of pay off. Otherwise, you could create a game with things that you just think up at complete random. Stage 1: rainbows, Stage 2: flesh eating iphones, Stage 3: cars made out of cheese. If you have no logical conclusion at the end, it almost doesn't matter what you do.
The other gripe with the story is the characters. Sadly, no one seems to acknowledge all the strange things, and the very few times they do, they are very vague. "There's something wrong with this place" - 9 chapters in. Really?
Not to mention that Jennifer Carpenter who played Julie completely phoned it in . Her performance is awful. And considering there's a story expension coming with her character in the focus, I am a little worried.
Visually, the graphics design, and the way it all comes together is almost masterful - and also, I adore the "warping" effect the game does sometimes - enviormnents transforming right before your eyes, daylight turning into night time, and so on. However, technically speaking, it's a mess. iDTech is not a good engine, sadly. RAGE, Wolfenstein and now The Evil Within also failed to be a smooth experience for everyone - and these are not cheap games made by incompetent people. Lots of people, even on configurations above the recommended are experiencing slowdowns and glitching. And, on top of that, the game's artifical limitations with the widescreen and 30 fps lock also add to the disaster. Personally, on my i7 with GTX 780 I didn't have a single hiccup, the game stayed at a steady 30 fps, but I've heard lots of people having issues. And still, after all these years, there's some serious texture pop in going on especially during cutscenes. Really disappointing, maybe it's time to put megatextures to the rest for a while.
Finally, I'd like to talk a bit about one thing I always loved about Mikami games. Replayability. Every single game directed by Mikami has excellent replayability; completing the game grants you bonuses such as new guns, outfits or abilities. Mind you, this is also the case here, you do get new guns that you previously couldn't access, so that's fantastic. Sadly, this is countered by one problem: the game's reliance on the narrative. Resident Evil 4 had a strong narrative, however, it was presented very well. You had cutscenes at the end of each chapter, and small radio conversations during it. The game NEVER took control away from the player, and you never had scripted sections. Sadly, TEW does.
In the end then, TEW is a mixed bag. Great atmosphere, excellent visual design, a story that definately grips you but kinda whimpers out in the end, countered by strange gameplay decisions and unfortunate limitations.
I looked forward to this A LOT, so i'm a little disappointed, but it was still a fun ride. Mikami took a few risks, and they mostly didn't pan out like before - but once you get over the shortcomings, there is a neat game to be enjoyed.

I finished the campaign on survivor difficulty in 13 hours.
PROS
-Your partner is Joseph Gordon-Levitt
-Sebastian does 360 no scope stomp attacks (stomp attacks will frequently make Sebastian spin lol)
-Some creepy environments
-2 really creepy bosses
CONS
-Those 2 bosses are re-used 3 times each. They won't be scary by round 2 and flat out boring by round 3.
-Bad pacing of scares/action.
-They start off pushing a clunky stealth system and then almost never use it.
-Enemy AI is terrible as far as alerting them goes. I shot one 10 feet from his friend and he didn't come looking for me. They also don't react to seeing the light of your lantern in an otherwise pitch black room.
-Non-existent character development. You'll know almost nothing about any of the exceptionally dry characters in the game by the time credits are rolling.
-They never address why the hell Sebastian was collecting jars of brain goo unprompted. I mean, it worked out that it's his currency for upgrade but was he just doing this on a typical day too? This guy has issues.
-The story is non-existent for the first half of the game and it's pretty awful once it gets going.
-The enemies trade in anything creepy for guns as the game goes on. It will just feel like a generic 3rd person shooter at times instead of one claiming to be survival horror.
-No dedicated punch and stomp button. Want to punch that guy in front of you? Too bad! Stomp on that corpse instead! You died lol
-Only 4 quickslot spots when you have more than 4 weapons alone. That doesn't take into account healing items or grenades. Time doesn't stop when you're trying to get your shotgun back out in a pinch.
-The ammo caps are set as ammo not in your gun currently. If you can hold 4 extra shotgun shells and you have 4 not in your empty shotgun currently, you'll need to reload before picking more up. This is especially bad with the crossbow and it's crafting system. Want 3 bolts? Craft one, equip bow, equip desired bolt, craft two more. Keep in mind this will be done in real time while enemies maul you.
-Lots of deaths just felt cheap. An underwater beartrap in front of a bomb. Are you ♥♥♥♥ing kidding me?
-Super widescreen aspect ratio that forces horizontal black bars on your screen. You can change this but then you're zoomed in horribly far and there will be graphical glitches where the bars should be.
-This game really chugs along. After using the 60 fps console command, I played this on a GTX 770 at 1920x1080 and it was averaging about 40 fps. It averaged 50 at 1280x720 on all the lowest settings.
-All the minor design and control flaws just make it feel like an offbrand RE4.

TL;DR the only difficulty mode that offers any challenge is almost literally impossible. Game has massive bugs and stability problems. Dev's seem very inexperienced. Customer service is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't play this game right now.
I used to enjoy this game quite a lot, but the devs seem hell bent on making it the most difficult game possible with little to no reward. The highest difficulty, Cataclysm, is nearly impossible for like 97% of the player base (check achievements) and Cataclysm is the only reliable way to get the best loot, which is a shame because you need more luck than skill to conquer Cataclysm maps with any frequency. Every difficulty up to Cataclysm is a joke and Cataclysm is absolutely brutal. You need a team of people with high end gear and who know every trick for the map in order to even have a chance and then, the game might randomly spawn Assassins (think Jockey from L4D2) as a sort of "♥♥♥♥ you". This can happen in the first 3 minutes or the last 10 seconds, literally.
The game has several bugs that make it even more difficult and unreliable, such as randomly dying for no reason whatsoever, invisible rats at times, rats that don't care about walls/objects/height differences and will glitch to attack you, etc.
Finally, their first "DLC" that they released was free, which was great and added some much needed features in order to adjust the stats and perks on your weapons. Then they released a hold out, wave style map. Cool. They teasted their next DLC for a while and made it known that it would be paid, but released no further details. Upon release, it was the exact same wave style mechanics as the previous one, but in a different map. It offered nothing new other than a different location that in no way changed how you played the game. I felt as though this was an extremely poor move by the developers. Instead of focusing on perfecting the current content and removing stability, balancing and various glitches, they released free DLC then basically a paid version of it that offered nothing new in any way. Great.
On top of that, their customer support is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing awful. At one point I had an older i7 SLI Laptop that ran the game fine, but would often crash. No matter what settings I tried to run the game with, I got the exact same crash every time. I compiled all of the information as requested, typed everything out that I could and made a support ticket, marked "Critical". It took them 3 or 4 days to get back to me, which is fine. They offered a solution, but as I was busy with other things, I did not get to test it for a day and a half before they closed my ticket. The solution changed nothing and was literally "This game does not support SLI. Disable it", which in my ticket I stated I had already attempted. So, I opened another ticket and then waited 2 and a half weeks for any response whatsoever. In that time I just bought a new desktop and continued to play on that instead of the laptop. Eventually they got back to me and offered more advice, which did indeed help, but not completely.
Overall, the developers seem to be extremely new to this whole "make game, foster community" sort of thing. I love difficult games that make me work for every single victory. I love increasing my skill. However, this game comes down far more to pure luck than it does skill. You can do absolutely everything perfectly and still lose because the game seemingly just says "Hey, ♥♥♥♥ you, you're not winning this map". No reward, nothing, just try again. Cataclysm is the only difficulty mode that offers any sort of challenge for myself or my friends and sadly, most of the community experiences great difficulty on "Hard", which is one step above "Normal". Above hard is Nightmare, which very few players have ever beaten and above that, Cataclysm. Even fewer people have been able to beat a single map of that, let alone every map. The developers are fine with that, so I'm fine not playing the game again and leaving a negative review.

The "revolutionary" turn-based combat system was created LONG ago in Final Fantasy Tactics for GameBoy Advance.
The "Open-World" MMORPG was done in EVERY MMORPG since UO.

I don't recommend supporting Sega. Even buying their good games supports bad practices.
Sonic in particular is high profile enough that any future games are likely to be affected by Sega's worst policies for DLC and DRM. This particular game doesn't include any 3rd party DRM but it probably would if it were more recent.
I have a soft spot for Adventure 2 but, while its engine was impressive for running at 480P 60fps on Dreamcast & its mechanics for Sonic improved on Adventure, the level design is weaker than its predecessor.
The speed levels have a lot more walls or elongated straight lines getting in the way of taking shortcuts & feel more linear in general; the hunting stages have a heavily nerfed radar coupled with a much larger scale that makes exploring them more frustrating; & the shooting stages are much slower & clunkier than Gamma was.
I don’t see why nearly everything except jump is mapped to B/Circle. Sonic seems to have a reputation for simple control schemes but this is the wrong kind of simplification with the light dash & bounce being a particularly unfortunate combination that will result in numerous lost lives.
There are odd graphical glitches which are exclusive to this port. On my hardware the worst issue I've encountered is all the objects in the Chao Garden retexturing themselves at random upon leaving the Chao Stadium.
On other people's hardware a glitch causes cars and trams to somehow get stuck to Sonic in the first level, apparently rendering it unplayable. Luckily it never happened to me even when I tried it on my laptop that's too weak to run the game at full speed.
Another somewhat infamous glitch exclusive to the HD port (on all platforms) causes the Chao key to consistently glitch in certain levels & send the player to a test level upon completion.
Sega never even attempted to fix these issues, leaving it to fans to help those who couldn't play the game.
The port does run at 60fps, less would've been inexcusable, but that's because it's locked at it. Any drops make the whole game slow down. Any increase makes the whole game speed up. I’m sure the Dreamcast original was capable of running at the correct speed at 50fps in PAL mode and 30fps/25fps in multiplayer but that’s not possible on PC.
As with the port of the original Sonic Adventure, texture and audio quality have taken a hit compared to the Gamecube port and the Dreamcast original in turn.
Once more there is no way to access or transfer content to or from Adventure DX's Chao Garden nor anything which required Tiny Chao.
I'll give credit for attempting to restore Big the Cat's cameos (removing some unreachable rings in the process) but for some reason one of them was left out.
A number of other touches I enjoyed in the Dreamcast version have been omitted too such as the hedges in City Escape spelling "Welcome" as opposed to the plain grass that's even more barren looking in this wide-screen version.
Likewise instead of inserting some of the billboards in the city that didn't make the jump between Dreamcast and Gamecube for variety's sake, Sega simply removed as many references to Soap as possible which means the billboards that are still there are repeated far more often.
No attempt has been made to recreate the Dreamcast version's DLC content either. Truth be told there wasn't much of interest but there are character skins, karts and at least one kart race that's not accessible in this version.
I don't believe the leaderboards of the console HD port are accessible on PC. No big loss, they'd just be hacked, but I wouldn't know because I mostly play in Offline Mode.
Why, then, would I have so many hours on record? The Achievement for raising a Hero & Dark Chao glitched out and refused to unlock until I started a new Chao Garden save & earned the achievement again while online. Every other achievement unlocks just fine in offline mode.
I don’t see why this game couldn’t have been sold on GoG or DRM-free on the Humble Store. Even before the PC port existed pirates already had access to the previous console releases so it’s not like DRM is saving them anything. At this point Sega are just turning down willing customers.
Lastly, as someone who owns and has completed the Dreamcast original, it irks me that Green Hill is exclusive to the Battle "DLC" when it was never exclusive to Gamecube. Every other bit of the DLC is pointless but Green Hill is probably in the top 2 levels in the game in terms of how fun it is to speed run.
I've purchased that game only for Chao Garden.

Hotline Miami 2: Blunt Force Commentary
It’s no secret that Hotline Miami was a commentary of violent video games. And the aspects of its point on being pointless stuck with me well after the fast paced action. That is to say, about a day and a half, because I immediately went and bought Hotline Miami 2.
Hotline Miami 2 is a much larger game that it’s predecessor, in terms of story, scope, and the overall amount of content. They packed a lot into this game for only $15. Hotline Miami 2 is simultaneously a prequel, side sequel, and a sequel. And it’s a wonderful value proposition… But I’ve been feeling that in adding so much to the game, it lost something in the process. That isn’t to say that Hotline Miami 2 isn’t good, on the contrary-- It’s great a great game.
But it doesn’t feel the same as the first.
And again I think that’s part of the point.
A lot of Hotline Miami 2 is commentary on … well a lot of stuff actually. The most obvious to me being ‘fandoms’, internet outrage culture, video games, and the people who play them. There were several times where I felt the creators poking at me in the dialogue of various characters. And I found it to be a very surreal and interesting experience, albeit a little hamfisted.
Commentary aside, I found that some of the changes they made to the gameplay have somewhat impacted my enjoyment of the game. The movement feels a tad slower in Hotline Miami 2 which took a bit to get used to. And actually impacted my performance in the first game, because it had changed my timing. But the thing I find disappointing is the game has a much larger focus on gun combat this time around. I never really cared for how the guns handled in Hotline Miami 1, and the larger focus on them doesn’t excite me. I find that they are tricky to aim, and really slow down the entire experience. Hiding behind doors, peeking out, shooting… it’s not nearly as engaging as stabbing the enemy. NSA, please don’t read this out of context!
Hotline Miami 2 is a much slower experience than the first game. Instead of bursts of fast paced action, Hotline Miami requires you to be even more methodical in your approach than the first game. And while this isn’t true of every level, guns become incredibly prevalent towards the later stages of the game.
I honestly can’t think of a stage in the sequel that doesn’t have you at some point dealing with firearms. That isn’t to say that melee has been made obsolete, rather, I would say it’s been made much riskier-- without a significant increase in reward. There are far fewer melee weapons overall, and most of them are slower, I don’t remember seeing any swords or machetes, unless your character started with one, until the final chapters. And the swing on weapons such as the bat and lead pipe have been slowed significantly.
And while this doesn’t sound like a lot, it actually impacts the feel of the game tremendously. Some might prefer the more methodical gameplay. But I found myself wanting levels to end, and becoming frustrated at the enemy’s ability to shoot me at almost any time. I finally cleared this section of the level! Now to move up to- [long string of expletives removed]
And while I might sound like I’m being harsh on the game, I actually really do enjoy it. There are more levels in Hotline Miami 2 that I don’t like, than I do.... But the good levels are really good. Sadly  the bad levels are just frustrating.
If you really really enjoyed Hotline Miami, I would definitely recommend the sequel. But it’s a tad long, and while the changes they made to the ‘formula’ weren’t to my taste-- Hotline Miami 2 is definitely a good game. If not as good.

That brings up another point, death in this game isn't very punishing at all. You just pop back to the nearest save point, which is usually only a half-screen or so away from where you were. Could be a positive or negative depending on how "hardcore" you are
, but for me, it takes the tedium out of it because you don't have to slog your way back through useless cleared rooms.
The controls feel great. There's a bit of floatiness to it, but it's part of the game style instead of being a poor implementation. You're floating in water in a heavy submarine, of course you're going to have some momentum when you turn or stop. Combat feels tight and really well-polished. You can enjoy fighting the enemies, not fuss over fighting the controls.
This is a seriously good game in the Metroidvania style. I've played (and 100%+) all the classics (Metroid, Super Metroid, Metroid Fusion, Metroid Zero Mission, C:SotN, C:AoS, C:DS, C:PoR, C:OoE) and a few new ones like Aquaria (*obvious inspiration for this game*) Axiom Verge and Guacamelee. This game comes correct with real respect for the genre and gameplay that keeps you coming back. Honestly, if you see negative reviews for this game, it's almost certainly from people who just don't like or get the genre. Not that there's anything wrong with people having their own opinion, but I'm just saying. If you like Metroidvanias, this game is a must-have.
One last thing I'll mention, though this isn't a multiplayer game, my wife is loving watching me play this. She plays some games (WoW, etc) and while playing Metroidvania games isn't her cup of tea, she's really enjoying the visuals and story of this one. If nothing else, this game gets a thumbs-up for turning a game that I would disappear to play for hours into a fun night of quality time with (bae? Is that what the kids say these days? I'm going with bae.) Especially since the narrator is Irish.

Mount and Blade Warband is truly a masterpiece, it's political aspect isn't as great as any other real strategy game, I mean, be fair. With mods it can be brushed up (It's no CK2.) and the graphics can be enhanced aswell. The options in Warband to be fair are limited compared to the advanced modifications. However, the vanilla game is fine, pretty good overall, you start out as a traveller after picking your back-story, and build up your renown, or you can go out as bandit, merchant, or whatever you wannna be in a medieval world. Building up your renown gives you offers from lords, (quite rare) who if you aren't sworn to any king, will actually INVITE you to become their vassal, if your renown is quite high enough. Being a merchant is fine, but doesn't enhance your fame. The marrying prospect is cool, but limited again. You can make your wife your "steward" of the castle but there is nothing further more to explore in the marriage category. Marrying her does cement an "alliance" with her relatives, however it's more symbolic to be honest. They don't back you up in schemes or such not unless THEY start the scheme. Schemes are essentially just quests with a tad bit of espionage and such, denouncing a lord, demanding they be cut off from lands, etc. However when you cement the alliance the relationship with her family improves. It also makes them actually vote for you when the king is giving out new lands and declaring a marshal. So actually, it's worth a while, but I would suggest you marry into the upper noble houses. It's disappointing to not be able to marry into the ruling dynasty, but hey, I think that's too easy for a rise to power eh? Combat is great, and the fact you control one character from a first-person view or third person view WHILE controlling a full-blown out army? (I suggest Napoleonic Wars DLC for that, it still can work well for warband vanilla) so yeah. There are even star wars mods for this, which is great mate. All in all, spectular game, I can't wait for Bannerlord.

Sonic Adventure 2 Battle was one of the first games that I remember playing. I had very fond memories of stages such as City Escape, Radical Highway, Pyramid Cave, and Sky Rail. Because of this combined with the cheap price, I decided to purchase Sonic Adventure 2 and the Battle DLC. After a rough start where my antivirus treated the game as malware, I was finally able to play it after years of wanting to. In my opinion, the game hasn't aged too well, but I still love it due to the nostalgia. The game is still quite solid because of my childhood nostalgia involving the game. I would definitely recommend the game to those who want to explore through Sonic's Dreamcast days or who want to simply relive childhood memories like me. Don't boot up the game expecting a masterpiece, as the game is old, but it's still incredibly enjoyable past the sometimes glitchy platforms, bad audio mixing, and plot holes.

I cannot recommend this version of the game over the console versions. The controls in the PC version are awful and nothing ever feels smooth with keys. I can say that this game has great music, gameplay and story... But the "gameplay" part is only bearable with a controller. I can't play a game that controls this awfully. I played through City escape when the game glitched and I had a car above my head, something that never happened on the consoles. I tried the level again, the car was above my head, blocking my vision. I tried again, it wasn't there but about a minute later it was. Every time I tried City Escape, that car was above my head, blocking my vision and I tried City Escape about 5 times. I can't say that the other levels have glitches in them like that, but I'm willing to bet that they do after City Escape. Overall, if you want to experience what this game really has to offer, go play a console version. I would recommend this game on the consoles but not the PC unless you have a controller and a fix for the City Escape glitch, which I have heard is downloadable or something. On it's own, with keys and no glitch fix, it is awful. Slippery controls make it hard to turn, moving the camera is not smooth whatsoever since it isn't set to a mouse by default, and glitches. I am in no way saying that console is better than PC. I'm just saying that the PC version of this game is horrible. The sheer fact that the creators never did ANYTHING to fix these problems and you have to go OUT OF YOUR WAY to solve these issues is what pisses me off. Without some modification, this game is unbearable with keys.
However, again, it is possible to play this with a controller and I have heard that there is a fix for the glitch in City Escape. You just might have to do some digging. Using a controller solves all the slippery controls and awkward camera. Again, I have not played much of the PC version so I don't know if there are any glitches further ahead. Just warning people what they're getting into.
Overall, should you get this game? Only if you have a controller you can use with your PC. Otherwise, don't bother.

The Evil Within is an almost perfect mixture of east meets west horror survival. It contains the familiar territory of Resident Evil and mixes in the insanity of Silent Hill while managing to stay coherent to a western audience - no horrible translations or ridiculous dialogue. It contains stealth elements and a minor RPG upgrading and crafting system, all serve gameplay well but can feel slightly out of place thematically. The game is genuinely creepy and beautiful, you will feel horror and amazement in various doses throughout your playthrough. The only negative I can add is that it can be unmercifully, face-smashingly hard, in the true Japanese fashion.
Many complaints have been lodged at this game such as the use of the ID Tech engine. I wouldn't have even known if someone hadn't pointed it out, but it works fantastic here. I've yet to see a single flicker, weird clipping object or crawling texture anywhere, it looks console-level polished. The black bars combined with the 30fps limitation, conspiracies aside, actually served to pull me further into the game - It just felt more cinematic to me.
The Evil Within is a fantastic and memorable game, and a true successor for the Japanese survival horror genre.

The Evil Within is a survival horror game that claims to be a throwback to the "roots" of the horror genre. It throws you into a twisted world full of psychological horror. You play as Detective Castellanos as he attempts to unroot the mysterious happenings that shift the world around him. Anyways, let's get to the review.
Now here's some complaints you might of heard already regarding The Evil Within, so let's just get them out of the way first. The game has some large black borders that attempt to give it a more 'cinematic' feel, you can disable these with some non-official fixes at the expense of some graphical bugs. The black borders tend to be kind of distracting, and sometimes pulling you out of the immersion for a while, until you get used to them. I'm hoping they'll have an option to disable them in-game in the future, as playing without borders really enhances the immersion. The next up is the 30 FPS lock, you can disable this using a console command to run at 60 FPS. I played the most of the game at 60 FPS and noticed no issues or problems regarding running at a framerate higher than intended. Now the optimization can be a bit poor at times. Some areas of the game give me a solid 60 frames, while others tend to drop to 45-50. It isn't terrible, but some of the textures/effects/graphics aren't very detailed enough to justify the drop, and it tends to happen in the strangest of places.
Now to the meat of it all, the game can feel pretty hit-and-miss early on. I felt the beginning chapters was probably the weakest part of the game, in terms of both horror and gameplay elements. It starts off slow and tends to follow every cliche horror games to a T. The intro is filled with many stealth and tutorial sections without invoking any real tension to the situation you're in. It's a very slow start, and it can probably turn-off a few people from playing past that point. Mid-way through the chapters, the game starts feeling more like a horror game. Each level is filled with twisted, and disturbing designs; enhanced only further by some of the most gruesomely lovely character and boss design I've seen. Once the game starts picking up, it's easy to get absored in the pacing of it all. These later chapters can feel absolutely tense, and creepy.
The gameplay is very similiar to Resident Evil 4 (both being Shinji Mikami games after all). The ammo is very scarce, and the game often encourages you to used them sparingly. Each engagement with the horrors that reside the twisted realm feel challenging, but never cheap. There's a lot of thought and tactics you can put into each battle, setting up traps using the Agony Crossbow, silently taking down each enemy with a knife to the head, or using careful well-placed shots to take out multiple enemies at once. Each bullet you spend can feel rewarding when it hits, enemies react wonderfully to each shot; from a head bursting, to falling over when hit in the knee. A lot of the game encourages using your head to solve the situation at hand than rather blindly firing all of your shots. The game also features a corpse-burning mechanics, as most enemies are weak to fire. You can find matches in the game that allows you set ablaze multiple objects or a downed enemy; this fire can spread to other enemies if they're over it resulting in an instant kill. The game also features some pretty awesome boss fights as well; although they seem to appear at random. Some chapters can have 1 boss, none at all, or even multiple. They kinda come inconsistantly, but they're lots of fun.
As far as graphics go, some parts of the game can feel really weak at times, while others looking amazing with great tension-building lighting, effects, textures. It's a bit of a hit-and-miss. Some chapters can look intense and eerie, while some suffer from muddy textures and some ugliness. The worse offender is probably the beginning of the game, where it looks straight out of 2008. It's great to see some of these strange and twisted enviroments come to life, the game often has a very nightmarish surrealism to it.
As for plot goes, it tends to shroud itself in mystery until the very end of the game. It seems that the almost non-existant plot for the first half of the game is only serves as a device to take you to each new area. You'll probably find yourself scratching your head for most of the game, and probably after it ends as well. The world is filled with some collectibles that give a bit of insight into your situation, and the plot can make sense if you read a bit into it. Unfournately, the characters are pretty bland. The main protagonist feels emotionless and almost robotic, making a few remarks to remind you that you (as the player) don't even know where the ♥♥♥♥ you are, such as, "Where am I?" or "What the ♥♥♥♥?" as if you haven't seen so much bizarre things already.
All in all, I enjoyed The Evil Within. Despite it's slight performance issues, sometimes muddy textures, slow beginning, and blind plot for the first half of the game. It's gameplay, artistic level design, and creepiness are more than enough to jump over it's flaws. It's a sickening lovely game that loves to play on the tropes of horror, and that's not a bad thing. It's a game definetly worth playing if you like Resident Evil 4 or just the horror shooter genre in general.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Total time to complete: 15 hours.
Difficulty completed on: Survivor (Medium)
Difficulty scale: Challenging, it's not an easy game that's for sure.
Total deaths: 98
Full price at time of review: 59.99 USD
Price paid for: 45.00 USD on Greenman Gaming
Price I suggest buying it at: 30-40 USD
Spookiness scale: It's not completely terrifying, but it can feel very tense at times; with a few scares here and there.
Pros (+) and Cons (-):
+Absolutely fantastic and challenging gameplay, requires you to think each situation through.
+Has some great creepy levels with plenty of supernatural elements to them, much like Silent Hill or Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem
+Wonderfully made boss fights and twisted enemy designs
+/-The graphics can look really good at times, and look absolutely awful the next.

You want a game that can be picked up by literally anyone, cause massive fun, and really reinvigerate the couch gaming experience? Then pick up this game. Let me start by saying that Tricky Towers is not a multiplayer game. It is a singleplayer game that you play with other people. Yes, you do participate in "battles", but the level of interaction between players is so low that the only real purpose the multiplayer serves is to put you under time constraints. Don't buy this if you're looking to have a blast with a friend.
That said, it is a *great* game and I definitely recommend it - especially if you like Tetris. If "Competetive Physics Tetris" appeals to you, then you'll probably enjoy Tricky Towers. Maybe wait until it's on sale, though - $14.99 is a rather hefty pricetag.

I picked this game up for $1 in a Humble Bundle but it's a complete steal for $7 as well. This is a very heavily tetris-inspired block building game that really shines with the multiplayer feature. Powerups and sabotages can really change the course of a match and makes the game all the more fun and unpredictable.
I have a few gripes with the game and some key features that were somehow not implemented on launch like the fact that a full lobby will start counting down regardless if everyone is ready or not. So if someone in your party needs a momentary break, you have to completely restart the entire lobby. Another thing with the lobby system is that you can't change game settings like the mode, difficulty or length; you have to remake the lobby with the desired settings. These aren't anything game breaking but still should've been implemented prior to launch.
I'd like to see some new themes and gamemodes implemented as well but those obviously take time.
Overall, I'd easily give this game an 8/10 in it's current state.

Tricky Towers is a twist on Tetris that doesn't distance itself too much from the original, which is a good thing because Tetris is a perfect game.
This particular spin-off features three game modes which revolve and cleverly use the mechanics of gravity: pieces will stick together as long as they perfectly fit each other, but "holes" (that wouldn't let you clear a line in Tetris) and misplaced blocks will cause your tower to become unbalanced and your pieces to fall into the water like Jenga.
In addition to that there are the omnipresent powerups, a "light magic" which will help you and a "dark magic" which f**ks up all the others. Needless to say, the excitement of messing with your friends and "NOOOOOOOOO"s as your own tower crumbles make for a great couch multiplayer experience.
The only part that bugs me is the price, which I deem too steep for the content. Otherwise great game, get on sale and only for local multiplayer.

Did you ever dream of becoming a researcher, helping mankind to unveil the mysteries of the universe? Yes? Then close Steam and go study.
Otherwise you might want to play some games, such as Boson X. Whereas the premise about the particle accelerator itself is merely illustrative, the game itself is fun.
The mechanics are pretty simple: constantly run, jump straight or jump+rotate right/left.  To complete a scenario you must stand on blue platforms which grant you "research points". Nearing 100% research points for one stage will increase the running speed of your Researcher (and thus the difficulty) and reaching 100% research points completes the stage and unlocks further stages. Otherwise, red platforms collapse once you step on them, and blinking platforms are actually moving. Stages are randomly generated, but you can clearly notice the "building blocks" for the randomization.
That's it about the mechanics. It doesn't change much during the game. The increasing difficulty comes from the initial speed of later stages, more complex platform structures, lack of shadows that will twist your depth perception and psychedelic textures that will confuse your naive brain. I didn't find it obscenely difficult, however.
Boson X is pretty inexpensive, has cards and the achievements are natural. The last achievement having 8% completion rate honestly surprised me. It felt more like a 2% achievement. I think I'd add the "casual" tag to this game.

Hotline Miami 2: Blunt Force Commentary
It’s no secret that Hotline Miami was a commentary of violent video games. And the aspects of its point on being pointless stuck with me well after the fast paced action. That is to say, about a day and a half, because I immediately went and bought Hotline Miami 2.
Hotline Miami 2 is a much larger game that it’s predecessor, in terms of story, scope, and the overall amount of content. They packed a lot into this game for only $15. Hotline Miami 2 is simultaneously a prequel, side sequel, and a sequel. And it’s a wonderful value proposition… But I’ve been feeling that in adding so much to the game, it lost something in the process. That isn’t to say that Hotline Miami 2 isn’t good, on the contrary-- It’s great a great game.
But it doesn’t feel the same as the first.
And again I think that’s part of the point.
A lot of Hotline Miami 2 is commentary on … well a lot of stuff actually. The most obvious to me being ‘fandoms’, internet outrage culture, video games, and the people who play them. There were several times where I felt the creators poking at me in the dialogue of various characters. And I found it to be a very surreal and interesting experience, albeit a little hamfisted.
Commentary aside, I found that some of the changes they made to the gameplay have somewhat impacted my enjoyment of the game. The movement feels a tad slower in Hotline Miami 2 which took a bit to get used to. And actually impacted my performance in the first game, because it had changed my timing. But the thing I find disappointing is the game has a much larger focus on gun combat this time around. I never really cared for how the guns handled in Hotline Miami 1, and the larger focus on them doesn’t excite me. I find that they are tricky to aim, and really slow down the entire experience. Hiding behind doors, peeking out, shooting… it’s not nearly as engaging as stabbing the enemy. NSA, please don’t read this out of context!
Hotline Miami 2 is a much slower experience than the first game. Instead of bursts of fast paced action, Hotline Miami requires you to be even more methodical in your approach than the first game. And while this isn’t true of every level, guns become incredibly prevalent towards the later stages of the game.
I honestly can’t think of a stage in the sequel that doesn’t have you at some point dealing with firearms. That isn’t to say that melee has been made obsolete, rather, I would say it’s been made much riskier-- without a significant increase in reward. There are far fewer melee weapons overall, and most of them are slower, I don’t remember seeing any swords or machetes, unless your character started with one, until the final chapters. And the swing on weapons such as the bat and lead pipe have been slowed significantly.
And while this doesn’t sound like a lot, it actually impacts the feel of the game tremendously. Some might prefer the more methodical gameplay. But I found myself wanting levels to end, and becoming frustrated at the enemy’s ability to shoot me at almost any time. I finally cleared this section of the level! Now to move up to- [long string of expletives removed]
And while I might sound like I’m being harsh on the game, I actually really do enjoy it. There are more levels in Hotline Miami 2 that I don’t like, than I do.... But the good levels are really good. Sadly  the bad levels are just frustrating.
If you really really enjoyed Hotline Miami, I would definitely recommend the sequel. But it’s a tad long, and while the changes they made to the ‘formula’ weren’t to my taste-- Hotline Miami 2 is definitely a good game. If not as good.

Breakdown:
Media (Audio/Graphics/Programming):
The game is visually pleasing. There may be a few small clips or graphical problems, but the game runs very smooth, since it does not have fancy shaders or modeling. Audio is fine. Background music is satisfactory, and the sound effects are very good.
Idea (Mechanics/Balancing/Marketing):
PVKII is a VERY good idea. As the title states, it is a three team battle. Pirates VS Vikings VS Knights. All the teams have three classes, which normally are: Ranger, Melee, and a medium-ranged fighter. The game is well-balanced, with many counter attacks you can make against other players. The community is amazing! The developers are awesome!
Fun:
PVKII is a FREE game. It's not filled to the brim with microtransactions like other "free" games. In fact, there is nothing to buy. (except HL2 to play the mod ) The game is very fun. Instead of your normal two team fighting game, this game is perfect for groups with multiples of three. If you have lopsided teams in other games, try PVKII with friends! All the classes are unique, along with the teams.
Overall:
Amazing, truly FREE game. Very fun three team fighting game! Developers are cool, and the game is amazing! The game itself runs very smooth, with a sacrifice of polycount. (but in an intense fight, you wouldn't care, and it's not THAT noticable as other games)
Buy it when it goes on sa-... wait... it's free! If you do not have the original game (HL2), BUY IT NOW. Play HL2 through, and then play PVKII.
The only drawback is the small community. Otherwise, this game is perfect. You probably want to play with friends though, so you can find people to play with.

I had really enjoyed Seduce Me the Otome, so I was looking forward to the sequel. Just like the first game, this one has a mixture of things I liked and disliked. Usually, I do pros and cons sections, but I feel like it might get a bit complicated if I use that arrangement.
While I didn't hate the artwork or anything in this, I did prefer the artwork of the first game a bit more. I think the guys looked prettier before.
The writing quality remained the same, which is a bit disappointing, but oh well. Some people have no desire to improve their writing skills. It isn't bad writing, but it could definitely be better.
In relation to the writing, I felt that the romantic scenes were "hit and miss," like last time. Sometimes, the scenes would elicit romantic feelings and other times I'd be bored.
Once again, Damien and Diana's story paths were the most interesting to me. However, Diana's path was much shorter than the others and I felt kinda cheated because of that, since she's the only female romance option.
I felt that the other brothers' wives/girlfriends were mostly pointless. They're merely inserted into the story for ... extra CGs? Only one of them has a role in the story, and that's only during one story path. Otherwise, these characters aren't developed at all and any scenes with them felt boring/uninteresting.
I really liked that one of the endings involves polyamory! It's such a rare find in media.
I was disappointed in the lack of people of color. It's a fictional world, so there really isn't an excuse for why there weren't any black or at least darker skinned characters. The brothers of the story are all HALF siblings, meaning that one (or more) of their mothers could've been a woman of color. They didn't need to be all white.
There were some typos, but I didn't come across any scripting errors.
Overall, it was definitely worth my time and I did enjoy it. I just felt like so many little things could've been improved. I do still recommend it, especially to those who like otome VNs.

Ever since I watched TheAnimeMan's mean-spirited review on the first Seduce Me, I've had a soft spot for Michaela Laws and the Seduce Me otome. The first "Seduce Me" is a cute, shallow visual novel for young girls with nice music, unimpressive (or flat out ugly, depending on your view) art, and weak storytelling.
I bought "Seduce Me 2" after following the developer's social media, eagerly hoping this one would be better than the first. From everything I saw, it seemed like it would be! I paid the full $15 for it, aaaaaaaaaand...
...I kinda wish I hadn't. Don't get me wrong, this is better than the first, but the prequel didn't set a high standard. The voice acting is good, as usual, and I appreciate hard effort behind the whole team. That being said, there is very little gameplay for $15, and the storylines get repetitive after a while. This is fine if you want a visual novel with fantastical elements, adventure and good music, but the writing could use a lot of work. I kept finding typos and repetitive sentences and imagery.
A lot of the pictures were very underwhelming, too. For example, Diana's battle scene plays out and all you see is a lazy drawing of Diana's back, with her wings obscuring the armies and enemy. I couldn't help but think, "That's all you could come up with? I understand it if you have a small budget, but couldn't you have made a more visually engaging artwork? How about Diana flying into the sky with the Demon Lord in the background? And later on, her snake is described-- why is there no image of the snake?"
Although this is a visual novel, the visuals are disappointingly lacking.
Another aspect I didn't like was the strong personality of the main character that took me out of the story multiple times. At one point in Erik's route, Mika (your self-insert) expressed disgust at the idea of having children. That would be fine if this weren't a self-insert game, but if you give me the option to erase her name and put in whatever I want, I'm going to assume she's a blank canvas I can project myself on to. I remember cocking my eyebrow then and thinking, "Interesting. I didn't remember having that viewpoint before, but it's good to know I do."
In short, "Seduce Me 2" is an okay game with a team of great people behind it, but the content is shallow, tiresome and disappointingly sparse for its $15 price tag. From my experience I don't recommend it, at least not as full price.

The Evil Within - a survival horror game that borrowed a lot from Biohazard 4 ( Resident Evil ).
I will refer to former Biohazard games a lot, since it is the same dev.
A lot of people say, that Biohazard went down the drain, when it tried to become a refreshing game, with a new playstyle, etc - well you can't please 'em all, right? Neither will The Evil Within be for everyone.
The Evil Within focuses on inflicting terror into your brain, rather than having jumpscares. The game looks more like a piece of wicked art, rather than a game - however it's a pretty much flawless piece of art to say the least.
TEW will let you experience disgust, fear and " WTF moments" - a lot. It features a dark atmosphere combined with fitting music. Compared to "older survival horror" titles TEW is no exception when it comes to action, as it is fast paced action filled combat - just as in Biohazard 4.
The PC requirements are a complete joke and should be ignored by 95 % of the folks who want to buy/play the game. TEW is a console port and shows it off proudly, by having 30 FPS lock and a weird FOV.
The 30 FPS lock can be easily disabled via Steam  " Launch Options " - even though the game runs surprisingly smooth on 30 FPS already.
A lot of people say that the BLACK BARS are a giant nuisance, however - they are sooooo important when it comes to atmosphere. Removing them will allow you to see above ledges, farther around corners etc and it WILL RUIN THE GAME.
As I've said before, TEW relies on terror and fear, leaving the player guessing where the enemy might be. Disabling the black bars will remove exactly this part of the game and will leave you with a generic horror shooter.
______________________
All in all the game is awesome. If you've liked BIo4 / RE4 - you will like TEW as well.
How scary the game actually is, depends on your brain alone.
The more you dive into the game - the more it will frighten you.
Oh and the voice acting is bad.

In reviewing this game, the first and most obvious point of contention is the developer's graphical decisions and the quality of the PC version that has been released. A lot has already been said about the FPS cap and the inclusion of black bars for a  more "cinematic" feel, and with the option to change these via the developer console there isnt much more that needs to be said about these inclusions directly. What I will say is that, while playing the game, a larger issue that popped up involved the developer's choice in the field of view (FOV). I had not seen much talking about this issue before purchasing the game, and found it to be a very large determent very early on. A large portion of the screen that you are able to use by default is taken up by the character, and with the low FOV this quickly becomes a frustrating part of the gameplay. There are fixes specifically for the FOV, but most of them appear to use the cheat engine or modifications of certain game files in the steam folder, which I would not particularly recommend anyone use.
Speaking of fixes, the developer console modifications for the FPS and the aspect ratio are certainly not without their own issues. Very early on I attempted to modify the aspect ratio and black bars, only to have multiple cut scenes glitch to varying degrees of annoyance. In one particular instance a cutscene glitched out that clearly allowed me to see something that was meant to be introduced in a dramatic fashion later on, and after experiencing it I decided to revert back to the unruly black bars that the developer intended. I have yet to encounter any issues that could be directly related to increasing the FPS cap to 60, and the game itself is fairly servicable outside of these points of contention as a standard PC game port. The game is by no means graphically intensive in appearance, so I would be interested in knowing how it plays on an average pc build to see if the system requirements are truly as crazy as they appear (for the sake of comparison for the review, I have included my PC specs at the end of this review).
Ultimately, the game suffers from a much larger issue than its initial graphical problems, and that issue is boredom. People who were drawn in to the game for an intense or horrifying experience are likely to be disappointed by a myriad of extremely slow, uneventful stealth sections. There is nothing particularly wrong with the idea of these sections, but their execution in the game is poor at best. In games that have employed these mechanics in the past, such as Amnesia, a large portion of the tense environment is in how you are hiding from enemies that are obscured or not easily recognizable to you as a player, making the player want to succeed even more in their successful completion of the stealth mission even more due to an intense fear of being discovered. In The Evil Within, most stealth sections consist of you staring at the enemy for a good 5 minutes in clear light to try to analyze its patterns.
Not that analyzing their movements will actually help you, as the AI programmed for a number of enemies in the game appears to be erratic and non-intuitive. This results in situations where an enemy or group of enemies will change their patterns halfway through a section, which often leads to situations where you are found and forced to restart at the very beginning of a scenario. A very early example of this happens in the first chapter with sadist, a chainsaw weilding enemy. While attempting to utilize lockers and dark corners to navigate to a far door to escape, you are given two potential paths to take and are tasked with not being seen. This would be a perfectly fine scenario, if you could reliably use either of the paths given to you. In attempting a path outside of the main room, the enemy would sometimes completely ignore the trigger for an event in which he must clear a box. In one attempt in this scenario it would happen as soon as I triggered it, while in another attempt it would take upwards of 10 to 15 minutes for him to do so. In taking the other path, the enemy would sometimes see you despite his view being a full 180 degrees opposite of your direction, regardless of whether you are crouched or not. This issue later carries on to later sections in the game in which multiple enemies are involved, resulting in increasingly frustrating scenarios where patience is both expected and punished with extreme inconsistency.
Outside of gameplay, many of the mechanics and elements of the story feel disjointed and inconsistent in their implementation. Some of the more important mechanics in the game, such as distraction creating, are not ever actually touched upon outside of the occasional loading tip. Certain items in the game are not properly explained, outside of screens explicitly telling you to use them to do something with them. The UI leaves a lot to be desired, as it becomes difficult to properly gauge your health against the capabilities of the enemy. Scenarios in which you have been discovered by an enemy quickly devolve into awkward messes of combat involving poor player cues and wildly disjointed enemy AI and animations. In multiple scenarios of being spotted I have encountered situations in which enemies will attack you before the game plays an animation or makes the enemy face you in such a way that the attack would even be feasible. This becomes very frustrating when you throw in the issues with the UI and general player's desire to conserve resource, as what appears to be a fairly easy single enemy encounter quickly turns into a game over without much consideration of how the encounter actually plays out in the game.
I cant speak much for the plot in itself, but I can say that from what I've played the game uses a variety of horror cliches and tropes to a confusingly explicit degree. Enemies and enemy types that would typically be eased into a game of this genre appear to be thrown in with little regard for their abiltiy to draw players in to the atmosphere. Many of the enemies in this game are simply not scary or suspenseful, and a large portion of that can be attributed to the way they are introduced in the games stealth sections. After an initial introduction you are given plenty of time to become acquainted with them, and after your first encounter you will likely find that they provide no feelings for you in regards to the game's atmosphere outside of personal annoyance. In playing the game I could not help but feel a weird house-of-the-dead vibe from the way cutscenes and interactions played out that was betrayed by very obvious attempts to make the tone more serious, most of which are not successful in doing so. It is possible that the story may improve, though it certainyl has not in the time that i've played it so far.
Overall I would recommend that people pass on the game, or at the very least wait for it to go on a substantial sale. The game is not unplayable by any means, but with the large number of games that are coming out as we approach the holiday months, there are so many more games out there that can provide a more enjoyable experience. People who enjoy horror, survival horror and stealth styled games are much more likely to get enjoyment out of other recent games such as Alien: Isolation. I intend to continue playing the game and will post further updates regarding how my feelings on the  game change, but after giving the game some time to draw me in it has ultimately failed to do so, and with a game of this genre that is certainly a bad thing that can ruin the enjoyment of other players as well.
