The Evil Within did as most well advertised games do.  It rode the hype train all the way to its release.  People boarded, they drank and ate frivolosly as they spoke of their excitement for the title amongst themselves (Myself included) But when the train arrived at a concentration camp and we were herded out to a firing line and systematically shot, we began to complain.  Is it our fault?  Of course it is, but all the blame does not fall upon us alone.  The Evil Within as a whole is not a "Bad" game.  Several hours of entertainment can be found within, but for those expecting to be swept up into a AAA horror look elsewhere.

Poor ports seem to be the bread and butter of the porting scene.  This game, although playable, is poorly optimized for its PC consumer base. A "widescreen" picture (Two large horizontal black lines at the top/ bottom of the screen) that can not be removed without some small degree of tech savvy file modding) takes away from the overall gameplay.  Frame locked to any degree is a sure fire way to♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone in the PC world off, and a windowed mode that doesn't truly allow for "Windowed mode" are just a few things on the list of recommended things to be altered, improved, or altogether removed.

Some may argue that issues arise with all games and to that I agree, to an extent.  There are simply too many variables to be able to cover all issues for all the varying degrees of hardware/software out there.  However, things like locked frames, although many say this issue is self fixable, should not be released in a AAA title with a price tag of 60 dollars.  Others will express that the fixes will come in time and to be patient.  To them I give a hearty, ♥♥♥♥ you.  Order a pizza dinner for 40 bucks have it show up three hours later and be the completely wrong order to which the proprietor of the establishment, after you are forced to call or suffer through the wrong order, tells you they will remake your order and send it out to you....most likely in another three hours.  Would you not be upset?  The concept is the same.

Is The Evil Within fun?  Mostly
Is it playable?  Yes.
Did it make good on its promises?  It didn't make any, it's a game.
Has it lived up to the "Hype" it received?    No.

Recommendation.  Wait for it to go on sale.

* Caveats
First of all, the caveats.  If you can't handle these, don't bother:
** Partial pay-to-win
Bonus XP and loot abound alongside otherwise-unatainable items for those who open their wallet.  I wouldn't call it a true pay-to-play since it's entirely possible to compete with people who pay, but it will take significantly more effort on your end.  The items may even make sense in some cases if they're cheap enough, but I would never recommend to anyone the booster pack or paying continuous fees for the new hero system  It's preposterous unless you have far too much money and nothing better to do with it.
** Slow
Tactical, turn-based combat that gives everyone 30 seconds to make their move.  With up to twelve players per battle (6 players per team PvP), there can be something of a wait until your turn.  For me, this is an advantage since I can plan out my approach more carefully, or even do other things while playing (the game makes a distinct sound when it's your turn), but people who prefer action will find it a bit troublesome.
** Confused
Wakfu sometimes wants to straddle the line between single player and MMO.  The scenes when following the main questline definitely try to feel like you're playing through a single player RPG, and those other players with you are all extras.  You, yes, you are the hero of prophecy, and it is your task alone to defeat Ogrest.  It's a neat approach, but the disconnect is sometimes a bit much.
** Trolls
Don't like being randomly killed by someome three times your level?  Might not be your game.  The only way to completely opt out of PvP is to stay in Astrub, where you'll never be able to level far.  Honestly, this doesn't happen often.  Once every couple months or so, it seems to happen to me.  The consequences of losing are pretty miniscule -- You reappear at your phoenix and there's a negative status effect attached to you for three minutes.  My suggestion is generally to ignore them because of this, but some people have strong emotional reactions to this, so they should be aware.
** Performance
My laptop is hardly top of the line, but it plays a number of my games with no problem.  It doesn't even slow down much on Minecraft most of the time, and we know how badly that was coded.  Why, then, does this 2d game sometimes completely tank in framerate even when the graphics settings are at the minimum?  Why can it then run quite well sometimes with the graphics set to max?  There's a wide variation possible based on what's happening at the time, both visually (there was a problem with the steam/smoke effect a few months ago that brought both machines I used Intel cards on to their knees, while my significantly older Radeon didn't suffer at all) and in terms of action (beginning and ending battles, loading areas, players suddenly logging in, etc. can sometimes leave Wakfu unresponsive for seconds on my laptop), so if your machine is fairly weak, prepare for occasional input or display lag.
** Documentation
My goodness.  There are tutorial panels that come up occasionally to try to tech you what's going on.  Some of them are massively outdated, some aren't descriptive enough to be much help, some come up at bad times and block your view, or even mouse (Though most can be dismissed with a click, I encountered one that could not.), at awkward times.  Frequently, the best option is to ask someone.
* The rest
Now, on to the good stuff:
** Class selection
There are a variety of classes that can represent a significant range in play styles.  The classes I love the most aren't neccessarily liked by my friends as I do not always like theirs, which I generally take to be a good thing on variety.  Even within classes, there are a surprising number of variants available based on the spells you choose to bring to battle and where you spent your points when leveling.  There are some respec opportunities available for free (as well as one for cash and one that requires you to collect a rather shocking amount of items), and it's relatively easy to level a character once you learn where to go and what to kill (so you can even discard a character and redo it all if you don't feel it's worth earning a respec).
** Fun combat system
It's not the best system I've ever seen (Makai Kingdom forever, man!), but the combat system is remarkably nice.  With the recent update, you are limited in the number of spells/abilities you can bring to battle.  This has significantly hampered one of my characters, who was a staunch generalist, but it has helped refine a few others.  The spells, active abilities, passive abilities, and attributes of your character are genuinely brought to life by a combat system that effectively allows you to translate your choices during character growth into sometimes novel and interesting results in combat.  It then goes further by offering additional challenges in combat that you can complete for bonus XP and items.  If you decide to go along with it, these can sometimes make a battle much more interesting.  Even enemies notably weaker than you can get complicated when you refuse to give up on any of the challenges, which can be a delightful way to keep things interesting when you need to gather items dropped by weak enemies.
** Graphics
The anime-style graphics are generally well done, with good customization for your character's appearance (Your equipment appears on your character, allowing for great flexibility in appearance if you're not too worried about having great equipment, or you can use costumes to hide it and choose freely.) and relatively fluid animation that feels quite right when put together.
** Story
The story itself is pretty generic, but it's realized in a remarkably nice universe with solid backstory and a wide varity of interesting characters.  Suffice it to say the world has a great feel to it.
** Community
Yeah, I mentioned trolls earlier.  They definitely exist, and there's no real way to control or contain them implemented.  They're a small portion of the population, though.  Some of the conversations and interactions between players are hilarious or intriguing, there's a wide variety of emotes to unlock, and even text smilies are brought to life with the vizage  of your character doing the expression above your head.  There's plenty of people to talk with, and sometimes random people just feel like inviting you to join their group.  Being an introvert myself, I was rather cautious at first, but I've grown rather fond of people randomly inviting me to go stomp through a dungeon or two with them, or to do a bit of this or that quest line with them.  It's really rather fun.
** Types
A bit of a note, the options available to players are a bit more vaired and detailed then Healer, Tank, DPS.  Obviously, there will be damage specialists sometimes, but they can specialize on distance or close combat if they can afford to sacrifice the other, there will also be those who specialize on moving allies or enemies to different spaces in the field to maximize the advantage for their side, characters who can use a great number of status effects on friend and foe alike, characters that place blockages on the field to keep enemies where you want them or who scatter automated turrets or summoned allies across the field to win with sheer numbers...  If you're expecting battle to always be straightforward, you're in for a surprise.
* Conclusion
While I hate some of the free-to-play nonsense, and I mourn the great potential the hero system had before it became the rent-a-slot deal it is, I have a great deal of respect for the effort and thought that has shaped this game into the remarkable thing it currently is.  I enjoy Wakfu a lot, and many of my fellow fans of tactical turn-based combat will likely come to the same conclusion should they give it a long enough try.  I wholeheartedly recommend Wakfu to those who enjoy a good turn-based tactical fight.

I typically like sub sims and have several, including Silent Hunter II, III, IV and now V.   Silent Hunter III was by far the best of the series for several reasons and while Silent Hunter V had a bunch of potential, it really falls short even for the low price.
Overall, I have to say this thing ought to still be in beta.  It's got more bugs than a cheap hotel in a third world country and Ubisoft has done nothing to fix them.  They are just there and you're going to have to deal with it.  Some examples are:
1 - The hatch in the conning tower won't stay open on some missions.  This means that your crew is going to sufficate before you can end the mission and there's nothing you can do about it except restart the game as the last save point.
2 - When you restart from the last save point, you will be facing the "surviving" ships from the original encounter with the appropriate level of damage and flooding and the proper amount of torpedoes and main gun ammo.  However, sometimes (more often than not) you do lose everything you've accomplished during that particular mission.  So, you lose the tonnage and ammunition you sunk and expended before you killed off your crew by not being able to open the hatch.
3 - Depth charge damage seems to be constant regardless of location of enemy destroyers.  So, if you have to crash dive to avoid destroyers, even if there isn't a ship within 500 meters, you are going to take damage.  Which means if you are spotted by an enemy, you are automatically gonna die.
4 - Navigation is tricky.  If you run at full time compression, plan to run aground sometimes even when there's no ground to run into.
5 - Setting the game parameters at the start of a campaign as "custom" settings is an exercise in futility.  No matter what you select and no matter what's showing in the menu, the game is going to play in one of the "standard" settings, usually "Medium".
6 - The TDC doesn't function correctly in that you cannot establish distance using the periscope.  For example, I knew the ship was 2300 meters away.  When I used the TDC to find range, it returned a value of 26445 meters.  But, I guess if you get to point blank range it will work that way.  (<---  attempt at sarcasm)
These are just a few bugs that I've found terribly annoying and, gamewise, fatal.
But there are other issues that just don't cut it.
1 - Movement around the sub is necessary to play the game.  I don't know about you, but if I were the captain of a U-Boat, I wouldn't run up and down the ladder and down the length of the ship to find out what's for freaking dinner tonight.  So, if you want to direct the sonar man, you have to go to his station and see what he will do for you at that time.
2 - Battle Stations are pretty much like any other day...  What's the point?
3 - The old axiom of "One ship, one torpedo" that made U-Boat aces during the war didn't play this game.  It typically takes 3 torpedoes to sink a modest freighter and sometimes more.  While I get it that not all ships would sink after one hit, a few did.  But certainly, after being whacked by 3 fish, a WW2 freighter would exhibit some degradation of performance.  Usually in this game it takes at least 3 hits and some deck gun work to bring a small freighter to a "dead in the water" state.
4 - If you are unfamiliar with this series, don't think the manual that comes with it is going to do you much good because it's pretty much worthless.  You will have to hunt and peck around YouTube to find tutorials done by well meaning individuals.  The few YouTubes I found made by Ubisoft were nothing short of shameless advertisements.
Let's talk about graphics...  Naw.  They really aren't that good.  But I guess they're acceptable.
No matter where you turn, people who are playing this game have it loaded up with mods to make it playable.  But I still hear there are many problems.
I could go on but what's the point?  After 22 hours of frustration I've decided that I've had my pocket picked
Bottom line with this one...  Not good.  Wolves of the Pacific (SH IV) wasn't very good but it was better and more playable than this version.
My recommendation is to let this one pass and wait for something better.

I didn't have a problem running the game, not sure why other people are having issues. The only mention of uPlay is when it synchronizes saves online.
As for the game itself:
For people looking for some casual submarine fun I do NOT recommend this game, cold waters is better for that kind of experience. SH5 has issues that require some extra effort to work around, it's by no means a plug and play game.
For people looking for a hardcore u-boat simulation experience this game is a must have, but not in its vanilla state. The vanilla experience is watered down in comparison to SH4, but there are a ton of mods available through
which make it a great successor to SH4, especially if you're sick of / not particularly enthralled by the restrictive interactions in SH4. You'll find yourself wandering throughout the entire length of your ship throughout each of your patrols and it really plays into a sense of immersion that no other game offers. If you don't want to worry about compiling a list of mods, installing them correctly etc I would recommend the Wolves of Steel modpack which introduces a ton of high quality mods which greatly enhance the immersion and overall experience, but at the cost of a somewhat steep learning curve. I've spent dozens of hours trying to master my use of the various instruments and measurements to compile a correct torpedo solution to the point where i can usually hit about half of all the torpedoes I fire, but I'm still constantly improving. Steam says i've spent 20 hours playing but I had to take the game offline for a couple mods which require some more extensive tweaking, I'd estimate my play time to be over 100 hours as of the time of this review and it inspired me to spend another 50 hours studying WWII submarine warfare and torpedo solutions to improve my tonnage each patrol. If you're a hardcore warfare sim fan who fancies the idea of diving to excessive depths to avoid depth charges, silently sneaking in among the ranks of a massive escorted convoy in the dead of night, or straining every last watt out of your batteries to move into a mined harbor unseen to take out Royal Navy battleships, then this is the game for you, and for $10 it's hard to go wrong.
Tip: in the campaign selection screen type "silentotto" to unlock all the missions. I haven't the patience to complete an entire mission just yet as each spans the course of a year or more in game time, and from what I've heard there's some issues with the game counting your progress in a particular mission to complete it so if you're looking for some variety after a few long patrols you can explore some of the other campaign missions, each having some unique challenges of their own.

TL,DR: The Evil Within is a bit unoptimized, but it's unbeatable in atmosphere, and insanity, so it's AWESOME.
Detailed Review:
Ah The Evil Within. Probably the most anticipated horror game in 2014. I saw the reviews, and I'm sad. Are graphics, and fps more important in 2014 than GAMEPLAY? Look at Crysis 3. It looks very fancy, but it's a simple FPS. However The Evil Within is different. Let's start with the negatives (there won't be a lot): 30 fps lock (people are bi*ching about this the most. It runs surprisingly well on consoles, but WE "The Glorious PC Gaming Master Race" (as some call it) can unlock the fps, so this shouldn't be a problem on PC. Bigger problem is the optimizing, or to be more exact, the loss of it. This game either runs on your computer, or not. You can't gain fps, by disabling effects, HOWEVER you don't need an i7 for minimum. I have an i3-4130K, GTX 660 2GB OC and 8 GB DDR 3 RAM, and I could run it on max between 40 and 50 fps. One other thing: The A.I. is dumb.You can easily hide from it, if you go round an object. After a round, the enemy loses interest in you, and you can kill it silently. These are the negatives, and now the positives. The game is VERY atmospheric. If you sit down to play it, you will want to complete at least that chapter, which you are in. Other positive, the levels are very unique. Not just in locations, but in gameplay too. One moment you are in an old village, but in the other, you are desperately trying to reach the exit of a hallway, filled with traps. This IS a true survival horror. You have to scavenge for supplies, try to find secret areas, and you have to SURVIVE. The game has an upgrade system too. Throughout the levels, you can find green goo, which you can use to upgrade your character in a place, called Asylum. You can find map pieces, and keys too, which you can use there. So are you ready for a journey through the twisted mind of Shinji Mikami?
PRO
+ atmospehric locations
+ interesting story
+ challenging
CONTRA
- unoptimized
- some minor bugs
- not suitable for everyone
VERDICT: If you like or liked Resident Evil 1 plus 4, and  you'd like a game like those, The Evil Within is YOUR game!

Gameplay: This game is a series of Dark Souls bosses. I seriously found myself having the same exact approach to each level as I would a boss. I’d start up a level and fail usually straight away. Often the level would seem impossible or unfair at first. I’d feel like giving up and often I did. But upon returning and attempting the levels more, I found myself slowly inching that energy bar up towards 100%. Essentially I was learning the levels move-set and its new tricks. Each level completion was such a release of tension and a sense of victory and accomplishment, that I failed immediately afterward, unable to rack up any bonus points. This game is a platformer, where you run through a hexagonal world of ever changing platforms. The game has 18 levels in which I spent over 10 hours. The levels obviously ramp up in difficulty, adding in new mechanics here and there to keep the player on their toes. The goal is to get your energy level to 100% and is achieved by running on the scarce blue platforms.
Design: The level design is randomly generated from a base set of platforming segments that all flow together nicely (when you do figure it out). This is important as each level segment has to flow into every other segment. You wouldn’t want a game to have these randomly generated combinations to run you into an impossible scenario, making the game unfair sometimes. The visuals are blocky and basic, but serve their function. The sound design is overall decent. The music can be a bit annoying at times and I found it’s not really any help (or hindrance) to listen or not. One level in particular, I finally beat when I muted the audio. But this could be due to the increasing pitch that is triggered as you ramp the energy up. That sound mechanic really adds tension to those final percentage points.
Overall: I’d recommend this game to anyone wanting a platforming/runner challenge.

You're led around by your coworker during a terrorist attack and take it upon yourself to save the world or at least yourself. You'll find yourself rushed along by something breaking and attempting to drown you every minute or two and being made to swim for your life, which is actually more controllable and less motion sickness-inducing than the normal imprecise, laggy movements you make on dry land. After you solve basically the only thing that requires the smallest bit of thought using your one superpower five minutes before the end of the game, making it basically the only practice you get with that power, you go on to use it to defeat the final boss, leading to the least satisfying ending I've ever experienced in a game. The best thing to be said for it is that it is short, and could be made even shorter than my playthrough if you're not trying to get collectibles (which I collected casually but was not about to replay to find the missing pieces) and if you're lucky enough not to encounter the buggy jump puzzle near the end of the game that I took nearly a dozen shots at, each requiring a full clear of the room and re-collection of the collectibles because of the illogical placement of checkpoints, before finding out it was a bug and not just me. Even still, there are thousands of other games on Steam that deserve your time before you slog through this one.

This is like 'Die Hard' on a boat, if the plot had been written by someone who isn't a very good writer. If I understand it correctly - a lot of the world is screwed, so the rich live on floating ship cities at sea.
Some terrorists are not happy about this, so they attack one of the ships, which you (as the security expert who provided their computer system) happen to be on.
There's a bit more to it than that, but to be honest - it's an interesting setup that isn't very well done in terms of the execution.
In terms of the gameplay it does make for a decent environment. Its a third person shooter with some platforming elements, that uses some very cool physics to simulate the ship getting flooded. The water in the game has some simple puzzle uses, offers a couple of exciting setpieces, and can be used to aid yourself in combat. Though its fairly self contained most of the time.
Unfortunately, despite it being a solid concept - it is lacking in several areas. The shooting is lame, and the "water tech" isn't that expansive in practice for solutions. Whilst it can aid in combat (generally by exploding conduits that electrocute it) the baddies can shoot underwater, and are seemingly gill breathers as they never drown.
There's the basis for a good romp here, but in its delivery it is somewhat lacklustre. The story is iffy, the voice acting is iffy, the combat is iffy, and the ending takes a rather nutty turn that doesn't feel earned (despite being nifty in some ways). On the plus side - the water movement looks ace.....
It's also reallllllllly short - took me 4 hours to finish...? something like that. Considering that its been dirt cheap in price - this is worth a look if you can see past what is, and enjoy it for what might have been (if that makes sense)
But for the average player who demands perfect execution in their games, it isn't worth it.

Update, this game isnt really one sided in favor of any nation any more. I applaud the game developers on their fix for overpowered allies, but would still not reccommend downloading. The game has MASSIVE balance issues. Specifically the fact that it is extremely pay to win. If you have a weapon that is not fully automatic, expect to lose. Also, if you are an infantry player going against tanks, expect to lose. Tanks have a massive advantage over infantry, and even the stupidest of drivers can hold up an entire match when camping. The reason tanks are overpowered is not because they are particularly hard to destroy, but simply because they have FAR too much range and damage against infantry. Tank weapons seem to have infinite effective range, with no accuracy drop off whatsoever. This means that any Call of Duty 12 year old that just got a tank can now sit at the back of the map, untouched, and proceed to farm fleshy infantry. There needs to be massive accuracy nerfs to tanks, and damage reduction against infantry if this game is to be even remotely balanced.

Ace of Spades started out as an excellent voxel based FPS, but it simply hasen't retained its value recently. Firstly this game has ZERO SINGLEPLAYER FUNCTIONAILTY, it is purely an online experience. This used to be a great thing that allowed for the developers to focus on the portion of the game that truely mattered to them. Now however the multiplayer UI (User Interface)and matchmaking service is simple unusable, the old UI allowed for easy access to every single active Ace of Spades game on the internet and had filters based on region. The newer UI forces you to use the "quickmatch" feature, this feature is neither quick nor effective, 9/10 times it will drop you in a game with no players other than yourself. Also it is now no longer possible to join other Steam users games, as me and my friends discovered to our surprise, this means you are entirely reliant on the broken matchmaking system. When you do eventualy get into a playable match the game is fun until you notice the extrrmely unbalanced weaponry such as the double barrel shotgun on the Engineer class. The shotgun has an effective range (one shot kill) of roughly 10 blocks, it will also two shot kill at roughly 20 blocks. For comparison the SMG does roughly 10-15% damage per hit and is effective when within a 30 blocks radius of an opposing player. This game used to be great, but now due to the broken matchmaking, and the inability to reliably find a game I cannot recomend this title to anyone.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is the "epic co-operative action combat adventure" set in the Warhammer Fantasy world. My threefriends and I played this cooperatively for a little over 12 hours. We had some fun times, but ultimately got tired of the grind.
You start the game by picking one of five heroes - Witch Hunter, Empire Soldier, Dwarf Ranger, Waywatcher. I played as the Waywatcher, who gets a staff that can cast some fireball spells and the like. Interestingly, there isn't anything like "spell points", but rather you can actually overheat (and take damage!) if you cast too many spells in too short a time. You can hit a key to speed cool down up a little, but you have to be constantly aware. I tried the Dwarf Ranger briefly but found it too hard to contribute, so I went back to throwing fire around.
Then you can pick a mission, either a side quest or a story mission. The ones we did were of the "clear out all the Skaven" (most if not all of the enemies are a kind of rat) to a delivery, where we had to pick up boxes and bring them back to a coach (or ship) that was waiting for us. These were always very difficult.
After a mission, there is a "die rolling", where you find out what kind of loot you get, if successful in the mission. You can earn more dice by finding specials or carrying a "book" that takes up a precious inventory slot.
And then there was the "crafting" or whatever the hell you want to call it. All in all, the leveling up system was hopelessly and needlessly complex. There are forges, and shrines, and all kinds of strange and unexplained things you can try to use back at the inn to get weapons and armor you can use. Because the die rolling gets you a completely random piece of equipment, almost certainly not for the class you want to play. But supposedly you can mix gems and items and the like to give it a better chance to create something you might actually use, but I never did really figure it out.
So that was the big negative - rewards just didn't match up with the grinding effort of the levels. If you die, you go to a special place on the level and can be rescued. But that didn't happen too often, because the rest of your team was just racing trying to survive. Make no mistake about it, this games is tough. Which I am normally a fan of, but the grinding was just too much. You just never could improve enough to take on some of the tougher challenges.
And there was plenty of sameness about it all, despite the really nice graphics and varied missions. You just killed a lot of Skaven. I know it is kind of a "horde mode" game, but that doesn't make much for a storyline.
In the end, all of our interest petered out after about 10 hours. We played a bit more, winning 3 or 4 of the levels, but just kind of gave up.

Ubisoft were at their peak with this game. Far cry 3 has a fun and enjoyable campaign with good and memorable characters. The protagonist Jason Brody while not really the most interesting and likeable character, his character changes the further you progress in the game. The more brutally and often he kills, the more experience Brody earns to become a better murderer. Jason’s gradual transformation from being a coward to a killer, unfolds in a believable way, which compensates for the narrow revenge premise. Losing control is a huge and important theme throughout the game.  Far Cry has always had the open-ended tactical choices available during each encounter, and the variety of ways you could take down targets. With aggressive wildlife and roaming pirates, your stealth and aggro options open up more than ever. I loved letting animals out of their cages in pirate outposts and let them take care of the dirty work for me. I claim the enemy’s checkpoint as my own and then kill the animals for skin. The games' setting, Rook Island, is a huge map for you to explore. The game also has great customization options. The game has a skill tree with different abilities for you to choose from, gun customizations, etc. Upgrading your arsenal motivates you to explore the island to find the things you need to craft, for example, a pouch to carry more items, ammo, medicine etc., and its worth it in the end because you will be more prepared for the various situations that you will encounter. I have to talk about Vaas because he is the best character in the game and one of the best villians in gaming history. Its his terrific dialogue and his mental instability makes Vaas so memorable. Vaas' manic outbursts make you fear his volatility. His insanity is amusing until he snaps. Far Cry 3 achieves greatness but that doesn't mean that it doesn't have its negatives. The multiplayer and co-op is what holds this game back from excellence. Multiplayer doesn't offer much and it isn't very fun. The co-op does not work. Loading screens that last up to more than 10 minutes, it just isnt possible to play it. Besides that, Far cry 3 should definetly be sitting in your library. With a campaign that's fun and memorable with a tone that is dark and mature, memorable characters, a huge island to explore, ridiculously effective tools for scouting every hostile situation, and so many clever intersecting systems to inspire creative ways to conquer them, Far cry 3 is worth your time and money. (10/10)

NOTE: This is coming from a joystick/throttle/trackir user who mainly flies in Sim mode, running Windows 10.
I've owned this game for a few years but never really spent much time playing it after my first big marathon. Why is that, you may ask? Well, back when I was using a mouse and keyboard setup, the game was playable but ultimately boring. But more about that in the pros vs. cons of this game.
Pros:
-The game is rather pretty for when it was released, the plane models are seemingly pretty detailed and the ground clutter is realistic for the period.
-The planes all handle quite differently, depending on their size and weight.
-The scenarios presented are quite good overall from a design standpoint, and the map really helps out with finding objectives without HUD markers.
-The videos between campaign section were a nice touch, too bad the voice acting was pretty mediocre at best.
-Many of the sound effects got carried over to War Thunder, which says something about them I would think.
Cons:
-There were quite a few either frustratingly hard or mind-numbingly dull missions included in the mix (even on lower difficulty settings), which while realistic are not exactly what one looks for when using a joystick. Simple missions can be difficult enough as-is, adding a timer generally doesn't help make it more fun.
-The damage model is extremely arcade-like in that getting just a few hits on planes snaps off a wingtip or sets it on fire in a Michael Bay-esque explosion.
-I had an issue where the game would freeze except in menus whenever it was minimized with a mouse click on my secondary monitor, or if I Alt-Tabbed out of it to do something else. It would force me to restart the game, which leads into my next issue.
-Having to use the game through YuPlay is annoying at best, as you aren't registered as quitting out of the game unless you find YuPlay in your toolbar and exit out of it AFTER exiting the game. Whenever it would crash or quit out, having this extra step is frustrating considering the GoG version is DRM-free. (And comes with the Luftwaffe DLC to boot.)
-The game has a lot of issues with controllers outside of the range that it supports natively. My X-56 is not on the list and the controls will get switched around seemingly at random almost every time the game is started up. For example, one button on my joystick is meant for turning the gunsight on and off, but after a few days, it was suddenly a part of the radio comms. At this rate, keeping the controls set up is just too much effort to bother with anymore.
-As well, TrackIR's field of view feels zoomed in when in use, and there is no way to reset the zoom axis for TrackIR in the game. This can make tracking targets a lot harder than necessary.
-Lastly, the diluted color filter on everything is a bit ugly in my opinion. I understand that they are trying to get a "noir" look to the game with it, but it'd be nice to be able to disable it. Shades of brown and grey get old very quickly.
So, would I recommend this game to the average gamer? In this day and age, no, not really. This game is essentially an older, single-player War Thunder, which isn't F2P and has worse compatibility with modern systems.
For a relative simmer like myself? Again, no. The game has some odd quirks with using newer joysticks and TrackIR, which cause enough problems to be off-putting even when they do work.
If this game were to recieve some updates to add in this content and fixes, then it would probably be recommended. But in its present form, sadly it's a negatory, ghost rider.

A bad port of a bad port of a bad game.
First of all, this game runs worse than on a dreamcast emulator. There are still frames every few seconds and tons sound issues like bad sync and just overall terrible quality, probably because it just emulates the Gamecube version of this game and that really poorly. I've also noticed even more glitches than in the original and that was already barely acceptable to begin with.
Other issues are not working lock on moves like the homing attack and terribly wonky controls. Like seriously, you only have to touch the gamepad stick lightly and you already run into an enemy or fall to your death and I haven't even talked about the actual game yet.
Which is also terrible. I like Sonic, even a lot of his 3D games, but this is just frustrating and I'm not even talking about the age of it. Of course it's a product of its time, so I'm not gonna complain about the graphics, the voice acting or other superficial things, but the game just isn't fun to play.
The Tails/Eggman levels are by far the worst, as all you do in them is hold the fire button and listen to an unbearable beep sound to progress. There's a little platforming here and there, but it's uninteresting as hell because it consists of still or moving platforms and nothing else. Did I mention the excruciating beep sound you hear whenever you press the fire button?
The Knuckles/Rouge stages are infamous for being bad but at least they are interesting to explore for the first time. Not terribly, just barely as interesting as Mario 64's hub world, but it's still something. The problem with these however is the task you have to fulfill, which is collecting emerald shards that are randomly placed everywhere on the map, which is not only unfair for those who want to get an A rank, but also very tedious, as it's basically a hide and seek game. On top of that, the sensor you have only detects one shard at a time, which means you can completely miss the other 2 even if you're right next to them, which means that you have to look for them on the entire map up to 3 times.
The Sonic/Shadow levels are by far the best thing to come out of this game and they are fairly mediocre. The biggest issues I have with them are the already mentioned terrible controls but also the camera angles. They get you killed a lot, especially towards the end. Level design is also a problem because a lot of them rely on jumping on extremely thin rails, which is borderline impossible with these controls, springs and rails that launch you into enemies, traps that you cannot see coming whatsoever and very long auto sections where you do nothing.
In conclusion, I do not recommend this game at all, even if you disagree with me about the game itself. If you somehow still feel the need to play this, just emulate the Dreamcast version instead, at least that one is playable.

If you enjoyed Seduce Me the Otome or are interested in the continuation of the story, the sequel is a must have. There was much that was improved in this game that I feel the content is worth the full price. The creator does occasionally put her games on sale for half-off, so it'd be absolutely worth it to pick it up by then.
There are 2 alternating stories while the demon war takes place: the MC's involvement in the war and your love interest's conflict. There are 1-2 good endings for each route and a few bad endings. Like the first game, there is a hidden password attached to some of the endings that unlock a bonus. The bonus provides an interesting twist and also (out of context)
.
+ A+ for voice acting. All of the cast did a phenomenal job. The bloopers were hilarious and well worth the effort to unlock.
+ Music has greatly improved. A few tracks from the first game do return, but there are some beautiful piano pieces that make me want to buy the OST. The ending theme song is especially lovely.
+ A majority of complaints from SM1 were repetitive scenes and choices. There is a greater effort in route variation. The choices give you a stronger sense of the MC's (or the player's) personality. The most repetitive scenes would be in the demo portion of the game, but there are plenty of choices added that make it worth re-playing through these scenes as you go through each route.
+ Writing has improved from the first game, but still feels a little stiff at times (during spoken dialogue and long explanations). I loved that there were more scenes where the MC was reflecting on her decisions and thinking about the weight of her situation- which I felt was absent from the first game. There were scenes where I felt tension, expecting a bad ending around the corner. There were scenes where I felt angry at certain characters; scenes where I felt depressed about the choices I had to make, but supportive towards the affected character. The creator did a great job in giving me more of an emotional attachment to the characters than in SM1.
+ The game provides a tutorial for Ren'Py shortcuts, covers content warnings, and goes so far as to offer brief explanations about the first game's story and route summaries. It was a very thoughtful addition that I appreciated having (served as a great refresher).
+/- The romance is already established since this game covers the MC's marriage. I felt the first game was more on the tame side, not being too smutty. Here, there are more intimate scenes added (3 per route with 1 exception) that takes it a step further while still being written in a tasteful manner. The sex scenes are still completely optional.
- Very minor typos. Again, some of the spoken dialogue came off as lengthy (such as explanations).
- Art still suffers anatomy and posing issues in sprites and CGs. The first game made them look older CG-wise. Here, they appear much younger. Some may be bothered with the new art, but I preferred the new style.
- The MC comes off as a Mary Sue during the war portion of the story.
- There were a few scenes where it seemed like there should have been sprites on-screen, but there weren't. I also found it a little strange that the boys were mostly shirtless for the majority of their routes.
- The wives issue, which are "the kickstarter backer-rewarded characters that are not canon".
Many people are mixed on the wives. Some are supportive of the idea (as it should be a logical outcome), while others tend to react negatively toward them. I can't think of any otome game where the other love interests moved on and hooked up with someone else while playing through a route.
No matter how you look at it, the wives feel shoehorned in and out of place. They are all inexplicably non-human and are already married before the start of the game (which is a 2 year time skip from the ending of SM1).
There are no scenes to establish their backstories. They just exist and have "off-screen" bonded with each other like a family. Outside of Sam's wife in James' route
, they don't add any support or value to the story besides their random interjections.
Personally, I disliked the scenes where you eavesdrop in on them with their spouse. It felt like you could have swapped the MC into those scenes and it would not have made a difference. This made me feel like the MC was not important to the incubus' story at all.
ENDING TIP
:
The war portion is a standalone story that does not directly impact the love interest's route. The outcome of the war is an addition to the endings, but the choices you make towards the good/bad endings are entirely dependent on how you treat your love interest.
Achievements are doable without a guide, but require a bit of trial and error. I wanted to point this out because some of the choices are vague in their outcome. You could pick one wrong option and be locked out of the good ending.

Seduce Me 2 is far superior to the first installment of the series. Besides the more straightfoward dialogue choices (in some cases in the first game, only a guide distinguishes the difference between some options), each route is unique in its main conflict while still adhering to one central plot, the outcome of which is influenced by you. My only complaint is that the outcome of the war is not linked to the best ending of some routes. For example, the game can end with the demon world becoming a
and you going back to the human world with absolutely no consequences for you and your lover. Besides that, it's a great game with good replay value due to multiple endings and war outcomes.

Three routes in and I've poked around the other 3 and will return to them, and I definitely recommend this game.
I absolutely adored SM1 and really got into the writing, character development, voice acting, music, sound, you name it, I liked every aspect. It pretty much pulled me further into visual novels of all types and I think it helped pull a lot more interest into the otome gaming business. I consider it a must-have in your Steam library.
This time, I still really like it, but I warn that it is different.
Once again, hands down, the voice acting really nailed it. Some of the actors really upped their skills and interpretations on the characters since SM1, while everyone of them made the story that much more. Mr. Ethan Nakashima, the voice of Matthew, really stood out, and even if you aren't a Matthew fan, check out the route, if only just to hear him, though that route's end has been the most entertaining, so go through for that, too.
Michaela's writing did not disappoint either, with intricate storylines, tons of MC choices and consequences, and *those* scenes being different for each of the characters and IMO is better than SM1. As stated, the story itself is different. You're not romancing one of the boys, that's what SM1 covered, now you're supporting them as a continuation of your relationship with the character. For the full experience, I agree with the other reviewers, play the free SM1 route of the character and then follow directly through with the SM2 route.
I have to warn, the writing is a little rough compared to the first. I think the timeline was way too tight for the amount of work and creative heart and soul the team poured into this game. The first was well edited and the writing tighened up quite nicely when it hit steam and I saw it and I can't help but feel if Ms. Laws had an extra three to six months to wrap everything up with a good polish and edit, it would have really helped with the typos and grammar that can be so jarring to some readers. Don't quote me on the numbers, but I believe she put out like 250K words of story in like 6 months. Insane when she's also programing the game. So complain if you want on the typos, but I can't help but be impressed at her dedication to getting this game out for us on time.
Once again I really enjoyed the music. One point, concerning what may have been an oboe and piano, actually had me pause in the middle of the game to stop, listen, and enjoy the entire song before continuing, which is a feat in itself, focused reader that I am. The soundtrack definitely has a place in my collection, right next to the first one.
I know the wives are a point of contention. They are a little weird, but Michaela is also not one to go 100% traditional in things, and frankly it was a good marketing tactic for the kickstarter. Others are doing similar though maybe not as obvious in their games. Literally a flash, bang, right in your face. Hah, Michaela does have style. I'm interested to actually find their little hidden paragraphs but TBH, I don't care that much to go through and really dig for them. If I stumble on them, cool. The other boys moved on, it happens after 2 years, and its pretty easy to ignore the 8 sentences of dialog they have, anyway.
As for the the story itself, a bit of spoiler.
And If they ever sell a Simon plushie, I hope I see it cuz, I'm definitely buying.

It's not tetris, but it isn't tower builder either. Tricky Tower demands precision and working within the confines of its somewhat rickety physics engine. However, if you get the hang of things you can usually start out pretty well...well until♥♥♥♥♥♥goes south. Since blocks can both interlock with eachother or just slip onto the one below, you can quickly end up with skewed towers that will make even the worst architects angry. The "nudge" move allows you to fit pieces into gaps, if you're lucky and precise. However, that's usually not enough to make your Leaning Tower of Pisa straight again. Therein lies the magic and agony of Tricky Towers. You can have the straightest arrow to the sky, only to see it go to the seven hells of misalignment in a block or two. If you're looking for the precise bliss of regular Tetris you probably won't find it here, because there are just too much chaos going on for that.
Multiplayer matches is where it's at, and with up to four players you are ensured tower mayhem in several modes including race to the top, puzzle modes and endurance. As long as you can get to terms that Tricky Towers has a rickety uneven core at its gameplay center, you can enjoy all the curse words raining from the sky from your fellow competitors. Or from yourself.

Tricky towers is a tetris-like tower building game but with physics applied to the blocks. There are single-player trials but where it really shines is the local versus. There are 3 modes in versus, all with their own unique stratgies: Race (build a tall tower quickly), Survival (don't drop blocks), Puzzle (place blocks beneath a line).
The game appears very simple at first, but there is quite a bit of strategy in placing the blocks in such a way that they interlace to provide as much support as possible. On certain difficulties, there is both white magic (power-ups that help your tower, like glue and morter) and dark magic (power-ups that harm your enemies tower, like weird blocks and ice). To cause the most damage possible, It is important to watch opponents' towers to cast spells at opportune times.
There is a certain wonderful dramatic arc to building your towers, regretting earlier placement decisions, and watching your tower sway and crumble to the ground. The aesthetics sound design are simple yet very pleasing. Overall an absolute delight.

No, I do not recommend this game.
Now, first, let me say that I fully support the ability of developers and publishers to actually make money from the products they create and produce.  There are many such successful models of the variants of the Free-2-Play model that exist in such a way as to generate revenue for the companies involved, while also respecting the playerbase (aka the "hand that feeds" the developers and publishers) with reasonable ways to play their games and progress without endlessly dumping money into a game that might otherwise retail for maybe $20 in a box.
With this said, the free to play model for Mini Guns was barely tolerable before the most recent update - now it is atrocious with the addition of a new "currency" that can be bought with real money (gems... surprised?) which is far less atainable through gameplay than the already existing currency.  They made this change at the same time they sort of pre-released a new "upcoming" faction to "VIP" members only, while still requiring all players to fight against this new faction (which is horrendously imbalanced).
Someone must have thought it was not bad enough already that in order to significantly progress via gameplay you had to (best case scenario):
- Play against people with stacked armies that are literally 10x your level
- Win against said opponents
- Get lucky enough to get a crate to drop upon winning a match
- Get lucky enough to get a good rarity crate to drop if one did drop at all
- Have and use an empty "slot" in order to use to wait, let's say... 24 hours OR ... pay the equivalent of 200 match wins (or more) worth of gold (the already existing currency which can also be bought with real money) in order to even open the crate
- Get lucky and actually get a good drop
- Get lucky enough that the drop is not only good, but a particular unit you are in need of
- Repeat every step in the process above multiple times (including all of the luck involved) in order to obtain multiple copies of the unit you are trying to level up until you have enough required to level up (varies per unit, cost increases with level and eventually requires multiple copies of multiple types of units in order to fulfil requirements)
- Use a "slot" to upgrade your unit that you have multiple copies of and wait another period of time (lets say 18 hours for a legendary level 1 unit) or pay about 60 match wins worth of gold to complete the level up
- Repeat this entire process above for each unit you want to level up in the faction the unit belonged to
- Repeat all steps above for each unit for each additional faction (you cannot choose which faction to play as during matches unless VIP, so you must level up units from both factions or the entire process will take twice as long, or three times as long once the third faction is "officially" introduced)
So... as if the process for leveling up a single good unit, as outlined above, was not already bad enough, they went and made it even harder by removing the ability to use gold "speed" things up and replaced the gold costs with equivalent gem costs... with only one catch - you cannot earn gems like you used to be able to (extremely slowly) earn gold by winning matches.  You can very rarely get a very small amount of gems from a crate (and maybe more gems at an even lower chance) - so I estimate at this rate I might have 100 gems in a month or so if I can manage to win most of my matches and the game manages to keep my interest with it that long and I play consistently enough during this time.
Or, I could pay literally hundreds of dollars to speed the process up to be equal with my competitors.  No thank you. Vermintide is a fun game for the first few hours, until the glaringly obvious game-breaking bugs become apparent. If you are interested in playing a game with strategic depth to co-op play that rewards good reflexes and accuracy, then this game is
what you're looking for. This game is
in its current state. Fatshark, the developer, has made it abundantly clear that they are more concerned with early DLC, cross-platform distribution (of an unfinished game), and randomized gear grinding than creating a balanced and functional game. The bugs are numerous and many of them have persisted since the first release of the game despite several patches. Here is my list of the most game-breaking issues:
There is little sense in how/when/where enemies spawn. Often you will catch waves of basic or special skaven spawning right in front of you. Watching enemies materialize in front of you not only destroys the immersion, but also increases the difficulty of the game in a non-meaningful way. Enemies will spawn directly in front of your path, trapping you in areas where enemies just beyond your line-of-sight can then attack you through walls, which bring us to the next issue...
There are several issues with hitboxes:
Skaven can attack you through nearly any object. It doesn't matter if you're standing behind a bookshelf or a wall, under a platform or set of stairs, or on top of a platform or pillar, because the skaven will hit you through them. They can hit you through almost anything as long as you're within melee range, and that melee range extends beyond the visible range of the attack animation. Sometimes they'll even hit you while you're blocking (even with full stamina). Additionally, horde events set skaven hitboxes in place even when the spawning skaven have not yet rendered. This means that it can be impossible to rush through narrow areas ahead of horde events because you will be blocked by collision detection with skaven that don't yet exist.
Many shots do not register hits, even when using hitscan weapons like the rifles. This can happen at any time. In my experience this happens more often when there are more skaven on the screen. A related issue is that high-penetration weapons (like the Soldier's rifle) will not register any hits whatsoever if the number of potential targets is too high (for example when a wave of skaven is stacked on top of each other). Additionally, your pushes can fail to register, seemingly at random.
Allied hitboxes are much larger than they appear. They seem to extend about 0.5m beyond the character models in all directions. This is very frustrating when trying to use ranged weapons to assist your allies. Shooting over an ally's head requires a steep angle. Additionally, allied hitboxes can clip through each other, so you'll end up shooting your friend who is standing 0.5m behind you because their hitbox is clipping through you without any visual cue to let either of you know.
Put simply, you will trip and snag yourself on far too many objects. Is that a lone decorative brick on the floor? STUCK. How about a gradual slope upward? BETTER JUMP CONSTANTLY, otherwise you'll get stuck on literally nothing.
The game runs like molasses and crashes often. Even with decent hardware (I have a GTX 650 Ti, for example) and the lowest graphical/physics settings the game can rarely maintain >50fps, even with zero enemies spawned. The game bogs down to <20fps frequently when fighting larger waves, tanks, or during finale events, further crippling anyone's ability to rise to the challenge. This happens to every single person I know who has played the game (about 10 people), even those with hardware vastly superior to mine.
*****
On top of these absolutely critical gameplay issues, there are
smaller bugs that become more and more annoying with time. Sound bugs (music, environmental effects, and horde event effects will sometimes stop playing for the entire level), graphical bugs (invisible and unblockable skaven), and lobby bugs (sometimes if someone leaves your party during a level then you will be unable to complete that level because the game somehow recognizes the former player as still being a player rather than a bot, and since the bot will not enter the wagon at the end of the map it won't allow you to trigger the map finish) are but a few. There are STILL more bugs to write about, but instead I'll finish with one last gripe:
Gear is an integral part of this game. The customization is welcome but it is also terribly balanced. Many traits are vastly inferior to the few good traits, and good gear is essential to being able to complete the hardest gamemodes. Since the gear drops and trait rolls are random, you had better be ready to grind your face off trying to get decent enough gear to continue playing the game. I know people who have played HUNDREDS of hours and don't have any orange trinkets.
4/10 game. Good music, good voice-acting, good art, and good lore. Everything else is terribly lacking.

After 400 hours I figure it's time I gave this game a review.
Obviously having that much time in the game I find it to be a challenging and rewarding experience. Those rewards, however, are intrinsic to a difficult game. Do not expect this to be a loot driven, MMORPG-esque experience. It isn't. In fact I daresay that if you play this game with loot on the brain, expect to be disappointed. This game is about taking three other people and doing some of the most challenging and visceral melee combat that I've ever encountered in a game. Completion of missions offers the reward of self satisfaction and, sometimes, maybe a piece of loot you can use.
There are five difficulty levels and the differences between each are noticable and substantial. Easy is basically a check to see if you understand mechanics and is good for the first map or two. Normal is a fantastic way to farm your first 10-15 levels. Once you begin playing Hard the hits will begin to hurt and you will run the legitimate risk of having a team wipe. Nightmare introduces friendly-fire and challenges players well up to level 100. Finally, Cataclysm offers the ultimate challenge. In Cataclysm difficulty, just four hits from even the most basic enemy can down your character.
I recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the four player co-op genre. Do not purchase this if you're not willing to work together with your fellow players in order to achieve a common goal. Do not purchase this if you're primarily concerned about the weapons/trinkets/items you recieve along the way. Loot isn't a big part of this game, ultimately. DO purchase this game if you enjoyed Chivalry, Dark Souls, or similar challenging melee combat titles. DO purchase if you enjoy being legitimately challenged in a group environment. You will need friends to keep up in Vermintide, and once you're in the zone, the experience is unparalled.

Far Cry 3 is an open world FPS game that takes place on two massive islands somewhere in the south Pacific. You are Jason Brody, a vacationing South Californian boy tasked with finding and saving your friends from a group of sadistic pirates, mercenaries and slave traffickers. In the meantime, you will need to learn how to survive in the hostile jungles teeming with tigers, crocodiles and other nasty creatures out to eat you. Throughout the course of the game, you will accumulate over 40 different weapons, drive a dozen different vehicles (the hang glider is awesome), free outposts from enemy control, hunt exotic wildlife, and meet a ton of very interesting characters.
Pros:
+The game looks beautiful. Every inch of the islands, from the forests, to the shantytowns, to the beaches and the surrounding sea, are incredibly detailed. Aside from generic shack interiors, everything looks and feels as if this could be a real, lived-in place. The game has a day-night cycle and even rains sometimes, and this is integrated very well with the environment. Something else that adds to this are the NPC interactions. There are always allies and enemies on cars going to and from places, always wildlife wandering around, and always a random skirmish breaking out between these three parties.
+The story is pretty interesting and the story missions themselves are fun. Even though the majority of the game is you just running around and exploring, the main story keeps you invested and wanting to find out what happens next. There is a nice combination of action-heavy setpieces as well as stealthier, slower sections.
+The characters are brought to life by top notch animation work, great voice acting and well-written personalities. Vaas, the main villain in the game, is incredible and some of the best scenes in the story feature him. But there is also a great group of supporting characters and everybody has a quirk to them.
+This game really is an open world. Aside from story missions, you can do whatever you want, whenever you want, however you want to. And boy, is there a lot to do. Aside from the story missions, there are a few main things that you'll be spending the entire game doing:
a) Exploring: There are 18 radio towers spread out across the two islands. To update your map and find collectibles, you need to scale each one and reconfigure the control panel. The twist is, every tower has a different approach to climbing it - its a puzzle to figure out how to get to the top of each one. Getting to and reprogramming each one is immensely satisfying. Once the map gets updated, there are also around 150 collectibles that you can obtain by exploring. These often reward you with interesting stories about the islands' past.
b) Freeing outposts: Also spread out across the map are outposts controlled by the enemy. Freeing them nets you a ton of experience and unlocks further quests. However, just like the radio towers, each outpost is different and they get progressively harder to "liberate", as there will be more and more enemies and they can call in reinforcements. How you go about eliminating the enemy is up to you - you can stealth the entire thing and free it virtually undetected. Doing so nets you an XP bonus, but is much more difficult than the other approach, which is going in guns blazing. Planning out the method of attack is really fun and taking over outposts is one of the best parts of this game. Also, you can release caged tigers and bears onto unsuspecting pirates and watch it kill all of them for you. This is the best way to clear outposts ;)
c) Side quests: There are a ton of quests given by villagers and allies, and although some of them are generic fetch quests, there are some great ones, particularly the ones where you have to hunt a rare animal to craft upgrades using its skin, and ones where you have to assasinate a target using a knife.
Cons:
-The UI is pretty mediocre. Everytime you want to craft something or see your inventory, you need to press ESC, then navigate to the appropriate icon with your mouse. Why there is no hotkey for these tasks is beyond me. It just takes too much time for so simple a thing. The map screen is better, but making it so that your mouse can move it is a terrible choice, as the map is never centered around your pointer and as a result it just starts drifting in random directions. The UI for buying/selling items is also terrible and clunky.
**IMPORTANT** Quicksave is F9. The game never tells you this for some reason.
-The story missions are pretty linear and restricts the player in most cases to a single method of approach. I can see why this is necessary, and there honestly isn't much to complain about because YOU can choose when to start these missions. it is annoying when you want to flank the enemy from another direction and the game tells you that you're "leaving the mission area" and prevents you from doing so.
All in all, a fantastic game. Took me over 50 hours to 100% it. Usually goes on sale for like $15, it is very much worth it.

This game is an utter tragedy. The context feels fresh (manuveuring around a sinking city-ship), has entrancing water physics which is modestly taken advantage of in puzzles, and wonderfully stupid lines like "I have two balls and neither of them are crystal." It also has an immense amount of collectibles which offer more insight into the philosophy and lore of the game's setting.
The rest of the game however sort of just exists for the sake of existing. The third-person shooting elements are absolutely rudimentary only kept from straight-up monotony due to the fact there's different ammo types -- even though it feels like you rarely need more than the default sonic rounds. There's 1 type of typical gunman mook with some threadbare AI (see player, find cover, shoot player. flank if out of line of sight.) and although you can sneak past them there's no incentive to do so over simply killing them other than an achievement.
Did I have a horrible time playing through this 4-5 hour title? No, not quite. Nobody can say I didn't have fun with it for what it was. It was an interesting little jaunt if only for the vaguely serviceable storyline; a fight against Darwinian terrorists who want to destroy the remnants of humanity in the water-world apocalytia because.. reasons.
The game was presumably intended to be episodic before the developers went bankrupt. The end of the game is perhaps the most abrupt cliff hanger I've ever seen in a game despite the game not being particularly worth a cliff hanger in the first place. it sucks, sure. But it sucks even more knowing the story is effectively abandonware.
If despite all of those negative marks that this game sounds and looks just cammy enough to catch your interest, it's worth giving the time of day when deeply discounted.

It occurred to me that I had never written a negative review for a game on Steam, so I thought about which of my games I actually considered to be bad.
Sorry, Hydrophobia.
Hydrophobia: Prophecy is the "updated" version of an earlier game, simply titled Hydrophobia, which Dark Energy promised would address criticisms of the first edition. It's actually the SECOND revamp of the game, if you count the update from Hydrophobia: Pure to Hydrophobia: Prophecy. So I ask, why does it still feel so unfinished? The water physics were the main selling point of the game, but you don't get your water powers until the game is almost over! As well, some have praised the water physics as the game's only standout, but I found the water hard to control in a game with already abominable PC optimization.
"I've got two balls and neither of them are crystal." I believe that line paints a pretty accurate picture of the quality of the writing. Let that line decide for you whether you want to spend a dollar fifty on this game during sales.
The story, like so many things about this game, has potential, but fizzles out without really answering the most interesting questions. Why exactly is Kate afraid of water? "Haunting childhood memories" are hinted, but never explored. How, then, can a person who's afraid of water learn to control it? The game mumbles "nanomachines" and goes no further. The blurb on the store page somewhat illuminates the matter, explaining that some very rich people intend to cleanse the world's water with nanomachines, but I don't recall this being explained in the game. Maybe there was a codex entry I forgot to pick up somewhere, but hiding need-to-know information in supplementary material really doesn't cut it. What is this "prophecy" the game itself is named after? That's a very mystical word for a game firmly entrenched in the genre of science fiction. And just what happened to Scott? He seems to just vanish at some point. Did he die? Was he abducted by aliens?
The story, like the gameplay, is a confused mess. It quite literally feels like the game ended at the halfway point. What I thought was a midgame miniboss actually turned out to be the "epic final confrontation" with the villain. It wasn't even a good fight.
It's honestly hard to believe that this is the REMASTERED edition of Hydrophobia. They released a bad game, took the criticism, and rather than blame it on budget cuts or outsourcing, decided to improve and re-release their game. Yay! Except... it's still sh*t. Either the Dark Energy team spent the time they should have used on making Prophecy flapping their lips and making silly noises, or the original Hydrophobia was somehow even worse than Prophecy.
On the bright side, the game is short. Not normally what I would consider praise for a game, but if you are curious about Hydrophobia, at least it won't waste too much of your time.

Poorly aged, and massively overrated. The Sonic/Shadow stages, while mostly enjoyable, still have some cracks that become more obvious with age. Some of them are really fun (City Escape will never not be a classic) but others, like Crazy Gadget, are obnoxious and grating. Sonic and Shadow's touchy movement controls make these stages and the boss fights an exercise in patience, especially with that awful camera.
Tails/Eggman are just okay; blowing up a bunch of stuff in a huge combo is satisfying as all hell, but it takes zero effort to do so, and the cookie-cutter enemy placement doesn't help much. They're brainless and boring.
But the creme de la crap comes in the form of Knuckles and Rouge's stages. Exploration and treasure hunting don't belong in a Sonic game. At all. The openness of the stages combined with the randomized nature of the emerald pieces adds the challenge here, and I can understand why they did it that way, I really can. If everything was in the same place every time you played, there would be no challenge. But even so, these stages are still a slog, even with the hints. The emerald radar only works with one piece at a time, so you're forced to go searching in the order the game wants you to. The controls in these stages are also really touchy- Knuckles and Rouge don't need speed here, so why is it that they can move almost as fast as Sonic and Shadow once they've built up enough momentum? Combat is also awful in these stages- just glide into your enemies, because your combo attack is useless and twitchy.
So what's left in a game that's only 1/3 good? A laughably awful story that reads like a 13 year-old's fanfiction, with acting that sounds like it was done by said 13 year-old and his classmates in a school play. This is a game about talking animals with superhuman abilities, but the story takes itself way too seriously to be enjoyable.
The only things worth salvaging about this game are the cheesy awesome soundtrack and the surprisingly enjoyable Chao Garden sidequest, which you could easily sink more hours into than the actual game as long as you only grind for animals and chao drives in the stages you enjoy playing. All in all, though, Sonic Adventure 2 is a mess of a game that tries to be as variety-filled as a Take 5 bar, but instead comes off feeling like a pizza with every single topping imaginable on it, drowning out that zesty pepperoni.

If something like the WH40k tabletop is what you're hoping for, just walk away. Regicide has two modes, Chess and horrible awful screwed up chess with poorly translated WH40k concepts heaped onto it. Winning isn't hard, but completing all the objectives is near impossible. The thing it does have in common with the table top is chance. Many of the objectives can only be completed through sheer luck, the npc chooses to move left instead of right, it fails an attack that would have ended your success, etc. The 'chance' of a action succeeding is shown in percentages, whatever it is though you need to subtract about 15 from that percent, if it says 54% or less, expect it to pretty much never hit. Even the computer, thankfully, suffers from this. Now, doing the same mission over and over and over and over wouldn't be horrible, except you only get the xp from doing the mission ONCE. So every single time you do it afterwards garners no reward, ever, except for IF you manage to complete that one challenge/objective. Regicide manages to ruin the design of WH40k pretty well, the Orks are evenly matched to Space Marines, which is not how they run on the table top. However, the Chess portion of the game is great. For those of you who want Chess, but more like wizards chess where the pieces kill each other and actually simulate some battle, then this is great. I bought the game purely for the chess aspect back when it had few other features. Thankfully. If I had bought this for the Regicide part of the game i would have been furious and actually, even though it is merely extra content, it is so blah it actually reduces my sense of value on the chess end, which is crazy since I got exactly what I wanted and more, that more though was just terrible. You can only play as one Chapter, the blood angels. Each leve of the reigcide campaign is pre-structured. So you can't choose which marines to take into battle or anything. Now I mentioned Xp earlier, just a side note, I have no idea what XP does. You gain it so slow that I have yet to 'level' up on anything for anything and the regicide campaign is so bad I just can't muscle through it to find out if it improves the experience. This is a bit like turn based gameplay, but if you're coming from Xcom or something good you will be completely upset over this, turn based games to date have set way higher expectations and standards than this does. In the end, if you are just looking for a cool chess game, this is it, this is literally WH40k battle chess between Orcs and Blood Angels. The rest of the game, well if you enjoy it that's great, really, but for me I just can't force myself to try to enjoy it anymore. So if you read this far, do I recommend this game? The Chess part, YES. The Regicide part, ABSOLUTELY NOT.

Alright, giving this game a review because why not?  I played Seduce Me The Otome on a lark because it was free, and I wanted to see what a free visual novel had to offer.  I was not disappointed and became slightly obessed with getting all of the achievements.  I was thoroughly surprised that the sequel was already out, and since I enjoyed the first so much, I was happy to plunk down 10 bucks to play the second.  I highly recommend playing through the first game, which is again free, so it won't cost you anything but time.  You don't have to, but you get more background into the characters than what K gives you in the beginning.
I really enjoyed this game, and it is a fine successor to the first.  Character development is very solid.  All of the boys have their own distinct personalities that are fairly consistent with the first game.  You also meet other interesting characters, like your trainers and Diana's personal guard Saero, who all have their own motivations, if you care to find out about them.  The voice acting is done very well, and I was very surprised to see a character from the first game come back and say "You missed me, ♥♥♥♥♥?"  I found myself saying "Yes.  Yes, I missed you tons."
The story lines are good as well.  It makes sense as to why you are in the demon world and what you have to do to get back to the human world, if you so choose.  The story lines could've been a little longer, especially Diana's.  I was able to knock her arc out and get all the achievements associated with it in about three hours.  It's important to note that what you say or don't say actually matters in this game.  Unlike the first game, which was incredibly formulaic and predictable in getting its endings, you have to pay attention to your paramour and his personality.  I am leaving Diana out of this one because in her arc, you aren't paying attention to her.  You're paying to Saero, who is a fantastic character and is easily my favorite new character.  I wish there was more of him in this game.
Onto the not-so-great stuff.  The art design for the game, on a whole, is better, except when it comes to the boys.  Some of their default poses are so unnatural looking.  It's like a few of their joints are at odd angles.  Also, Damien's character model was the most drastically changed.  While he is the youngest of the five, in the first game, he didn't look or act like the youngest.  That was reserved for Matthew, and I understood it because of their personalities.  Now, Damien definitely looks the youngest and sometimes acts like it too.  No bueno.  Finally, the wives.  As a whole, I like the fact that the boys that you don't romance move on and find love.  That's awesome, but with the exception of Carrie (Sam's wife) in James's arc, they have nothing to do, and it really pisses me off.  I want to know about these ladies!  I want to know about Irene's fashion sense, Noryn's cat leggings, and Iridessa, who looks to be of Native American descent.  I still have a bit of the game to play, farming achievements and such, but if over 20 hours hasn't revealed anything yet, I doubt another 10 will.
Despite all of that being said, this game is worth your money.  Doubly so if you've played the first game.  The good endings are satisfying, the bad ones are heartbreaking, and the voice acting is superb.  Good job, Ms. Laws.
