One example is how each secondary weapon (bombs, rockets, etc.) had a different button assignment vice a single button and when you
map them to the same key, you get an in-game error telling you that the secondary weapon is not available.
Overall, Wings of Prey did a good job with display and realism. But, like many games of its kind, mission variety is rather lacking but it's the crappy control scheme that makes it hit rock bottom. As I said earlier, this is just my experience with it but I highly recommend looking elsewhere.

I don't know what an Undying Bear is exactly, but I've vowed to kill it. I hope it's just a name. This is a mission for the island's Rakyat tribe, and Rakyat tradition dictates that I must defeat the creature with the infinite-ammo pump-action shotgun they've given me. A recent tradition, I would guess, but one I'm happy to honour. The truth is, I have an ulterior motive for finding and killing the legend: I'd really like a new rucksack.
A lot of what you do in Far Cry 3 raises perplexing questions: why would a rucksack made from the skin of the Undying Bear hold more than the one I made from four dead dingoes earlier? Can't I just make one out of six dead dingoes? What is it about Undying Bear skin that facilitates a particularly capacious rucksack design? And more to the point: if it's never died, how would anyone know?
But as I scramble away from it, panic-firing my traditional tribal pump action, what I'm actually wondering is this: when did Far Cry 3 become so good?
We'd been told it was an 'open world' game, but everything Ubisoft showed of it made it look like a monologue-heavy, tightly scripted adventure, its freedom limited to small mission areas. That is in there, it turns out: there's an absurdly long series of missions about rescuing your friends from the pirates who've captured them. But it's just one of the many different games you can play on this vast, freely explorable tropical island.
Hunting wild game to make bags out of their skin is another. Guns, money, syringes and all types of ammunition require their own special container, and every size of every container can only be made from the skin of one particular species of animal. And while guns, money, syringes and all types of ammunition are abundantly available on the island, its people have apparently never invented the bag.
So you, American tourist Jason Brody, must bring your container technology to the island by personally inventing and reinventing various types of harnesses, wallets and sacks, culminating in your magnum opus: the Undying Bear Skin Rucksack, a masterpiece of dermatological engineering capable of holding up to 96 leaves.
If you're going to ask players to buy into a system so hilariously removed from its origins in real-world logic, it had better work. It does. Making the island's wildlife the fodder for your personal upgrade system turns you into a hunter, forced to study and understand the jungle as you explore it. The place teems with life, to the point that you'll often just sit in a bush and watch it. Check out the leopard stalking those boar! What are those dogs howling at? Ooh look, a Komodo dragon mauling a villager!
Something's actually happening over there, and you can go and find out what. Maybe steal its skin.
They don't just fight amongst themselves: the island is dotted with pirate outposts, and the roads are travelled by trucks and cars full of pirates, Rakyat rebels, and civilians. Almost any pair of these have some reason to scuffle if they blunder into each other on their randomised routes, and hearing it happen around you makes the place feel alive. Distant gunfire or beast growls are never just ambience: something's actually happening over there, and you can go and find out what. Maybe steal its skin.
Those outposts are what the game is really about, and conquering one demonstrates everything that makes it great. Your first job is to scout: you've got an entire island of free space to circle this small settlement, and the zoom lens of your camera to study it with. The first Far Cry let you tag enemies with your binoculars: once seen, they're marked on your map in real-time. Far Cry 2 ditched that for being unrealistic. Far Cry 3 brings it back with a vengeance: not only does your camera mark enemies on the map, it lets you see them through walls from then on. As with the skin-crafting, the philosophy is clear: screw reality, this ability makes the game more fun. It does.
Once you've scoped and tagged the 5-10 enemies guarding the outpost, you have perfect situational awareness. You could open fire, but at least one of the pirates will make it to an alarm panel. That brings a truckload of goons to reinforce, and things get very messy. So priority number two is to disable the alarms, and the systems for this are deliciously clever.
You can shoot them. OK, that one's not clever, but it has an interesting complication: only the panel you shoot is disabled, and even a silenced shot will make enough of an impact noise to send the guards running to the others. If it's a small camp, and you've scouted it thoroughly, and you're sure you have line of sight to every panel, you can speed-snipe them all before the guards can set them off. This is cool.
Trickier, but cooler still, is to methodically eliminate each pirate without alerting the others. This is tough, but your tools support it: you can lunge for any unwitting enemy nearby and impale them on your machete before they can call for help. A perk system lets you spend experience points to upgrade stuff like this, including a great trick that lets you steal the dying guard's own knife and throw it at someone else for a second silent kill.
My favourite method, though, is often more practical. If you can get to one of the alarm panels in person, you can tamper with it to disable them all . It's silent, instant and comprehensive. But the panels are always in the heart of the outpost, watched by everyone. Getting to one requires perfect scouting, obsessive planning and steady nerves.
Advertisement
That generally means creating a distraction, and that's another thing Far Cry 3 is great at. You have a dedicated button for throwing a rock, and the sound will distract any idle guard in earshot. It's not a new feature for the series, but short-sighted enemies, more predictable AI and the see-through-walls thing make it massively more useful this time. And those same factors apply to other distractions: a car-full of rebels showing up, a stray bear wandering past, or the pirates' pet leopard suddenly finding its rickety bamboo cage shot open.
Last time I did the cage trick, the leopard savaged every pirate in the camp, waited for my Rakyat allies to show up and take over, then savaged all of them too. That camp is under leopard control now. I gave him sovereignty.
Part of what I love about all these systems in Far Cry 3 is the way they chain together. I find myself hedging my bets: I want to take an outpost down undetected, but I'll try to sneak in and disable the alarms first in case I screw it up. And before I do that, I'll drop some C4 under a nearby truck: if I'm close to being discovered, detonating that'll take their attention off me. Often, halfway through carrying out my plan, the guards catch sight of something they want to attack outside the outpost walls, and rush off to shoot at it. So you have to be ready to restrategise on the spot, and sneak through any window of opportunity that opens up.
Once, when I couldn't get to an alarm panel, I was rumbled halfway through eliminating the guards. I finished the rest off before the reinforcements arrived, but that left me trapped in an empty building with eight angry pirates hunting for me. It was heart-poundingly tense. I'd peek out of windows to tag them with my camera, then watch their silhouettes through the walls until one strayed close. I couldn't risk leaving the huts, so I'd just throw a stone near the doorway. The sound would lure him inside, I'd impale him on my knife, drag his body out of view, then wait for my next target.
If you do manage to disable the alarms, your reward is an even more satisfying second phase to the fight. You still have to eliminate all the guards, and it's still good to remain unseen, but now it doesn't matter how panicked they get as their friends drop around them.
Far Cry 2 had outposts too, though they were smaller with fewer ways to approach. They were also the source of my biggest prob

Fun game, but not yet.
Sadly I keep falling into early access traps the day they come out. I guess I should say they aren't traps, but I do often get caught by the "Look at these cool features" list and wanna play the game bad. I'm also a sucker for engineering and physics games, so this one similar to Space Engineers but simpler really caught my attention. Needless to say it needs work and many more additions to the game before it's worth the  buy. If you want to support the devs, by all means do so since these guys have a real gem on their hands.
Now for the actual review.
Graphics: For the style of the game, top notch graphics. Zero complaints and runs smooth as a butter.

Controls: Easily the best sandbox world controls I've ever player. Every button is where you think it should be. Not once did I ever think of switching a control. Definitely shows these devs are true gamers and know how hands work on a keyboard. More than I can say about most engineering game controls and simplicity.
Replay Value: Once they have more object in, I'd say it has the replay value of Minecraft. Most games like this have 150-200 assets to be used in game, this one has like 25. So pretty much after you've used the small amount of blocks and decoration blocks you're left with your imagination. However, you are limited and a lot of the joy comes from that limitation and trying to find a way in game to work around what you want to do. For example, they have only one real tool that you program, the bearing. The Bearing only works in rotational movement, meaning if you want a linear straight line  for something like a sliding door, you would need to literally make a contraption of six or so moving parts and a bunch of basic logic programing to do so. This in no way takes away from the game as it allows you to explore what you have in front of you. Eventually things will be added to avoid these work arounds so people can play more efficiently without wasting 45 mins on a single sliding door.
Gameplay: This game feels fairly polished in terms of how everything works, surprising since this is an Early Access game. By polish I don't mean everything works, but everything feels like it works. UI makes sense and looks final, everything is textured, world objects like trees and grass are all animated and look great, terrain is great, movement, controls, animations, etc. Everything in the game at the moement feels very good for how early on it is.
Overall: The game is solid. A definite buy, but only if you're really into building machines. It's not like Minecraft where your focus is on a main building, but more a machine. 10/10 times I made a house I somehow made it into a land vehicle or a flying fortress. I've seen people build rail guns out of wood and metal, gundams, vehicles that launch planes, etc. There is also no Survival or anything of the sort just yet, but there will be. For now all we can play in is Creative.
On a side note I would like to give a kind of prediction with this being one of the best survival games to date. I've come to this conclusion based on the materials in the game and how other games used similar styles of survival. There are things like air conditioning with a bunch of assets for ventilation and a duct system, food storage and other storage, ability to make your own defense, launch pads in the game (Potential Space), there's O2 storage for Oxygen. Basically it looks like it's going to turn the love child of Space Engineers and Minecraft with the creepy uncle Rust influencing it.
I do recommend, but not yet to buy.

Warhammer 40k: Regicide is a fun game,
only if you're interested in playing chess against an AI. As of the 13th of February, 2017, after going server hosting upgrades, the multiplayer is not functional. The developer's webiste and forums are both inaccessible and none of them are replying to the questions on the Steam discussions page either. At this point, this can only be understood as a deliberate suspension of multiplayer funcionality, under the disguise of "server upgrades" as the developer is no longer able to support the game.
Which is a damn shame as the chess mode is rather well done. The game nails the feel of the WH40K universe and all of the pieces look and sound believable. They even went as far as to get some voice actors from the Dawn of War series, like Brian Dobson and Steve Blum. The animations the pieces perform when walking and capturing the opposing player's pieces have weight behind them for the most part, but aren't immune to getting repetitive.
On the other hand, the Regicide game mode, which lets units attack and use special abilities, as well providing the player with some Commander abilities, is SEVERELY undercooked. Simply put, its boring, lacks the depth and immersion it should have. The majority, if not all of the animations for these abilities and attacks are either laughable or non-existant. Not to mention that whether your unit will hit their attack or ability is determined by RNG, just like in X-COM, except here it completely boggles the mind how your pieces miss their attacks when the enemy is
right in front of them. To add insult to injury, the game may show the enemy piece being hit (or a piece in the background because you missed your attack) just because of how close it is, but it won't register as a hit because that's what the RNG determined.
Oh, but that's not enough, is it? The 50 mission long Space Marine campaign is done in this mode, as opposed to the classic chess mode, and the achievements don't work. So even if you do what the achievement requires you to, you don't get it. Not to mention that the Ork campaign has to be bought with in game currency that you earn from matches and by beating missions in the Space Marine campaign, but you're not able to get it as, as stated, the online component of the game is busted. This entirely
the somewhat interesting story the game tries to present through nicely voice acted mission briefings.
In addition to in game currency,  the game has daily log ins, as if it were a free to play game. These award you with more currency, but you're unable to utilise them as, again, the online isn't bloody working.
To sum it up, WH40k: Regicide's chess mode is fun, but not worth the $15, and only if you're interested in playing Singleplayer as the online component of the game is
. I'd be fine with this if they had the decency to admit it
The Regicide mode on the other hand feels like it never left the Early Access stage of the game which was back in 2015, two years ago.
I've been meaning to hold off my review of the game until we get some word from the devs, but seeing as the game is now on sale, 60% off and will be for the next 10 days, I feel like people need to be warned.
And if we never do get a response, I hope that Hammerfall Publishing at least has the decency not to show their face on the Steam Store ever again.

So, Hydrophobia: Prophecy; What a weird name for a game where the main protagonist isn't afraid of drinking water, nor is there any mention of a prophecy of sorts in the story. It's like the devs skimmed through a list of words with a hydro- prefix, picked the one that sounded cool, and added the "prophecy" subtitle so it looks like there's going to be a grand "chosen one" adventure. I think that they were trying to tie the title's name with their in-house "
", but in my opinion, they should have gone with something that represents the game properly.
Hydrophobia looks like it was made to showcase the HydroEngine (which is impressive), and that's kind of where the problem stems from. Everything about this game is bad; the voice acting, gameplay mechanics, and story are all lackluster, compared to other indie games within the same price range. Sure, the water simulations are great, but why didn't the devs use that as the core gameplay mechanic, instead of shoving it as a background element? The player could have controlled the water ala waterbending, used it so solve complex puzzles, and employed to create tension in some stages - all we were left with is a so-so TPS, with a hodgepodge of game mechanics that's borrowed from other titles.
Regarding the story: well, the story is forgettable. They've got this protagonist who has all of the excuses and skills to navigate a sinking ship, with a voice actor who is clearly trying to sound American, but slips in her native Irish accent once in a while. She's got some kind of a backstory that's shown in the opening cutscene, where aquaphobia has troubled her all her life, yet she swims like a pro - and it doesn't get mentioned ever again throughout the game. After the intro, everything regarding character development is thrown out of the window, in favor of a story that's all about escaping flooded rooms.
If someone could pick up this IP, and revise some of the decisions made before, I'll definitely have a look at it. The industry rarely tackles games like this, and it would be a shame to just let a concept like this one die out. But choose a better name next time; something like "Hydropower", or "Hydroelectric". Better yet, name it "Aquaphobia".
And there you have it.

This is probably one of my favourite games of all time.
I can't explain
. Not eloquently, anyway. There's a few things in particular that stand out; the truly cinematic battles, the endlessly fascinating policital intrigue, and how Calradia really feels like a living, breathing continent. Wars break out, Lords defect or are driven out by their king, merchant caravans travel from city to city, rivals torch villages and take their enemies' castles for themselves, bandits harass towns before moving on to greener pastures, and it can all happen wile you're just sitting in your tent, curled up with a good book.
There are lots of little things, too. It feels like an old-school RPG - you're pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥when you start out, but eventually hone your skills to a point that even rivals the kings themsevles. It feels like you're taking a journey in this place, and what you do really matters as to how the future unfolds.
Also, taking out foe after foe with Crossbow headshots never gets old. Or seeing your Nord Houscarl take out an enemy Knight with a throwing axe. Or winning a tournament after having bet on yourself at every opportunity. Or knocking a godforsaken Khergit of his stupid horse.
Not that there isn't complaints, there most certainly are. But Warband shines so brightly in all the areas where it counts that they're swiftly forgotten.
Oh, and mod support. Lots of mod support. And the developers are totally on board with it, which makes it so much better.
Bottom line, this is more than worth the $20 asking price. In fact, I'm so bold as to suggest it's a steal at twice the price.

This looks like Tetris. Don't let the appearance fools you. The resemblance is superficial only, this is nothing like Tetris. Unlike Tetris, this is a physics based game, so if your pieces aren't properly supported, they'll tilt and possibly fall, possibly trashing your foundation layers. You have some harmful powers you can use to hinder your opponents along with some beneficial ones to help yourself build better.
Grab yourself some friends for some local multiplayers. There's some fun to be had for an evening or two. You probably won't be playing this for hundreds of hours, there's too few modes; a race to reach a certain height, a survival which consists in not losing pieces longer than your opponents and a puzzle mode where the winner is the one who manages to put the most pieces below a certain height. Each of these three modes has three difficulty settings which changes what powers are available and how much wind you'll have to deal with. There's online multiplayer has well, but I haven't tries it.
There are some single-player challenges but they're pretty much limited to the same game modes with set objectives instead of opponents.
This game definitely has good but limited value.

I bought Tricky Towers a few months ago and was initially super-amazed at how fun it is in multiplayer.  After playing a few games I realised that some of the physics weren't consistent.  This meant that two players placing down the exact same block could have different outcomes.  Granted, these situations were few and far between but it introduced a random factor into the gameplay.  My review was initially negative as this broke the game for me.
I raised this issue with the devs and they worked on an update and the physics now seem to be pretty much consistent.   Now, after ploughing a few more hours into it I can certainly say the game is fun, and more importantly fair!!  I won't dwell on this point further as it is fixed but really wanted to mention the proactiveness of the devs to fix this big issue!
We have three game modes in the game : Puzzle, Race and Survival.  Each mode requires completely seperate strategies to be successful.  To mix it up there are then different variants of each mode : Easy, Normal and Special.  The format I play the most is online cup which randomly chooses a mode and a variant of that mode and you play over until one player earns enough points to be the champion.  This format was introduced recently and works really well.  A cup run could maybe take 10 minutes so it's perfect to pick up and play.
I've played at different times of the day and can always find others to play with around the clock.  It would be nice to have some standard chat phrases like "gg" or "unlucky" etc after the game a bit like Rocket League system.  When you win you do get a chance to whizz around the screen shouting in a weird voice, but this is more a victory lap as opposed to an opportunity to handshake.
There are also a number of challenges and a couple of endless single-player modes that include leaderboards meaning there is some game there if you want to take a break from playing in multiplayer.
If you like Tetris, like physics and like multiplayer then Tricky Towers really is a no-brainer.  This for me, is one of the best games of 2016!

Pro's:
-  Something that's great for a few friends together in front of the same monitor, without feeling squeezed.
-  Builds on an old game that so many people are immediately familiar with
-  Games are quick, nothing feels drawn out
-  Game uses some of the single player puzzles to transparently teach some of the concepts.
-  Admittedly, the game has replay value, but only with multiple players.
Con's:
-  *WAY* too little content for the price
-  Same goes with art, music, etc.  The opening music (in the game setup menu's, etc.) is a 30 second loop.  This becomes grinding *REALLY* fast.  There are only 4 avatars for 4 players?  I mean that's just lazy.  The characters only have a handful of reactions/emotes at best, I didn't count, but I think a "handful" would even be generous as a term.
-  When playing locally, you can't even name your character, they all use your steam name.  What's up with that, seriously!
-  A lot of the game is frustrating, and not in a good way:
The placement "rules" for what sticks, and what does not, are entirely inconsistent.  IE: sometimes putting own a "T" shaped block, using the bottom section of the "T" to latch sideways to a cliff will hold, try it in another spot, on a similarly solid surface, and it just won't.  Why?  Who knows!
The last bit just ruins the gameplay.  The game has a few things built in to up the ante (wind, swaying towers, offensive spells, etc.), but having the rules of placement changing arbitrarily without any rhyme or reason is just poor game design.
Bottom line, what you see in the video's is basically the entire game, front to back.  There isn't much to the game, and while it's fun, you're effectively paying $15 for less content then you'd find in a typical flash game.

I have had this game for years now and here are a few things on why this game is bad. You may skip this review thinking I'm angry at it, but I'm actually disappointed.
First, the game was in early access in 2013. I've spent the last 4 years patiently waiting for what I thought would be an eventual full release. I turns out, the full release was in 2014. In the state that it was in 2014, it was very incomplete and very broken. Now, it still seems incomplete with one of the game modes being in beta for almost 2 years now.
Second, the game devs simply don't care anymore. The last time they said anything on steam about the game was last halloween in 2016. This game is still incomplete and they haven't said anything in over a year. This is bad for their community engagement. If they are going to treat the player base like this, what's the point of making the game.
Finally, the game is very much dead. The matchmaking is virtually empty, there are sh*t loads of modded servers with crappy modifications, the player zombie is overpowered (player respawning as zombies in the first place is a huge problem to begin with for a realistic zombie game), and starting a match without a private server or lan as an option makes it impossible to play with friends.
To be honest, it is a very fun game. But unfortunately, the devs don't care anymore, the game is still incomplete, and the player base is almost non-existent. It is worth it if you can set up a lan party with friends that live nearby, but otherwise not worth the purchase at this point.
This is simply not how you should treat your game or your player base.

A beautifully dark, Gothic setting; the Warhammer Universe, a small band of heroes; a Bright (Fire) Wizard, a Witchhunter, an Elven Archer, a Dwarven Ranger and an Imperial Soldier and a horde of armed, man-sized (and occassionally larger) rats. What more could you want from a co-op slaughter experience?
Combat is wonderfully visceral; melee is the focus and it really delivers; a simple (but not too simple) and satisfying system that makes you want to dive in for more. Each class has overlapping areas of proficiency but each really feels unique (Getting used to dwarf height is a challenge in and of itself). Ranged combat tends to be a matter of either Ammo management in long term for most classes, or Overheat management in short term for the Wizard, which is a nice diversity.
10+ missions of varying length, around about 15 hours if you storm through them. I really was excited for this game and I really wanted to like it; the graphics are charming, the music is catchy, and the gameplay is fun, however it's heavily pay to win.
Essentially the game is you sending units down little paths to the enemy base, certain units counter others: for example, airborne units counter most infantry, some infantry counter tanks, tanks counter some vehicle-type units.  It's pretty simple and straightforward.
The downside is that when you start, you have 1 "inventory space".  These inventory spaces are used for timers to open chests or upgrade units, and range anywhere from 10 minutes to 8+ hours.  You either forego extra chests from winning battles; or upgrade your units.  You can buy more inventory spaces using the golden "freemium" currency, starting at 250 for the 2nd space and 1000 for the third space.  You do start out with 250 currency when you begin the game but it doesn't last long.  You can also earn more currency from battles and achievements, but it's slim pickings compared to just buying the currency outright.
All the unit upgrades in the game are based off cards you gain from loot boxes (similar to Clash Royale), and of course the best units come from the large boxes that cost a ton of the freemium currency.  Which means that people who pay money will almost always be ahead of you, whether its unit types or unit upgrades.  More coins = more inventory slots = more chests = more cards = better units.
I'd much rather pay $10-20 for a game like this and get rid of the pay2win elements, but I guess the developers would rather go the mobile game pay to win route to keep people buying.

The plots are all fascinating, well-developed, and different. The boys\' routes have similar starting points but vastly different subplots that make each one interesting in their own right. Each character - the love interests and the new side characters - have wonderful development and are excellently voiced.
It feels more like an experience and less like a dating sim - not that I dislike dating sims, clearly, but the environment here is epic and grand.
The music is gorgeous, the art stunning, and the atmosphere all encompassing and engrossing.
My one criticism would be that I really wish we knew more about the wives. For those who haven\'t played or gotten very far, each of the incubi that you AREN\'T playing the route for has a wife, who is brought along with them on the journey to the Demon World. Personally, I loved having more female characters in the game and I really enjoyed the way the wives were drawn and the scenes where all ten of them (the incubi, the wives, and the MC) were bantering together. But with the exception of Sam\'s wife, we don\'t get any backstory on them. We don\'t know how they met their chosen husbands, how much or how little they know about the demon world and how they know it. I would\'ve loved more on them but I do understand that it\'s the MC\'s story, after all.
And what a story it is. I highly reccomended this game. It\'s well worth the cost.

Its almost a good game, I've given it several chances but ultimately there are just too many stupid decisions in the design. The main ones that keep comming up for me are:
- If one team cant move during the movement phase the game is a draw, so if you corner your enemies obejective piece... draw... the AI will seemingly try to make it so it cant move to avoid loosing too. This is the biggest problem IMO.
- In the campagin the hit percentages displayed are not what is actually in use, it starts off that way but as you progress it deviates, I ended up keeping track of hits and misses and it wasn't even close in the later acts (I know, I know, there is a degree of randomness but over time the results should trend toward the percentages).
- When you get down to just a handful of pieces left the AI will often just run away, you can chase it all day long but you wont get anywhere (bearing in mind you cant corner it or it will be a draw...). It feels like a bug when this happens because more often when the match has clearly been won the AI will just throw the remaining pieces onto squares for you to capture so as not to drag out a already foregone conclusion.
- When the AI makes a 'hail mary move' (i.e. if everything in the following round doesn't go its way the move would cripple its position) it seems to always workout for it, these dont happen too often so perhaps I've just had bad luck but given how other parts of the game work I cant help but suspect not everythings random and I've seen the same move repeated on the same map several times as if it were scripted.
- If a round lasts too long (like when you are chasing down a couple of final pieces while trying not to end in a draw) the game starts lagging between each action.
If they cleaned these up and some of the other less frustrating bugs I would have happily recommended it as the concept is neat, its the execution that wears thin.

Chess based strategy game with Warhammer theme. Very similar to the old Battle Chess. Can use traditional chess moves to take pieces, as well as fight with guns, grenades, special abilities to destroy enemies health down to 0, going through their armor and sometimes shields in the process. Different ways to play like solo and multiplayer, pick between classic chess or regicide mode, with custom board layouts to mix things up.

I don't know who it was that thought a heavy dose of random chance would make chess better, but it's ridiculously frustrating. I generally don't mind dice rolls in games, I have no issues with XCOM for instance, but when it's combined with the deliberate nature of chess and the ability to take pieces in a single go by capturing them it becomes surprisingly infuriating. The whole point of chance in games is to force you to adapt your plans to whatever bad luck may transpire against you, but as it's still basically chess it fills extremely tactically inflexible. To put it succintly: If chess is about thinking several moves ahead, how can I do that when there is pure chance involved?
I know there is a pure chess mode in the game, but the selling point is Regicide mode, after all. Maybe I just need to git gud, but having played through the first Act of the campaign it feels like there aren't any interesting consequences to bad luck, there's just restarting.
Add on to that all the issues with having to sign up for an account and that the game is very poor at explaining things like the levelling system, or the range of abilities, or what those abilities actually do before you get the chance to use them...

If I could leave a neutral review on this particular game, I probably would.
If you're looking for a melee-focused, first-person, shield-and-slash kind of loot-farming L4D-like game, this game's for you.
I've played enough of this game to have a lot of fun with it, but this is one of those games that's almost unplayable without people/friends. Sometimes there's not enough teamwork to succeed either, and eventually you might just get tired of playing the same maps over and over with very little entertaining end-game. Some players might continue though, because of the randomized loot system, which, although randomized, still feels pretty rewarding. Sometimes.
CONTENT AND MISSIONS - There's a bit of a lack of content for Vermintide, not that there isn't enough to feel like a 'full' game, but you'll end up replaying maps quite soon into it. This is sort of to be expected of an early access title, but it needs more missions to play somewhat badly. Also, I think the game should be finished and released out of early access before they start making paid DLC's. Sure, the first is only $2.99, but it's a slippery slope.
But on the topic of missions, it almost feels like the variety doesn't matter since most people just run Horn of Magnus to grind loot, with a handful of other missions... It's a little disheartening for only 1 mission to be played so consistently.
TEAMWORK - You'll probably spend the first 10 hours having fun and learning the game's mechanics. After that, you'll try your hand at the Hard, Nightmare, and Cataclysmic difficulties, as there isn't much of a point to run Normal or Easy difficulty if you want good loot. Sometimes you'll get teamed up with people who fall all at once and fail the mission, but you'll just have to keep at it to get better. Along with that, the bots are sadly not a viable alternative. In my early playtime, I tried to play Horn of Magnus on NORMAL with bots, got to the elevator at the end, where 1 rat hit me, knocked me to the ground so I'd need a revive, and Kerillian (the Elf bot) and Bardin (the Dwarf bot) just stood over my corpse, they didn't help me up.
LOOT - Next 20-30 hours, you'll get some Greens (Commons) and Blues (Rares), an Orange (Exotic), maybe even 1 or 2 Trinkets, which really help out as their effects are independent of the Hero you're playing. These'll help you survive and deal better damage.
But I have some extreme gripes with the rewards system, as you collect special dice in missions that are used at the end to get a random reward of a loot item. It's either a weapon or a trinket, but on a very rare chance, it's a hat. But in order to get even this chance, you have to BEAT the mission, make it ALL THE WAY to the end and succeed. If you don't, all you get is exp, and even if you make it to the end but DON'T beat it, all you get is 8 CRAFTING TOKENS. The dice give you better chances at getting higher tiers of loot, but only if you win. And even then you might not get loot for the character(s) you play.
Overall, it's a really fun and hectic game. It's visually great and pretty fun when things go right, but it's not without problems.

This game is solid, through and through. Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide is a dark fantasy, FPS from Fatshark. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
There are a lot of things I could drone on about here, but I will try to keep things relatively brief. For starters, I have always been more of a melee guy than a ranged guy. Rushing in and decapitating things has always been more rewarding to me. Vermintide (which plays pretty much identically to Left 4 Dead) allows me to do just that, maintain me value as a member of team, and actually do some good. Melee weapons will doubtless be your most commonly used form of weaponry in Vermintide. Each character also has a ranged weapon as their secondary and, while they are also fun to use, bullets run out quickly when your group is getting overwhelmed and (depending on what difficulty level you are on) fresh ammo can be scarce.
Secondly, the Skaven (for those of you unfamiliar with the Warhammer Fantasy universe, “Skaven” are ratmen) are an incredibly fun enemy to cut your way through. I feel like most people are a bit burnt out on zombies at this point in time and the market is flooded with subpar zombie games. The Skaven are a refreshing new take on horde enemies in a video game.
The level of violence and gore is simply beautiful. Gibs, decapitations, severed limbs, Vermintide has it all. Not to mention sound wise. When you swing your bladed instruments at something, you hear it connect with meat. It is glorious. When you shoot something; meat. What more could you ask for?
There are (currently) five playable characters in the game. Each one brings something different to the table, uses different battle strategies, and is genuinely fun to play as. Sure, you’ll decide on one or two favorites, we all do. But, each character is actually fun to play and that is a good thing.
Weapon, item,  and map design are beautiful. Seriously, if the city in the game wasn’t crawling with slobbering rat people who want to eat your intestines, it would be a very cool place to sight see.
The Bad
The one complaint I have about Vermintide is the loot rolls. At the end of a mission (assuming your party completed the mission) you will have a chance to get new equipment. This is done by rolling dice and, judging by how many x’s you get, that’s how rare of loot you receive. Most of the time you’ll end up getting crap you won’t be bothered to use.
The Meh
I got nothing here, sorry.
Verdict: Yea
If you’re a fan of Warhammer, Left 4 Dead, gratuitous violence, or anything that I mentioned above, Vermintide will be a good fit for you. The price tag feels about right for the game, but I haven’t seen it go on sale much. As always, thanks for reading.

Oh boy. First things first, if you want a good voice-acted visual novel with awsome artwork, then THIS is the game. Seduce Me 2 is a direct sequel to the first game (which is free if y'all wanna take a look). In short, you play as a human girl that is about to be married to one of five incubi brothers (or a beautiful succubus princess ;D). Unfortunately, things don't go as planned and you get dragged into a Demon War that you maaaaay or may not have had a hand in...
Story: Mmmm THIS is where games are a deal breaker for me, as I love reading and writing stories. SM2 is beautifully written and each path you choose is unique in its own way, which is a definite improvement from the first game. The choices your MC make are relatively open most of the time, and my favorite part about this is you don't HAVE to have sexy time with your demon to get a good ending. The SM team is very big on proper consent with your partner. You don't HAVE to sleep with someone just because they're a sex demon or etc. Not only that, but there are so many different endings you can get, to the point where sometimes it can get frustrating. For me, the hardest was Erik since I kept dying, haha. But it's really satisfying when you see every single secret and ending the game has to offer since you really have to work for your results.
Characters: You definitely see the character development throughout the game, and it was even more apparent if you also played the first game. Like damn, that's my other weakness in stories (I'm so proud of my green sinnamon roll). I was also very surprised with how all the new characters interacted with each other. Usually you'll have minor characters that are there simply for decoration or for a bit of extra dialogue. In SM2, each side characters has a story of their own and further expands the world of the Abyssal Plains. You'll spend a long while revealing secrets, such as who Diana's guard is, or why Sergeant's horn is broken, etc.
Sound/Music: YES! I loooove the music, so good job Christopher Escalante. Also to Jonah Scott too for sound design. It was a huge improvement from the first game and I found myself crying and laughing many times while playing. I'll admit that sometimes the music will suddenly shift in an awkward place, but it's not too distracting.
Artwork: Not going to lie, when I first saw the changed art style, I had my reservations. BUT the more I played, the more it grew on me and I actually found myself loving it. The CGs are really well drawn/colored and the backgrounds are GORGEOUS. They really help paint the image of the Abyssal Plains while I play. The only complaint I have are some of the characters' arms are in awkward positions (especially noticeable when in demon form). Nothing huge and I can't fault the artist since it's better than having everyone in the exact same pose.
Bugs/errors: As with all games, we'll have our share of bugs and errors. Luckily I haven't had anything game breaking happen to me so far, but occassionally you'll get a strangely placed character when skipping a few lines. Before the recent update, some lines weren't matching up with the vocals, or if you
. I THINK these were fixed in the most recent update, but I haven't had time to test them all just yet. But anyway, the bugs aren't that gamechanging.

The game has a lot to go and huge shoes to fill. I think it to be the nature of MMOs that each one is compared to others, be it WoW or AQW. The game honestly needs a lot of fixing, refining, and overall polish.
In my time currently in AQ3D (20.2 hrs) here are a list of grips I've had:
-Out of combat healing feels slow
-The lack of a healing button/animation makes it feel like your time resting is unproductive
-Enemies aggro for far too long of a distance
-A glitch where you fall through the floor is common in dungeons and on respawn, the glitch continues (needs /unstuck)
-No sprint button
-No version of enchanting
-Finishing a zone has no real indicator beyond no more quests from the quest vendors
-A lack of an overarching storyline (Not  a huge grip given that it is in open beta)
-Moving with the forward key while turing the camera still means your character moves in the original camera's foward
-Instances of areas exist but aren't stated, nor can you join a yulgar-9999 type of instance to meet up with friends, meaning if you have a large group, meeting up in one area is hellish ( /join graveyard(party) would be stellar
-The barbershop costs 500 gold however you can't rotate your character model to see the back of the hair (female characters are especially a victim to this)
-Quests with random drop requirements do not drop the same for every player, meaning if you're doing a quest that requires a box that has a 20% drop with a friend, you may finish ahead and need to wait for your friend
-Sound is incredibly lacking
-Some items don't have descriptions, which is disappointing
-Inventory is not sorted by item type but by order obtained
-Mana gain in combat is laughably unnoticable
-Eye color choice would be nice, a choice from the entire color pallet would be great
-CC gear would be nice
-Hide helmet, cape, pauldron, etc would be great
So in short, there are many flaws with the game. However, as with AQW if you think you may get into it, it's best to start now. It's an investment, a promise that when the game gets good (which I do believe it will) you'll have been there from a very early point, meaning you have very rare items (at least by AQW standards, in which the older, the rarer).

Sonic Adventure 2 is a weird game for me.
I routinely critique it for not having aged well and being buggier than a spider ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ party, yet I own it on every single platform and have 100%'d it about 12 times.
It hasn't aged well, let me just reiterate that. The voice acting is wonky, the stages are short and kinda flat, the plot is a bit laughable, it has the pacing of a heartrate monitor during an electrical storm, and the non-speed stages break up the flow like a bullet to the brain.
Yet, in spite of those issues. I still like the game. All things considered, it's a fantastic time waster. Plinking away at levels and their sub missions whilst dropping into the Chao Garden to take part in the cutest eugenics experiment on Earth is admittedly quite therapeutic. While the non-speed levels might break up the flow, they're not at all bad in my opinion and having the option to do something else OTHER than speed stages isn't an unwelcome relief. Sure, the game would've been better if the alternate gameplay modes didn't exist, but it is what it is.
And hey, if you're looking to add replay value, why not try

Everyone says this game is just 40k chess but it is so much more than that.  While there is a "classic" mode that is basically just chess with 40k skinned peices and battle chess style animations, the real highlight is the rest of the game which is a strategy game where your troops move in chess like patterns, but feels completely different from chess.  This is because each stage has a different set of "pieces" and starting points for both sides as well as different conditions for winning and special abilities like boosting health, armor, firepower and even stunning enemies that add an extra layer of strategy that makes you forget you are playing a "chess" themed game. There is even a campaign mode with a story and typical 40k style voice acting.  I say if you like ANY strategy games, chess or not,  and the 40k universe, this game is well worth the money and time invested.

Beside those two things it is an incredible game. Especially to think in the ways of chess but also shooting Orks in the face, just to spill Blood For The Blood God!

It does what it promises and not much more. It's chess, with an added round after each move to make a few attacks and wear down an enemy's HP to eliminate pieces, rather than just capturing them through chess moves. Does chess really need the addition of random chance (to hit), however?
The graphics are poor for something that came out this recently and they reused assets as often as humanly possible. Most of the units look exactly the same, minus a bit of equipment swapping. Unlocking other factions gets you different colored guys.
I played through Act 1 of the campaign, which mixes up victory conditions and setups enough to keep things from getting overly stale, but honestly, everything merely swung between being too easy and being annoying.
Maybe worth a buy on sale if you're really into chess and Warhammer. Otherwise, there are probably more polished and engaging ways to spend your time.

I spent a good year or so playing this game, developing a guild, making some great new friends. But if I were to be absolutely critical, this is my review:
Wakfu is a strategy MMO with a battle system remniscent of games such as Final Fantasy Tactics. It features several unique classes, a world with a rich story and lore comparable to Warcraft's, and a fun, playful art style you could probably only find from a French game.
Its parent company, Ankama, has recently put in a lot of work to developing the earlier game (levels 1-100, basically) but overall... you basically need to be social in order to have fun with this game. Without friends, without a guild, the grinding can get pretty boring pretty quick. Further, the community is small and the PVP a little under developed - a recipe for disaster.
Overall, I would still recommend this game, but with a huge grain of salt. If you can get past the grinding, the "highschool" mentality of the social scene, and the dupers, its pretty fun!

TLDR: Get when 5 dollars or less. It's a good physics demo but not a good game.
The water physics are worth experiencing.
The game is very interesting for a showoff of a well developed water physics engine. That's really the whole point of the game and it is the protagonist and antagonist. You play as a security detail that suddenly gets flooded in during an uprising of the facility with the invisible guidance of your totally-not-boyfriend in a puzzle/shooter while racing or working against water for the most part.
The shooting elements aren't very interesting. You have a few ammo types and an infinite ammo type but these fights are nothing to write home about. It's just a third person shooter.
The story wasn't all that moving. Rebels are uprising against the water-bound facility and you're trying to overcome your personal fear of water to stop the bad guy who somehow ties into this.
Now the selling point of the game is intended to be playing with water. You shoot out glass barriers and open doors to flood in a large current which turns the whole place upside down. Unfortunately the whole water-bender magic only happens in the last chapter of the game which is a really short time. You don't get to play with the magic as much as you should.
For a tech demo, I'd say it's worth it when five bucks or even on sale for less than that.

I was drawn to this game by the graphics and water physics which looked amazing, and it didn't disappoint in that regard.  The water and water effects are pretty impressive.
Overall gameplay:
From the start and through most of the game it is a relatively simple game, mostly solving minor puzzles and navigating around obstacles, and taking out enemies when they present themselves.  All in all most of the game right up near the very end is not very difficult at all.  More on that later.
There are a number of flaws in this game however and here is my take on them.
Story:
Firstly, the story and plot are nothing remotely new in the general sense.  Evil bad guy trys to take over the world (figuratively speaking), you must stop them under time pressure blah blah blah.  There is nothing unique or nuanced about it, it's fairly textbook without any major surprises.
Controls:
The controls for this game appear to have been designed for console gaming where there are not a lot of buttons/keys to press and so they have to be creative with how they present weapon selection user interface etc. in the game in order to allow players solely using a game controller to fully access all of the games controls.  This is a pet peeve of mine because if you use a keyboard and mouse you have a lot more buttons available that would give you more intuitive control over the game, but games like this purposefully do not bother to use the available hardware options and instead force everyone to use a console-like interface instead.  I hate having to press and hold a single button in a game to get an on-screen menu of weapon or ammo choices, then point out the one I want.  I'd much rather have a one button press like you'd find in a standard shooter like Quake to select my weapon/ammo.  These popups force me to lose immersion and have to think about an on-screen display instead of just hitting a button without leaving the game.  Very immersion breaking.
Combat flaws:
The weapon/combat mechanics are very awkward and unnatural feeling.  That is a combination of the third person perspective and difficulty determining where your weapon's line of sight is compared to what you see and think versus what the game engine considers a line of sight.  This makes it often very difficult to aim your gun at the target accurately when shooting around cover from the left or right.  Even though you personally have a clear line of sight to the target, and the trajectory from the end of the gun to the target is clear, the game repeatedly acts as if the cover to the side is in the way and your bullets hit the cover instead of going where you can see that they should go.  You're forced to put your self deep out of cover into harms way to get around this quirk and it's rather irritating and inconvenient when it happens.  You usually end up taking fire, whereas in real life you'd keep your body in fire and just hold the weapon around the cover.  Other games get this right, so it's designed this way on purpose and more or less makes hiding behind cover partially useless.
Sometimes you have a weapon/ammo selected and it wont shoot, it just hangs until you select other ammo then reselect the ammo you had.  Very frustrating bug that occurs occasionally although not often.
I always felt like all of the weapons were very inaccurate, having to spray bad guys with endless ammo to take them down while they take you down with 1-2 shots.  Also, you can pretty much visibly see the ammo travelling to the target at a much lower velocity than real weapons would fire, so the weapons just had this lame feel to them.  I often wished I could just run up to the enemies and Mortal Kombat their arses face to face with bare hands than fiddle around with the lame weapons in this game.
Respawns:
Enemies respawn out of thin air unexpectedly.  If you're looking for an arcade-like game experience then that might be fine, but I like more realism and immersion in my games, and when enemies spawn in out of thin air I find it really annoying, especially when I've completely sweeped an area and there is no way in.  IMHO, encountering enemies in a game should always feel natural, and visible or other obvious spawn-ins really takes away from the realism and immersion in a game IMHO.
Final Boss:
Without any spoilers, the final boss fight is a severe challenge.  The entire game up until that point was relatively easy to mildly challenging, but when you get to the final boss it becomes extremely difficult and for me it felt down right impossible.  I tried over and over countless times to defeat the final boss and it just got tedious and repetitive and wasn't fun at all.  The whole time you're getting your butt kicked the boss is laughing at you and firing off World War III in your face.  Be prepared to die like 50 times while wanting to smash your keyboard and punch the monitor.  The final boss fight is just totally not fun at all.  I ended up giving up and just watching a Youtube video of someone else defeating the final boss who also was upset at the game for being so impossibly difficult.
Final verdict:
I found the game to be an interesting diversion with nice graphics and physics, but the story and gameplay were lacking.  The combat mechanics were awkward and the final boss scene was severely unbalanced and far too difficult to be fun.  I like a good challenge, but it has to be fun not frustrating.  Overall I think there are much better games out there worth the money than this one, and I think all but the most die hard gamers will simply give up on the final boss fight if they make it that far.  Save your money and watch a youtube playthrough of this instead.

First of all, it's hard to justify recommending this game despite how much I've enjoyed it because this game is very exclusive to the US region.
Statistically, the game lobby lists ~70% as US games, the rest mostly EU. Asian players make up <5% of the 300-500 active players during peak hours.
I have seen too many players buy the game and give up quickly because they have no one to play with, which was one of the reason I created a steam group for our region and remained active for quite a while.
The game itself is extremely fun and challenging. The survival of the players depend heavily on team cohesiveness and communication which adds another layer of enjoyment. It can get overwhelming and frustrating in pick up groups without this layer for the loner player.
Due to the reserved culture/nature of Asian players, initiatively opening up to players through VOIP is not common, hence the game doesn't thrive in our region.
The game failed to establish a foothold outside of US and EU. No point wasting money to buy since the game is dead in Asia/SEA region.

I really enjoyed the first game, so naturally I got this game thinking that I would enjoy it just as much, if not more.
I played for about 3 hours, got a few different endings and was generally disappointed with this game. It was pretty convoluted and went off topic a bit so the flow of the game kept getting interrupted.
I'll give a few examples.
*SPOILERS AHEAD*
It made no sense and in fact was a terrible idea that the boys brought their wives with them to the demon world, they are human and therefore would have no way to protect themselves. They were in the story just to be there; they had no importance.
The malicious voice in the main character's head also killed it for me a little bit, it got to the point where it was just annoying.
I appreciate the attempt at all the little side stories such as Diana's love with her guard and her team wanting her dead, but the way it was introduced was jarring.
Long story short, this game isn't worth $10.00 and if you liked the way the original ended then don't bother playing this one.

The game has a lot to go and huge shoes to fill. I think it to be the nature of MMOs that each one is compared to others, be it WoW or AQW. The game honestly needs a lot of fixing, refining, and overall polish.
In my time currently in AQ3D (20.2 hrs) here are a list of grips I've had:
-Out of combat healing feels slow
-The lack of a healing button/animation makes it feel like your time resting is unproductive
-Enemies aggro for far too long of a distance
-A glitch where you fall through the floor is common in dungeons and on respawn, the glitch continues (needs /unstuck)
-No sprint button
-No version of enchanting
-Finishing a zone has no real indicator beyond no more quests from the quest vendors
-A lack of an overarching storyline (Not  a huge grip given that it is in open beta)
-Moving with the forward key while turing the camera still means your character moves in the original camera's foward
-Instances of areas exist but aren't stated, nor can you join a yulgar-9999 type of instance to meet up with friends, meaning if you have a large group, meeting up in one area is hellish ( /join graveyard(party) would be stellar
-The barbershop costs 500 gold however you can't rotate your character model to see the back of the hair (female characters are especially a victim to this)
-Quests with random drop requirements do not drop the same for every player, meaning if you're doing a quest that requires a box that has a 20% drop with a friend, you may finish ahead and need to wait for your friend
-Sound is incredibly lacking
-Some items don't have descriptions, which is disappointing
-Inventory is not sorted by item type but by order obtained
-Mana gain in combat is laughably unnoticable
-Eye color choice would be nice, a choice from the entire color pallet would be great
-CC gear would be nice
-Hide helmet, cape, pauldron, etc would be great
So in short, there are many flaws with the game. However, as with AQW if you think you may get into it, it's best to start now. It's an investment, a promise that when the game gets good (which I do believe it will) you'll have been there from a very early point, meaning you have very rare items (at least by AQW standards, in which the older, the rarer).

Mount and Blade Warband is quite possibly one of the best games of it's genre. Despite being somewhat aged, the modding community is still active and you'll be able to find your pick of game changing mods that range from adding a couple tweaks to diplomacy and battles all the way to ones that turn the game into feudal Japan or even Star Wars.
The combat, which is where a large chunk of the game is, is exciting and takes skill. While fairly basic in nature, move your mouse in the direction you want to swing or block, you will often engage in intense one on one duals, where even a slight mistep will mean your death, in multiplayer as you clash swords with the opposing faction.
The game does have a fair share of issues though. One such being the combat AI for NPCs. I often find that in battle the AI will only do one of two things; hold their ground and wait for you to come to them or charge you. In no way shape or form has the AI ever attempted to do anything other than those two basic options and so combat can become boring in the late game when you amass a larger force.
Another issue with combat AI is that the soldiers will often clump up in huge piles and attack one specific enemy, ignoring the cavalry that might be attacking them from behind.
Although the multiplayer is where the game shines the most and I would suggest getting the Napoleonic Wars expansion just for that purpose. Huge sieges will be fought as waves of infantry will charge a wall, dodging artillery fire as the sound of drums and pipes spurs them one from the musician classes. Line battles will occur where organized groups of sometimes over 300 players will join a server and fight more proper and historical battles.
Mount and Blade Warband is a great game if, for nothing else, it's mulitplayer

This is my first review on steam. But we all start at some point ... :-)
Btw, English is not my mother tongue (but German), but to have a global reachout I decided not to do "German first".
I bought SH5 nearly a week ago and after about 10-12 hrs of playing I am already bored and disappointed.
Also pointing out that I am playing hardly more than 2 hrs a day overall.
First some pros:
Good atmospherte overall. The languages in speaking and subtitlles (German/English ) do not match always exactly, but its good enough for me. The U-Boat does perform as I was used to it in SH3 and the different settings allow for pro players (doing the math) and amateur Captains as well (simply aim the target, give some orders).
A good feature was done by assigning points to the crew. Guess that pays off in later missions.
Now some cons:
There is an intro but overall you are guessing what to do. Not the navigation or attack, but the standard navy procedures.
When do shallö use the radio? What orders shall be given in which order to do it properly?
As I did not serve the navy (doing my time in the army) I am not familiar with that but basic military knowledge telles me that there are some procedures for every step you to :-)
The missions are quite strange. (I admit I stopped early, so maybe I miss something her). You are ordered to sink specific
tonnage or ships but even if you do so in many cases I wondered why it did not count.
I ended up ignoring the mission orders and huntng as I seemed appropriate.
Also strange that you need to walk to each station to give orders yourself. I expected that you should be able to give orders more easy.
And finally - although most ships do show the battle scars afetr being hit by torpedo or gunfire, the big ones dont. (transporters, carriers), or I simply have a bad hardware.
Overall I would not recommend to buy that game now. Maybe some bugs might be fixed in the short term, but as long as mission controls and order controls are not clear this is justr giving you frustration.

Are you tired of horror games being "wait in a locker for a guy to pass" snoozefests? Look no further; The Evil Within takes horror games back to the high standard of RE4, and even improves on it in many ways.
The gameplay is pretty standard stuff, but with some great innovations. For starters, enemies have ALOT of health; and will typically required to be burned via a limited number of matches you carry to finish off. This leads to alot of tactics, as you can burn multiple enemies if they are all down by eachother. Another cool twist is the 'crit" chance, which gives every headshot a chance to proc  'crit" resulting in a super juicy head explosion. This is INCREDIBLY satisfying not only because of the fantastic audio visual feedback, but having a super tough enemy die from a single, random headshot in a potentially life threatening situation feels like the epitome of survival horror.
Another key twist is the bolt crafting. Very early on you will find a "Agony bow" that can fire many different types of bolts from standard to rediclous; harpoons, explosive bolts, even ice bolts, which can all be crafted on the fly with parts you accumulate from disarming traps. It adds a whole layer of strategy; do you disarm a bomb to craft an arrow, or leave the trap to shoot when an enemy goes by?
Stealth is also a viable option in most cases. Bottles can be thrown for a distraction ,and sneaking up on an enemy will allow you an instant kill headstab. It just really adds a great feeling of survival; A typical scenario being "ok theres a bunch of guys up ahead, how many can I sneak kill to save ammo?" getting spotted of course isnt game over, but will surely cost you some ammo. Hiding in lockers and under beds is also an option.. but honestly seems a shoo in to appeal to the more gimmicky horror games of late.
The story is a trip, but not one id honestly say is a highlight. Most of it is just mindtrip nonsense (intentionally) and when it does start to make some sort of sense its very late in the game, and by that time its just kind of like "oh". All thats really important to know about the story is that Its going to be mindf*ck nonsense which honestly is just an excuse to put you in the scariest places in-humanely possible.
The graphics look nice... but dated, and it unfortunetly has a myriad of strange technical issues; Id summarize the graphic performance as "rough". The aspect ratio can be adjusted and the framerate cap removed, but I found messing with the aspect ratio bugged some things out (blood on screen effects will stick to default aspect ratio bounds). Besides the blunders it does have some very nice lighting, and the best use of film grain ive ever seen in a game.

The overal aestetic however is great, and truly calls to horror game's finest. Plenty of rusty enviorments harkening to Silent Hill, deserted subways and towns, even a bizzare medieval castle/dungeon. Even with how dark most of them are they all stand out and feel distinct.
The audio is fantastic; from the screaming of the zombies burning to a toast to the haunting melody of the safehouse, there really isnt anything bad to say about it. (Extra points for the super satisfying sounding headshots!)
Overall, Id say the Evil Within is a worthy Shinji Mikami game, and a true marriage of classic survival horror games that ironically "breaks the mold" of horror games being made these days. Try to brace the somewhat shoddy visual and technical issues and you will not be dissapointed.

Hydrophobia: Prophecy is a typical adventure game, with lots of innovative uses of water. At its core, the gameplay is similar to other games in the genre, but the game uses its setting and environment to its advantage. The result is an interesting game and experience as players navigate through water filled environments.
The game is set on a floating city, which is attacked by terrorists who take control of the entire place. Kate, a systems engineer, gets involved in the mess and has to escape to safety, fighting the terrorists along the way. The story for this game is quite linear and not exactly an amazing story. There are a few good lines by the characters though to break up the flow of the story a bit. In addition to the linear story are optional objects and documents in the world, which provide additional backstory and perspectives on the characters and events. With a decent story to keep players interested in the game, it functions well enough to fit the main gameplay attractions in and provide a bit of depth to those interested in reading up about the world.
For the most part, gameplay consists of getting to certain objectives on the map using a single route. Getting to these places is done by some platforming, climbing, or swimming. There are tools that are unlocked later on, which are a scanner and a firearm. In addition to getting to places on the map, there are also some puzzles that need to be completed to go on to the next area. The gameplay is honestly a bit on the simple side with these mechanics being pretty basic, but it’s serviceable to play through. The biggest part of the game is the water as the title suggests. Due to the water’s realistic nature in this game, it has a major impact in how players have to work with and use water to their advantage. Opening a flooded door sends water rushing in, which fills up the room with water to swim in. This water feature can play a huge role in firefights, as the battles shift to fighting underwater in flooded rooms. Littered around the map are various objects to collect, which can be collected for achievements. These objects make the game focused more on exploration for players that try to soak up their surroundings and find things around the world. It makes for a nicer experience to step back and see what hidden things were placed around and to try and find them. The simple adventure gameplay might be off-putting for those wanting something more complex, but the usage of water is done in a great way that makes the game play and feel unique.
The setting is a floating city in the near future. On the whole, the game uses a realistic style, though at times the graphics do look a bit dated. The water looks amazing though, with some of the best water visuals around. The developers really nailed getting the water to both look and flow in a realistic manner. Since the water is such a major component of the game, it’s good that the water effects are very appealing when playing and interacting with it.
Alongside the realism focused graphics is the soundtrack. The music for this game is comprised of both traditional and electronic instruments. It’s nothing particularly distinct, though it does help that the music is dynamic based on ingame events and helps to give cues on what’s going on. Overall it’s the water graphics that shine the most, with the other content looking good enough to make a fine game.
Hydrophobia has some standard adventure gameplay and a straightforward plot, but the usage of water does make things interesting. The short length and typical story and gameplay might not be wanted by some. For those wanting a short game that is simple to pick up and play and has some awesome use of water, Hydrophobia is a good game in that regard.

I have been excitedly waiting for this game to be released for months and I must say that it did not disappoint. There was so much more detail and depth compared to the first game and the stories were unique to each individual character. The soundtrack is just so beautiful and enhances the experience immensely; Christopher Escalante did a truly wonderful job on it. I have played through all of the routes and, while I enjoyed some more than others, I thought that they were all exceptionally done.
My favourite routes were definitely Erik's and Sam’s while my least favourite was Damien's. Damien's route was still well done, but personally I found his story to be a little too redundant. Additionally, I found Diana's route to be too short and thought her story should have been expanded and delved into a little more. I also really did not like the 'wives'. They had absolutely no significance to the story and were seemingly only there to spout a few throw away lines every now and then. I'm not against the other boys being married, but I feel a mention would have been sufficient.
There were quite a few grammatical errors and a few instances where the spoken dialogue did not match with the written dialogue. It did not detract from my enjoyment of the game though so I was able to overlook them for the most part. What did bother me a bit were some of the endings. The dialogue for some of the endings are not accurate when it comes to the fate of certain characters. Hopefully this will be rectified in an update at some point in time.
Overall, I would absolutely recommend this game. I really liked the first Seduce Me game but I would venture to say that I love Seduce Me 2. I am so pleased that it was able to live up to, if not exceed, my expectations.

First of all, it's hard to justify recommending this game despite how much I've enjoyed it because this game is very exclusive to the US region.
Statistically, the game lobby lists ~70% as US games, the rest mostly EU. Asian players make up <5% of the 300-500 active players during peak hours.
I have seen too many players buy the game and give up quickly because they have no one to play with, which was one of the reason I created a steam group for our region and remained active for quite a while.
The game itself is extremely fun and challenging. The survival of the players depend heavily on team cohesiveness and communication which adds another layer of enjoyment. It can get overwhelming and frustrating in pick up groups without this layer for the loner player.
Due to the reserved culture/nature of Asian players, initiatively opening up to players through VOIP is not common, hence the game doesn't thrive in our region.
The game failed to establish a foothold outside of US and EU. No point wasting money to buy since the game is dead in Asia/SEA region.

It's not always an issue, and if you're the host, you'll be fine if you're connection is stable.
Otherwise
The game itself is great! The gameplay feels amazing and the weapons have nice feedback. You can feel the force of the hammer or greatsword as it hits. Killing rat men is terrifying and fun at the same time, and the game is always tense. I think it's safe to say that NO run will be a walk in the park, even on easy difficulty, and if you don't coordinate at least a bit, you'll most likely fail a run. BUT this also scares the COD kids away and what you're mostly left with is a pretty good community of people who don't♥♥♥♥♥♥around. You'll get the occasional guy who just runs through and gets killed alone, but it's rare.
The enemies are varried and always fun. The earth quaking after a Rat Ogre appears is so damn terrifying, and the same goes for the appearance of a gutter runner and the hook rat (can't remember it's name). You just instinctively want to run the hell out of there, but again, the best thing is to stick together at all times and cooperate.
The item system is also really well done, but can feel slow since you only get 1 item per run, and at easier difficulties, the dice will most likely just give you another common quality item. Forging items to get better quality items requires 5 of the same quality, and unless the items are all the same type, you'll get something random. It's still all very well implemented but just feels slow at times.
It's the most grim, terrifying, satisfying, and tense game that encourages people to help each other and work cooperatively. Work as a group and you'll have a hell of a great time!
