Before the actual review.
The devs finally added framerate cap and letterboxing options. Enabling console doesn't prevent you from getting achievements anymore. While these options should've been there from the beginning it's nice to see that these issues have been addressed.
Actual review.
I'll keep it semi-short, I don't want it to be bloated. Story spoiler-free.
Short introductions.
The Evil Within (TEW) is an oldschool survivor horror game with semi-tanky controls. If you'd ask me which games does TEW remind me of then I'd say Silent Hill, Resident Evil 4, Outlast and Alone in the Dark. If you ever played any Silent Hill title then you'll notice the familiar dirty, rust and blood covered dilapidated locations, scary mental hospital with beds and wheelchairs all over the place. The game is medium paced, which is good and bad at the same time. It's good because it doesn't get boring. it's bad because it decreases the horror factor. Puzzles are there, but really scarce and simple.
The visuals.
The game has some really nice lighting, reflections, shaders, particles, post processing effects and dynamic shadows. Depth of field and film grain make a really good combo here and add a lot to the experience. The locations are well made, a lot of attention to the detail, even though there are some cheap visual solutions (like 2D rock textures on water). The polygon count on most of the objects is medium, texture quality is mediocre at best. The worst textures I've noticed were the beginning (the city) and mostly rubble, no notable HD textures. City destruction is nicely looking, but is entirely scripted. Most of the animations are smooth, jerky ones have been fixed in the first patch.
The enemy types.
This contains some partial spoilers. Throughout the game you'll be greeted with different types of zombies (Haunted) and their sub-mutations. Just like in Resident Evil 4 you stumble upon angry villagers. Some of them will attack you with bare hands, some of them use torches, knives, hammers, sickles, molotovs and even crossbow, guns and sniper rifles. Notable mutations: invisible zombies (barely visible, fully visible on hit), two headed monsters with a surprise (AlterEgo). There are also mini-bosses and actual bosses.
The combat, mechanics and AI.
Many people mentioned that it's like RE4 on steroids. Semi-tanky controls, you can't dodge or counter. If you get hit you're usually given time to recover and fall back. Unless it's an instakill attack. Oh yes, there are plenty of enemies in this game that can instantly kill you. But unlike in RE4 you can actually move while you aim and now you have the option to use stealth.
You can sprint (uses stamina), run and duckwalk. You can't shoot while you're duckwalking as it's meant for stealth kills (you sneak up behind enemies) and trap disarms. There are two types of traps: hidden ones that can be simply disarmed by holding the button (bear traps, string triggered dynamite, etc) and more obvious, but dangerous sticky bombs. You disarm them by pressing the button at the right time, otherwise it explodes. Each trap gives you crafting material. Check weapons sections for more about that. If you accidentally activate a trap then you can expect: small to high health loss or instant death.
The game has RPG elements. Throughout the game you'll find green gel (that is used to upgrade various physical abilities and even weapon effects), ammo, materials, collectibles and matches. There's health regeneration. If your health drops below ~20HP then you'll be unable to sprint, but you're able to recover it back just by standing. Your melee consists of slapping and kicking enemies. Useful for finishing off or pushing away zombie type enemies, but generally not recommended for more serious enemies. Stamina bar enables you to sprint. The default sprint time is around 3 seconds and when stamina is below 30% you slow down to usual speed. If it reaches 0 then you stop completely and catch your breath (completely vulnerable).
You can upgrade your ammo capacity and weapon efficiency (damage, fire rate, reload times, accuracy, clip size, etc).
Stealth is a nice addition (works only on Haunted). You sneak behind the enemies and instantly kill them. This works in following scenarios: a) the enemy is standing in one place; b) the enemy is patrolling back and forth. You have a lantern which is your own source of light. It really helps to see where are you going, makes you clearly see the traps but also gives away your position to the enemies. Making loud noises (slam open a door) also can catch enemy attention. Knowing that you can use glass bottles to either distract them or stun them by throwing the bottle against their head (after that you're given time to stealth kill them). Stealth killing is a nice way to conserve ammo and if you have the chance to do so - go for it. If you get spotted then you can deal with them the usual way.
Enemy attack patterns are worth a mention. Most simple ones are punches (or swings with the weapons), kicks and dash attacks. Dash attacks of melee zombies are quite dangerous as they go into berserk mode and try to hit at least 3 times. Crossbow/gun enemies usually take time to aim at you and then shoot. Sniper rifle enemies hide behind cover and then take their time to shoot at you. Shooting a zombie in the knee usually makes them fall. All of the enemies are weak against fire. if you have matches then you can burn corpses (REmake style), hay or even downed still alive enemies (hence shooting in the knee). Igniting something will set on fire all nearby enemies. You'll stumble upon plenty of corpses throughout the game, some of them can be used to ignite other enemies. Some of them can become alive depending on your actions (so it may be wise to burn some before you pick up an item or activate a mechanism).
The enemy AI is also mediocre and could've been better. As soon as they spot you they'll start moving or running towards you. Detection sometimes fails and they spot you when you're behind them, crouching. Sometimes they might get stuck, run in circles or simply charge at you and end up running against the wall. I've also seen some weird patrol patterns. Like I mentioned before loud noises alert them (be it doors or you stepping in a trap). To avoid direct confrontation you can either hide in closets or below beds and tables or use the traps against them. Most notable con is the big amount of enemy invulnerability frames (you shoot, but they don't react / take no damage).
In some chapters you'll stumble upon your partner. Shouldn't be too problematic as you can heal your partner by just standing next to 'im and holding a button. No need to share your ammo either.
Weapons.
Semi-traditional Resident Evil layout. Handgun (revolver), shotgun, crossbow (with different bolts), sniper rifle, magnum, rocket launcher. Most are upgradable, crossbow is worth a special mention. You find different bolt types for it, after that you can craft them from materials gathered from the levels and traps. Bolt types: harpoon, proximity explosives, flashbang, electric shock, freeze and DLC ones. Useful in combination with other weapons.
Due to character limit I'll have to wrap it up aka tl;dr version.
TEW offers a nice oldschool survivor horror experience, the locations and atmosphere are nice, but it's far from perfect either. Some chapters are more action centered and the game becomes zombie slaying action game (like Resident Evil 4 Chapter 5 island parts). I don't think that arena style battles (especially against enemies with weapons) was a good idea either. There are cheap deaths, especially in escape sequences, but in the end even with all its flaws I would recommend the game as it's entertaining and fun to play.

Okay, first, let me say that it is (as far as I can remember) my first public review, so excuse any formatting, or coherence errors I may have made during the writing process. The reason I decideed to voice my opinion is that, as the numerous posts in the forum indicate, there is an unreasonable (yes, unreasonable) amount of hate surrounding this title, and I wanted to create a completely unbiased review, with the (perhaps too ambitious) desire that some people may read this first, instead of all the not-very-constructive whining, and decide based on facts. So here we go:
I had been waiting for this title since it has first been announced. Therefore, saying that I'm biased, would be reasonable, so let me just say that I'm very much aware of its faults. Let's get the technical stuff out of the way first, so that I can focus on gameplay, story, and more relevant stuff more. While the 30 fps cap is admittedly substandard in modern gaming (and I don't want to defend it by appealing to console standards, I never had a console) and it is true that the developers should have paid more attention to making it  a matter of preference, it is by no means detrimental to the enjoyment of the game. If you are one of those people who get vertigo/nausea etc. easily, you should avoid it though. Basically, if you unlock the fps with the launch parameter, then use Afterburner to limit it to 40, you will get a remarkably consistant framerate, with no drops, stutter, etc. even on a 2 generations old GPU (660). One potential counterargument may be, that end users should not be bothered to use console commands, etc. While this argument has some merit, I personally believe that the defining advantage of PCs over consoles, is their wide area of application. If you own a PC, you should not be so lazy that using a console command is beyond your comfort zone, period. Even if you have "standards and principles". Let console owners use pre-defined settings.
Second, the issue of black bars: while they are certainly disturbing on some occassions, I found myself getting used to them in about an hour, and since then, I barely notice them during gameplay, except some cinematic moments when I think to myself: "Wow, that looks like a movie". I'm saying this despite the fact that when I first heard about the supposed "conceptual reasons" behind their implementation, the first thing running through my mind was "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t". In practice, it works fairly well to create a cinematic atmosphere. As a disclaimer, I do admit that they should have made it an optional feature, for people using screens with different aspect ratios, but on a 16:9 screen (which the vast majority of gamers use) it is perfectly serviceable.
Third, the engine: I am one of the people who hate ID5 more than the plague, since (at least for me) both rage and wolfenstein14 were unplayable, with copious amounts of texture pop-in being omnipresent. TEW however, was a pleasant disappointment in the engine. Texture pops are still present, and the texture quality is below what some modern games (BF4, crysis, etc) have been treating us to, but the megatexturing allows for the use of highly detailed, beautiful environments, are despite the recommended settings, it is actually rather tame, as minimum req goes.
As gameplay goes, the game signals a return to the oldschool survival horror era, and some sections reminded me of the best moments in Silent Hill 2/3, and resident evil 4. The only disadvantage I can think of is that towards the end, the action sequences become more abundant, but I think this is excusable.
Storywise, things are less shiny. While I find the story interesting, and there are many subtle hints and references (Again, in the vein of SH) I still have pretty much no clue about the bigger picture, and I'm almost at the end. I have to say though, that I'm very much interested in the outcome, and even though it is not extremely complex, the story keeps me hooked.
Overall, the game reminded me of Alan Wake (which I love to pieces), the SH series, Dead Space 1, RE4, and amnesia on numerous occassions. Of course, it is not only the positive parts of said games that gets adopted, for example I found the parts where I get a follower somewhat forced, and not true to the roots of survival horror. These sections are in the minority though.
Overall, I firmly believe that the technical issues people are complaining about, while do exist, and some of them may be considered fairly serious from a programming standpoint, are not severe enough to negatively impact the enjoyment of the game if one has an open mindset, and loves horror games. This game is a remarkable representative of a (unfortunately) dying genre, and although it also attempts to appeal at modern audiences (action sequences, etc.) at its core, it is very much a traditional survival horror game. The bottomline is, if the abovementioned cons are enough to discourage you, do not buy it, or wait for some mods, patches. On the other hand, if you have an open mind, can tolerate some technical shortcomings, and have the money to spare, think no further, you will enjoy the hell out of it.
My score: 9/10 (I would give it a 10/10, since I personally love it, but I wanted to be as objective as possible, and there definitely are some weak points)

Hotline Miami 2 takes things a step further in this sequel to the successfully brutal, bloody top-down action shooter of crazy-aimbotting enemy AIs who have the reaction time of a zebra on steroids and psychotic junkies who eat pizzas everyday yet have the killing skills better than an elite black ops soldier.
Whereas the first game was rather simple in scope, mostly revolving around the main character Jacket, Hotline Miami 2 features a diverse cast of characters that stretches throughout the story.
It may have turned out to be too amibtious, as the story immediately gets convoluted with a
frequent change in setting, time period and characters. Even halfway in the game, I still
barely understood what the ♥♥♥♥ the story was about. Or I guess that also has to do with the fact that I just didnt care much about the story.
The music is just great but hardly anything that stands out. It aptly accomodates the whacked atmosphere of the game.
The 'scenes', the actual gameplay, is what makes HLM1 so exceptional. In HLM2, the devs decided to take a different spin on the action, all of which has only impeded the game's quality.
Perhaps one of the most noticeable change here is the significantly more open level design.
Numerous enemies patrol large open spaces that make you one big walking target for them.
To assist the player, the game gives you ability to look beyond your FOV. Seems useful, but not
when enemies have an eagle vision even wider than yours. It's easy to get killed out of nowhere
when enemies can spot and snipe you, even when completely out of your screen's expanded view.
How can you even scan across your environemnt 360 to ensure complete safety while also shooting enemies in front of you? You can't.
Most annoying in the enitre game is the utter lack of customisation given to players.
Controls are not quite as fluid and hindered by unresponsiveness and inconsistency.
Want to try executing that guy lying helplessly on the floor? *presses spacebar, yet nothing happens.
Press again after 2 more tries, the player finally goes for the execution too late as another enemy comes and whacks you dead.
Want to pick up that handy baseball bat lying right below your feet? Nope, the game makes you pick up this useless gun without ammo lying nearby instead.
Run out of ammo and need that fresh new machinegun over there? Nope, the game makes you pick up some puny knife instead.
I don't know how the devs even thought it was a good idea to limit the controls so much, they even have the key binding for executions being the same key for the Corey's Dodge/Roll key binding (which btw is a very useless ability).
And the crosshair...the crosshair...it's annoying as ♥♥♥♥ to deal with.
The devs have stubbornly chose to keep the crosshair white, a color suitable for some levels, not for others. In bright levels like Stronghold, the crosshair near completely camofladges with the background, making it extremely frustrating trying to play through the level.
Simply offering some crosshair customisation option would have fixed this nicely. Again, the devs didnt bother.
You know what else they didnt bother? No brightness setting, no gamma setting, no video settings at all. Howdo hoo, whereas all other games out there would offer at least these crucial settings, the only thing this game allows you to customize is its very, very limited controls.

This proves in the final Act 6 level Catastrophe, where Dennaton once again thinks it'd be 'challenging' to make a level so ♥♥♥♥ing dark, enemies like the black dogs and large black thugs are almost invisible to the naked eye yet are able to spot you from afar like it's in f***king daytime.
It doesnt help that I dont have that good of an eyesight, the lack of any gamma setting simply made me falling prey to such a disadvantage.
It doesnt matter how good the player's skill is, if you cant even see the ♥♥♥♥ing crosshair or the enemies, that's just extremely BS game design.
Furthermore disappointing is the removal of several masks from the original game, all for the sake of the story.
In fact for most of the levels, you dont even play with a mask. This all depends on the characters
you are forced to play as. Playing as 'The Fans' give you the most options on picking masks but
for all other levels, you're pretty much forced to play by the set rules.
In Hotline Miami 2, Dennaton Games tried aiming high on target but instead hits all places wrong.
Being quite a fan since the first game, having played to the fullest and achieved plenty of A grades and even S grades, this wonderful sequel has only managed to turn my initial enthusiasm into regret and dismay.

With its unpredictably bad and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥lazy level design, unfixed bugs and glitches of enemies clipping and utter crap controls and options available, HM2 has made it more of a huge annoyance to  get through than a game to enjoy anymore.
+ Music is the same great list of soundtracks.
+ A more ambitious story
- Sh****t open level design
- Controls are unresponsive and badly implemented
- Lack of choices, lack of masks
- Intentional lighting issues of some levels being too bright, others being way too dark
- - Too unpolished and rushed, with too many bugs and clipping issues in levels

Let me start off by saying I was a huge 40k fan before TET Vermintide, and still am; however, this game was one of the reasons I started diving more into fantasy.
The Game is a Left4Dead style co-op experience where you play as either a Soldier of the Empire, a Witchhunter, a Dwarf, an Elf, or a Witch battling hordes of ratmen known as skaven. The campaign takes place durring "The End Times", where basically the forces of Chaos are moving to wipe out all life. Though much of the talk around Games Workshop's End Times story is hated by hardcore warhammer fans, Fat Shark does an excellent job capturing what one owuld think the end times would truely be like. As the campaign progressed, the sense of grim darkness and dispair thickens.
The Combat is excellent, incorperating the base Left4Dead style formula of enemies, with a few major improvements which make gameplay mroe dymanic and less repetitive. There are the standard ratmen who will charge you and kill you like undisciplined banshees and are extremely easy to kill, and there are 'Specials' which have unique abilities that can be a real problem to handle in crowded situations.
Vermintide incorperates a refreshing melee combat I haven't yet seen in, what is for all intensive purposes, a game produced by a small developer. Enemies are extremely reactive to hits, and will realistically move and dismember according to where you stab, slash, or shoot them. The AI is also relatively smart (when it isnt bugging). The lesser skaven will move to surround you in open areas while specials try to sit back and hit you from afar, only moving to grab and obduct you if you stray too far from the group.
Weapons are earned through a chance based 'Loot' System, where players can roll dice at the end of the round, the better the roll, the better tier the loot. Players can also collect items such as tomes or grims and occasionally loot die to increase their odds of better loot at the end of each level or round, but at the cost of less max health or not being able to carry as much equiptment.
Bugging is a problem, one that I know the devs are actively fixing. Enemy AI sometimes gets stuck or will run in place. This is especially problematic with events such as 'patrols', where entire packs of armored units might get stuck looping in a building, and you are forced to engage them to progress, where as normally you could just hide to let them pass. The game also has balancing issues for weapons. The current problem is Red "Veteran" Tier items having poor traits upon aquisition (added special bonus effects to the weapon), and the staffs for the witch are all underpowered. Other issues with the game include the ability to find any lobbies to play a game you want. On easier difficulties it is relatively easy to find matched with other players on almost any map, but as the difficulty gets harder, hardly anyone plays and it is relatively impossible to find cataclysm difficulty matches on any map, even Horn of Magnus.
All in all this game is worth the but desipte its current bugs. I encourage community members to purchase it, if nothing else: to try it out. I was suprised that it was as good as it was.
Pros:
- Good AI (When it's working properly)
- Loot system, no Pay to win.
- Graphics
- Melee combat system
- Lots of content
Cons:
- Frequent bugs
- Balancing issues
- Not alot of players
- The End Times

Vermintide, on its surface, is "Left 4 Dead with rats". While in a general sense that may be true, Vermintide is much more. With fast-paced, very difficult action, a rewarding loot/crafting system, excellent visuals, subtle yet engaging characters, and a terrific setting, Vermintide isn't just "Left 4 Dead with rats". I'll say it; it's better than Left 4 Dead.

The left4dead with rats comparison would be accurate, if left4dead had a simple yet engaging melee combat system with a large variety of ranged and combat weapons that had interesting abilities and changed play style allowing for plenty of hours of fun. The visuals are also very nice and enemies are easily distinguished which is important in the game because there's a good variety of enemy types.
Progression in the game is good enough to keep you wanting play and the different grades of weapons means that you want to keep playing in order to find out what interesting and unique items you'll get.
There's 13 maps in the campaign mode with 5 difficulty levels so all ability types are covered. Finding games is easy enough but the way your rewards scale based on difficultly could mean that later on the community has moved up to the top 2 difficulties and new players would have trouble finding games.
Atmosphere in the game is absolutely great. The sound design is immersive and you'll use it in game to find out what's happening in the level.  It runs worse on ADM processors but don't let that put you off buying the game.
All the heroes play in their own way but some have 'shared' weapons, for example the witch hunter and Empire soldier both have two handed swords because some heroes deal damage and others are more crowd control, allowing you to play in different ways.
At the end of the day it's a good game well worth buying. The devs are also continuing to support the game with updates and some future DLC, so it's not going to drop off the face of the earth anytime soon.

Reminds me of a a hack and slash (mostly) L4D2 hoard style, team objective game with the added bonus of character progression in the form of a unique rng based loot reward system and additional player mechanics including the ability to dodge and block.

BLESS THIS RAVAGED BODY
-Vermintide is Left 4 Dead set in the Warhammer universe. Using melee weapons, guns, and bows, your party of four has to carve a path through rat-men to various objectives. At the end of each mission you roll a series of dice to gain new items. Like Left 4 Dead, story is conveyed entirely through the remarks each character makes to one another.
-First person melee combat is very difficult to pull off, but Vermintide does it well. Each hit feels like it makes and impact and the block and shove techniques at a lot of depth to your confrontations. If you enter the game hacking and slashing without thought, you won't survive long in further difficulties.
-Mostly you'll be fighting rat minions, but every so often a special enemy appears (again, like Left 4 Dead). The typical bunch will pounce on you and force your team to help you out, but others require other tactics. The ratling gunner, for example, will lay down suppressing fire on whoever takes the most agro. Using someone else as bait, the other teammates have to take advantage of the gunner being distracted. Most of the specials are copies of the Left 4 Dead types, but there are a few twists that make them a lot more fun to face. While in Left 4 Dead they are more of an annoyance, Vermintide presents them more as cooperative challenges.
-Graphics are also quite good. It takes a powerful machine to run it on the higher settings, but even on the lowest quality it is still a good looking game. That, and the game take the gloomy aesthetics from the Warhammer tabletop (and it works surprisingly well). While most of the environments seem to be darkened streets and abandoned fortresses, it's still enjoyable to work your way through them and discover all the secret areas.
-The loot system randomly generates a weapon or trinket at the end of a level. Unfortunately, these rolls are not specific to the character you're playing. Most of the time you'll get a weapon that belongs to one of the other classes. This encourages you to switch around and play everyone, but a lot of times you have to choose your character based on which one isn't taken in a party. It'd be much less of a grind if you could specifically roll for a character. They've added some measures to prevent this, but you can't get into it until you have a collection of weapons that you are comfortable with salvaging for materials. Overall, the loot system could be a lot better. It encourages grinding and exploiting maps in order to get the best rolls, which is very unfortunate.
FINAL VERDICT
-Overall, I'll say this is a better game than Left 4 Dead. The maps aren't incredibly varied, but the combat is enjoyable enough for me to get over that. The enemies and the setting are much more appealing for players who enjoy fantasy rather than typical zombies. It's cheap for the amount of content you get. Even if you decided to just play through all the levels once and be done with it, I would consider Vermintide a worthy purchase. Get some friends and you'll have a lot of fun killing Skaven with one of the best melee systems on the market.

This is actually my first review, but I feel like this game definitely warrants one. While the price tag is a little hefty, the gameplay is well worth it (assuming your computer can handle it). This game is a Minecraft meets Beseige open world creative game that is just in it's birth. I've logged only a few hours and have already made a secret hidden lab similar to Breaking Bad that transforms into a quaint house. And did I mention the whole thing can drive away? But here's what I like and didn't like about the game.
Pros:
Scrolling placement with blocks (not one by one like Minecraft)
Custom vehicles that work regardless of skill or engineering knowledge
Beautifully laid out handbook to help you in any aspect of the game
Beautiful graphics for being cartoon-esque
Plenty of item for such a new game
Infinite possibilities. Your imagination is your only limitation
Hints at what is going to be coming in future updates like farming
Almost feels like a puzzle game at times but really rewarding when contraptions work
Cons:
Controls are a little finicky at times, just experiment with sensitivity and find a comfortable setting
Mistakes are costly. Very little forgiveness with deleting and replacing parts. Whole limbs of vehicles fall off and can't be reassembled.
Controls sometimes feel like you're driving a boat.
Creative mode needs a fly feature
Overall, I 100% recommend this game if you like Minecraft or Beseige. This is a happy medium with less destruction. The game is not 100% complete yet, but there is obvious attention to future updates. The base game right now if still incredibly fun. Make sure your computer can handle it, then click the buy button because you won't regret it.
Hopefully this helps!

First of all, i want to say that i love the game. Once you're actually playing it, with friends or strangers, it's an absolute blast. When i'm at work i think about the game and want to go home and play it, and a game like that is pretty rare to come by nowadays. So for the actual game play it's 10/10, I f*cking love it.
But what don't i like? Literally everything else.
There is no/barely any single player. You can't race the AI so if you want to play the standard online game modes by yourself you're going to have to play a local game and make it so you're playing with the controler, and the other player are using the keyboard. Then you can play 2/3 game modes by yourself in a sort of practice mode were on the other payer (your keyboard) simply drops the pieces into the abyss until you win. So you don't have a controller then you’ll never play the “practice modes”
But that is not single player, that's simply Local Battle.
If you chose single player you're presented with two options, Trials or Endless.
In trials you race to complete the game modes with special challenges. But often these trials are unfair and not very fun, but they work in themselves as trials. So in the end i can't really complain, but it's by far not what you want when you want to play single player.
The second option is Endless, where you play the Survival game mode on the special mode and compete with other players who can get the most blocks down. Your score is saved on the global leaderboards. Now Endless is not too bad, since is it basicly the closets the game offers to a practice/single player mode. But if you want to compete on the leaderboards you're going to have a bad time. Because every game has randomized negative powers used against you, and some are inherently not as bad as others. I've had runs were i've gotten high scores simply because the powers that were used against be were not as severe as other games where i've barely gotten a fifth of my all time high because i was f*cked over by the negative powers within the first few waves. So in the end endless is the best single player game mode, but not competitive at all, or at least not fair.
Well now we got the single player game modes done with, now to go on the the f*cking disaster that is the online battles.
Again a want to clarify, once you actually get into multiplayer and do a propper battle against friends or strangers, its absolute great fun, the most fun i've had in video games in a long time. But the process of getting in a battle is an absolute mess.
When you enter multiplayer you're greeted with 2 options, "Finds match", and "Play with friends". What's the difference between those lobby types? Absolute NONE. If you select private lobby, i.e. "Play with friends", it's not actually private and anyone can still join, the only difference between the two lobby types is that the "Play with friends" lobby has an invite button. But if you make a regular lobby you can still invite people manually with the Shift+Tab menu.
"Play with friends" (i.e. private lobbies) are not private what so ever and anyone can still join.
So imagine this scenario. I host a private lobby for me and my mates. I join and so does my 2 other mates, but then a stranger joins and therefore fill the lobby so my 3rd mate can join. In any other game it would be a simple measure of just kicking them, and if they still join back, just ban them. Guess what? No kick/ban option. Once someone is in your lobby you can't get them out. The only way to make someone leave is to create a new lobby and hope they don't join it before your friends.
So you might think, why not just ask them to leave? No in game chat. No text chat or quick chat or anything. There is literally no way for one player to communicate with another player what so ever. If you need to speak to another play your ONLY options is to add them on steam and chat with them there. And if they don't add you, you're f*cked.
So now you might think "oh how very rude of that guy to join your private lobby" and the worst part is, there is no way for him to know what he was even doing.
Let me explain how to join a multiplayer game in Tricky Towers.
In the lobby creation screen, as i explain earlier, there are 2 options, "Find match" or "Play with friends". So to find a game you select "Find match" and then your game mode, but if you just want to find any match you have to select the gamemode random and hope there are any matches hosted. Why must you hope? Because there is LITERALLY NO indication anywhere of what games are hosted on. It doesn't tell you what lobbies are open, it doesn't tell you if they are private or not. It doesn't give you a list or anything.
So if you select random and it just puts you in an empty lobby, you're just going to have to assume that there are no lobbies hosted. And even if you join a lobby it doesn't say anywhere what kind of lobby it is, just the game mode. Last night i tried finding a game. Which i did luckily enough. But as soon as i joined the host left, why did he do that? I thought and searched for a new game just to be put into another game with the same host. This time he didn't leave and a 3rd player join and we were ready to start the game i thought and readied up. Now 5 minutes pass and suddenly the host adds me on steam just the explain that it was a private lobby and he tried to play with his mate.
But how could i have known? The game never told be it was a private lobby, nor could he kick me or tell me this ingame.
Oh and one last thing, once you have a lobby running with your mates, you can't switch game modes. If you want to change any gamemode, or even the settings of the lobby, everyone has to back out and the host has to recreate the lobby. It also doesn't show you ping or wins or any other useful information. Oh and also there no match making and the levels aren't clear so when a stranger joins its extremely hard to figure out his skill compared to yours, and even if he's way too good compared to you, there's nothing you can do to kick him.
Right now this review has gone on for far too long so i'll summarize
-No practice mode
-Unbalance challenge mode (endless)
-No Ai battles
-Absolutely terrible matchmaking
-No private lobbies
-No ingame chat
-No kicking abilities
-No switching game modes without having to remake the lobby
-Hard to estimate skill of players
-General lack of useful information
+One of the most fun games i've played in a long time
So even after all these negatives why is this review positive? Because under all of this sh*t there is a great game hidden that is so much fun to play. It's an absolutely awesome game with so much potential it's just that actually getting there and playing that awesome game is so hard.

It is a game about maintenance engineer who gets the points for destroying systems of his ship.
Graphics are good, full voiceover, interesting feature of fluids filling the rooms.
And thats it in general.
I played game with mouse and keyboard [havent seen gamepad tab in options so i guessed it is unavailable - which is not true and probably game runs great on gamepad] and controls are really annoying. Game can have bad visuals, simplistic story and no vioceacting but pristine controls will do the job. Remember first Prince of Persia, or Doom. You start playing and you are the one with the avatar you control. Here you fight with controls to make the character move, climb, jump or dismount the ladder. Mouse sensitivity changes depending if you are in game or in menu or in 3d map or even between scenes - first i adjusted settings in starting room, then it changed when i was in the elevator so i tweaked it again just to revert back when i went out of the elevators shaft.
Gameplay is about runing here and there, following waypoints, doing some basic shoot-and-cover. Bit of climbing with separated buttons to release the grab - like good old crouch wouldnt do the job.
Hacking minigame is really easy but really fresh and well executed in it s simplistic form.
Then comes swimming... and this is disappointing - i thought that maybe other controls are bad because all effort went to hone underwater action. But not. Camera changes angle if you go under or over water which makes you disoriented a lot and causes 'major annoyance' when simple task like swimming forward is impossible because sometimes your heroine emerges over the surface - changing angle of the camera, so you counter, then she submerges but you changed angle so she swims upward, so again automatic change and counter again and again and again and you struggle to just swim forward. Then there are fast-swim-buttons - and to swim fast you press crouch and do dive you press sprint - just to mess with your mind :P. And you can swim fast in many directions... by using many buttons. So if you aim upward, press swim fast forward you will swim fast forward... in global coordinates, not in your current orientation [it means you will swim horizontaly, you wont swim upward].
On top of that water is usually crumpled with floating junk and you cant get the right feeling of enjoying little diving and uderwater sightseeing.
Fire will kill you instantly all of a sudden. You won't get warning that this little flaming desk is lethal, you will come close and die. Just like that. And first you think 'what happened'? but your character wasn't set on fire, didn't have the chance to step back - just come in the area for 1s and died. You can die easily in situation when there is somethink on fire swimming on the water and you just resurfaced close enough. Unnecessary and simply annoying because it doesn't provide any challenge or platforming difficulty - it is just unexpected sudden death in the areas you have to pass by.
But for sure it is not a game that nobody cared to make. Game looks good, works without glitches, water mechanic is quite unique. It s just possible that there were too many technical and art guys making this game and not enough 'game-feel' experts or somebody with clear idea what this game should be about. Or maybe it was about making visually appealing tech demo of fluid mechanic?

The only good thing i've heard come out about this game is it's water effects.
Turns out they were right. It's literally the most impressive thing in the game...

The Good: Ever changing environments makes the maps interesting, the modes included are fun, whimsical graphics, fast paced action, 24 players
The Bad: Everything feels floaty and unbalanced, seeing endless blocks will hurt your eyes after some time, only 4 classes, limited amount of modes, no reward system, shoddy hit detection, no customization of any kind
I normally don’t like Minecraft clones because they are pretty bad, but Ace of Spades looked exciting. The 8-bit style graphics with a Call of Duty multiplayer base seemed exciting, and it is, for maybe the first few matches then it gets boring. Ace of Spades lacks modes and classes which would make this game much better. Hopefully more content is slated for the game, but as it stands it feels very bare bones.
You can pick up to 4 classes which are heavy machine gunner, sniper, assault, and engineer. These are cliché FPS classes and the game really needs more or at least a way to make your own classes. There is no customization to speak of, which is really boring, but what is here is fun for a while. There are a few modes such as Team Deathmatch, Diamond Mine, and Zombies to name a few. I love Team Deathmatch so I went in here first. Playing with up to 24 other players was really fun, I dived in as a machine gunner and started fragging the other team. I soon realized that the spade comes in handy to dig your own fox holes or holes in walls for your sniper rifle. The environment is ever-changing and this is something that can make online fagging really unique and fun. You may run across a building then 5 minutes later it is completely destroyed forcing you to change tactics. I soon realized that you aren’t given a fair enough amount of ammo to start with and ammo drops are very scarce. The sniper rifle has 4 round clips and the reload time is really long, so there are some balancing issues.
I started to see the issues during my first match of Zombies. Players can climb on top of the level (on the edges) and just kill everyone down below. You have to take your blocks and make a floating path up to stop them. I also found you can get lost forever if you start digging in a wall of a level. I spent 4 minutes trying to dig my way out. That isn’t fun at all. This game needs barriers and limits on things to make it a more balanced FPS game.
Once you play around with the four classes and stick with one you will venture off into other modes like Multi-Hill or Demolition. These modes are fun for a while, but after maybe 6-8 hours online you will get pretty bored. The game just feels very stiff and uneventful. There are no rewards for killing anyone (not that they are necessary), but there is no incentive to even go back in after a while. I honestly felt the aiming was a bit off and floaty and you can jump way too high. The art style is nice, but seeing flat blocks everywhere will hurt your eyes after a while, not to mention a lot of people are tired of the Minecraft rip-offs and clones. If the developers spent more time on this game it could really stand out on its own.
As of today the servers are pretty empty. They were really full when I first got the game, but now you’re lucky if you can find one or two full matches. This game has so much potential, but it feels half done. The hit detection doesn’t feel right, the guns don’t feel right, and the lack of classes, modes, and rewards will bore player early on. I recommend waiting for some major updates before purchasing, but if you really want a Minecraft type fragfest then go ahead.
--Score: 7/10

You can probably guess from my Steam name and avatar that I'd probably be interested in a horror/sci-fi game set in icy environs. Unfortunately, this is not the snow-drenched horror game to best Kholat, nor is it even the Lovecraft game to replace the epic shortcomings and bad memories of Dark Corners of the Earth.
Is there potential here? Yes. Definitely. Is it anywhere near even the Early Access stage yet? No. I don't believe so. There is still an awful lot of work to be done to make this anything other than "potentially interesting" and "admittedly atmospheric", the two most positive things I can say about it at this point in time.
Will said work ever get done? That is for the devs to know, and the rest of us to find out. In the meantime, I can't, in all good conscience, recommend this at the preposterous price of twenty dollars when there really isn't a playable game here yet. Hold off a bit longer, and in the meantime we'll all hope this isn't yet another disappointing footnote in the history of Cthulhu-themed video games.
Verdict: 4.5/10.

The framerate thing for which I did not buy the game for a long time seems to be solved, or at least it is playable. The graphics are not great, but hey, most Cthulhu mythos stuff we get is usually low budget, so I can live with this.
2 things however bother me:
The first one is the invisible walls and collision in general. Sometimes I get stuck in a minor obstacle and have to jmp/push/load my way out. Also there are lots of invisible walls which prevent you from exploring, yet it is very unclear what direction you need to go to.
The other thing is narration. I am royally confused what is happening, sometimes short cutscenes come in with no good reason and I did not really get the strory, or what the games wants me to do.
All in all, I only recommend this if you are a HUGE Lovecraft fan, and want to support the devs. You can see that they put effort in it, the atmosphere is somewhat good, but they really must focus on storytelling, as it is one of the core principles of Lovecraftian pieces. Suspense, good storytelling, constant fear of the unknown.

The graphics are decent and lighting is really good, but animations are dreadful. I found the gameplay extremely offputting to the point where I couldn't go on. But I really want this game to get better and playable. I want this to be perfected, but at its current state I cannot reccomend it.

I'm a huge H. P. Lovecraft fan and love to get into anything related to his world. I'm sorry but this game is terrible. The graphics are sub-standard but I could get past that if the story were engaging. Admittedly, I'm only about an hour in, but the story is extremely vague, not in the good, Lovecraftian way. Madness!
The voice actors are fairly inept and are made worse by trying to create some sort of unique 20's French gangster accent and failing, mostly while reciting very awkward and confusing dialogue. The quotes from Lovecraft are left for you to read as they fly by. Madness!
The figure skins are nostalgic and harken back to Doom II days, although I don't think it's intentional. The map is filled with arbitrary boundaries that don't match the landscape at all and much of the non-snow constructions have no mass at all and can be walked through at will. That's the madness!
Much of the time, you are wandering aimlessly, wondering why you keep hoping to find some shred of interest in this awful mistake of a game. I think this is the true genius of it! The longer you wander...the more fragile and thin your desperate mind becomes...as the insipidness of the graphics and terrain and animation wear you down and down...you realize you've truly reached: THE MOUNTAINS OF MADNESS!
Oh, the sound effects and music are pretty good. Unless my twitchy brain was making them up.

Boson X has been a favorite of mine ever since I bought it off the App Store during Christmas of 2014. The shape-shifting platforms, progress updates, and scientifically enhanced optical illusions are what set this apart to many other rage games.
You're placed in this massive particle accelerator, which could arguably be the Large Hadron Collider, where you must land on cyan colored platforms to raise the peak energy of the particle you're attempting to unearth. Reaching 100% energy results in successfully discovering a new particle, and each particle (level) presents you with new gauntlets of varying speeds and obstacles. The gameplay is a tiny bit similar to Super Hexagon, where you must traverse a shapeshifting polygon to progress towards level completion.
The game's base price should suit the amount of time you'll get out of it. Boson X isn't as hard as Super Hexagon, but it's still a great endurance test that'll enhance your reflexes. Plus, the achievements are very straightforward and simple to obtain.
Quite fun, some of the levels are a bit random for my taste, but overall if you like fast paced platforming give it a go.

Remember HM1? With the nice nonlinear levels, that allowed you to experiment and try new things? Remember how when you died, it felt sorta fair, like you messed up and you needed to try something new? Do you want to get more of that Hotline Miami feeling?
Skip this game then.
The level design in this game is plain frustrating, with every level giving you many cheap deaths. What do I mean by cheap deaths? Practically every level has at least 1 guy with a gun who is out of your field of view, who will shoot you the instant you step out into the open. Many of the levels have gun guys in wide open spaces with no cover, and most have many glass walls, which enemies can shoot you through.
Several of the levels additionally feature melee enemies who are positioned right next to where you spawn, guaranteeing at least 1 unavoidable death.
Instead of having the ability to pick enemies off one by one by playing well, the new enemy AI seems to consist solely of bumrushing you.
Furthermore there are far less masks in this game than in HM1, and many of them are locked off depending on the level you are playing.
The game's story is told in a non linear manner, jumping between the perspectives of many characters. It was novel, but I found the story to be a tad hard to follow at times. The game is also much longer than the first game, which can be a good or bad thing. Personally I found it to drag on, especially considering as I did not much like the game in the first place.
Pros
+Good music
+Cool atmosphere
Cons
-Unrealistic difficulty
-Bad level design
-Confusing story

This game, with freely available Mods installed from
, really brings home the tensions and flavor of operating a UBoat in WWII.  It is a Fantastic game (as you can tell from the number of hours I’ve played).   But be warned: this is way more than a "torpedo game".  You have to survive getting resupplied by sailing thru enemy blockades and patrols, learn to conserve torps by using a deck gun, learn to recharge your limited underwater batteries , learn how to navigate and compute target speeds and course angles, and learn various evasive maneuvers against the  threat of Airplanes, Destroyers, Sonar and Depth charges.  Some of these skills you learn by watching YouTube vids, some by asking others online, and some from the school of hard knocks.  In this regard you can Save and Reload your game to try different engagement scenarios, which is what I do till I perfect the best possible strategy.
Out of the box, the game can be played in a simplistic mode, and everybody starts there, but the real thrill comes from learning to take more control of your boat and the little things that make it work efficiently.  This is where the MODs come in.  They can enable things and actually completely transform the game into a serious UBoat simulation.
Principle among skills you’ll need to learn is how to aim and angle a torpedo for real (and there are plenty of YouTube vids that cover this).  The torpedo has its own gyro compass and you can “program” it to turn in almost any direction except directly around and hit your own sub.  Mastering the TDC (Torpedo Data Computer) is key, and  its faithfully recreated in the game.    With it, in the midst of a convoy you can now target and fire at a number of different ships in seeming rapid fire, without turning your sub, as soon as the torpedo tubes are reloaded.
Watching your torpedoes propel forward toward their targets can be nerve wracking.  You can watch them zoom off toward their predicted target intercept locations, but sometimes you can't wait to verify a hit... because You’re too busy setting up the targeting solution for your next target while they're enroute.  Thank goodness, you can speed up, slow and even stop TIME, so you can work out what has to be done and in the right sequence.  There's some work involved here which develops into a Confident Skill.  The game becomes addictive then.  There's a big disappointment if some of your torpedos miss, a huge feeling of satisfaction when they all connect.
Can’t say enough about the game really.  If you’ve ever had a secret desire to run  your own Submarine, this is definitely it.
One last thing, the sea and sky simulations are really beautiful, and I sometimes I take a break and just “ride” my sub on deck and watch the clouds, sunsets, and storms.  Cameras can be moved anywhere, inside or outside the boat, in the sky, even underwater.   Some of the images you get look photo real.  Very very beautiful game.
Hope this helps.

An extremely enjoyable legally distinct block placing game, which uses steamworks, and has a fun physics element. In Tricky Towers you use different shaped blocks to build towers under certain restrictions, depending on what game mode. There are 3 game modes available (+1 special modifier for each) and supports up to 4 player multiplayer. There are also a large number of singleplayer stages to complete.
In Race mode, you must build a tower faster than your opponents to reach a certain height.
In survival, you must use all of the blocks given to you, however you can only have up to 3 collapses.
In Puzzle, you are given a piece of terrain in which you must carefully place your blocks to build a tower with a given height restriction (But the terrain you start on is extremely narrow, so the challenge comes from using the blocks to expand horizontally).
The physics element adds a lot, which means rickety, shoddily-based towers will likely collapse, which may be fatal depending on the game mode. There are also magic spells, named light and dark magic, which you can use to buff your own tower, or sabotage your enemies. A light magic spell example would be a binding spell, which binds the next block you place with those surrounding it, making it stronger and more stable. A dark magic example would be fog, which clouds the enemy towers and makes it difficult to see where to place blocks. The magic spells all drastically affect the outcome of the game, and you can even use light magic to turn an enemy's dark spell that has been used on you to your advantage.
Puzzle went from my least to my most favourite mode, as block placement needs to be careful and precise, and you need to plan ahead with how the tower you create will take shape. I would say the hardest mode would be survival with it's special modifier, as in this mode you must survive with waves of dark magic thrown at all players.
I'd like to see more functionality, like a chat or even a simple VGS system. However this doesn't affect the game much. In the future I'd perhaps like to see some kind of coop game mode.
It's relatively inexpensive and I strongly recommend this game.

Sonic Adventure 2 is a game many people have nostalgia for. And, of course, its cutscenes and voicelines have led to many jokes. However, if you weren’t on that train as a kid, I still think the game holds up. I haven’t played the Steam version, but I have a good amount of time in the Gamecube version (which is largely the same), for the record.
Sonic Adventure 2 has two campaigns that tell the same story from both the heroes’ and villains’ perspectives. While the sequence of events is the same, each is different enough that they don’t feel samey, aided greatly by the fact that no stage is repeated. The story itself is nothing to write home about, but it’s asinine enough to be enjoyable in a sense.
The gameplay is split into three modes for both campaigns. Speed stages are you general 3D platforming stage. These are generally described as the most fun by most people. Mech stages have you in a mech where the 3D platforming is toned down in favor for shooting at enemies. Due to its slow pace and easy lock-on ability, most people aren’t a fan of these ones (but I think they’re okay enough, not a complete drag). Finally, the Treasure Hunting stages see the player gliding, climbing, and digging around a big, open 3D area to find three pieces of an emerald. People seem lukewarm on these ones, as I think they can get frustrating to look for but are satisfying to beat.
There’s also a side mode that people are a fan of. The Chao Garden is where you raise little adorable creatures called Chao. You mainly give them gems (that raise their stats) animals (that change their appearance, too). Then, once you think they’re ready, you can put your chao in races and karate tournaments, where you have limited control of the chao and they’ll win if they have good stats. It’s definitely more laid-back than the main game and needs some grinding, so some people might not be fans, but seeing your little chao succeed is rather satisfying.
Sonic Adventure 2’s a curious case where I think it’s generally given positive feedback, but there are aspects certain people don’t like. I personally like most of it and tend to replay it every so often. The bad parts usually just make me laugh. I think it’s worth trying out yourself!

The visuals and music are both appealing. The feel of the game is great and it all comes together well. Despite retrying levels endlessly, the music still works and adds to the experience without becoming annoying which is always a possibility in games like this.

percentage of completion than those attempts. Didn't stop me from retrying the level though...

Ok so when I saw this was free to play my first thought was 'Oh great... here we go again, another pay to win or donate your life savings into this game to be decent', but its turning out not to be the case at all.   This game is grindy and takes time, but if you want to just push buttons and feel good about yourself immediately, then this may not be your game and that's OK.  Sometimes however, effort required to do something makes it have more meaning, and if this is your thing you may just like this :D
The fact that I can do more in this Free to Play MMO -without restrictions- than I can when I buy a full version of a Total War Game which then gives me the 'chance' to buy a bunch of DLC, is a commentary in itself (on both games, despite different genre / game type and I am a HUGE Total War fan).
*Items- lots of sense of humor with pets, armor, and misc items.  Sort of like the humor of Borderlands, but not quite.  (There's an NPC in a sewer named Donallangelo who essentially is a pun of Ninja Turtles, and pets like a Ghast have descriptions which read 'I ain't afraid of no ghast!' and so on)  Also, importantly, no restrictions on items that I can tell so far if you are free to play.
*Great community - helpful and teamwork is essential.  Let's face it, many MMOs don't care to pretend about requiring teamwork - it's just login, get achievements, and feel good about pressing the level button.  This game is not that.  It's teamwork, has depth, and requires thought.  If that's not your thing - great!  Don't play.  Leave it for people who do because this makes for a great community that works together.
*Graphics - pretty charming and actually really awesome artwork.
*Class system - did I say there were what, 700 million classes?  Well maybe not THAT many, but at least 16. Yes 16, which if you can count as high as WoW classes, well then this is a LOT compared to many MMOs.  Beyond that, yea it's complicated "Oh noes! Don't try! Too hard!", wrong!  A game with some complexity is a great thing, its not going to hand you things, but its not going to stomp your face in either by giving you experience debt you need to clear by using item shop items (Runes of Magic).
Butt weight, there's more! (and yes those awful wrong use of word errors got your attention!):  You pick a class, then you have 5 tabs of stuff to put points into, so not only are there a ton of classes to pick from, but there's a very custom way you can build your char.  If you're not sure, look it up or ask someone.  Find a guild -
*Guilds - did I say find a guild?  Find a guild!  Guilds matter in this game, and apparently there's even complicated politics with certain Nations owning certain regions etc.
*Crafting - there's several paths to take, and you can do all professions.
*It's free, and they give you a House, 5 character slots, you can wear all the gear, they let you use the AH, you can sell items remotely too apparently by dropping a bag and selling.
*Gathering - there is this very cool anti-bot system, where if you are gathering it comes up like a 'fight' with this npc, but actually you and it just stand apart from one another and you have to select the same images around you as it has.  If you do this correctly, you get bonus resources and not just a few either.  Pretty sweet and easy!
*Biomes - I don't even know what this is and I'm excited!  (:S  review pending here)  Also plenty of environments it seems and cool stuff in each.
*Nations- player driven, can elect govenors of Nations, collect taxes, set foreign policy, control regions, etc.  Like Eve but without the crying about how broken capital ships are.
*Pvp is a thing, more to come (tm).
I'd say overall, having not spent any money on it, having joined a guild where folks are really helpful and kind, I would say check this game out.  It's free, all it costs you is bandwidth for a bit and you may find you like it. If not, you tried it and can move on to other games.

Remember HM1? With the nice nonlinear levels, that allowed you to experiment and try new things? Remember how when you died, it felt sorta fair, like you messed up and you needed to try something new? Do you want to get more of that Hotline Miami feeling?
Skip this game then.
The level design in this game is plain frustrating, with every level giving you many cheap deaths. What do I mean by cheap deaths? Practically every level has at least 1 guy with a gun who is out of your field of view, who will shoot you the instant you step out into the open. Many of the levels have gun guys in wide open spaces with no cover, and most have many glass walls, which enemies can shoot you through.
Several of the levels additionally feature melee enemies who are positioned right next to where you spawn, guaranteeing at least 1 unavoidable death.
Instead of having the ability to pick enemies off one by one by playing well, the new enemy AI seems to consist solely of bumrushing you.
Furthermore there are far less masks in this game than in HM1, and many of them are locked off depending on the level you are playing.
The game's story is told in a non linear manner, jumping between the perspectives of many characters. It was novel, but I found the story to be a tad hard to follow at times. The game is also much longer than the first game, which can be a good or bad thing. Personally I found it to drag on, especially considering as I did not much like the game in the first place.
Pros
+Good music
+Cool atmosphere
Cons
-Unrealistic difficulty
-Bad level design
-Confusing story

All in all, I think this game would be a lot better with some clearer objective instructions and intelligible dialogue.

Unfortunately, I have to change my review at this point. I usually like to cut a game in EA some slack, but I was under the impression that this game was very early into its development. Apparently, it isn't, and the current state seems to be quite advanced in the view of the developers, and I just don't think that that is a fair assessment.
Here are my issues:
- The game performs horribly. I am aware that optimization doesn't usually happen until the very late stages of development, and it might improve the performance, but right now, it runs terribly on a system that can run many current or very recent triple A-titles (Division, Witcher 3, GTAV, Hitman etc.) at medium to high settings. Motion blur, horrible framerate.
- The voice-acting is terrible, and if this is more than a placeholder, is a big minus, as atmosphere is so important in HPL-games IMO, and this ruins any immersion.
- Load times
- Invisible walls that kept me from climbing even slight inclines, which felt odd.
- Floating objects. If you look at, say, a can of beans on a shipping box, it floats.
- Weird textures... the tents look like some silvery river surface. I guess they're supposed to look wet and frozen, but it just looks like some weird T1000-thingy. Same for a hut close to the starting area, which looks like the ghost of a hut, very unfinished.
- Lack of explanation for things
- I am not sure, but I read that the later game will involve quite a lot of fighting, which to me, kills the immersion. Yes, there was a bit of action in MOM (the novella), but it should be only a small aspect, where story, setting and atmosphere should be the focus.
- Weird animations
- Save game bug...where saving won't work, and puts you back to the start when you try to load. According to the devs, this is only on the first map, but there are reports of it bugging out later too.
I am sorry, but if this is considered close to being ready for release, it really deserves a downrating, especially at the current prize... I don't mind big problems in an EA game if I know it's the very early stages, but 18 EUR to get into EA for a game that has severe performance issues and other bugs just isn't ok.
I will keep an eye on this, and hope it can get improved a lot, as in another half a year or year of changes to the performance, layout, voice acting, mechanics, UI etc. If it does perform better eventually, I might change my review, but right now, this just isn't worth the money they ask for, and if a game based on such an atmospheric story is turned into a shooter or combat-focused game, I, as a longtime-HPL-fan, will stay away for good.

I don't typically write reviews, and certainly don't bother with actually writing negative ones, but man is this a special case. With the sheer amount of garbage that is classsified under Early Access, saying a game is too early even for Early Access feels pretty damning and yet perfect for At The Mountains Of Madness. There's a lot of jumbled thoughts to put together, so let's break it down into points.
-The actual performance is terrible, sitting at about 22 frames on average. However, when I loaded my game after dying in the middle of talking to an NPC, the game dropped to a stubborn, stable 5 frames for no discernible reason. Turning down the graphics had no effect on the frame rate either time, just made the game look even worse. Of course, this is something that could be fixed in Early Access via optimization, but it leaves the initial impression that the developers have no idea how to go about doing that.
-The voice acting is worse than abysmal. Likely recorded by the devlopers and their friends, all of the spoken dialogue sounds like non-english speakers phonetically reading dialogue off a paper. This could be placeholder dialogue again, but based on the budget it seems unlikely that the developers will be able to replace it with different voice actors more familiar with english. Perhaps it would have been better to record it in the native language with subtitles?
-The gameplay is pretty awful and bland so far. There's no explanation of the health, or what the white flashing that kills you is supposed to mean. I thought it was freezing to death, since you can collect firewood and start fires, but eating a can of beans made it stop so who knows. Once you collect the plot mandatory flashlight and walking stick and get into the main gameplay, you're dumped in a dark, hideous looking ice cave. You need to find a fossil (which was just floating in mid air) and a hammer to extract it (from the air I guess?). This seems like the majority of the entire game, going into increasingly larger caves to find these fossils. It looks like there's eventually combat, but I can't imagine it being much fun at these stuttering frame rates.
-The developers themselves. While this isn't immediately tied to the quality of the game, with Early Access the developers become much more important for determing whether the game will be able to improve. These developers seem a bit over enthusiastic for what was apparently originally a school project, claiming above that they're confident they already have a solid game here. Furthermore, I was banned from the game's forum for pointing out that deleting threads (or creating a Trash section to dump them in) with criticism is a pitiful, cowardly tactic that is frequently employed by indie developers on Steam who can't face criticism of their pet project/money laundering scheme. That's one thing that immediately removes any positivity or leniency for a developer, and the same is true here.
-It's not fun. Ultimately this is the big problem that it boils down to. There was never an enjoyable moment in what I played, never a time when I went "Huh, that's neat." This felt a lot like many of the free Unreal Engine and Unity engine messes that I've tried, cobbled together from a pile of assets without any real design philosophy or concern for coherence. It's a real shame, because I'm always looking forward to a good game based on Lovecraft's works, rather than just inspired by them. But At The Mountains of Madness isn't one of them, and likely won't be for a year or more, or perhaps never. Save your money, wait for The Sinking City for a quality H.P. Lovecraft game.
It's bad, and it likely won't get better without being a mostly different game from what's here. I'm refunding this, and I suggest you stay far away too.

Ok so what we have here is a true survival horror game. Keep in mind I dont have much time to play games these days so Im only on the 3rd chapter. Also I'm not judging this game on technical issues. Back then the hardest thing about finding a true survival horror game was trying to decide which of the many available titles you wanted to spend your B-day money on. Fast forward almost 20 years(dam that long already) and aside from a few unpolished indie titles and the genre is almost dead, what new life emerges(Dead Space 1) is quickly scooped up and assimilated into the Gears of War co-op action clone in order to reach mindless masses incapable of any coeherent thought and unable to use any tactic other then pop up from cover and shoot, shoot, shoot another and another shooting gallery blah blah, but I digress. The Evil Within is what Resident Evil 5 and beyond should have been. It even feels like RE4 but better. Even certiain features like the RE remake for gamecube where you can burn bodies or just decapitate enimies to prevent them from unholy resurection. Exccellent level design, enemy AI, creepy Atmosphere great blend of action, stealth tactics, running hiding it all works great and makes for a fun and intense, and challenging  experience. True survival horror fans should not pass this one up.

If you watch interviews with Shinji Mikami he never claims he's trying to revolutionize survival horror with this title. Hell, he doesn't have to because he already did. However,
Right off the bat, I don't think the choice of armies was the best. In terms of fluff, you have a chapter of 1000 super soldiers facing off against a force so large it's called "The Green Tide". You'll lose over a dozen of these prized soldiers in a single battle. I'm sure GW wanted their Space Marines instead of IG, but it really just doesn't make sense.
Second, I find that (in my opinion) the Regicide Orks are overpowered compared to the Space Marines. SM have a lot of skills focusing on defense and maintaining the line, while Orks are very agressive.
For example: Space Marines have abilities that...allow units in a 3x3 to shoot more accuratley, another that regains armor, and one that grants extra toughness when an enemy is nearby.
Orks, on the other hand have abilities that allow them to regain health on attack, shoot twice in a single round, and they have several units that increase critical hit chances.
My problem is that (assuming every hit is successful) it takes 4 snapshots from SM pawns to take down a single Ork pawn. Orks can take down an SM king (non-assault) in 2 turns (or less) through a mixture of snapshot and more dakka (Emperor help you if they get a critical). Orks are aggressive to the point where all you can really do as SM is create a wall of bodies to hide behind.
In assault, Ork pawns deal 4 damage to Space Marines. SM pawns only have 8hp.
Without bonuses, SM pawns deal 3 damage to Orks. Ork pawns have 12hp.
Space Marines do have more armor and can hunker down better than orks, but it doesn't really matter in the campaign mode. Why doesn't armor matter?
Here's an example:
An SM bishop with +1 damage does 5 damage to a normal armored Ork.
If an Ork has no armor, you now do 6 damage.
However, that bishop can only shoot once a turn and no unit does more damage than a bishop. Regardless of whether or not an Ork has armor, under the best possible circumstances, it takes a minimum of 3 hits to kill an Ork Pawn and only 2 hits to kill a Space Marine Pawn.
Additionally, Orks are oriented toward assault (melee) combat while SM have more shooty bonuses. Problem is that on an 8x8 game board, (and especially when the majority of your units can only move forward) units will more often than not end up adjacent to eachother, which is ideal for Orks. I could see this working as 3 dimensional chess (perhaps with 40k style buildings instead of just barriers), but as it stands it feels like the Space Marines are simply outgunned at every opportunity and forced to agressively use defense bonuses in the campaign.
Here's a prime example because this will happen to everyone either in campaign or skirmish:
You have 2 SM pawns. There is 1 Ork pawn adjacent in front of you. You have 3 initiative. Assuming you hit twice, that 12hp Ork is now down to 6hp.
Now lets flip the script.
You have 2 Ork pawns. There is 1 SM pawn adjacent in front of you. You have 3 initiave.
Assuming you hit twice with assault, that SM is now dead.
Third, the campaign can be pretty annoying. Not because of anything to do with the gameplay, but because if you ever need to restart the scenario, you can't just get back in the action. You need to watch the dialouge scroll and the primary, secondary, fail objectives again. Why yes, there is a skip button. It doesn't actually skip the dialouge and objectives though. It just makes them all load faster. You still have to sit through all of the dialouge and objectives every single time you restart a mission, despite that the objectives are conviently located on the left side of your screen. In any other game, this would be the equivelent of having an unskippable cutscene for every single combat encounter.
Finally, there's cosmetics. You may notice in the promotional video on Regicide's Steam page that one of the cosmetics is an Ultramarines Captain (with a big Roman crest). Yeah. That isn't in the game. You just get a reskinned SM King. About the most advanced cosmetic in the game is either that Dark Angels terminators are bone colored or that Blood Axes have camoflauge. So why have promotional videos with content that is not in the game?
So although I enjoy the game and will continue playing it, I really can't recommend it to others.

Warhammer 40k + chess.  Absurdly stupid idea, I said.
I read about, it sounded stupid, and it dropped off my radar.
Much later, I bought on sale and figured if it could give me a few days of enjoyment, it'd be worth it.
It's 3 weeks later, and I'm still playing it.
Pros
1. The campaign, by itself, will take anywhere from 40-50 hours to complete, especially if you buy Ork campaign for 99 cents.  There is something like 60 missions plus another 40 in Ork campaign.  Although hard, I really enjoyed each mission, as it plays out completely differently and is like a challenging puzzle.  I'm sure many people never finished the campaign because they got "stuck", but I really enjoyed figuring out how to win each one AND get the secondary objective.
2.  The abilities and the chess merges very well together, once you get the hang of it.  It's not like 2 seperate games, but actually a deep strategy game that is more about positioning than piece trading like in chess.
3. Overall, the flavor is excellent, and despite the "chessboard", it really does feel very 40k.  The animations and abilities really help a lot, and it's not like playing chess, but a turned based Warhammer 40k game.
4.  Balance. Really well done, especially between the different factions of Space Marines and Orks. Each one plays differently, but none feel strictly "better" than the other.  SM and Orks are balanced too, although I'd say the Orks are a bit too strong, and need nerfing.
Cons
1.  The game's gameplay and graphics are very polished, but there are mistakes in the text.  Some objectives are just plain wrong.  In about 100 missions, there's maybe 2-3 missions with incorrectly marked objectives, so it's not too bad.
2.  Slow release schedule.  Where is the 3rd faction?!
3. The secondary objectives are absurdly hard.  Some of them may be nearly impossible (lose no units with 12+ units on each side?!). Still, it keeps you coming back to missions to try different things.
