I recommend this game at full or at sale price, because the core gameplay is well-thought-out and, the vast majority of the time, fun.
The game is also well-animated and attractive. Fixes for many bugs have been introduced, with the devs prioritising the bugs that make most sense to prioritise. They interact with the community and on the whole seem professional and somewhat amenable to receiving and acting on some amount of community feedback.
It succeeds in adding a new twist to chess. The battle system is fairly straightforward. The main feature that significantly affects gameplay is that it allows units which are close-up to deal high, reliable damage. In such an RNG-heavy game, high reliable damage up close generally results in more cautious, defensive play. Expect to see fewer flashy forks from Knights and fewer Devastating pins, because these will typically put your pieces at risk. Expect to see more small-scale♥♥♥♥♥for-tat exchanges, because these allow you to both swap a piece, dictate the opponent's next moves, and deliver an up-close assault, which gives your pieces a small edge.
In general, the most satisfying Chess moves are not viable, and the least satisfying moves are viable, and you can't plan far ahead in a tactical, precise manner - instead, you must focus on a more fluid general strategy. It is lucky that the 'game-feel' is spot on, making combat feel incredibly satisfying, and that the additional special moves add more than enough interest and nuance to make up for the lost tactical depth in the movement phase. Sapping potential threats of their strength before they can develop, suppressing units at key moments, lobbing Krak grenades, preserving Initiative points for use on a later turn, all these actions and more feel fun and impactful.
For these reasons, it is enjoyable for people who would consider themselves beginners, intermediates, or casual fans of chess (rule of thumb - if you can't remember a complete opening or haven't memorised the solutions to the most common endgame setups, you *probably* fall in this category). Slightly more advanced players might find the game frustrating in that it rewards a very different, less aggressive, more cautious playstyle. I currently fall in the former category, but in the past would have fallen in the latter, so I feel as though I can talk honestly about both. Actual advanced chess players may disagree on this point.
Where it falls flat is the single-player level design and attention to detail, especially with respect to secondary objectives. Many secondary objectives are poorly described; others in the past suffered from significant bugs that make them unachievable (these are fixed when found & reported to the devs); others are so RNG dependent as to be incredibly dull to seek and achieve. The AI is poor, making bad decisions from both a Chess and a Regicide point of view - often it will make moves that lose it the game, but ruin the chance of a secondary objective. Needless to say, this adds to the feeling of frustration when going after these objectives. Equally often, it will exchange a high-health piece with a Shield for a low-health equivalent piece that would die to a scratch from a Shoota Boy, or try to retreat a low-health piece that will die anyway at the cost of a full-health piece that will now be taken the next turn. It will spread fire between multiple units, when concentrated fire could score a kill. It will move pieces into positions from which they will clearly be taken for no apparent reason, seemingly being confused by the way Knights move - which is expected from a beginner player but not so much from an AI.
However, the single-player campaign is not really the point. And the secondary objectives are not really the point of the single-player campaign. So the weakness of the AI and the poor design of the secondary objectives are not significant detractors from what is, on the whole, an enjoyable game.
What may actually sway your decision is that the Orks Campaign comes in the form of an additional premium DLC (Only about £1, far from a deal-breaker for me considering I'm a Total War fanboy), and you need a third party account in order to play. I haven't found these to be obstructions, and so far the third party account works fine and hasn't got in the way at all.
If you are swayed by these factors, you're missing out on a strategy romp that weirdly enough feels similar to Advance Wars with RNG added in. It's a great game for hitting a sweet spot between the ultra-precise requirements of tactics-heavy games like Desktop Dungeons or, uh, Chess I guess, and the RNG-heavy strategy of games like Faster Than Light, XCOM, or Darkest Dungeon. It feels somewhere between a casual and a core game, and as such I've been really enjoying it.
Typically the game has been receiving scores of around 7/10 in the press, and although scores are usually a bit arbitrary this is genuinely a good representation of the game - an enjoyable experience with minor flaws that don't detract from a solid game with committed, though not fanatic, developers.

The overall gameplay is well implemented. The different classes are fun to experiment (however, I tend to focus on one class and try to best equipt it) with and the basic outline of the game makes for a fun mix with high replay factor as long as you have a few friends to replay it with. The models are very well done and the engine shines. While the mission design and narrative are fun in themselves, the level design could use some finishing touches. Missing walls and floating elements all around - things, any community created map for any game out there would be destroyed for. That doesn't make the game bad, it's just something I tend to notice.
Be prepared for lots of repetitive grinding, though. The drops are dice rolled at the end of every mission and trying to find a specific item or even an item of a specific class is time consuming. Fatshark is tried to improve this by introducing a reforge type mechanic where you can replace or improve the enchantments on any item, but there are still problems with this system. A friend reached level 35 without a single trinket drop. So he got 3 open trinket slots, but only the start trinkes to choose from. A simple gift or trade mechanic in the party would easily improve that.
Overall, a fun game I would recommend to anyone as long as you can stand the endless grinding or are lucky with your drops.
Side node: Bots are midly unintelligent and I dream of the patch that introduces basic command ability such as "heal up" or "pick up this heal god damn it, you have none and stand right in front of it" (happens rarely) or "yeah, there is a ratling gun but that does not mean you have to run back to confront it" or "we just dropped of this ledge please follow us or else you will be attacked by a gutter runner and will 100% die... yeah, though so - so long."

After CHapter 4 the frame rate got so bad my game went into the menu screen and froze.
The list goes on, but if you want to find out more read the discussion forums before committing your cash to this one. Make sure to check the discussion sub forums for feedback too because they are deleting posts and banning people giving negative feedback. Honestly, one of the best free-to-play Source mods out there, although with some stuff worth mentioning.
With a flowing and balanced melee system I've never seen anywhere, interesting classes and nice (and very fast!) gameplay, it truly earned it's place in my heart.
People expecting quick updates will be disappointed: updates are made rarely, due to the developer team's small size. New classes are usually released per 2 years, while smaller updates take many months.
While the developers obviously care about their game, the actual player population is rather small, made of around 200 players who faithfully play the game, and other random people who either stay, or get discouraged by the seemingly hard melee-system. The player count goes up exponentially when major updates are released, or during summer though.
The only true negative aspects about the game is it's miniature community (mainly) being composed of brain-dead people, but you can encounter nice folks as well.
Another thing is how high latency / ping can affect the reach of your melee weapons, meaning that people with 200 ms and the likes will prove to be a problem, both because of their lag making them harder to hit while their "longer" weapons make it much easier for them to hit you. Same thing happens with tw ats who decide to play around with their in-game rates via the console.
Overall, I recommend the game. It really is fun to play, not easy to get into but if you actually spend time playing and learning the melee system's mechanics it can become quite an enjoyable experience, minus the problems I've listed. Those can be off putting but try your best to ignore them.

. An fast-paced indie platformer that requires a lot of memorization of patterns to get you through.
It seems that the objective is to help two (or three if you consider a robot one) scientists discover three particles by traveling through some visual starfield. The goal is to run along blue platforms that emerge from the endless void around you, building up enough energy to spark a particle. This task, as you progress, isn't as easy as it seems as newer stages bring forth new obstacles, may it be moving white flats, fragile red flats, thick walls, and even rings that emit electric currents. All this game really needs is mind power and complete concentration.
Boson X has proven its to be a worthy challenge, taking nearly months to actually beat all levels (for me anyways). At first glance, I truly thought I had what it took to beat it, to little avail. Up until you reach a certain point, the game provides a nice, minimalistic and basic gameplay that can be enjoyed... if you're into games like this one, of course. The music that plays in the six stages is also pretty fine as well.
While this game doesn't a lot, I can't seem to find a lot of bad things to say about it aside from no real replay material implemented into it. That's... about all I can point out atm.
It's a pretty intense but exciting little game that I somewhat find kinda funny too if you manage to envelop yourself deep into the game, not pressing to strive straight for instant wins or even trying to beat the game. And if you're one to shoot for those top ranks on the leaderboards, I wish you greatest luck for you. I'm sure there are very many already high up, but who's to say you can't get up there?
--Hermix.

Sonic Adventure 2 is an excellent inclusion to anyone's library, and a great way to introduce someone to the Sonic series. Gone are the adventure field hub worlds of the previous game but in their place is a tighter and more streamlined experience where one level ends the next begins.
While some folks might groan at the mech and/or treasure hunt stages I never found enough to complain about, There's something enjoyable about patrolling the skies of Pumpkin Hill and Meteor Herd (though it isn't until each mech is sporting their hover jump that *they* really come into their own), and there's just a ton to do in this game besides the main campaigns.
SA2's possibly still the best attention to multiplayer the series has had to this day. you can grab a friend and head to the foot races, kart races, or any of the other gameplay styles though the races are easily the most addictive. Last but not least raising virtual pets in the chao gardens is a master stroke that ties it all together.

The devs have clearly taken a break, also because the community has been very small, but there's always at least a couple lobbies open 24/7. Hydrophobia has a memorable level design and visual themes, along with rather impressive water flow simulation, and an average, but decent TPS system. Still, all of these feel a little unpolished, awkward when playing, resulting in a mediocre game at best.
Dark Energy Digital spent years with developing a game engine with fluid simulation, and Hydrophobia was supposed to showcase its capabilities. Sadly, the game tanked so hard that it drowned the company, but not before they salvaged some of it by releasing the Prophecy update that more or less ties up the loose ends of what was originally meant to be an entire trilogy.
Not that there is too much story: set in the somewhat near future– where overpopulation has caused the rich to flee to a floating city, away from society’s increasing problems– we play as Kate, a system engineer who ends up in the middle of a terrorist attack. She spends about 3-4 hours trying to survive while getting off the most damaged parts of the ship, aided by the mandatory tech guy guiding her from afar.
The game mechanics are basic third-person action adventure: climb, jump, shoot the two available enemy types (normal and heavy trooper), and try to use the water to your advantage when it is not trying to kill you. It’s not really boring, but the level design does get repetitive.
The showcased water mechanics work well; at least up until you get the power to control it. (Despite what the store suggests, that happens only about 10 minutes before the end of the game.) This was intended to be used only in the upcoming games, and they didn’t really have much time to put into it, so it’s rather awkward to control and just looks ugly, in stark contrast to all other water mechanics.
Could Hydrophobia be a better game? Probably, but we will never find that out. As it is now, it is still enjoyable, to a degree, but it will feel lacking in all areas, if you decide to try it.

Chess and Warhammer.

When I heard
1. Warhammer
and
2. It's like chess
I was sold. Unfortunately, it's not "like chess," the classic mode literally is a chess game with a Warhammer skin. That wouldn't even be so bad, I like Star Wars Chess as much as the next guy, but the "sets" of humans and Orks are all so samey-looking that it's hard to tell a pawn from a knight or a rook at a glance without zooming in on them. So it's ultimately not even a particularly usable chess game.
Beyond that is a second mode, which seems to be the "game," but which is also just chess with some weird extra powers. It's still a chess board, with chess moving pieces, and the fact that they can shoot and use other "powers" to do damage to the health bars of various pieces is novel, but ultimately harmed by the difficulty distinguishing between types of pieces.
Ultimately, Regicide is a cute idea, but can't seem to decide if it wants to be a TBS with a heavy chess influence, or a Warhammer-skinned chess game. Either way, better attention to making the pieces distinguishable at a glance would go a long way toward making it playable.

This game is like Avorion, except that there's barely any content, the gameplay is frustrating, and its generally terrible.
Some examples:
- The first two hours of the game consists solely of warping to "?" markers in space, dragging modules from their wreck to your ship (one by one! ), then warping to a station to reset your ship and thereby sell the modules for money ("wex"). Early combat is impossible as you can't afford any decent ship and don't have any good weapons unlocked.
- Even after you get a few weapons, you can't use 90% of the ship designs as you have to wander the galaxy unlocking every single part they use before you can use them. Finding the parts is random. So you're stuck on low-tier designs. I had 20 Wex but couldn't pilot anything larger than a destroyer (that costs ~2 Wex) as I was not having any luck getting modules to drop. Why on earth would stations refuse to sell you their merchandise until you already have one? The entire point of a shop is to sell you what you DON'T have. The game does not seem to understand this.
- Combat in this game is not fun. The first ship I encountered was called 'Knife' and its strategy was to ram me with its armored hull. Seriously? In a game with all kinds of weapons, your best strategy, and the one NPCs use, is ramming you with an armored hull? That's really dumb. It doesn't say much for the weapons in your game when the first NPC players see thinks ramming you is a better strategy than using any weapon.
- The game has almost no content. Compared to avorion (which has quests, many tiers of ship components, trading, etc)... this game has none of that. The wiki talks about 'quests' but they're disabled. There are only three areas in the galaxy and three basic materials for ships (junk, industrial and alliance). There is no friendly AI to play with. There is no trading system beyond stocks. I haven't seen any multiplayer support and almost nothing in terms of community features. The best resource for the game is the wiki, but even that is often disappointing. Basic, basic questions, like "how do I quickly loot all modules from a derelict ship?" aren't answered. Instead, it seems to be a catalogue of ship modules, which is rather useless information as you can't actually USE any of these modules until you manually hunt them down yourself, and good luck getting them.
- The dialogue in the game is a waste of time. Sometimes, when warping to an "?" in space you will encounter neutral ships. This is a waste of time, as you can't get anything from them except poorly-written dialogue. Some of them say inane things like quoting sentences you can read both forward and backwards. Really? There's nothing interesting enough in this game for the NPCs to comment on? That's what it seems like.
I could go on and on, but suffice it to say: this game is not worth your money. If you want to play a game like this, but that is actually good, I suggest Endless Sky, or Avorion. Endless Sky is free. Avorion is $15 to $20, but its miles better than this.

One of the best games i've ever played, until recently suffering updates that focused massively on removing mechanics that helped the players instead of also focusing in fixing the glitches that ruin the game. Now let's talk about the balancing and debugging.
-They have now removed block revive, which was a strong and vital part of the game, if you go down on cataclysm during a horde, you are bound to die, unless all of your teammates have distraction on their weapons, this did not use to be the case, the block revive used to be a counter part glitch that helped the players to the overwhelming ammount of glitches that sought out to punish the players (i.e. rats hitting through walls, under the floor, or through the ceiling).
So if you decide to remove a glitch that actually was a good mechanic in the game, why not also remove one of the most hated and frustrating bugs in your game? It does not add up.
Weapon variety is a joke, specially on the wizard, who only used the beam staff which now got ridiculously nerfed, making her virtually useless, i won't even mention the other staffs, even after the buffs, they are still a punch in the gut to the players.
Did you know crossbows existed?
Did you know the Witch hunter had an axe?
Did you know the Captain can use a 1 handed sword and prettend to be the wizard?
Did you know Kerillian has a shortbow?
Kerillian can use a single sword, why?
This.Is.A.Joke
Now, on to the specials
Globadiers - Globe rat resistance has been nerfed shortly (90%-60%) after massively buffing the globadiers. This has resulted in situations where if you have a horde and a globadier that you cannot spot, you are already wiped, and even if you do spot him, goodluck using your handgun to headshot a small, glitchy head in the middle of the horde, because they are just that tanky.

Built around a simple but smart series of tools to allow you to create all sorts of dream contraptions -- think Gmod, but more Popular Mechanics and less Ragdoll Poser. Two months out of the gate that momentum was already dead in the water. Two
down the line, we are just now getting the first vague details of Survival Mode biomes and random landscape generation... in a game that was supposed to be about

Avoid.

Well, I'm surprised. I think I rode the hype train a little hard on this one, but here goes...
The Evil Within is a survival/horror game, or at least that's how it bills itself out of the box. I've only had about two hours of experience at the time of my review, so I know I'm going to be critical pretty early, on what amounts to being a 12+ hour game upon first playthrough.
First and formost, this is a regrettably poor console port. Having to use commands to 'fix' issues with the game (30fps cap, removal or adjustment of the black bars, etc.), and no native disable of Vsync, and relatively skimp graphics options, already show a clear sign this was done last minute. The controls are passable, but not impressive, with it being fairly easy to pick up with a keyboard and mouse. Finally, the in-game menus show much more pandering to console controls, which are controllable with the previously mentioned setup, but still irritating enough.
The pacing of this title is much too... bizarre. Within ten minutes of the game, you're dropped into a surprisingly difficult stealth mission with 'chainsaw badguy,' only to quickly die at least a handful of times to him before realizing that every enemy you'll encounter has third eyes and ears. Stealth is tricky, cumbersome, and at best, you'll provoke at least one or ten Haunted before progressing to another area.
I've gotta say though... I'm still somewhat excited to finish this title. Maybe it's because I've got a very deep sweet spot for Resident Evil 4, or maybe it's just the well designed environments, the curiously  intriguing characters, musical score, sound effects, and quite possibly that I'm just going through horror withdrawl.  I don't think this is a title worth 80 dollars in Canada (taxes, currency conversion, that fun stuff :P), but maybe once some patches and fixes come out for the glaring problems, this'll be something more worthy of your time after a successful Steam Sale. Until then, I wait with patience, and an almost childlike sense of intrigue.
This is NOT a game I'd suggest as an entry into Survival/Horror, but as a supplement to a library of titles like this. I'll be adding more to the bottom upon completion of this game.
Tl;DR:
Positive
- Dark, disturbing environments
- 'Inspired' Enemy design, still seems fresh
- Solid, if at times silly, voice acting
Neutral
- Stealth is too tricky, if useless at times
- Game feels too dark in some areas, lots of video effects (disable film grain, and lots of the issues go away)
- Tutorial feels awkward and sped through
Negative
- Poor console port
- Even on a PC that exceeds the Recommended specs, game runs poorly
- Poor pacing for story
- Lack of user configurable options
- Use of console to 'fix' game issues

While I have a slight preference for aspects of the first Sonic Adventure (including better shooting sections with Gamma), this game still a worthy inclusion in the Sonic series, and earns the respect it gets from fans. The gameplay and controls are a lot tighter when compared with the first Sonic Adventure. City Escape is an instant classic (and was rightfully included in Sonic Generations). While personally not a huge fan of Shadow the Hedgehog and Rouge the Bat, they are by no means 'terrible characters', and the game at least did a decent job in regards to their involvement.
However there are few critiisms. First off, Tails' sections (and Eggman's) are pretty poor gameplay-wise. Emblem collecting feels more difficult than Sonic Adventure, and (from memory) this arguably due to difficulties in obtaining a higher rank, when compared with Sonic Adventures more straight forward zone emblem system (e.g. simply collect 50 rings or beat a certain time and that's it). This is subjective however, and it doesn't necessarily hurt the game too much given that it's optional.
One final criticism however is a problem with optimus laptops. Unfortunatly, I'm prevented from having the full experience performance-wise. This is something to consider when purchasing the game should you be in a similar position. That said, the game is still playable with integrated graphics, but this is extremely unfortunate and really deserves a proper fix.

Basic Information
Title: Lightspeed Frontier
Status: Early Access
Developer: Crowdwork Studios
Publisher: Riveted Games
Genre: 3D Space Simulation
Release Date: 7th of March, 2017
Type: Singleplayer
This is going to be my first (out of many, I hope) preview for a Steam title, instead of a review. What does it mean? Well, that “P” is an important distinction. You wouldn’t mistake Prussia for Russia and in the same manner, my previews shall differentiate from reviews, by not containing a final rating. The games in question have been provided by the developers for a more informative role than my usual constructive criticism. Anyway, I’d like to think that I was never too harsh in my writings and that you will enjoy reading even my occasional previews. I shall not skimp on the details, no matter how often I have to adapt my style to the needs of my sponsors, so you, as my readers can always expect an in-depth analysis from me.
Lightspeed Frontier is a 3D Space Sim that wishes to offer an open-ended experience for its players, within a singleplayer mode designed to accept both randomly generated assets and complex customization options for the spacecraft itself. An ambitious project from a debutante dev team, but so far they haven’t given me any reason to doubt their potential to actually come through with their first Steam game. If you know me by now, you probably noticed that I rarely care for the multiplayer component and even if there are many space sims on Steam or otherwise, few of them come close to the liberty and exploration found in 2003’s Freelancer. That was singleplayer experience that combined trade, combat, intuitive control scheme and an intriguing cast of character & storyline, with the sheer vastness of space. And no, Freelancer is not available on Steam or any other digital distribution platform.
It’s an obvious Early Access stage in which the developer wanted to focus on the core gameplay mechanics, before adding a proper story. Lightspeed Frontier has some mission elements implemented already, but they aren’t yet consolidated enough to form narrative coherence. Disparate assignments that have you warp jumping from one solar system to another and reaching some coordinates that frequently prove to be elaborate traps involving space pirates. It gets old fast but I’m certain the fully released version of the game shall offer a campaign worthy of Lightspeed Frontier’s potential.
Judging from the title’s launcher, I presume it’s running on Unity Engine 5 assets so eye candy is more or less present along with enough customization options to satisfy even the most creative digital spacecraft designer/player. The ship components act like near-literal building blocks that can be manipulated to such an extent, to which you can recreate famous space ships found in Sci-Fi films or TV series. And there are already a handful of skillfully crafted examples, ready to be downloaded from Lightspeed Frontier’ Workshop page.
Performance-wise, the game is running maxed out and at 4K resolution without so much as a frame-rate dip if you use anything other than a huge ship design (which would still require copious amounts of in-game currency). I can imagine that running the game at only 1080p or 2K resolutions, ensures buttery smooth performance no matter what gets shown or blown to bits, on your monitor. So the lack of glitches or frame rate instability proves that Lightspeed Frontier is not your typical Early Access indie game on Steam. This dev team isn’t beta testing its game on your own expense and spare time.

Sounds might need an overhaul and perhaps even the soundtrack would benefit from a few added songs. The ones already present tend to repeat themselves way too often. Also there’s no voice acting whatsoever. Not for the tutorial or even the chat of sorts, being simulated. It’s all a much too silent playthrough and so far, a missed opportunity for some really epic tracks. Space sims deserve them almost as much as games belonging to the fantasy genre.
As soon as you start the game, you can pick beween Campaign and Endless modes. True, no unified story is present yet and the collection of slightly repetitive missions may not seem like much, but exploration is encouraged regardless. Space stations represent crucial hubs for any activities you undertake in Lightspeed Frontier. These massive orbiting structures feature everything you need. A marketplace is the perfect spot to unload the minerals you mine and components you capture after a space battle. It is here, where you can buy new “modules” which act as spare parts that help upgrade your ship by your heart’s desire. When you’re not trading in the classical term, you can try your “luck” with the in-game stock market, which features a simplified version of what real life brokers have to deal with. It’s still a nice addition and shows that the developer wants to add personality to the game with the inclusion of stock prices for their faux brands (that are also highlighted through billboards on the space stations themselves).
Stations feature refueling docks and resupplying your ship, costs Wex (the game’s currency) but repairing the vessel seems to be free of charge. I’m not complaining since earning enough cash in Lightspeed Frontier isn’t an easy task, when you constantly have to replace the destroyed bits and pieces you lose after most battles. For all their extra armor you may install, the ships still seem fragile and the weaponry present already is divided in three categories from lowest damage output to the highest: gatling gun (bullets), laser beam and plasma shot. Three is apparently the magic number for current ship style/template, with themes such as rusty brown metal plates with yellow lights, modern white/aluminum look with shades of blue and my favorite, the darker design which features lots of red to go with those black plates. Nothing spells “friendly trader” more than recreating Star Wars' Slave I or a Star Trek Borg Cube (if only green lights were available).
As I mentioned above, when you’re not blasting randomly spawned foes (there aren’t any neutral or allied vessels yet), you can earn Wex by mining the asteroid belts around certain planets you find in most of the solar systems you visit. The game’s map is huge to say the least so I do hope it may get filled with activities and special locations and characters eventually. As with most other controls, travelling from one system to another is as easy as opening the map and clicking on the warp command. Going from one planet to another is also as easy as engaging the warp mode and pointing your mouse cursor towards your intended destination. Even players that aren’t accustomed to space simulations, can simply pick this title up and Lightspeed Frontier’s tutorial shall prepare them for any challenge ahead.
Final rating or not, I still recommend you purchase Lightspeed Frontier even in its current Early Access stage. Its lack of a storyline or campaign is vehemently offset by the presence of a stable and diversified gameplay which won’t bore you. On the contrary, should you wish to craft a space ship worthy of your dreams, you can even do so with the safety and unlimited budget present in the Endless mode. As you will find out, nothing’s gonna stop you from exploring the ever shifting universe of Lightspeed Frontier and no, the sky was never the limit!

They don't aim particularly at your other systems (fuel, engines, weapons etc).
The only good use for the radar is that it shows blocks, that are left behind when you destroy an enemy and you can scoop them up using it as a guide on where to fly. It doesn't scale geometrically thus making it useless to detect ships very far away and enemies show up as red [ ] brackets in large distances away from the ship outside of the radar but in the main playfield.
Weapon selection is very limited (I'm not sure if it gets bigger if you progress further in the game and travel deeper into the galaxy). Some act as fixed, some gimbaled and some are turrets. Some can't penetrate shields, others can so even though you have lots and lots of shields, you might still be very vulnerable against certain enemies, that will have those few weapons, that do penetrate the shields.
Shields in the game are kinda meh. There is no clear information on how much shields you have in total, what's the charge rate for them, the penetration values against weapons, that can pass through them etc.
Also you seem to have a functionality in the game to turn on/off shields and also turn on/off power generation. Based on the fact, that it's not that difficult to get enough power generation to support all your weapons and shields, there is really no need for both of these options at all and I didn't even bother to "manage power".
Mining isn't anything fancy in this game, you just shoot them with any of your weapons and bunch of ore blocks pop out and you can collect them in your cargo containers, nothing special.
Even if the description of the game mentions, that there are different corporations, that you can do missions fore, there is no real benefit of doing them, since it doesn't affect in any way how hostiles ships are spawned in the system.
Game needs factions - pirates, neutral, traders, haulers, miners etc. There needs to be some option to interact with other ships, hail them with options like threatening traders/miners to drop their cargo, bribing hostiles to make them go away.

Construct your ship, fly around, defeat random hostiles, rebuild your ship from their carcasses, and repeat, while enjoying the stellar/planetary scenery.   After each battle, you'll have some time to collect the fragments of destroyed ships.  Return to the in-system station for repairs and reconstruction, or rebuild your ship away from the station and get jumped while doing so.
There is a learning curve: It takes some time to get used to the controls.  You also need remember in what mode you are currently in -- constructing or flying.
Because LF is still in early access, there are still some bugs, but the devs are open/responsive and have been rolling out fixes.
Note that the game as it stands now (19 Mar 2017) is great for casual play, but lacks a compelling reason to play for an extended period of time.  Each system is different on the surface (different star, different number of planets, etc), but the number of unique and interesting things to do in each system is limited.  However I expect this to change as more content is added.

TL;DR. One of the best games i've ever played, until recently suffering updates that focused massively on removing mechanics that helped the players instead of also focusing in fixing the glitches that ruin the game. This company has also failed to meet it's deadlines, it seems like that they spent too much time something that was broken, but fun in it's own unique way, instead of actually adding promissed content.
Please be aware that this is a review from somebody who solely plays on cataclysm, if you play on another difficulty please don't bother.
Now let's talk about the balancing and debugging.
-They have now removed block revive, which was a strong and vital part of the game, if you go down on cataclysm during a horde, you are bound to die, unless all of your teammates have distraction on their weapons, this did not use to be the case, the block revive used to be a counter part glitch that helped the players to the overwhelming ammount of glitches that sought out to punish the players (i.e. rats hitting through walls, under the floor, or through the ceiling).
So if you decide to remove a glitch that actually was a good mechanic in the game, why not also remove one of the most hated and frustrating bugs in your game? It does not add up.
Weapon variety is a joke, specially on the wizard, who only used the beam staff which now got ridiculously nerfed, making her virtually useless, i won't even mention the other staffs, even after the buffs, they are still a punch in the gut to the players.
Did you know crossbows existed?
Did you know the Witch hunter had an axe?
Did you know the Captain can use a 1 handed sword and prettend to be the wizard?
Did you know Kerillian has a shortbow?
Kerillian can use a single sword, why?
This.Is.A.Joke
Now, on to the specials
Globadiers - Globe rat resistance has been nerfed shortly (90%-60%) after massively buffing the globadiers. This has resulted in situations where if you have a horde and a globadier that you cannot spot, you are already wiped, and even if you do spot him, goodluck using your handgun to headshot a small, glitchy head in the middle of the horde, because they are just that tanky.
Previous to the nerf, globe rats still spammed enough globes and poison to the point of seriously injuring the players, but giving them a chance to survive a situation you are cornered in.
Continuing on this trinket, it seems fatshark forgot the purpose of these trinkets, you have a maximum of 3, and on cataclysm, you do need the grimoire resistance, or you get 1 shot by a rat that will hit you through shove, or through the wall. You also need poison resistance, or once you have both grims, the sheer impact of the globe would kill you instantly. And then you have the choice of another trinket. So all this "great variation of gameplay" brought by trinkets are a massive joke, even more so now, where you waste a trinket slot to deal with a specific kind of special rat, and it won't even do that anymore.
Packmasters - Ah yes, the ghosts of vermintide, ethereal beings that are imune to unit collision, marching towards you during a horde, ignoring every rat possible, grabing you through all the rats or a wall and draging you to a death that is certain, even if your team is around, best case scenarion would be to go down, and helped by your team during the horde by block reviv... oh wait..
After 300 hours playing this game, i have defended it constantly and passionately from its critics, but update after update i have become more and more tired and disapointed in the direction this game is taking.

I've bought this game twice now, as I've refunded it before.
The first time I played this game, I was very hard on it, as one of my friends expressed distaste torwards it, causing me to refund it. However, I now realize that I was too hard on Vermintide. Yes, it is very similar to L4D. Yes, many of the enemies or carbon copies of L4D enemies. But that changes nothing. Just because a game is similar to another game, that doesn't mean it isn't fun. Vermintide IS fun. There are other examples like this all throughout gaming. Skullgirls is similar to Streetfighter, Battlefield is similar to CoD, Xenonaunts is similar to X-COM, literally all tower defence games are similar to others in its genre, DoTA 2 is similar to LoL. Dispite the similarities, no one has ever claimed they are bad because of this. I just hope for others to take the same approach to Vermintide.
Now that I've got that out of the way, on to the actual game. There are 5 classes, each with a unique feature that greatly differentiates their gameplay. So far, I enjoy all of these except the Bright Wizard. The Enemies are pretty well varied, and you will rarely go longer than a minute or so without seeing a special enemy (if you are actually in combat, and not just scouring the area for resources). While yes, some are just simply reskined L4D characters, others are unique to this game. For instance, I've never seen a giant rat with a minigun anywhere else. Loot is aquired through a dice game after each sucessful mission. You can get better dice, and therefore better rolls, by completing optional objectives, i.e. completing a game with grimoires and/or tomes. Picking up grimoires reduces your teams max heath and take up you healing item slot, whereas tomes take up a potion slot. Tomes can be dropped and picked up later, but once a grimoire is dropped, it's gone.
All in all, I rate this game as a 8.5/10.

I picked up Mount & Blade: Warband on sale during the 2014 Hoiday Sale on Steam. I had recently gotten the original Mount & Blade for free during the
Winter Sale and had been playing it. The original leaves a lot to desire and Warband actually does a pretty decent job of adding more content.
The premise of Mount and Blade is simple; You play a charcter who has traveled to the medival realm of Calradia which consists of multiple constantly warring kindoms. You can mind your own business and simply kill bandits, be a bandit, help villagers, or even start your own trading operation. Or if you want, you can ally (or just start and uprising) with one of the kingdoms and TAKE OVER THE WORLD!! (Well, not quite the world, the GAME world.)
The graphical differences between the two games are minimal. TaleWorlds has changed some armor and weapons and has added a bigger map with a new faction which is meant to resemble Arab cultures. If you've played the original, you'll also note some differences in how weapons are swung, while they are definitely more realistc, if you are used to the original then it takes some getting used to know when to release the mouse button to swing the weapon.
In War Band, TaleWorlds has added more quests and other things to do. Bandit quests are more present, you can get married, the role playing aspect of the game has been improved overall. And the premise of the original game has been preserved as well.
Overall, even if you own the first M&B, Warvand is well worth the buy for the added features and I absolutely reccommend it.

I can't remember exactly when I started playing this. It was pretty early in development, but still had the basic gameplay. I didn't start playing it a lot, though, until a year or two back. Let me just start by saying it is an amazing game through and through. The ideas are pretty original or adaptations of good ideas, there's humor, the developers are nearly always in contact with the players, and other than the random fools that will join, the community can be entertaining and inviting.
I will admit that there are cons. There are true cons and then my opinion of bad things. The largest con, I think, is that there is not a large playerbase behind this game. And that is a con in two ways: not a lot of people to play with, and the developers thrive off the fans' feedback. With only a small knit group of players supporting the mod, I feel it's a waste; not because the game is bad but because it's a diamond in the sand that no one will ever see. This mod needs people to help work on it and to help give it publicity. The second major con is the community. I said earlier that they can be entertaining and inviting, but because they are so tight knit, some players will immediately reject new players. And a part of me feels that this isn't because the community is full of bad people. I've met a lot of the community and they can be nice people. It's just that there will be a lot of rotten apples, and the regulars will get really sour with these apples, because they're usually new players goofing off. It's more a defensive thing: the fanbase wants the community to look amazing, so they are very apprehensive towards new players. But it goes both ways: if you're not a tool, they will gradually accept you.
The combat system is fun, but I'm pretty neutral about it. Sometimes I love it, and sometimes it makes me shake my head. This could be a variety of problems: lag or connection, plain luck, balance issues, or the high learning curve on some characters. This game isn't that easy to "dominate" in without practice. You can get one or two kills without any knowledge, but to really do well you have to dedicate time. I personally like this as it shows skill and how much time you've put into the game, but I know it can be a major put-off for people who don't want to learn. There are even people who criticize the combat system and say it's too easy or simple compared to other games. I honestly can't say for sure, since I don't play other games like this, but that's because I don't really enjoy other games with similar systems. This game keeps me entertained.
In the end, would I recommend it? Of course. Does it need work? Of course. Nothing's perfect. But it's a hell of a game that not many people seem to realize exists. And it's free, so why not?

I love this game and even though it's similar to Left 4 Dead (which I love equally), it's not necessarily a bad thing to bring a familiar element from one game to another before introducing new ideas. It's a nice way to ease a player in, instead of risking to lose people due to there being more than they are willing to learn/handle. While some people love games with groundbreaking new ideas that create their own identities, I think this establishes it's own spot while being something someone can pick up to play with friends who know nothing about it firsthand The fact that they can identify that it's similar to Left 4 Dead allows them to immediately adopt the core play style they are familiar with to be able to get through a majority of the game and enjoy it on that premise alone. From there on they can discover the things that are new and different like aspects enemies have and the pros and cons of different charms with their abilities, stamina management used between blocking and shoving, letting the caster cooldown or risk exploding because you need 1 more spell to save someone, weapon types, weapons with unique attributes gotten through drops, a crafting mechanic, a loot system and a way to make the game harder without raising the difficulty as a whole that rewards you (in a sense, probability can still screw you on a dice roll) if you can make it to the end(bonus dice, tomes and grimoires). I find one of the things this game does even better than left for dead is making the party stick together to maximize teamplay elements. The primary means of disposing enemies are melee weapons. They give you ranged weapons but they teach you to ration ammo which is generally on a much shorter supply (cooldown for the caster) due to the unique enemy types because it's better in most cases (although not impossible/doable) to kill those guys from afar while horde fodder is much more easily handled with melee. With Left 4 Dead I find people mowing through enemies and rolling past hordes because they can and doesn't really force people to think as much. Guns are everywhere and ammo is bountiful, people get screwed over more by people who HAVE to speedrun EVERYTHING and get the group separated or more so by the environment (death charges, tight spaces, etc) with the exception of a well coordinated infected attack (a feature not in Vermintide yet due to no vs but we may get there). Melee combined with the horde spawns keep you together where as in Left 4 Dead 2, it was more of a neat bonus. You only really used it if anything got close enough to you, were good enough to get the smokers tongue or were hopped up on adrenaline. Different paths can have different means of getting to places based on map memory and can help in avoiding confrontations and lead to potential items for current or end based gain (rolls). It invokes more communication between players imho. While I will praise this game for what it has offered, the only things (apart from no vs mode yet) I will admit to not being a fan of two things: no chapters/checkpoints on the maps and the rng loot dice rolls. It's all one long run and if you fail, you start from square one on the map or start a different level altogether. It makes the game REALLY hard to enjoy as much when you get so far or get a lot of bonus dice like items to see it all go down the drain when/if you die and even if you do make it, sometimes even with all the bonus dice you can get to boost your chances at good items, get boned because rng hates you like 50% of the time but it feels like 100% of the time and even with the level up bonus loot you get, it dosen't get good until a certain level point which turns the game into that much more of a grind unless you are having a real good time with friends and don't really care all that much in the end. Are the games similar? Certainly. Are they the same? No. It's harder for youtuber groups like these to really find that out because a lot of the time, they record their first time playing or don't bother to play/learn before hand because a lot of this is the fun of getting to play with friends and a lot of attention is more found going in that direction. All we can hope is that enough of what is made an obvious difference between the two is enough to encourage these groups to explore further, play more, and fully enjoy the games full potential while still enjoying the similar essence of what Left 4 Dead 2 gave it

I don't normally write Reviews, but here I go.
Ever play Fire Emblem? Final Fantasy Tactics? This game follows the same mechanics by fighting within a grid system. The game is vast when it comes to: grinding for gear, harvesting: plants, trees, ores, fish and trapping(Taking Mats(materials) from mobs or collecting seeds(essentially spawning certain mobs)). Aside from harvesting to get the mats you need, of course you have Crafting Profressions. They can range from Single-Target Weapony to being a Tailor to weave armour. There's plentiful Profressions to choose from and you better get ready to invest a lot of time in this game. That's probably the biggest aspect of the game is Time. To get what you want, you must be ready to grind hours on end. Of course that's to be expected in a MMORPG.
Outside the Crafting aspect, the world can be shaped BY the PLAYERS through the ecosystem mechanic. Remember those Seeds from Trapping? You can control the population of the mobs in certain locations. You can even control the plant life that can be grown in those locations as well. Maintaining Balance is key for not only you but the community as well! It's a 3 Star System, in better lack of words. Have 3 Stars in that area? Everyone will have an added bonus for keeping the ecosystem balanced, however Riktus and/or people who don't focus on keeping the balance will hinder that and cause the area to lose stars, essentially losing the bonuses at the same time. Just through that, there's always an on going war so to speak, but of course you don't have to look at it so darkly, haha.
I digress though, the classes you can play in this game range vastly as well and each class will have 3 specific elements you can choose from. You can focus on one, two, or all three elements if you so choose to! Try not to let guides determine your playstyle or mindset on how to play the game. ENJOY it how YOU want to! Play your class how you like and learn the tactics that you come across when facing foes that may work well against you and vice versa.
Of course, the game isn't for everyone and I'd say it's best to have a set of friends or a close community to play with as the grindings will be tiresome at certain times and you'd like to have people there with you to help or even spice things up. The World of Twelve has a lot to explore and I'm still learning new things every chance that I get when I play this game. Though, if you're so crafting types, like me, I think you'll enjoy with the content that's offered.
But remember, HAVE FUN!

This game is bad. It is frustratingly slow, and contradictory. It combines chess, the slow methodical boardgame where long term planning is based on a set of simple movement rules, with a random number generating action point system which makes that long term planning impossible.
Most units special abilities work about 70% of the time or less, so you are gambling everytime. However, moving units like regular chess results in a 100% kill, so there is no consistency. You will restart mission after mission because your amazing space marines refuse to hit with their 64% chances over and over again.
It is also very painfully slow. If you enjoy watching two sides move about slowly while shooting (and almost always missing) at each other, then this is the game for you. There is no auto skip, so you will be mashing spacebar in order to make the seemingly interminable missions go a little bit faster.
There is very little variety, each unit has a handful of animations that you will get sick to death of within an hour. There are three acts to the campaign with WAY too many missions in each. You basically replay the same battle over and over with a slight shake up in unit composition. It's dull by the end of act 1 and then you realize that you're going to do it 2 more times, but with less and less of a chance each time.
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.

Updating my review because it's been a long time since the issues have been fixed and wanted my review to reflect the experience I've had with the changes.
Performance: Constant 60fps during gameplay with everything on high and no black bars. I have a GTX 970 and a Xeon E3 1230 V2.
Gameplay: 8/10
- Very satisfying and rewarding gameplay.
- If you like resident evil 4, you will love this game. It almost feels like a sequel to RE4, which isn't a bad thing.
- Some refinements have been made to the gameplay and mechanics over 4 and overall I find it much better. I like the new weapons, upgrade system, sneaking and cover mechanics, knifing, matches, etc. Feels like a mix of RE4 and RE 1 Remaster.
Graphics: 7/10
- Not as great as it could be, looks like a previous gen PS3 game. I guess they were limited by the last gen engine they used.
- That said the environments are varied and interesting, dark and grimey, just what you would expect in a survival horror game.
- The bosses are really cool too. Some people don't find them scary, but there were a few that creeped me out.
Story: 5/10
- Very confusing and hard to follow. I don't like how it's fragmented and all over the place. I've played the game a few times and there is still things I don't understand.
- The game got its inspiration from Inception, Matrix, and Shutter Island, so you can imagine what they were going for.
- I would have liked for the world to feel more connected, but you just go from one seemingly unconnected area to the next, there's no flow from one area to another. It broke the game up too much for me with each level not feeling connected to the last, but that's probably a personal preference.
Overall: 8/10
- Very good game overall, especially if you are a Resident Evil/Silent Hill/Survival horror game fan, it blends a lot of elements from these games together.
- The gameplay is very fun and rewarding, especially sneaking up on enemies and killing them silently to conserve ammo. There are many ways to play and strategies you can take.
- The story is a mess so what really motivated me to continue was the gameplay, The game was just very fun, story was really just an afterthought for me. If they can develop a better story for a sequel and iron out some of the issues with this game, they will have something great.
- The game is also very replayable, just like RE4. There's tons of challenges you can do once you complete the game, with other modes unlocking.

Having played quite a few other Sonic games and hearing that they were inferior to Sonic Adventure 2, I was excited to finally buy the game on sale. I've beaten the Last Story now, and while the game is a solid and fun experience, I couldn't help but wonder why classic Sonic fans put this one on a pedestal. Nostalgia is strong for them, I suppose - as a first-time player I couldn't help but be slightly underwhelmed, though I did enjoy the game.
Gameplay revolves around three different playstyles - the speed-based platforming of Sonic and Shadow, the mech-shooting of Tails and Eggman, and the treasure-hunting of Knuckles and Rouge. Personally, I felt like the Sonic/Shadow stages were the best-executed and are the ones that are legitimately fun to play; they involve high-speed movement combined with being on the lookout for alternate paths and bonuses. If you've only played the 3D Sonic games after Heroes, the constant changing speeds might be a little bit alienating, but it works quite well for the game.
The mech stages involve moving through a level and shooting just about everything you can. Your mech can lock on to enemies, item bubbles, and stage components, allowing you to blast them, rack up points, and clear a path through the level. These stages are probably the worst of the lot, mostly because your mech controls really weirdly and someone thought that putting in platforming that would be easy to mess up
the aforementioned control issues and the broken camera (more on that below) was a good idea.
The treasure-hunting stages are definitely not bad, but they have the most potential for tedium and frustration. Your character is tasked with finding three plot coupons in wide-open levels, and they're given a radar to help them find said coupons. These stages suffer from random placement of these targets, however; one time through the level they could be incredibly simple to find, while another time they might require deep exploration of each part of the level. Compounding this problem is the inability to view more than one of your targets on the radar, leading to not one, but three wild goose chases across the level if you're unlucky with the order of the targets. Parts of a level do little to distinguish themselves from one another, making exploration feel like a chore sometimes.
There's also a slight Metroidvania element in the game: an upgrade in each regular stage gives the character obtaining it a new permanent ability. These feel somewhat flawed as well: the ones needed to progress in the game are pretty much handed to you, while the ones required only for the additional missions are in tough-to-reach areas, which would be fine if the game didn't require you to get a good time to acquire an A rank.
Aside from the fun, though flawed, main stages, there are side games like kart racing and the incredibly-popular Chao Garden. Both of these activities are required for full completion, and they're both less than perfect: kart racing has little depth and difficult controls, while Chao-raising doesn't progress quickly enough (in my opinion; I can see the appeal of Chao raising, but I'm not a huge fan of it). For all of its rough edges, the game does have plenty of content, especially for completionists. There's also a 2-player mode (disclaimer: I bought the Battle DLC along with the main game) that is fun to mess around with, though it's certainly not the most deep or polished experience.
The game's aesthetics are dripping with cheesy early 2000's charm; whether that's a good thing or a bad thing is up to you. The graphics are bright and colorful, although they're definitely dated. The voice acting is pretty terrible, with Knuckles and Eggman being the only major characters with decently-voiced lines more than half the time. The soundtrack is excellent, as is usual for Sonic games, with different styles accompanying each character; if you don't like cheesy lyrics, you might be displeased with Sonic and Knuckles' stages, but I think they work really well in the game. The camera deserves a dishonorable mention here: it hinders every character's stages and has led to more than a few of my deaths playing through the game. It's especially egregious in Sonic's penultimate level, where gravity gets flipped while the camera doesn't, and the controls start acting weird to go along with it.
At the time of writing I had 24 hours put into the game and over half the emblems; despite the game's flaws, it's a lot of fun, and I definitely intend to go for all 180. Whether you'll enjoy the game will likely depend on whether you can look past the imperfections to see where the game shines. If you enjoy Sonic games, I'd definitely recommend you try this one out, possibly waiting for a sale; if not, Sonic Adventure 2 probably won't change your mind. It's not the end-all be-all of Sonic games, but it's a fun experience nonetheless.

Coming into this game from Hotline Miami is quite the suprise. While both game are superficially similar, it feels like they were built on completely different priorities; hotline miami 2 trades some of the first game's amazingly well designed gameplay for story depth and level variety.
+The soundtrack manages to outdo the first game. A wide variety of tracks and artists complement every level.
At times the game feels more like a rythm music game than a gritty, ultraviolent action game.
+The game tells an interesting narrative: the levels bounce between different characters, settings and time periods to expand on the first game's story.
+There are many different levels; where the first game saw the player clear dozens of mobster infected apartments, wrong number sees you fighting in jungles, boats, hotels, warehouses and banks, all drawn in wonderful pixel art.
~ There is a massive difficulty increase, compared to the first game. Beating wrong number one provides a hard mode that somehow pushes the challenge even further. By itself, it would not be a problem if not for...
-Weaker level design. While the levels themselves look georgous, they are often very frustating to play. Wide spaces filled with gun using ennemies that see you before you see them. Unlike the first game, there are quite a few levels that
feel cheap, or railroad you into using a particular strategy.
-Removal of the mask system: Wrong number lets you choose from 0 to 5 variation on your character for each level. It's no longer possible to choose your playstyle from level to level, or to retry a level with a different strategy.
For whatever its flaws might be, Wrong Number did not fall in the trap of being a mission pack sequel. It feels like a worthy addition to the first game's story, and provides more of its hectic gameplay and excellent music. It's a must play for any fan of the first game.

I would go as far as saying that Wings of Prey is not a simulator despite being advertised as such. Visuals in the game are great, but it plays more like an arcade shooter than a serious attempt at a combat simulator. It is not, however, all bad. Simulator styled cockpit view coupled with arcade-ish gameplay allows for greater "ace pilot" feel, since you'll be spending more time in the cockpit shooting at enemies, than floating slowly towards the ground with a parachute.
I would recommend this game to anyone who has maybe felt dissappointed after having a shot at IL-2 or other more realistic sims, and ended up on the ground in flames one too many times.

Brief summary of Wings of Prey:
A "Holywood" flight combat sim. Looks and sounds great, exciting to play, but lacks in mission design, AI and flight model.
+Lots of missions and planes.
+Great visuals. Variety of day/night and weather conditions. Nice effects: glare, cockpit scratches, damage (bullet holes, damaged ailerons, broken gauges etc.). Cockpits look great.
+Immersive 5.1 sound.
-Some of the missions in the campaign are frustratingly difficult. Some are bugged (e.g. objectives not triggering correctly).
-Stalls are a bit unrealistic.
-Poor documentation: Some things are never explained, like how the I-16 engine will die if you pull negative Gs, or how to use propeller pitch and radiator.
-Haven't played MP, but looks like online is basically dead.
~TrackIR is a big advantage, both for watching your six in dogfights and for spotting ground targets.
~Joystick (preferably HOTAS) is a must. Gamepad or keyboard+mouse won't cut it.

50-Mission Campaign (DLC Ork Campaign for $1)
2 Playable Races (Ork and Space Marines)
Skirmish Mode (Hotseat Multiplayer or Human vs Bot)
Online Multiplayer (Asynchonous and Real-Time)
2 Game Modes (Regicide and Classic Chess)
Multiple Factions (2 Space Marine, 2 Ork Unlocked at start, with more unlockable via in-game currency)
I personally found this game quite enjoyable, and it actually has rekindled my interest in chess. The combat animations and dialog add a unique flavor to each piece on the board, as well as each army. Kills are bloody, and satisfying, though if you wish to skip the animations of moving or the combat, just press spacebar.
The online multiplayer could definitely benefit from more players though, as sometimes you can find that there are not many people on at certain times of the day. Still, you can occasionally find yourself playing against one of the Developers themselves.
The Regicide Mode is played as a combination of Chess and a turn-based shooter, allowing you to kill units with both chess captures as well as unit abilities. More than once have I been saved by a unit ability in a game where defeat looked certain. Rule of thumb, Space Marines have more armor and more accurate guns, while Orks have more health and deadlier close-range attacks.
The campaign consists of entirely Regicide Mode, with various objectives (and secondary ones for bonus currency and experience) to mix things up. Currency can then be used to purchase more Ork Clans or Space Marine Chapters to play as online or in Skirmish, which have different abilities in Regicide. If you don't want to wait for one of your favorite chapters, they currently cost $0.99 each. (As does the Ork campaign)
All in all, this is an entertaining twist on chess that deserves much more attention than it currently has.

I'm going to be honest, I really wish Steam reviews had a neutral because I can both recommend and not recommend this game depending on the person. The nostalgia hits hard right off the bat and the game has a really good foundation to build upon. That being said the game/devs have a lot to work on and there are still a solid amount of glaring issues with the game. I almost think it's a bit unfair to judge the game in the current state because it really feels like EARLY EARLY ACCESS.
I've been a fairly long time player of AE games and hit level 15 before writing this review.
Progression while having a good foundation and core is pretty frustrating and most of the time not fun at all. Leveling feels a little to long past level 4 with quests just being repeats essentially (EX: Kill 4 Skeletons, Kill 7 Gargoyles, then Kill 10 Skeletons). It's utterly painful to level past 12-13, as there are only enough quests to get you there basically. After that your best option is to go to a bridge and spam 2 abilities the entire time until you're level 15. It's really honestly quite terrible because it's to much of a grind basically doing nothing. The main reason a lot of people automatically dislike this game is because you don't feel like your progressing essentially at all. The first few zones are fine but once you get a little deeper into the game the flaws really show. On top of that you will enter some zones under leveled/under geared due to there not being enough quests to level you up.
On another subject we have gear. Gear progression is surprisingly not terrible. In each zone the mobs drop crafting materials that you turn into gear. The gear then costs a bit of gold to craft and takes a certain amount of time, you can however pay to speed up the timer (not worth it at all unless you're extremely lazy/can't wait), timers range from 5 minutes -> 5 hours (with some minor items being 24 hours that you don't need) but generally fall into the 1-2 hour period. It's a really cool foundation for gear progression but can definitely fall culprit like level progression to feeling grindy at certain points. Level 15 is where the flaws start to show. You're basically forced to build more tanky to a degree because of how hard some mobs/bosses hit. Build diversity isn't great which is another glaring issue.
Honestly just making more enemy types to give variety would be a great addition to the game and give it a little flare. I understand AE is working on some more zones so we will see how those zones turn out.
Combat is fine, it's like any other RPG. You have your basic attack,  3 other abilities,  and basically 1 ultimate (although it just feels like 4 abilities). It can feel buggy at times due to what it feels like lag so that might just be the servers. You can animation cancel some abilities which is cool and adds a slight skill ceiling to the game. Aggro on the other hand needs some work. Right now the mobs target the biggest threat (aka the guy dealing the most damage) which is a pretty big problem. One class, The Guardian has a taunt of sorts but right after you use it if someone bursts really hard the boss automatically goes over to them which kinda sucks because Guardian is the one meant to be tanking. I get Artix doesn't want traditional tanks in a sense so the game isn't to easy but this leaves little room for DPS builds to shine due to how hard some level 15 mobs can hit (even the trash). Combat is honestly fine right now but can definitely be improved upon, hopefully we see some improvements in the future.
Oh boy you finally hit level 15 how exciting. I mean it is exciting to a degree, but there's not much to do. You do have a few options though. You can go back and finish off some quests you didn't do, farm the level 15 dungeon and craft some sweet new level 15 gear (you can also get some cool gear drops from the bosses there), farm Acevorah for Vorah dagger, farm event dungeons (if there are any going on if not you're out of luck on that front), go back to the bridge to farm Gold, help people and just mess around elsewhere. As you can see there isn't much to do. Sure there are some 1% drops you can get but that's honestly just fake progression that really doesn't amount to much other then showing off. While feeling powerful and carrying people through the final dungeon is fun it slowly loses it's exciting feel and goes back to being a little grindy especially on some Holiday content. Artix has said we can expect raids and stuff in the future so I still have hope. Like everything else it has a good foundation it just suffers from the game being so early into development.
I'm not gonna sit to much on this because there are only 4 Classes in the game. Mage (DPS), Rogue (DPS), Warrior (Tank/DPS), Guardian (Tank). It's to early to judge but it looks like they're going the route of all their past games with how they make classes. I urge Artix to look at some other cool mechanics they could use to make classes (a resource other than mana, 2 form characters (etc)). Classes are pretty cool but The Guardian class is locked behind a $20 paywall and is arguably the most fun class to play (well for me personally).
Oh boy. You're probably expecting this game to be filled with them everywhere due to it being an Artix game and also being able to be played on mobile. I'm gonna be honest, I was surprised at first with the lack of not being able to literally buy progression. Sure you can speed up crafting and stuff but it's ultimatley not worth it. It's headed in the right direction so lets hope and pray Artix doesn't screw it up and it ends up like basically all their other games. The only major paywall is The Guardian pack. You can pay either $20 or $50. The $20 version gives you the Class, 2500 of the games currency (Dragon Crystals), Guardian gear (which is fairly useless after early levels you can however upgrade the weapon to 15), access to the Guardian Tower with some fairly useless quests (I shouldn't say useless they've stated it will lead somewhere but for now it's pretty useless, Founder/Guardian Badge. The $50 on the other hand gives everything above, 7,500 more Dragon Crystals (10,000 in total), Dragon Guardian armour/wings (again useless past a certain point), and a pretty cool looking mount. These packages are actually a pretty good deal for the game, but are quite expensive for what the game is in its current state. These packages are a great way to support the Devs however so if you wan't to do that it's a great idea! Overall while you can pay for the game to progress faster it's not littered with micro-transactions YET.
I don't mind the graphics personally but I can see why you might. What they're going for is a classic feel back to their older games while still keeping it a bit fresh/updated in 3D. I personally like it but it definitely looks/feels outdated. You could blame the fact it needs to play on mobile as well. I know a lot of people care about graphics but honestly judge for yourself. Gameplay is a little buggy at times but overall fairly smooth so no real complaints there.
Honestly I'm bit hesitant to thumbs up this game due to some of its glaring issues. But Artix seems committed (well they kinda have to be due to their Kickstarter) so we will see what happens. Not to mention I sorta enjoyed the game even with its flaws. Like I've said multiple times the foundation the game was built upon is honestly fantastic and just needs to be worked on. I urge Artix not to rush the development and not release the game itself to early unless they're 100% satisfied with how the game works. Artix has a huge issue with its past games in the form of micro-transactions. So far it seems to be under control but we will see what the future holds. I will keep this review updated if anything drastically changes in the future.

Simulation-cake is a lie.
Handling is wack, probably broken by design. Drifting and slip is broken because the wheels dont seem to turn proportional to the car. Instead steering is proportional to some arcade vector.  I couldn't figure out why the game was handling so weird until I watched the car in 3rd person in replays.
For example, when you hold the steering wheel at +0% during oversteer - the car will straighten out towards your intial vector as if you are counter steering hard. (read: fishtail) If you want to drift or flick a 4WD/RWD, you have to keep oversteering while applying throttle because you are steering against the directional vector, not the actual slip angle! It's like joypad mechanics are hardcoded in the physics.
It takes a couple of hours of play to unlearn counter-steering, among other good habits. If you need to correct, carefully center the wheel instead.
Also, you need to disable most FFB to be able to play because the steering physics is so broken. Wheel friction, tire friction and tire slip FFB need to be set to 0; everything else can be adjusted to preference.
The game is actually fun to play once you learn steering techniques that will kill you the next time it snows on your way to work, and when you adjust the FFB the game isn't trying to steer you into a ravine and you can do some clean stages.
Everything else is OK. The co-driver is bad at keeping pace on procedurally generated tracks; and why is there a helicopter making a dust storm on a brake-point before a hard 3?

Don't buy, unless you intend to casually play with a gamepad.

If you're looking at this and wondering if you should get this game, you probably should. I can't believe I nearly passed on this great game because of mixed reviews on Steam. If it's on sale, buy it now.
I'm a sim racing fan through and through, but given the varied difficulty settings I'd recommend this game to sim and arcade racing fans.
For those that have played Dirt Rally:
This is not a sequel to Dirt Rally! That said, you could easily justify having both these games in your library, because they offer slightly different experiences that are both great fun in their own way.
I'm not sure which is more realistic in terms of driving physics, but Dirt 4 is definitely less brutal than Dirt Rally. Dirt Rally was hard to learn, and very hard to master. Dirt 4 is easy to learn, and potentially hard to master if you increase the difficulty settings. Use simulation handling, turn off all assists and crank up the AI difficulty and this game is a real challenge even for Dirt Rally veterans.
What makes Dirt 4 easier to learn is the tracks being slightly wider. It may not sound like much but it makes a big difference compared to the extremely narrow tracks in Dirt Rally. Both are great in their own way, but the wider tracks encourages you to push your car to the edge consistently.
Where Dirt 4 really seperates itself is in the experience itself, it really makes you feel like a rally driver with small touches. Here's what's new in Dirt 4 compared to Dirt Rally:
- You have to launch the car yourself instead of simply waiting for the countdown to finish.
- You can't just fly across the finish line and abandon the controls, you have to slow down the car and bring it to a stop in front of the marshal.
- The damage repair section is a lot more in depth and realistic. You can wash the car and do inspections to get more accurate estimations of the damage and how long each component will take to fix.
- The career mode is a lot more fleshed out. Different licenses as you progress, the option to race for other teams or your own, hiring staff, improving team facilities, buying cars new or from the classifieds, sponsors, livery design, etc.
The pros:
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Great sound design
- Graphics
- Immersion (lots of small touches to make you feel like you're in a real rally competition)
- Rally training facility
The cons:
- Only 5 countries for rally racing
- Damage is perhaps too forgiving (similar to Dirt Rally), some more settings here would have been nice
