The water looks fantastic, and there are a lot of really good elements to this game, but there are some unfortunate killer flaws that bring me to not recommend it.
The first and most important issue is there is a point in the game you simply can not go past due to a design issue.  Forums indicate that this is somewhat random and may be passable by messing with video settings.  The problem there is your card/driver/settings should never impact the mechanics of the game, and the issue is a jump that can't be made due to distance.  Very odd, and it was the nail in the coffin for this one.
Up until that point I almost had to stop playing it several times because the number one way the game lives up to it's name is by making you sea sick.  The camera follow is abysmal, whipping around randomly as you go in and out of water, up and down from ladder to platform, and even just trying to swim around under water.  The violent thrashing of the camera, and some times inability to look past a very confined point when you need to look around is just terrible.
Had those two issues been addressed in the years since release, it would at least be an enjoyable play with some engaging visuals.  It has a good balance of strategic shooter and light puzzle solver familiar to other games of the genre.
Past that however, you note a couple other problems.  For one, it's very short.  Given what I read from those who were able to play the whole game, the killer point I mentioned is quite near the end.  That means the total play time is 4 hours or less.  Also, while they clearly had a great back story to the game world, very little of it is shared in the game.  This leads you to feel lost while things are being talked about in a very matter of fact way.  While not entirely unusual in similar games, the fact that bad guys just appear out of nowhere with no reason (didn't come in by door, just popped up) is off putting.  It's also quite obvious the bad guys must have gills, because unlike you they can stay under water indefinitely.  There is also the matter of the water control powers.  Apparently you get those right at the end, so I never got to experience them, but saving something like that for the last 20 minutes of the game?  Odd choice in my opinion.  In the end, other than the sea sickness there really is never a sense of fear of the water, which makes one wonder if there was an element the developers just failed to convey given the implied back story.
All told, if you take a sea sick pill and get the game on a super steam sale for $1, it will pass a couple hours, and how hard can you complain for $1?  Well, I guess about as hard as this review...

Aeon Command is a linear game, where your mother ship is at the left end of a space area and the enemy mother ship is at the right end.
You mine resources and then use the resources to build ships (there are extra ships to unlock, research to be done, and upgrades to be had).
The unlocks are on the main menu; not in game, as I had expected, so it took a while to find them (doh).
As soon as you build your warships, they head off to attack the enemy.
You can't issue commands to your ships, such as getting them to attack a particular enemy, hold position, retreat, or whatever - so that sucks; it limited the tactical abilities of the game severely.
As an aside, I'm not sure if one achievement is broken or not, "Destroyer: Destroy 5,000 ships."
Despite destroying many ships, I have 0/5,000 for this achievement.
Maybe it's only for multiplayer games (if it is, it certainly doesn't say so), but when I tried to have a multiplayer game, there were no other players available - so, maybe that says a lot for the game in itself.
This is a very limited game. It might be ok for 5 to 12 year olds, who don't have high expectations.
Apart from that, I wouldn't bother with it - unless you have some time to waste and nothing better to do.

This is a cute, attractive, colourful, cheesy, funny and entertaining co-op dungeon crawler. You are an ugly little naked goblin who can partner with up to three more folks to work your way through a randomly generated dungeon, collecting coins, killing bosses and buying upgraded gear. It's a roguelike; if you die and your team mates can't resurrect you, you lose your coins and it's bye-bye back to the checkpoint. The checkpoint is the beginning of each dungeon level; so if you're still on the first set of rooms it's game over. If you've progressed a bit further, you will save some progress and your level.
The rooms are varied, with chasms over lava, the occasional platform to jump on, obstacles to avoid and so on - allowing for plenty of kiting. And kiting is what you will be doing for the majority of the game. Most of the enemies are damage sponges but can be killed by evading them and using a ranged weapon. Some of them have different strengths and weaknesses, such as shields that need to broken, enemies that explode in melee, enemies that have ranged attacks or special attacks etc. There's also bosses which are pretty cool and unique.
You get a special ability that's on cooldown that is pretty powerful, and a weapon ability that's slightly powerful and on a shorter cooldown and can buy new weapons and armor from the shop after looting all the things to upgrade your attacks. I found some hats (top hat on a goblin?! Yes please!) and changed my chest, but I couldn't find any pants. This is actually quite critical in this game, since you're a naked, male goblin and I really don't need to see goblin ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (apparently steam censors anatomical words, okay) all day long. Is it really practical to be dangling that about with fire and swords and crossbows?
You collect mushrooms to heal and to throw at the enemies. If you get a bad mushroom, you also suffer the effects of it, so you've got to be careful you don't get poisoned or stunned or set on fire because those things really don't feel very good. There is an element of PvP in that you can actually stun other players too and then steal their money - quite rude. You can also mount your friends, if that's your kinda deal, and stacked on top of each other your special ability becomes more powerful. I don't know what kind of friends you have, but if I was going to knock mine out and then mount them, I'd probably get a few complaints.
The problem is in the playerbase, as is so often the case with any co-op game. I couldn't find many people to play with - I did host a game and have a couple of people join me, but they ended up snowballing (mushroomballing?) me at annoying times and I can only imagine they were giggling to themselves as I died thanks to my "team mates". I'm not sure that mechanic is well suited to random groups. I'm sure there are some players out there who aren't jerks, but the playerbase seems to be absolutely tiny so you've not got a lot to work with. You're also encouraged by the achievements to attack and steal from your fellow players, so I can't really blame folks for doing it - but when it's people you don't know and costs you your life, it can get frustrating.
Ultimately, you really need to bring your own friends to the party. You can always play by yourself, but it really feels like the game is designed to be played with a full party as you won't have any option to be rezzed, to upgrade your special ability or to work as a team when kiting, so loners may need to give this a miss. I did manage to get to the boss on level 2 by myself several times, but alas, he bested me repeatedly. I don't want to sound like a total pariah, I do actually have a few friends - but not willing to drop £10 on this game right now. Perhaps the playerbase will increase during a sale.
I do want to love this game; but a lack of friends makes it a lot duller than it should be for me. I'd love for this to get a big population so that there were easier ways of finding folks to play with.

Looterkings, developed by Looterkings, published by Looterkings, and released in August of 20Looterkings, is an indie cooperative roguelike for up to four players. The premise is simple enough, you and up to three others are lowly goblins fighting their way up from the dungeon depths, gathering as much loot as you can along the way, purchasing upgrades, and competing to earn upgrade cards.
The game is potentially very fun. The rooms that comprise the dungeon are varied, with plenty of monsters to fight and gold to collect. The weapons and armor are varied, and are where the
game shows a great deal of it's humor. Armor ranges from diapers to tee shirts to top hats, and the weapons vary from toys to trash to furniture. It gives a very appropriate impression of poor but clever goblins improvising wargear. These pieces of wargear also all contribute ingredients to form the 'god ability', a powerful spell on a relatively long cooldown. Killing bosses awards stat boosts for the current run, and at the end of each level, the players are awarded gems to contribute towards permanent discounts. Card based permanent upgrades are awarded based on whoever completed the special challenge, such as taking the most damage.
This forms the gameplay loop, and is a workable backdrop for palling around with three of your friends, but it's not without issues. Ranged combat lacks a crosshair, and shots will often head
in seemingly arbitrary directions, especially when firing of a slope. The melee combat doesn't feel much better. The goblins have no defensive maneuvers outside of some of the god powers to
avoid damage, so running into the arms of the enemies to attack just becomes a boring way to kill yourself. Both forms of combat have special abilities with agonizingly long animations, making
them almost unusable if you don't think you can afford the damage.
Finally, the studio is trying to form a cooperative experience with true interaction between players, but the choices they made for this seem odd. Players can throw excess mushrooms at one
another to stun and rob each other. Although this certainly fits in with the mischievous nature of the characters, it risks turning the game into a near constant snowball fight. It feels
unnecessarily adversarial and is ripe for frustration. Secondly, the 'stacking' mechanic is weak. One player can mount another Freak the Mighty style. One player attacks, the other runs, and both god powers are upgraded. Aiming your weapon while riding on top is difficult and confers little bonus, and being legs is simply boring. The only reason to stack is to utilize the upgraded spells, but is inconvenient enough I don't even want to bother. I would have loved to see the stacking either removed as unnecessary or wildly buffed and given a special cooldown.
Looterkings allows for a 4-player roguelike romp which is a rare treat, and has hours of content with more on the way. However, with it's current control and design quirks, it should probably be regarded more as a casual party game than a 'serious' rogue entry, for better or for worse.

If you count the time before it's Steam release, I think I've been playing this game for a couple thousand hours.
First of all: The game is still called a "Beta", because the developers plan to add even more content in the future and don't want to call it a "full" game, yet. It is not some bug-haunted piece of software without any content to it, if you are afraid about that.
Secondly: You don't need to own any Source engine game to play PVKII. Just go to the Steam Store and start downloading it!
And as a third point: Some negative reviews criticized the unrealistic damage displayed for some attacks. The damage display is a plugin for "SourceMod" and has nothing to do with the PVKII base game. It is known that this plugin is not optimized for PVKII and sometimes displays improper damage. Therefore, most people use it only as a "hit detector" on certain servers.
Speaking of the game itself: It has so much love in it, you can see it everywhere: The voice acting is one of the best I've seen in a game - even retail ones. The voices and the beautifully crafted, slightly comic-styled models give each class a real "personality". The design of the stock maps fits the game's theme perfectly and the community has created a lot of good custom maps so far.
I have to admit that the population in the game is not the biggest, but it is always possible to find a full server or fill one quickly. The learning curve is steep and you will encounter many good players with hundreds or thousands of hours play time. While this could be frustrating for new players, it keeps the fights always challenging. In the end, the game is all about team play and even good players might not be able to win a game against a team working together really well.
The last thing I want to mention here is the rate of updates: There aren't as many updates as in other games, but it already takes quite some time to get into the game. You have to practice with each class for a while to be good with it. Creating classes and doing other major updates takes time. Especially since classes are not random models, but - as I mentioned before - real personalities and have a lot of references to literature and movies. There is also a lot of actual play testing by experienced beta testers involved before a release. This means that none of the updates has brought any balance problems with it so far. It always became better and each new class has been integrated really well.
I can only recommend to try out this game and want to thank everyone for reading my review!

(Note: I have the game on iOS and have logged additional hours there also. - I consider this game to be far better on iOS due to the platform and game-time opportunity.)
Regicide is a polished, well-assembled, turn-based strategy game set in the Warhammer 40K universe.  With a great musical score and absolutely top-notch graphics/aesthetic design, Regicide uses chess rules combined with an expanded TBS framework to provide an interesting twist on turn-based warfare.  It is important to clearly underscore that the Regicide graphics are the finest representation of space marines and the Warhammer 40K universe ever presented within video gaming.  While the game is very tightly assembled, the game does lack a significant amount of depth.  A game with vehicles, and multiple upgrade options, as well as races would do a lot to justify its 30-40 dollar price.
Still, for a chess-TBS hybrid set in the Warhammer 40K universe, Regicide is a worthwhile diversion.
7/10.

Great game, although it is still in development and it still will be until about mid 2017... If you wanna play a complete game with lots of features, tons of content, and little to no bugs, you'd best wait until then... However if you wanna give it a try anyway then you're in for a different kind of MMORPG experience. First off, the game is true-cross-platform. What does that mean? It means that the game is playable on Steam (on PCs and Macs) on Google Play (for Android devices) and The App Store (for iOS devices), but get this... Regardless of what device you're using, you will be playing the game on the same server as everyone else, regardless of what device they're using. I could be on my iPad while you're on your Android phone and we'd still be able to play together! Pretty cool, right? But don't worry, the Steam version and mobile versions each have their own user interface which are constantly being improved. If you've played any of Artix Entertainment's previous games (especially in the early stages) you'll enjoy this latest edition to their line up.
You're all probably wondering my game time is so high for a game that isn't even officially released yet... (I'm not even gonna talk about why I have 6 in-game accounts >.>) This doesn't even count the hundreds of hours I spent playing on the web version before the game got moved to Steam or the time I spend playing on mobile, so yeah, why is it so high? That's because I believe in this game and its future, not only that but the game is really fun!! I'm a proud Kickstarter Backer and I've been playing games from this company for over 10 years. It's like a dream come true to watch one of my all time favorite games be remade in 3D. Artix Entertainment is a small company with a ginormous dream. People laughed at them and said they couldn't do it, but here they are, making the impossible possible. The game is far from finished and has tons of room to improve, but it will. Because that's how AE works. They listen to players and make the game something that everyone can enjoy. If they make a promise, you can count on them to keep it.

I would love to give an honest review about the story, characters, development etc, but I can't play long enough to progress in the game without getting motion sick. I feel a little bit guilty for writing a review of this game before writing one for SA1, but that's just how it goes sometimes. I played probably well over a hundred hours of SA1 on the Gamecube back in the day, but haven't played the PC version to its fullest, which is why this SA2 review comes first. So, here we go.
It's a fun game. We can debate about whether it's a good game, or better than SA1, but that's besides the point right now. It's an enjoyable experience that does suffer from some clunky gameplay. There are 6 playable characters, split into 3 playstyles which all have their ups and downs.
-Sonic and Shadow: Doing your standard running and stuff you'd expect from a sonic game.
-Tails and Eggman: Shooting up robots.
-Knuckles and Rouge: Treasure hunting and flying around.
So I guess it's time to talk about the quality of the gameplay of each of these categories. I will try to avoid comparing them to SA1.
(sidenote: Play this game with a controller)
The running stages are fun the second time through. Some may disagree, but I have to stick by my statement. Look, we all remember playing the Sonic Adventure games and feel that the running stages were easy. But that's because we played them so much we practically had every turn and jump memorized. So take off the nostalgia goggles, and try to imagine a first time run through a stage. It's tough. It's super tough. So new players, just understand that you're going to have a tough time with these. But when you go back through to unlock the extra emblems, these will be much easier. I've grown to consider the running stages to be well designed, but that's because I see them from a casual speedrunner's perspective.
The shooting stages are alright. Hold "B" and let go to win. It's really just a matter of timing and spinning to get through these stages. There's some "platforming", but not in the way we think to 3D platforming games, like Jak and Daxter. Playing through the first time, it's just a quick run and gun through each of these. But you end up revisiting these stages the most after completing the game to get the little glowy things for your chaos. I will revisit that later.
Treasure hunting is... different. It's not that it's bad, it's just that some stages are astronomical in size. I spent close to 30 minutes in "Meteor Herd", and if given the choice, I would not play that stage or the Rouge variant again. A common complaint I hear about the treasure hunting is that it's "Too slow for a Sonic game", and you know what, it probably is. But an important thing to remember is that franchise names do not dictate gameplay. Think of treasure hunting as a bonus, a time to let your nerves calm just a bit after a Sonic/Shadow sprint. The difficulty of each stage it dictated by its size, because of the radar system. On the basic missions in each one, the placement of the emeralds is random, which makes getting an "A" rank tough sometimes. The only thing tougher in the game is the driving missions.
So there it is, a complete Sonic game. But if that was it, why is this one of the two most praised Sonic games of all time? Oh yeah, because there's a frick ton more content.
First off, multiplayer. It's supposedly the best Sonic multiplayer of all time. I wouldn't know, I don't have friends over much these days and we're usually too busy screaming while playing through Outlast to bother with Sonic multiplayer. From what I can tell, the multiplayer has several modes, the stages are well layed out, and you can even race your chaos you raised in the garden.
Emblem collection is a pain. It really is. Every stage has an additional 4 missions to complete, and some of them are annoying or straight up difficult. If you want to 100% your achievments, you need to commit to mastering this game and not play anything else. The hardest achievments are to earn every emblem, and to get an "A" rank in every mission. I'll see you in a year when you're done. Good luck.
There's a boss battle mode, which is timed. There's a kart racing mode, which I can't win to save my life. And then there's the best part of the entire game...
THE CHAO GARDEN! A game developer could spend billions on R&D and never come close to creating anything as well crafted, cute, and satisfying as the chao garden. You start out with a couple eggs, they hatch adorable little chao babies, you pet them, feed them fruit, send them to school, name them, then pump them full of steroids and watch them beat the crap out of each other. It's awesome, I have no other words for it. I am not ashamed to admit that close to a third of my hours in the game have been spent on farming Prison Lane for vials of glowy stuff to feed my chaos. You thought Stardew Valley had a lot of farming? Nah, this game takes the cake and will never be unseated. Your life is now owned by your chaos, and you will be happy about it.
Overall, I think it's a good game. It has its many issues, but I believe it makes up for it in its charm and replay value. This game is considered a classic, and for good reason. Many video games have fandoms that push people away from them because of how obsessive they are over loving their game more than anything else. Not this game. This fandom is too busy screaming and throwing crap at the SA1 fandom, and vice versa. So if you're a sadist looking to watch little creatures beat each other up, and join a borderline-violent fandom, this is your game.

I was leary about buying this, but it's cheap and I figured what the hell. My experience pretty much went like this: installed the game, then it installed uPlay, which crashed repeated. Found solution was to uninstall uPlay and then re-install it. Okay, then it made it to the game and I started a new career. Went through the minimalist tutorial and then discovered the missions are glitched and won't show up on the first attempt at the career. So you have to restart it and skip the tutorial. Fine. I start out in port on a new patrol and realize there's a glitch where your periscope always starts raised. This basically continues... you play a while, and find another glaring bug or the game crashes.
On the brightside, it looks pretty and is fun in an arcady way when it works, but it should never be considered a simulator. I waltzed into Scapa Flow totally surfaced and sank several ships without the British even showing the slightest sense of alarm. I almost deckgunned a battleship to death there and probably would have been successful... but the game CTD'd before I got the chance. The AI just sucks. The only chance of death in this game is from running aground or hitting another ship in time compression.
Furthermore, what really annoys me are the fundamental flaws with this game that fancies itself a simulator. For instance, when I started out, realizing I hadn't adjusted the difficulty and had unlimited fuel, I decided to just go on a joyride. I'll leave Kiel and head up over the north pole and over to Alaska and down the coast of Asia, I thought. Then I realized the map is horribly flawed and the developers apparently believe the world is a cylinder and not the oblate spheroid I was taught about growing up. That meant my "shortcut" over the pole wasn't going to be so short. This also means it reduces the range your sub has from what it would be in reality. I liked this game more than I disliked it, that is why I clicked "yes recommend" this game.  The reality is this game is, for me, very average and disappointing in many ways.
My biggest complaint about this game is that it was short.  Like really really short.  It has 3 stages and then it ends, though the stages are fairly long it doesn't really help the matter.  Stemming from that, the story for this game was very ill-handled, by which I mean it wasn't handled.  You get a bit of backstory about how the world basically turned into a new, uninhabitable Pangea, with one giant ocean that a giant city on a boat sails on with all the sane/not criminal members of humanity, and there's a terrorist cell that lives/was exiled to the dried up husk of a continent who think humanity is ruining/ruined the world and needs to die.  There's a lot that they could have done with this to flesh the story out and be something unique or unique-ish, but the story is basically in the background the whole game.  The worst part of this complaint focuses on the main character: an engineer on the ship named Kate Wilson who it is implied by the title has hydrophobia.  This would be a really interesting twist considering how much of the game revolves around water in different gameplay elements (haha, pun) but the only times it really comes up or affects anything is in the beginning when her coworker tells her she can do this, and when she stays underwater for awhile you hear a little girl laughing, which hints at why she has hydrophobia, but it's never explained or explored, and otherwise she might as well not have it at all.
The only other complaint I have concerns the water-manipulating aspect of the game, which you don't "unlock" until the 3rd stage, and when you do all you do is raise water into a pillar to splash something or raise something in the water up into the air to touch something for some reason or another.  I can get why they would start out with only this because she's new to this ability, and if the game were longer maybe they would develop that further so she learns how to use water differently, but sadly the game ends before it can get to that point.  At least we got to see the cool-looking glowing effect on her arm for a little bit.
I lied earlier, I have one other complaint that I would have tried to go back and integrate into the first complaint paragraph but I don't feel like putting in that kind of effort right now.  The ending itself is really disappointing.  You (spoilers!) kill the terrorist leader and kill the nanites that are giving you water-bending powers from eating your insides out, then basically pass out of relief and the credits role.  No thought is given about the giant ocean-liner with a city that has hundreds of people living on it that's sinking into the ocean, and I guess the rest of the terrorists that were stealing more of those deadly nanites gave up when some psychic call went out about their leader dying.
The gameplay was pretty fun, reminded me of Tomb Raider like it reminded everyone else of Tomb Raider.  The graphics looked good, nothing fancy but was nice to look at.  And of course the water physics were exellent.
I may have been slightly drunk while writing this.  I'm sorry.

I quite like this game, but unless you have some pals to play it with, I can't really recommend it. Even on Normal, I feel like the AI never cease to let me down.
There's some things I think the game needs improvement on:
- The AI is remarkably stupid. They can't defend themselves from special rats and don't prioritize saving others. They usually end up staring at you getting dragged away until they notice something's off.
- Rat Ogres feel like they have way too much health. Unless it's because I usually play with my one friend and us two are the only ones who are actually hitting it, then that kind of just goes back to my first point where the AI is sort of useless.
- It seems like getting decent loot for the character you want takes forever. Yes, a trinket was added to increase the chances there, but even so, unless you play on higher difficulty, you'll be stuck with white rarities for a while. For the most part, it's really just luck. There's a chance you'll get what you want quickly, and there's also a chance you'll be stuck getting crap over and over again. Some sort of boost to help speed this along would be great.
- No checkpoints. This is good and bad. If you just want to casually play through the levels, it'd be nice if there was some sort of checkpoint system, since some stages can seem to drag on. Plus, if you lose the stage you get a pity reward of some shards that can be used for crafting which is a rather meager reward. Maybe something like sacrificing a dice to restart at a half-way point, opposed to having start over from the beginning.
- Empty chests. I don't know if this was intentional, but it's a bit annoying. A lot of chests you open simply have nothing in them. To me, it would make more sense to have less chests on the map, but guarantee there was something in them every time.
Anyway, since I posted this as a positive review, I should probably list what I actually like about it. The setting is unique and very cool. I really dig the abandoned gothic fantasy feel it gives off, and the rat enemies are creepy and fitting. I like how powerful you feel mowing down hordes of rat babies.
While, I dislike how luck orientated the loot system is, I do like the idea of stats and weapon choice for this sort of game. It gives a bit of motivation to complete levels and a good reason to try harder difficulties. It would just feel more rewarding if it was something you would actually use.
Coming from someone who finds L4D2 somewhat boring, yes I can see how easy it is to compare the two. They are quite similar in formula and structure. However, it's worth trying out even if you dislike L4D2 because you might actually enjoy this game.
Also, apparently a DLC pack is coming out with some free aspects to it, so that's cool.
I give it a high-five / 10.

Big win.  If you loved the L4D games, you'll be right at home here.  I like this even better.  It feels like L4D just suddenly evolved into this different world but at the same time, offers enough new change and a bit of loot based progression to make me feel much more invested in my character.
It has very intuitive controls, and a nice fluid feel in combat.  While it's easy to just pop on and play and even do fairly well, there is also a lot of room for skilled players to set themselves apart from the pack.
The visual and audio elements are done wonderfully.  A great soundtrack to go with the maps, audible clues as gameplay notifications, and it all sounds very clean and clear no matter how messy things get in battle, except when it shouldn't, like when you're about to bleed out.  ;)
The graphics are great, nice high res performance, rich textures, and plenty of eye candy options if you want to push your GTX 960 to the edge, like I do.  On an older card, like a GTX460(tested this) - you'll still get pretty nice quality video, nothing that you'd ever sneer at, and with very acceptable performance.
At first glance, the game doesn't seem to have the story at the level L4D did, but as I play it through, the interactions of the characters continue to bring out more and more, bit by bit, and it all comes together very nicely.
At full price, this game is absolutely worth the money.  It will remain especially so if the developers produce some more DLC, preferably maps and game modes, so that it doesn't become repetitive.
If you catch it on a steam sale, buy more than one copy.  You'll want to give some to your friends.  The community is very nice, as a refreshing change of pace, but it still feels a bit small.  I'll definitely consider future titles from Fatshark.

This review might change in the future, but for now it's this.
While at first it looks promising and it does deliver a few things to tinker with, it's still quite barebones.
My review is kind of biased, since I'm getting tired of all these 'sandbox' games, that feel more like tools the developer made to create the actual game, but never did. As of writing the review, the game version is 0.1.11, which means that it has a long road to go, until it gets to the complete version. It might get faster after it's up on steam, but at this point it's believing on the promises the devs made, and I already have trust issues with most early access titles in the past, that seemed really promising, but did not go in the way I thought they would.
See, the problem is, I see this as a promising game, but when it gets to thinking about the future of it, it can go many ways, and only a few make me want to play it. There are a lot of questions that the game does not answer. And we are not talking about the creative mode, we are talking about the other gamemodes, that will actually make the game challenging.
Will it be more like Factorio, where you make automated factories for extracting resources, or do I have to grind everything like Minecraft?
Are most of the stuff cosmetic, or would they have an actual use? The electricity panel, the pipes, etc.
Would my car run out of fuel, so I'll have to extract fuel to make it run?
Is it going to get more in-depth, or is it going to get more content to work with? I prefer the former, since I'm already tired of all the games that provide the second. Can you promise me that? No.
For example, I saw 'Multiplayer', and when you first hear multiplayer, you are thinking about a server list to join in. Nope, you make a world and invite your friends to play with. I personally am not fan of that kind of 'multiplayer'. I want to join and do stuff with random players, not convince my friends to buy the game, so I have to play it, in a specific hour, and a certain period of time. I don't want to be dependent on that, I want randoms that go around in circles and do stupid stuff, so I don't feel like the last person on the planet.
Will it improve? Probably. Can you promise me that? No.
The game currently doesn't give me any info on how is it going to be developed further. Sure, I can ask the developers, but there are two factors - Player feedback, and realization. If most of the players want more content, and it gets more content, then I paid for a game other people want, not me. Then it's the realization, I might speculate all day how it's going to be done, but in the end, they are going to do it their way.
So, should you buy it? Depends.
Do you want minecraft meets GMod? Yes.
Do you want in-depth resource management, and complex contraptions that go beyond a house-car transformer? Wait, and see how it goes.
In the end, we've gotten to a stage where 'Early Access' titles are not even in Beta, nor Alpha, but merely Prototypes of the actual game.
Basic controls. Check.
Core mechanics. Check.
Map to explore. Check.
And by reaffirming the devs with all the positive reviews, and that it looks 'promising', you are going to see a lot of future titles, that are no more than prototypes that look 'promising'.
Castle story also looked 'promising'.

4.7 Hours on record - here's what I think.
All in all, I enjoy the game.  It's not a particularly complex, or in-depth strategy game, but to those who enjoyed the flash game Age of War, it will be entertaining.  The interface allows keyboard commands, which increases playability significantly.  There are campaigns to go through, but my favorite part is playing scramble in scenario mode, where each unit is randomly selected front one of the playable races.  It's generally a resource management game, where you try to mine as much as possible and upgrade your units as fast as possible while keeping the enemy at bay so you can eventually overwhelm them.  It is surprisingly replayable, because there are times that I have had matches lasting 3 minutes, and sometimes they last 10.  I would recommend this game as an intermitten time waster, because if you sit down and drill through, you will beat this game very quickly.

Warband was used for most of the CGI work in the movie Gladiator, as well as Troy, and more recently Thor: the dark world.
MBW provides a fun and interactive programming environment that is robust and utilitarian. Warband has become the staple programming language used in software development of FIlms and video games. It has even surpassed Java and provides a steadily growing competitor to HTML5 for most web based applications recently.

Greetings!  Welcome to my review of The Evil Within.   I don't generally post reviews before completing a game, but if you're anything like me you enjoy reading what other intelligent gamers like yourself have to say about something before plunking down that AAA cash.  Grab a drink and snack, we have some ground to cover.

I noticed while reading through initial reviews marked "most helpful" that all of the negative reviews seem to discuss a couple of similar points, so we'll start there.  The aspect ratio, or should I say THE ASPECT RATIO!!!!11  seems to fuel the majority of these negative feelings.  TEW utilizes a 2:35:1 cinematic aspect ratio.  I didn't find it to be an issue at all, but I do believe that the size of your screen and your relative distance from it could play a part in your personal enjoyment of the game.  On a larger screen or a small screen right in front of you it creates a mild sense of claustrophobia and panic, even in outdoor areas.  Given that the aspect ratio was discussed at length multiple times on a variety of forums before the game was released, I didn't feel at all surprised by it.  Furthermore, as everyone currently playing the game had access to the same information before release, negative reviews based on the aspect ratio should be taken with a grain of salt.  The "black bars" efffect isn't something that everyone will like or appreciate, but ignorance is never a good reason for a negative opinion.
Not to be outdone by aspect ratio negativity, that old favorite frame rate rears it's head in a multitude of reviews as well.  Out of the box, TEW is locked to 30fps.  It runs smoothly at 30fps and feels like you're watching a horror movie from the 80s.  The preivews and interviews I read leading up to release did not mention that it would be set to 30fps in the PC version specifically, so I can understand the frustration with the frame rate a bit more than the aspect ratio.  I would suggest playing the game initially as presented, but Bethesda has already posted a concise guide on how to alter the frame rate and the aspect ratio via the console if you so choose:
All standard disclaimers apply to utilizing the console.  It may impact your playing experience negatively as it is not a officially supported way to play the game.  That being said, Bethesda does plan to fix glitches associated with playing the game at 60fps in the future.
Let's now move on to "optimization".  The phrases "poorly optimized" and "well optimized" are thrown around so much they mean very little.  Without an explanation all I hear is "it doesn't run well on my computer" or "it runs well on my computer".  These opinions are important as they give a statistical point of comparision.  It does need to be pointed out however, that based on how the information is presented to you the source(s) may have no idea what they're talking about.  TEW runs well on a variety of systems.  I've had the opportunity to test it on three different computers and with some setting changes it ran at a steady 30fps on all three.   I consider the game to be well optimized not because it runs well, but because it can be adjusted and runs well on very different computers.  I did adjust the frame rate to 60fps on a PC utilizing an Nvidia 800 series card and other than some minor animation and pop up issues experienced no problems at all despite it being currently unsupported.  Keep in mind you will need a powerful rig to "max" the settings and run the game at higher than 30fps.  This should go without saying, but I will say it anyway: Update your video card drivers BEFORE you start playing the game.  If you are going to be playing TEW on a laptop with an Nvidia card and Nvidia Optimus, create a new profile for the game in the nividia control panel BEFORE you start playing.  This will eliminate the most common startup issues with TEW.
Everyone still with me?  Good.  If anyone would like more detailed information on the computers TEW was tested on and the settings used to achieve the test results, please drop me a line.
Okay, on to the fun stuff.  TEW is a brutal but loving tribute to a survival horror era gone by.  If it was released in 2004 instead of 2014 I believe it would have been a game of the year nominee.  It looks alot like a Silent Hill game and plays like a Resident Evil 4/The Last Of Us greatest hits mash-up.  If you long for the PS2 era of survival horror games this game was made for you.  The environments are a sight to behold, disturbing and beautiful in equal measure.  The gore level is intense without being ridiculous.  The enemies you face are detailed and terrifying.  The sound effects and score set the tone very well.  The controls are tight and feel very natural with a controller.  The only thing that pulled me out of the experience was the other human characters that you interact with on occasion.  The textures and voices for these characters really don't fit with the look and feel of the rest of the game, and the effect is jarring.  This was most noticable to me in the opening cut scene conversation.  The feeling of hit and miss textures and voice acting is a fleeting one though, you will spend most of your time killing or being killed by some of the most detailed nightmares in gaming.
To answer what is in my opinion the most important question about any game, TEW is a great deal of fun to play.  The scare tactics used aren't original, but they are varied and used to great effect throughout.  If you enjoy horror games The Evil Within is absolutely a must play.  9/10
EDIT: It has been brought to my attention that although the aspect ratio is said to be 2:35:1 it actually is not.  Al informed me of this (Thank you Al!) and I have verified it.  The game is locked to 16:9 with letterboxing (or pillarboxing if you prefer) when played on a 21:9 monitor.

Every negative review I have read seems to just be complaining about how the games looks/runs or black bars or fps locks and whatnot, but not saying anything about the actual game itself. I personally have no problems with fps, and I don't mind the black bars at all. The game is very enjoyable and feels very much like Resident Evil 4 which I loved so much. I'll keep this short and just say if you enjoyed RE4, get this game. It's a little more stealth based and you have to make sure you conserve your ammo, but it's quite enjoyable and is pretty challenging.

I've never written a review before but I felt compelled to because of a release week flood of ridiculous hate reviews. They are written like children whining about two things, fps and aspect ratio. Both of which are very subjective details. I am honestly having a great time with the game. My graphics card only has 2 GB of Vram and it is running this game like a beast. If you like Survival Horror games with bit of stealth, this is right up your alley. Resource management is key and the game has mechanics from the RE remake (burning enemies) and the general gameplay of RE 4 plus a bit of stealth. The frame rate is locked to 30 fps but it is rock solid with no hitches for me. The aspect ratio is kind of weird at first but by the time the intro played out I didn't even notice it. Maybe it's because I'm playing on my TV, I dont know. The negative user reviews for this game were appallingly immature for a time and threw a lot of undeserved hate at the game due to it being a straight port. The developers announced their plans for the fps and aspect ratio weeks ago so any complaints about those is void in my opinion. With that said, if you get simulation sickness, you may want to look at some videos of the game to make sure if it will bug you or not. The people who made many of those negative reviews were either uninformed or were planning on complaining anyway. It is the same game that is on next-gen consoles (PC may look a little sharper I haven't seen the console versions).  The game is very playable and it is not a broken port, at least, not for me. If you were a huge RE fan I think you will have a very fun time with The Evil Within. So far I am having a blast. There hasn't been a game quite like this in years.
You might need a controller. I cannot speak for the controls on mouse and keyboard. From my experience playing any 3rd person game works better with a controller just like first person shooters are far better with mouse and keyboard. I have been hearing that playing on a
TV negates the shock of the aspect ratio a bit so do your research if you are playing on a monitor. And for the love of god DO NOT come to this looking for a brilliant story! While Silent Hill games have had some pretty good stories the RE games have always had a sort of cheesy B movie plot. This game comes from the creator of Resident Evil so The Evil Within seems to naturally be going for the cheesy plot, though they seem to have dialed it down a bit. Voice acting is comparable to RE 4... serviceable but not award winning though I will say there seems to be less annoying characters like Ashley.

The real draw of this game is going to be the gameplay. Guns feel extremely satisfying to blast enemies with and they all have well done sound effects. The controls are designed in a way to make you feel unsafe at all times. You can move while aiming though I wouldn't advise taking a shot while moving because you will most likely miss unless you are at very close range. While your aim is initially inaccurate you can become more accurate as the game progresses by spending points in the games upgrade system. The upgrade system also includes things such as weapon capacity, damage, reserve capacity, reload speed, melee damage etc. The upgrades seem to allow for multiple play styles which is pretty cool.  Artificial intelligence isn't very smart but most enemies are bringing knives or claws to a gunfight so they are kinda dumba#$es to begin with. In other words, enemies with close range attacks are only going to have so many patterns because they eventually have to rush and kill you. I have not experienced any outstanding AI glitches but I have seen minor things like enemies hugging to close to corners and getting hung up for a second. Enemies are more dangerous in numbers than individually but they can be surprisingly fast. Headshots work best but if you knock one over you can light him up with a match or, even better, wait for other enemies to walk over him before burning them all. There are also multiple environmental dangers that you can use against your would-be killers. Tactics and precise shooting combine to make a very fun combat system. I am finding that I am dying less from regular combat and more from instakill bosses which can be frustrating to some. Nothing excessive though. Overall, the game balance is very good and I am making steady forward progress.
The Evil Within takes a lot of inspiration from Silent Hill in its environments. So far I have found a range of asylums, hospitals, labs, hellish otherworlds and so on. Character models and environments  look very good and the lighting is done particularly well. But this is not the game to benchmark your new rig on if thats what your are looking for. Some players report it as somewhat of a resource hog (maybe CPU?) but I am still finding no dips in the frame rate but I will make a note in the review if that changes.
The game is very dark, gory and intense if not necessarily scary. However, to be honest, I have never been utterly freaked out by any video game before. I am still finding it to be an awesome game. Unless I run into some absolute disasters on the way to the end (musical numbers), I believe genre fans will absolutely love this as long as they don't expect a full return to pure survival horror. The game does get a little action heavy toward the end featuring some gun-wielding enemies. Overall, though, I found it much closer to the tone of the original 3 RE games than 4 was. And there is no coop to be found, except for some AI partners (no, you don't have to share ammo) for brief instances. I am very glad for that last part.
If you are new to Survival Horror games know that the game is a little harder than your typical action game and you are expected to take your time and make your shots count. You also have less health than in most games but you can upgrade that as you progress. Your health only regenerates to a low amount if wounded and medkits and ammo are harder to come by than most games. You will be down to your last bullet in some fights. However, enemies will drop a couple of bullets (like 2 or 4 at most) every now and again and if you explore you should find enough rounds and matches to keep yourself alive. The game won't make things impossible for you. But you will rarely be flush with supplies.
Edit: Whether you found it helpful or not, I want to say thanks to everyone who read the review. Like I said, I've never written one and I wasn't really expecting more than ten people to read it. It's a pretty cool unexpected surprise. I also wanted to throw some specs out there in case they help someone out. I will make any necessary changes to the review when I have completed the game.

Did you like Shinji Mikami's Resident Evil 4? How about Silent Hill? How about lots of gore and excellent gunplay? If you answered yes to 1 or more of those questions, I would advise you to check this game out!
I have now completed the game and I can only recommend the game more, the gameplay holds the weight of the overly ambitious story. The combat feels intense and becomes increasingly scary due to your constant lack of resources, the horror isn't stacked on too thick with little to no jump scares throughout but you do always have a feeling of dread as you never know what is coming for you next (this is in part because of the games incredible music and sound design. MANY of the noises the enemies makes are bone chilling and because of very effective lighting effects).
The gunplay is very rewarding and "crunchy" as in you can feel the heads limbs and other areas being hit and often exploding (I actually shot an enemy in the face and blew its face clean off with only a hole left in the middle of its head it continued to chase me around).
Now that I have completed the game I still stay true to my opening statement and would recommend this game to anyone looking for a cool new 3rd person shooter or  a very nerve racking and often terrifying survival horror experience!

I love this game as much as I love the original HM. I replayed the latter quite recently, and this new one doesn't feel all that different, gameplay-wise - at least to me. I'm the silent assassin type. I use firearms for the big guys, mostly, and stick to melee weapons most of the time. I jump the nearest enemy, dash for cover, check the map, analyze enemy routes, move to the next safe corner, play peek-a-boo with the next enemy, wait for him to come closer, then whack him, etc. It's hard -- infuriatingly so, a lot of times -- but if I can beat the game, with my butter fingers, anyone can ;) Yes, the enemies can spot you from far away, outside of your field of view, and despite sticking to one route/staying in one room most of the time will occasionally randomly walk out right behind your back while you're busy performing a fatality -- so all you can do is try to off those sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s when you can early on... or just keep your fingers crossed. I've gotten used to that while going through HM1 with just the drill.
To me, though, it's not just about the gameplay. It's the moooood. The soundtrack is insanely good. Those dark, scary, angry tunes get you so pumped up and ready for action. Carpenter Brut, Perturbator and M|O|O|N really shine. But what really stands out are the slow, mellow tunes by The Green Kingdom or Modulogeek -- a nice breather between sequences of adrenalin and rage. And all of it goes SO well with the story. In HM1 I loved Jacket's weird encounters with the three masked figures, the little-glimpses into his mundane life, the upbeat store clerk, and the world changing as Jacket descends into madness. The sequel takes that narrative of "What you're seeing isn't necessarily what's really there" even further -- and also really fleshes out and expands on the thing mentioned in the Biker's secret ending. There's also a lot more interactions -- even if most of it is just chit-chat with little significance for the plot. In HM1 I wished Jacket would talk to the girl at least once. So Wrong Number was refreshing in that sense, especially seeing one of HM1 villains presented from a completely different perspective through his interactions with someone close to him. It'll take some effort -- and preferably some extra reading -- to piece the events together chronologically, but it's really rewarding.
A couple of things really annoyed me, though. I don't know whether it's a faulty hit detection system or just me -- but the katana-wielding guys in the last bit of the penultimate level would usually kill me if I came running at them. My best chance was to stop and stand still while throwing punches -- but even that didn't always work. So I can't count the times I got offed by that last samurai after clearing the whole level. Dogs would also get stuck on the stairs in that chapter sometimes -- and since I chose brass knuckles, I couldn't use a gun to kill them. Also, if you finish an enemy off next to the level borders, you might end up OUTSIDE the level, with no way to go back in or do anything else. And lastly -- a couple of levels are very, VERY dark. HM1's graphics were so great because everything was so hypnotically colorful. That's why I like it so much. Here, one level is so gloomy and brown it feels like I'm playing an Arkham game (a visual treat similar to watching your own colonoscopy) -- and two others are so dark you'll have a hard time spotting the damn dogs.
Overall, a fun game. Whether you'll enjoy it will depend largely on your playstyle -- and I totally understand why some people hate it. I had a blast. Yes, it annoyed the heck out of me, many, MANY times -- but so did the original. I rage-quit and uninstalled HM1 - TWICE! - only to re-install a couple days later, replay and PWN it, A+ on all levels. It's just that kind of game. It's designed to push you -- and you'll either hate it for that, or decide to accept it for what it is, with all the design choices, and say "Challenge ACCEPTED!"

The first Hotline Miami came out of nowhere. Bringing a bit of social commentary along with some arcade reminiscent gameplay, it ended up being a smash indie hit in 2012. The internet exploded with love for this unknown game.
Making a follow-up had to be a daunting prospect. Was there really any way to top the original? I honestly don't believe so and Hotline Miami 2 doesn't do much to fill one with confidence. The game is as solid as ever, but it's incredibly scattershot narrative and lack of any real change hold it back.
For starters, you control a lot more than 2 people in this game. Hotline Miami 2 follows the exploits of a couple of people following the events of the first game. You have gang members who are trying to copy the killings of the first game, a writer investigating what really happened, an angry fat guy with strong political beliefs and a crooked cop.
It makes for some cool setups, but after the first few levels, everything becomes easier. You learn all the AI limitations and guns still overpower the opposition. Stationing near a door and slowly firing is almost a guaranteed way to succeed in any level.
There are different masks that allow one to augment the gameplay. Some have deadly throws for your weapons and limit you to only punches, but the strict camera gets in the way of truly going all melee. The levels have expanded in size, but that also means you tend to get killed from off camera a lot. It's frustrating, if not for the AI's relative stupidity.
The soundtrack is also not as bass heavy or angry as the first game, though there are a tremendous amount of great tracks. Every level gets it's own song now and it does help to make certain segments of the game more defined. Some of the best tracks from the original repeated, so you'd often forget which level they were associated with.
The boss battles from the first game have been pretty much removed. There is one that happens later in the game and it's total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but it seems the sins of the past haven't been forgotten. It was always agonizing to have an enemy basically lock-on to you and never fail, so it's nice to finally be able to plan ahead in most levels.
Though honestly, I couldn't find many new weapons. I know there is a chain, a machete, dual SMGs and a katana, but the only real dramatic change is one mask which allows for two characters. The other character takes on guns while the main player wields a chainsaw. It's fun, but isn't given enough use (not to mention it does little to fundamentally alter the game).
Then there is the pacing. Since you're constantly fumbling between characters, the game seems to crawl a bit. You don't get enough time with any one person to come to terms with them. The best new character (The Writer) even changes the focus of the game from murdering all to non-lethal, but his final level is a bonus unlockable.
The game is definitely longer than the first, but I don't know if I'd call that a plus. The first game was so lightning fast and intense that you didn't even know what hit you. You'd die a bit in some rooms and effortlessly dominate others, but with 2, you're constantly playing. It ends up dragging and sucking a lot of the impact out of it's bigger moments.
The final level is a treat, even if it does include a boss fight and some ridiculous visual effects. It closes out the chaos of the entire Hotline Miami series pretty well. Lots of people have always compared this to taking drugs and killing people, so I guess push came to shove.
Either way, Hotline Miami 2 isn't a bad game. If you are still on the market for an experience like this, you would be better served going with the first title. It's more focused, offers better replayability and doesn't feel like a slog. 2 is mostly for the hardcore fans, which is not that bad of a thing.

Alright, pro's and con's outt'a the way real quick.
+ Wonderful soundtrack, my goodness.
+ Improved engine and art.
+ Underrated story, with a lot of key elements for the Hotline Miami universe.
+ Neat environments and unique characters.
+ A pacifist character!!!
+ Not gonna lie, I really dig the ' flipped level ' aspect of Hard Mode.
+/- Not really a whole lott'a options for masks, and ' masks '. Some characters don't even have 'em.
- Adding onto that, restrictive gameplay. Late game is ranged central. Melee may as well not exist from Act 4 and upwards. Remember that pacifist character I mentioned? In order to beat a Hard Mode level as him, you have to go against that mechanic.
- Atrocious AI
- Windows are no ones enemy, it's how they're centered around almost all the ' difficult ' aspects of this games challenging demeanor that makes them such a toxic mechanic.
- Doors are practically a bug altogether.
Do I recommend this game to people who like/are interested in Hotline Miami, and wanna get more into it story AND gameplay wise? Yeah, man.
Do I recommend this game to people who want a similar experience to Hotline Miami 1? Who want to ♥♥♥♥♥ it out, get all their achievements and do everything there is to do? No. Get it while it's on sale or something.
Starting off, I have Achievement ♥♥♥♥♥'d both games. I've done all there is to do, and I've seen it all. I've sat for hours on end, getting my A+'s. I've grinded the kills for Genocide. I've felt the relief of walking into that golden, rainbow pathed gate at the end of Hard Mode Apocalypse. And I wish I could say I regret all of it, because the more time I put into this game, the more I hated it.
Before Act 3, the game actually has great level design. Moving Up is one of my personal favorites, and there isn't really any other level like it. There seems to be an ebb and flow to all of it, until you hit Dead Ahead. This is where you're introduced to the sloppily thought out room design, annoying enemy rotations, frustrating window placement and clunky AI.
Yes, it's kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to constantly compare the sequel to it's shorter predecessor, but it's kind of important to my reasoning. Hotline Miami 1 was short and sweet. The difficulty left you blaming yourself, and it felt good to learn from your mistakes. You could rush in, and be done in no time at all-- Because you learned the area, you got comfortable with your actions, and learned from your previous ones. Hotline Miami 2 was an RNG-based bait fest, filled with intentionally placed windows that completely throw you off your groove and result in yet another frustratin off-screen or sudden death.
The magic of Hotline Miami 1 was how much it could afflict a player within it's short, action-packed levels. Hotline Miami 2 just wants to see how long it can drag its fingernails across the chalkboard of a droned out, lengthy level filled with lengthy boards that want you to play by it's rules. Every level in the sequel is like a puzzle that you can only solve one way, and one way only-- Through means of large enemies, dogs, unique enemies and windows. This becomes very apparent in Hard Mode.
Again, this is a good game. It's just... kind'a lazily made. I doubt I'll return to it for level editor, as I've had my fair enough share of blood and neon. I'm not gonna give it a rating, because it's sorta different for everyone. I'll repeat, if you want a new experience and are overall new to Hotline Miami, go for it. If you're a veteran who craves more, wait for the fanmade mods Midnight Animal and Hotline Miami:Redial to quench your thirst for combo's and anger.

A curious mix of Minecraft-esque building and FPS action is to be found within Ace of Spades.
And surprisingly, they were ablel to pull the mix off fairly well.
While the graphics style might be a little low-end for some people, this game actually plays fairly solid.  I spent several hours mining, digging, exploding, and blasting my way into enemy bases.  Playing with friends is more rewarding in this game than in most FPS's because you could - say - quickly construct a fort / defense / offensive position with them.  Or mine your way to the enemy base unseen - working together to make the trek much faster.  This makes for a completely unique experience.
The weapons are fun, and pretty much what you would expect in a first person shooter.  You get classes (Soldier, Tech., Ect) but these don't go beyond anything you would normally see (save for a jet-pack and being able to rocket jump).  They all perform as you would expect and they do not disappoint.
Overall, I'd recommend this game if it is on sale.  I would warn people away from paying full price just because it's a game that can get easy to put down, and if you aren't playing with a friend or two, the gameplay value is cut down severely.

A surprisingly simple but very okay game.
I'd vote against getting this if you expect some super dramatic and graphical spaceship war game, but if you know what you're looking for - a basic Build-and-Watch tactical game - then this would be a very good bet. I'd not call it 'bare bones' so much as admit it's a very simple game that focuses more on the planning and gameplay than anything else; that's not to say that they ignored everything else, but you can easily see what their best aspect is.
Difficulty-wise, I'd say it's too easy. I like a challenge now and again, and the thing here is that with a simple game comes a simple A.I. - one that needs a bit of a boost (resource-wise) to keep up with an actual planning player (and will nearly always still fall short to one who's actually on their feet and assiging commands properly). That's not to say the game's not fun - there's still a simple satisfaction in playing it and seeing your amassed army do the dirty work for you.
Achievements-wise, this game will take you a while. Aeon Command is a deceivingly challenging tug-of-war game with strategy elements that almost reminds me of an RTS. You don't have to command units, they automatically attack the enemy. The only thing the player does is manage resources, applies powerups (buffs, debuffs), deploys weapons (nukes, emps), and purchases upgrades for units. The more obvious thing players must do is build units. I found it relaxing, rewarding, and late games were challenging and exhilarating.
There's 3 factions to choose from and they all have their own unique appearance and they all have their own weapons. However, they have similar basic unit types which keeps it fairly well balanced. I say fairly because there are some different support units for each faction. The similarities will be noticeable in attack units. I had little trouble identifying an enemy ship and launching the appropriate counter. Watching the space battles unfold is quite interesting, it reminded me of Battlestar Galactica for some reason. A word of warning, this game starts off unforgivingly and you may lose many of your first matches. Does it get better? Yes it does, because of two types of upgrades. There are game-wide upgrades that you can upgrade from the main menu and these are purchased using "gear parts" you acquire from destroyed enemies. These upgrades are applied to every game thereafter. The second type of upgrade is the in-game upgrades which must be purchased with scrap and these only apply for the duration of that match. Generally, upgrades modify weapons and armour but there are also resource collection upgrades which I researched first because the best economy almost always wins.
The campaigns are short and aren't full of narrative. If you want a deep story, you won't find it in this game. HOWEVER, I recommend this game because of high replay value and the gameplay is well polished.
The soundtrack is more like ambience and I found it added to the atmosphere. Sound effects from weapons to explosions are also well done. The only sound effect that drove me nuts was the spacial anomaly sound effect which you'll only hear in 1 or 2 campaign missions anyway.
I had a lot of fun with this game and I am absolutely astonished that (as of purchasing this game) no one in my friends list has this on their wishlist or owns it. So if you're reading this, I highly recommend it for it's replay value and the great gameplay. 8/10

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Looterkings is currently in Early Access.
Looterkings is a three-dimensional action dungeon crawler in reverse: you play a goblin living at the bottom of the dungeon, ascending through the levels in search of more and more loot, until you eventually break through to the surface and the court of the Elven Queen.
Graphics - Graphics are colourful and cartoon-like, with more lifelike textures than many other cel-shaded games, especially on the goblin skins. The goblins themselves are great, although with only a few skins to choose from, there's not much variation. They're well modelled and animated nicely, and they have a certain cuteness to them. Enemies are also nicely modelled and animated, and fit in well with the general theme. Unfortunately there's only a small number enemy types so far. I hope there are a lot more planned as the game moves through Early Access.
Weapon and ability effects are okay, if nothing jaw-dropping, and lava looks a bit meh, but the fire and smoke particle effects are good, as are the dynamic lighting and the water. The room graphics range from okay to excellent; I think they get better as the game progresses.
Graphics settings are limited: one single detail level setting, as well as vsync and window/full-screen options. The game mostly performs well, but can occasionally slow to a slideshow in large rooms when there are many enemies about.
Sound - The music and sound effects in Looterkings are good, but very limited in scope.
There seems to be only one music track, which is played only on the title screen and menus. It's a jaunty sort of tune that fits well and sounds good
The goblins' sound effects are great, but there aren't enough of them, and it seems to me that they need some volume normalisation, as some are too quiet.
There's also a nice touch where sounds are dulled and lowered in pitch when you're close to death, together with a corresponding visual fade.
Overall, the few sounds and lack of music in game leave the game feeling a bit lonely and empty. I hope more will be added soon.
Gameplay - Looterkings is action oriented. You control your goblin from a third-person view with WASD, using mouse for aiming and weapons and a few other keys for jumping, running, etc. There is no controller support, but the gameplay is really asking for it.
The game is divided into multiple levels, each with a procedurally generated layout that changes every time you play. This is performed through the use of a relatively small number of set rooms connected by short hallways in a modular fashion, so although each time you play the layout is different, the rooms you see are all very similar to what you've seen before. The limited enemy types -- the bestiary lists eight -- make everything seem even more repetitive, too.
Each room allows you to enter and then locks you in, immediately spawning a number of enemies of a single type, up to a predefined maximum. As you kill them, more spawn to keep the room maximally populated, until you've fought your way through a predefined number of enemies for that room. Once they're all dead, the doors unlock, you pick up your loot and experience point glowy-things, and move to the next room. The game's difficulty stems from swamping you with enemy numbers.
For the time being, ignore the 'RPG' category tag on the store page, as this game doesn't include any of the traditional elements of RPG games: inventory, quests, character customisation and meaningful progression are all missing from Looterkings.
The 'loot' you find is simply gold. It's used to buy items from the shops (one per level), but you can only have one weapon, one mask, and one suit equipped at a time. One original aspect of the game is the way in which the items you equip change your god abilities. It's an interesting mechanic, but it can be a frustrating one: I bought a suit of armour, but didn't like the ability change it forced on me, so I ended up not wearing it at all.
Progression in the game is also very simple: kill enough enemies and collect the XP left behind, and you go up a level. But all this does is unlock a new item in the shops. You don't get better at anything, or gain any new abilities. The game features permadeath, but your level and the associated item unlocks are carried across after you die. Unfortunately, though, you lose all gold and items, so there's no real increase in ability. Some sort of level-based stat or ability increase, or better starting weapon options, or even being able to keep one item, would all add to the replayability. As it is, it feels like progress is all but lost with each play.
Looterkings is designed to be played with three friends in a cooperative mode. So far I've only been able to find one other person with a game that I could join, and that only lasted for an hour or so; the rest has been singleplayer. In either case, combat is very basic and tends to involve kiting enemies until they trap you, then using your god ability to run away and start again. The alternative is to take advantage of the poor AI and jump up higher than your enemies, in which case they tend to ignore you. Teamwork makes it more fun, but the basic combat mechanic needs improvement.
I also found the following bugs and questionable design choices that I thought were worth mentioning in passing. Bear in mind that the game is still in Early Access, though.
. There are three modes: normal, casual, and twitch. Only 'normal' is available at the moment.
. Poor grammar and spelling.
. There's no map.
. It's easy to become stuck on geometry in some levels.
. Some enemies can sometimes shoot through geometry sometimes.
. The statistics screen is funny, but some of the stats are wrong.
. Starting weapons get duplicated in the shop.
. There's no way to eat a mushroom once you've picked it up; you can only throw it.
. Poisoned mushrooms cause too much damage.
. Sometimes the 'loot' just disappears.
. The crossbow doesn't always aim at the crosshairs, particularly when you're trying to shoot above you.
Pros:
+ Excellent graphics
+ A fun game idea
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Procedural generation needs more components
- Combat is repetitive, especially with no real progression
- Not enough monster types
- Not enough items
- Not enough people playing yet
- Other minor bugs and issues (see above)
Looterkings isn't quite what I expected it to be. It has a lot less RP in it than I thought it would, and the combat needs some work. It's very pretty, though, and there's a good core game idea here.
At the moment I recommend it if you can pick it up at a discount, and especially if you can play it with friends.

Now for the bad thing about this game. You will be extremely lucky if you get someone in a game with you. I personally have played alone most of my playtime but still.

Upon completing the available content of Looterkings I hereby bring upon a few words of wisdom regarding the current state of the game.
It is very apparent that allot of hours have gone into the making of Looterkings and it shows in its own quirky way, the character models are very well done to the drunken happy look of the goblins expressions down to the anatomy that you will notice upon your first few minutes in the game. The visuals from the hoards of rats and beetles that you will encounter are very well polished as are the dungeons in which you progress through, are very detailed and beautiful.
That pretty much covers the visuals and character models in which I give the game a double thumbs up, however lets talk about the game mechanics and combat system below.
The overall combat system in terms of flow and smoothness is excellent, the party up system with having a fellow goblin ride on your shoulders is a very cool perk and rewards the players for doing so with more damage and the ability to stack your ultimate abilities. The level up system could use some more polish as the only reward that I could notice was just the ability to unlock additional items. I would add in the ability to customize your character stats in some way (Adding in more attack speed/hp/armor/regen upon leveling up)
The current state of the mob scaling versus the state of the goblins is in need of some TLC, I say this due to the only way to clear some rooms, mainly the armored beetle rooms is to stand on high ground and cheese the mobs with ranged weapons. You will find yourself standing on tables and perches to avoid incoming damage and an inevitable whipe.
This can easily be fixed with reducing the amount of mobs on the map at a time versus how many goblins, lowering the hp pool of said mobs and tweaking the mechanics and scaling to a point where it is doable without cheesing the game mechanics.
In the later levels there is reduced access to mushrooms, this can be rectified with buying items with regeneration on them and using your terrain. I also would like to point out that you should be able to pick your ultimate ability instead of having to restart the game over and over looking for invulnerable heal or invisible heal to progress though the first floor.
Overall I give the game a 4/5 Shrooms, the game has allot of potential but still needs some more polish. I look forward to coming back when new content is released to make some more videos and do a follow up review.

Sonic Adventure 2 is considered, by most, the best 3D Sonic The Hedgehog game. Some people might think that we say that because of nostalgia, but this game offer so much more contents than the newer titles from the serie that we see nowadays.
This game had two story modes, and a total of six characters. There was three types of stages: With Sonic/Shadow, it was the classic race-to-the-finish. With Tails/Eggman, you could shoot stuff with a Mech. With Knuckles/Rouge, you had to find hidden treasures within an area. The best thing about this game was arguably the Chao Garden. This side minigame had you raise and level up little creatures called "Chao" with various powerups that you could get from destroying ennemies during an action stage. The Chao Garden made replaying a level feel rewarding, as you could powerup your tribe of Chao after completing a level.
Sadly, the newer games just feels bland. There's rarely any other character to play as other than Sonic (or Classic Sonic, if this feel like a different character to you), and they ditched the well-loved Chao Garden, which we never ever saw again.
As for the porting, SA2 is greatly ported to PC. It has slighty better graphics, and most features are still in the game (except the option to transfer a Chao to a GBA). The price is also really low, especially when the game is on sale.
