The first Hotline Miami came out of nowhere. Bringing a bit of social commentary along with some arcade reminiscent gameplay, it ended up being a smash indie hit in 2012. The internet exploded with love for this unknown game.
Making a follow-up had to be a daunting prospect. Was there really any way to top the original? I honestly don't believe so and Hotline Miami 2 doesn't do much to fill one with confidence. The game is as solid as ever, but it's incredibly scattershot narrative and lack of any real change hold it back.
For starters, you control a lot more than 2 people in this game. Hotline Miami 2 follows the exploits of a couple of people following the events of the first game. You have gang members who are trying to copy the killings of the first game, a writer investigating what really happened, an angry fat guy with strong political beliefs and a crooked cop.
It makes for some cool setups, but after the first few levels, everything becomes easier. You learn all the AI limitations and guns still overpower the opposition. Stationing near a door and slowly firing is almost a guaranteed way to succeed in any level.
There are different masks that allow one to augment the gameplay. Some have deadly throws for your weapons and limit you to only punches, but the strict camera gets in the way of truly going all melee. The levels have expanded in size, but that also means you tend to get killed from off camera a lot. It's frustrating, if not for the AI's relative stupidity.
The soundtrack is also not as bass heavy or angry as the first game, though there are a tremendous amount of great tracks. Every level gets it's own song now and it does help to make certain segments of the game more defined. Some of the best tracks from the original repeated, so you'd often forget which level they were associated with.
The boss battles from the first game have been pretty much removed. There is one that happens later in the game and it's total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but it seems the sins of the past haven't been forgotten. It was always agonizing to have an enemy basically lock-on to you and never fail, so it's nice to finally be able to plan ahead in most levels.
Though honestly, I couldn't find many new weapons. I know there is a chain, a machete, dual SMGs and a katana, but the only real dramatic change is one mask which allows for two characters. The other character takes on guns while the main player wields a chainsaw. It's fun, but isn't given enough use (not to mention it does little to fundamentally alter the game).
Then there is the pacing. Since you're constantly fumbling between characters, the game seems to crawl a bit. You don't get enough time with any one person to come to terms with them. The best new character (The Writer) even changes the focus of the game from murdering all to non-lethal, but his final level is a bonus unlockable.
The game is definitely longer than the first, but I don't know if I'd call that a plus. The first game was so lightning fast and intense that you didn't even know what hit you. You'd die a bit in some rooms and effortlessly dominate others, but with 2, you're constantly playing. It ends up dragging and sucking a lot of the impact out of it's bigger moments.
The final level is a treat, even if it does include a boss fight and some ridiculous visual effects. It closes out the chaos of the entire Hotline Miami series pretty well. Lots of people have always compared this to taking drugs and killing people, so I guess push came to shove.
Either way, Hotline Miami 2 isn't a bad game. If you are still on the market for an experience like this, you would be better served going with the first title. It's more focused, offers better replayability and doesn't feel like a slog. 2 is mostly for the hardcore fans, which is not that bad of a thing.

Alright, pro's and con's outt'a the way real quick.
+ Wonderful soundtrack, my goodness.
+ Improved engine and art.
+ Underrated story, with a lot of key elements for the Hotline Miami universe.
+ Neat environments and unique characters.
+ A pacifist character!!!
+ Not gonna lie, I really dig the ' flipped level ' aspect of Hard Mode.
+/- Not really a whole lott'a options for masks, and ' masks '. Some characters don't even have 'em.
- Adding onto that, restrictive gameplay. Late game is ranged central. Melee may as well not exist from Act 4 and upwards. Remember that pacifist character I mentioned? In order to beat a Hard Mode level as him, you have to go against that mechanic.
- Atrocious AI
- Windows are no ones enemy, it's how they're centered around almost all the ' difficult ' aspects of this games challenging demeanor that makes them such a toxic mechanic.
- Doors are practically a bug altogether.
Do I recommend this game to people who like/are interested in Hotline Miami, and wanna get more into it story AND gameplay wise? Yeah, man.
Do I recommend this game to people who want a similar experience to Hotline Miami 1? Who want to ♥♥♥♥♥ it out, get all their achievements and do everything there is to do? No. Get it while it's on sale or something.
Starting off, I have Achievement ♥♥♥♥♥'d both games. I've done all there is to do, and I've seen it all. I've sat for hours on end, getting my A+'s. I've grinded the kills for Genocide. I've felt the relief of walking into that golden, rainbow pathed gate at the end of Hard Mode Apocalypse. And I wish I could say I regret all of it, because the more time I put into this game, the more I hated it.
Before Act 3, the game actually has great level design. Moving Up is one of my personal favorites, and there isn't really any other level like it. There seems to be an ebb and flow to all of it, until you hit Dead Ahead. This is where you're introduced to the sloppily thought out room design, annoying enemy rotations, frustrating window placement and clunky AI.
Yes, it's kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to constantly compare the sequel to it's shorter predecessor, but it's kind of important to my reasoning. Hotline Miami 1 was short and sweet. The difficulty left you blaming yourself, and it felt good to learn from your mistakes. You could rush in, and be done in no time at all-- Because you learned the area, you got comfortable with your actions, and learned from your previous ones. Hotline Miami 2 was an RNG-based bait fest, filled with intentionally placed windows that completely throw you off your groove and result in yet another frustratin off-screen or sudden death.
The magic of Hotline Miami 1 was how much it could afflict a player within it's short, action-packed levels. Hotline Miami 2 just wants to see how long it can drag its fingernails across the chalkboard of a droned out, lengthy level filled with lengthy boards that want you to play by it's rules. Every level in the sequel is like a puzzle that you can only solve one way, and one way only-- Through means of large enemies, dogs, unique enemies and windows. This becomes very apparent in Hard Mode.
Again, this is a good game. It's just... kind'a lazily made. I doubt I'll return to it for level editor, as I've had my fair enough share of blood and neon. I'm not gonna give it a rating, because it's sorta different for everyone. I'll repeat, if you want a new experience and are overall new to Hotline Miami, go for it. If you're a veteran who craves more, wait for the fanmade mods Midnight Animal and Hotline Miami:Redial to quench your thirst for combo's and anger.

A few frustrating design decisions hinder what would otherwise be a notable sequel to the fantastic Hotline Miami. The worst of these forces the player to play levels with certain characters, who impose pointless restrictions on how you can play - examples being characters who don't use guns, or - even worse - only use the one gun their character holds, unable to pick up any others. This inevitably results in the player having to conserve ammo, and forces you to play the level the 'right' way - both tactics which fly in the face of the brawling, free-for-all carnage for which the original was so lauded. Add to this the fact that you can't change these characters - and therefore the restriction placed over the level - and what should be an adrenaline-fuelled carnage fest quickly becomes a tiresome, frustrating chore of constantly redoing the same level over and over again, struggling more against the arbitrary penalty imposed upon you than the hordes of machine gun-toting enemies you're pitted against.
Hotline Miami was a game deserving of a worthy successor, and it's a shame Dennaton decided to mess with their formula in a seemingly thoughtless attempt to 'make the game harder'. There's a thin line between a well balanced, challenging game that punishes you for mistakes
make, and a frustrating, get-shot-by-a-guy-offscreen game that punishes you for mistakes
makes. The original Hotline Miami fell within the former category, but unfortunately the sequel edges towards the latter. Pick up this game if, like me, you loved the original and want more, but wait for a sale.

So I just finished playing Hydrophobia. Here's some thoughts.
Flow and mood are excellent. The scenes were well-directed.
Puzzle-solving was... it would have been good but there was a lot of hand-holding; you basically follow a carrot on a stick through the whole game, which feels largely on rails.
They sold the game based on the idea that you'd have cool hydrokinesis powers, but you only have them for the last 15% of the game if that.
The hydrokinesis is cludgy to control and not all that useful. You can't use it from cover and it's less powerful as a weapon than the sonic stun bullets you use for the other 85% of the game.
You also get real bullets but they suck so I never really used them. The sonic rounds have more stopping power and accuracy so why would I use semiauto or fullauto?
There's some stealth for about 5 minutes but you end up shooting everyone in the face anyway.
After the game ends you unlock a "challenge room" but I don't care.
---SPOILERS BELOW---
There is one boss fight, a robot gun thing. When you kill it, the antagonist gets electrocuted, you cure your water-power poisoning, and then it fades to black, roll credits.
You never get the deeper explanation of the conflict, just "crazy cult wants to cull humans". you never meet up with your pal who helped you through the first 75% of the game over the radio.
I'm glad I played it. I'm also glad I got it on sale.
I want more in the world of the game but I know it won't happen.

If you're looking for something more hardcore and intense, then this game won't be for you. Way too many issues out of the box.
Moving past the Uplay issue (Hint: install Uplay beforehand, have an account ready), which is annoying but not groundbreaking, I still can't recommend this game. On Win8.1 at least, had to uninstall every 2008 edition of Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable just to load past the menu, as it would just crash upon loading into the game. I don't know why it was that specifically, but thanks for the heads up, internet. Do your research before calling it a day.
The vanilla game itself feels considerably rushed. Fewer subs, poor AI, graphical glitches out the wazoo.
Sure, it looks nice, but the changes from previous games are, at least initially, disorienting if you're coming from an earlier game. It might seem petty, but remapping all the controls to fit in the finnicky 'walk around the sub' mechanic (which is admittedly a nice touch) screwed with my muscle memory for at least an hour. Managing to get my sub glitched inside a larger ship thanks to time compression didn't help either.
It does a couple of things right for casual players though. Having a toggleable map might take away some of the challenge, but it does wonders for situational awareness. Crew management is, for the most part, a non-entity, which for me personally is a... semi-welcome change from SH3, but again removes a lot of the challenge. Instead of rapidly throwing crew members from room to room to min-max their rapidly decreasing energy in SH3, we get running around the submarine talking to the senior officers. At least, I think that's the intention, but you never seem like you're forced to do it. Morale doesn't increase or decrease at a noticeable rate, except when you botch a conversation for the first time.
AI crewmen can't be set to fire the deck gun or AA gun without you expressly selecting a target, which might seem fine for ships, but is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥when trying to pick out planes. And yes, I know sneaking away from the planes is the preferred solution, but if you're going to give us the option, Ubisoft, why make it so darn difficult?
Honestly, some of my gripes would probably fade away over time, but I don't believe Silent Hunter 5 is a product worth investing into, especially not for the asking price. If you can get Silent Hunter 3 or 4, do that.

I'm a bit torn on this one - it's a perfectly decent 'endless runner' (actually not quite endless but you know what I mean) but the control system lets-it-down a bit.
The thing games like this is you should be making last-second decisions and JUST making it (or not) - but the control method here is "make a jump direction choice - live with it" - which means there's a time gap between hitting a button, realising it's the wrong-one - dying and there's nothing you can do about it.
Furthermore, the need to plan-ahead works with the speed of the levels/draw-in of the platforms to sometimes make the game outright unfair - in some cases you'll have to 'guess' or 'take a chance' because you can't see the thing you need to make a decision to jump towards (or at least the thing after it which is a dead-end or whatever). It's not HORRIBLY unfair - but it can be.
Admitedly that's in the tougher levels but the game doesn't mess about - the first level is fairly easy and then it gets a LOT harder!
End of the day I'm erring towards 'Not Recommended' simply because I think it lacks that "ahhhhh,,, yes!" or "ohhhh - no!!!!!!" factor which I tend to want in my twitch games - I don't like having time to realise I've made a mistake before it actually happens ;0
YMMV however - it's a competent game, just maybe lacking a bit of excitement and having a bit too much "unfair!"

Wakfu is a turn based mmorpg with a cute anime-like style. The combat system is similar to final fantasy tactics and players are able to shape the the environment. But there are not a lot of quests that will tell you what to do and lead you the way, it's more of a sandbox game where you decide what to do and where to go.
If you prefer quests from Lv. 1 to XXX this game will not appeal to you.
When you create your character you will get your first quest chain until like Lv. 12-15.
I think the next is around Lv. 35 to get your first mount.
The next one is at Lv. 50
Then there is another one around 90~100
...
As you can see, there is alot of spare time between those main quests. So, if you don't like to explore the world yourself, you will be stuck after each quest chain ends.
There are 16 classes to choose from, each once has its unique fighting style. These are no archetype classes you'd normally expect. Except like 3 classes which are similar to Warrior, Archer and Assassin. But you probably won't know which one is the warrior, if you see them, they are more like a mix of a Barbarian, a Warrior and an idiot (The game calls them stupid, not me I swear). There are also Faries, Bamboo-Milkoholics, Machosists, Robots, Human-Plants, Gambling Cats, old greedy Farts, Terrorists and a few more...
But there is no higher class change at a higher level or something like that. You will be stronger when you level up your Class abilities and elemental spells.
There are 4 Elements: Fire, Water, Earth, Air. All Spells in the game are categorized in one of them.
Each class has access to 3 Elements, 5 spells for each Element.
Each class also has 10 Class specific supportive abilities. 5 of them are active spells, the other 5 are passives.
What are the elements for? Everything has Elemental Damage and Resistance.
If you have a lot of Fire Damage, your fire spells will deal more damage, if the target you attack has a lot of fire resistance, you will deal less damage with your fire spells.
Elemental damages can go over 100% to infinite. Elemental resistance has a maximum of 100%(which would block 100% damage of that element), but you cannot reach that. I have about 60% resistance at Lv. 105. So you can at least reach that :)
For your first 20% resist in each element you will need 100 points in resist, which are 5 points for each % resist.
After that it will slightly increase the amount needed for each % resist.
The best way to level up your character is probably by doing dungeon runs. You get a wisdom bonus in there, which increases exp gained. 20 Wisdom = 20% more exp after the fight. To enter a dungeon, you will need the corresponding key, which are usually not too hard to get. If you know what monsters are inside the dungeon, kill the same monsters outside of the dungeon, they will drop it sooner or later. You can also craft keys by using the items those monsters drop. Usually its 7x Item X.
There are also daily quests in each zone of the world, which tells you bring 10 items of the monsters that are lurking around. If you collect 20, you don't need to hunt them tomorrow, just accept and finish the quest immediately. Those quests give you a decent amount of exp.
I think in all zones except the first one in each nation are also timed events with a small variety of quests. There are either monsters appearing, or other random stuff you have to interact with before the time runs out. Those are highlighted in green if you see them while the event is ongoing. There is a new event every 10-15 minutes I think and the exp is also decent if it's around your level.
There is a lot more to talk about this game but if I tried to explain every detail I know, I would need 2+ hours to write this review. I will try to end this with a short Pro and Con.
+ High Variety of Classes (16 Classes)
+ 10+1 Crafting Professions (the extra profession can't be leveled. you can create in game money called Kama with it, if you have the materials)
+ 6 Gathering Professions
+ Battles get more challenging at later levels (monsters gain passives, you can't always ignore to win battles)
+ You have your own home, which is a bag and is accesible from almost everywhere (You can put furnite in it, plant stuff and there is an item storage)
+ A lot of costumes for customization. Also everything you wear, besides the belt, can be seen on your character, haven't seen that in many 2D games.
+ If you don't have friends, you can have 2 Sidekicks fighting by your side.
+ Shape the world, Kill monsters, replant them, cut trees and flowers and plant them where you want em, but be careful, in the open world everyone has access to this.
- Bugs, Glitches. The longer you play, the more you will find. Some are just minor bugs that don't matter much, others are killing you in battle. The worst battle bug I know is that you can't do anything for 1 round. I have that once in maybe 2 weeks. The friend I play with has it every 25-30 battles. I guess, it depends on your computer.
- lack of guidelines
- Most crafting professions don't feel satisfying to level (only a few things you can craft are better than hunting equip)
- Some gathering professions are really slow and boring to level (Ex.: Trapper, most stuff you collect from monsters to level up will be thrown away to save item slots)
I play and like this game because the combat is fun and challenging to me. In an even battle, every wrong step you take, might cost you or your party members life. The special effects are also pretty well done.
If some bugs and glitches scare you away, you won't be playing for long.
Give it a try if you like most of the things I have mentioned about Wakfu. If the bugs you find don't affect your gameplay experience too much, you will enjoy it.

I don't know what the hell happened to this game in development. It had all the ingredients to be as good as the first but it falls flat on it's face which is very apparent from the offset.
Hotline Miami was a great game because of it's fast paced think on your feet melee action, guns were used as relief from a crazy situation. Hotline Miami 2 breaks this fundamentally from the very start of the game and carries it through right until the very end. Nearly every level requires the player to plan ahead and before you can move you must check as far as the camera will move for enemies with guns. It's not often you find yourself in a situation where you need to use melee weapons as gun drops are provided almost constantly. Almost all I can remember is enemies with guns and never melee weapons.
Later on in the game you are placed in a jungle and it's these levels that show how bad some of these decisions that the developers made can be. These jungle levels are so tedious as you find yourself being shot from all kinds of directions. This ruins the pace of the game and makes you wonder how they perfected the level design in Hotline Miami. It becomes hard to look back on anything prior to it in fondness.
The story is largely forgettable. It doesn't carry any of the shock content that the original game had and it's not nearly as inventive. The end of the first game was almost funny in it's attempt to shrug it's harsh content off and say "it was because we are bored". Hotline Miami 2 tries too hard with it's story and it ends up becoming a convuluted broken headachy mess.
My last sentence sums up Hotline Miami 2 for me quite perfectly. It feels like a game trying too hard to become another classic without knowing how it became one in the first place. The addition of too many firearms, bad level design and convuluted story make this extremely difficult to recommend.

Having been able to play the game since Closed Beta, I can highly recommend it!
Even after over 30 hours of playing, the game is still absolutely fun. That is, if you play together with others (each room can have up to four players) or with friends, which in my opinion is the best and funniest way to play the game.
So let's break it down:
You start out as a teeny tiny goblin deep in the caverns your kind dwells in. Your job is to take all loot from the nasty elves and deprive them off anything shiny and glittering. Conveniently, the elves have put everything into crates, barrels and chests located in the rooms you will roam.
However, you aren't quite alone and left to just stealing all the gold. In each room, you will encounter enemies you have to defeat before being able to progress. They are numerous and they hit hard.
However, there are several things to aid you in your quest.
First of all, you will encounter mushrooms in almost every room. They can heal you should your health drop low; you should be careful though, since some of them may stun or even poison you, leaving you vulnerable to being looted by your fellow goblins. If you're on full health, you can collect up to three mushrooms which you can use to stun both enemies and fellow goblins alike for a brief period (and you may take some of their loot if you manage to stun one of your mates!). Furthermore, your weapon has a special attack and is empowered by one of four gods.
Your most powerful tool is an ultimate ability that you can use once in a while. These abilities are assigned randomly at game start. There are many different types such as becoming invisible, healing, becoming invinvible, thorns etc. The type of your ability depends on the combination of your main god and its ascendant. These factors are influenced by the equipment you wear. There are many combinations, but they are fixed, so I recommend noting what combination results in which ability.
Also, bear in mind that once a member of your party dies, you will NOT be able to use your god's ability until you revived them!
Once you managed to level up from killing your foes, you will unlock random items in the shop. There's one in each of the five biomes. You can use your loot there to buy different weapons such as crossbows, staffs, daggers or different helmets and armor. These are all infused with one main god and ascendant too, so you can plan your buys in order to change your ability.
Regarding the difficulty, the game is hard. Period. You will probably die a lot, especially if you play alone or an incomplete party. You can revive fallen teammates, but once everyone in your party dies, you will have to start out from the beginning and do it all over again. Teaming up is absolutely key in this game, so never play alone! Also, you may stack up with a fellow goblin, which will greatly increase your damage and the power of your god's ability!
As for the replay value, the rooms are randomly generated each time, so none of your runs will be the same. Furthermore, you can play over and over again to unlock new items that help you in quest.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Looterkings
Update Version: 0.7.1
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Before I get started, I need to clarify four pieces of information that have no baring on the final verdict.
- There is only one difficulty setting currently available. Hard makes solo play rather frustrating and downright boring if you play it safe.
- You must be online to play this game. While you can play this solo, you are still forced to create a lobby in order to enter the game.
- There is nudity in this game in the form of goblin genitalia.
- Options default the region to Europe, so if you do switch to US, be advised the lobbies might not be as populated.
It is worth mentioning the visual aesthetic is pleasing on the eyes with very few clipping issues in terms of character animations. Texture quality is above par, the lighting is effective across the board and the user interface is clean cut with minimal screen clutter. It is a pleasant change from the usual pixelated decor and complements the subject matter beautifully.
Utilizing the mouse, you can use a standard attack and a special attack unique to each weapon. God powers are also present, randomly created at the start of each round to provide your goblin with either a elemental attack, invincibility, invisibility, or even resurrecting a fallen foe to fight at your side. In multiplayer, these God powers and standard attacks can be empowered by stacking on your teammates or by allowing them to stack on you. If you happen to get knocked out, you will lose all progress including loot amount and gear, but retain all experience you received during your journey. This is easier to avoid in multiplayer due to the abilities to revive allies as long as one person is still up. Mushrooms can provide a little pick me up (or be used as a stun grenade) and are scattered throughout the game in varying shapes and sizes. Each mushroom type has some effect that will either heal you, damage you, or in terms of my third play through, instantly kill you. All this morphs into a combat system that favors teamwork with a simple, easy to use structure.
Each game might have procedurally generated levels, but the standard dungeon crawler process is followed to a T. You roam a level filled with connected corridors and slay monsters that spawn in order to move on. Chests, pots and barrels clutter the corners with the promise of shiny emeralds and gold figurines to collect for equipment upgrades later on. You can have the loot to purchase new gear, but you also need to locate the shop on each level in order to view their wares. To progress to the next floor, you must locate the elevator or the boss room depending on the circumstance. It is a simple prospect in theory, but the alternative motives of your fellow goblins can make this adventure an absolute track wreck.
The promise of loot and new equipment is a great incentive and your teammate's worst enemy. Chests spawn a limited amount of loot, which is the only way to purchase new gear. This means you either team up to eliminate the enemy and share the bounty or abandon the notion entirely for a chance to loot everything before they can. This conundrum is the reason this game is so difficult; even the death of a colleague will yield profit in the form of dropped loot. You lose the ability to use your God powers if anyone is knocked out, so keeping everyone alive is a good counterweight to the profit debate. I will be the first to admit that going it solo is entirely easier than dealing with potential multiplayer issues, but the frustrations of dwindling cooperation is also what makes this game enjoyable (if you are with your friends at least).
Thanks to a great Godpower combination (Invincible with healing), I managed to complete the game, solo, in under two hours. Eight monster types inhabit the dungeon with five different levels currently available. Each floor is designed in their own unique way from the style of architecture to the type of chest/breakable container. Weapons and armour range from the hilarious to the practical in the form of unique special attacks and passive enhancements. I have only unlocked nine equipment items thus far (items are unlocked based on your overall level), but according to the Early Access statement, there is 16 weapons and 10 pieces of armor to satisfy your monster crushing needs. Content is sparse for the time being, but what is here is at least polished.
I am rather impressed with the technical function of the game, nevertheless I did notice some issues. Loot can get stuck between the chest and the wall depending on the angle the loot is produced. Enemies can stand in place, ignoring you completely while you wail on them with your weapon. Some achievements activated without me being anywhere near the required number. None of these are game-breaking or overly annoying, but rather beneficial in the long run.
This game is meant for those with friends, especially with the current difficulty. You can find yourself having a blast dealing with the issues of looters and team players, but when it is all said and done, the price is a little heavy for five floors. I am not recommending this title on the grounds of content, but I will commend the developers for the technical stability. I will revisit the game in six months to see how it has evolved.

- Technically, I haven't run into many issues

ABSOLUTE DISGRACE TOWARDS PC GAMERS.
- Horrible performance.
- Huge letterboxes that takes 30% of the screen.(removing the black bars via console commands will drop fps drasticaly)
- 30fps lock (unlocking it does not help because the game still performs terribly)
- Very limited PC configurations in the options.
- Straight up console port.
- Camera stutters when moving around and tends to hit walls behind you.
- Insanely small FOV.

I don't know what everyone's griping about. The game runs smooth as silk for me at 60 fps. Yes, I had to enter a console command to change the max framerate, but so what? It's easy and it works. The aspect ratio is annoying at first, but you get used to it, and even if you don't like it, you can change it as well. Be warned, though, because doing so will change the FoV and it may make the experience uncomfortable on your eyes.
As for the game itself, it's a wonderful blend of action and horror. There have been some extremely tense moments where you're running from a hideous (and incredibly designed) monster, or are struggling to use the few resources you have to fend off a rush of enemies. It's very similar to RE4, with many similar elements; however, TEW is more focued on horror and gore.
The downside to this game is the story and characters. The story is intriguing, but it is fed to you so piecemeal that it seems nonexistent. You're constantly thinking "What is going on? Why am I here? Who is that? WHAT is that?" While mystery is important to horror, there has to be something threading you along that mystery, revealing just enough information to keep your intrigued. TEW isn't great in this regard, and as a result the mystery is just confusing rather than horrifying. Also, characters are completely flat and one dimensional. Voice acting is dull, the writing is bland, and the the protagonist is so, so boring.
Still, the game is fun and interesting enough to keep you going. There's some mind-bending and horrifying areas, mixed up with satisfying gameplay.
Overall, the optimization IS FINE. It's not the best, but it's not unplayable, it doesn't lag or stutter, and YOU DO NOT NEED 4GB VRAM TO PLAY. I have a GTX 760 2GB Vram and I get 60fps with zero problems.

This game is simple and fun.
You just build ships with resources that you collect to defeat the enemy.
Though it's much more complex than that. If you don't make the correct ships at the right time, then it can cost you a lot of wasted resources, and an injection of resources or energy from your destroyed ships.
It still needs work, though. For one, the tutorial is just an extremely basic overview of everything, and the actual tutorial is in the campaign. So I would recommend to make the CURRENT "campaigns" into the tutorials, and make the campaigns more difficult as you progress, with maybe even some changes in rules sometimes to give some missions a bit more of a challenge. It would also be great for tooltips to exist, or at least a "library" of sorts with each ship's information. Perhaps give the game some more visual flair to make it look better.
All in all, it's still a pretty good game. I would recommend it to anyone who wants a rather cheap game with a rather simple concept and some little bits of fun. I just wish more people were playing multiplayer...

A WW II Fps MMO ! and it's free to play! A great game to play with friends or solo and it is very highly addictive. Choose a side of axis or allies and start off as a infantry man in the great war. A quick Tuturial  called First Blood (witch I personally think needs a little more to help out with game play and what exactly to do in in matches) As you gain  rank exp into the war you can use your ingame points/cash to upgrade and buy weapons/vehicles and to (when you rank up enough) change combat rolls to Tanker, Pilot, Recon and eventually you can make it to all mighty general. As a genral a whole other part of the game opens up. You get to actually controll what happens in the matches, infantry, tanks and planes and tell them where to fight. This itself directly inflounces the outcome of who wins the overal war. The war itself after so many victories by the generals of a side will be handed a victory. Then the war starts over as the winning side gets bragging rights. Last I checked the Germans won the last war! Also once you reach the Feild Officer rank, during matches you can have direct control over assualt teams for that match. This can turn the tide and is important  in matches when you are or going to out number someone for an objective.. You can also use real money to purchase upgrades/weapons/vehicles. Matches are won by capturing or defending objectives and/or killing off the other teams. I played myself as the Germans with my friends and brother. I found, I favored the SMG MP34 over the starting SA Rifle G43 and hunting down tanks with the H3 or Tellermines. I also had the option to buy the starting German Infantry vehicle, the Kubelwagon. A bucket shaped jeep with a MG34 mounted on it. Addictive, for you want to really upgrade your weapons/upgrades/vehicles or work to get  ribbon exp to unlock a new one. Getting kills and capturing/defending objectives and doing other such things  in a match also gain you ribbon exp as well as rank exp. Gaing ranks is easy, but sometimes grinding is needed to unlock certain ribbons. The ribbons themselves unlock new combat badges and weapons/vehicles/upgrades. Combat Badges are perks you get through upgrading your ribbons and you can only equip one. Combat Badges include my favorite, Heavy Set. Where you take less damage. It helps against pesky snipers and gernade blasts. A smooth game it runs well with its expected lag issues from time to time. Also maybe close combate could be worked on.  I learned a lot about WW II weapons and vehicles in this game. Just the name of SMG's and tanks. It's fun good stuff and I'm sure the game will grow and grow. Very Positive outlook.

I don't know what the hell happened to this game in development. It had all the ingredients to be as good as the first but it falls flat on it's face which is very apparent from the offset.
Hotline Miami was a great game because of it's fast paced think on your feet melee action, guns were used as relief from a crazy situation. Hotline Miami 2 breaks this fundamentally from the very start of the game and carries it through right until the very end. Nearly every level requires the player to plan ahead and before you can move you must check as far as the camera will move for enemies with guns. It's not often you find yourself in a situation where you need to use melee weapons as gun drops are provided almost constantly. Almost all I can remember is enemies with guns and never melee weapons.
Later on in the game you are placed in a jungle and it's these levels that show how bad some of these decisions that the developers made can be. These jungle levels are so tedious as you find yourself being shot from all kinds of directions. This ruins the pace of the game and makes you wonder how they perfected the level design in Hotline Miami. It becomes hard to look back on anything prior to it in fondness.
The story is largely forgettable. It doesn't carry any of the shock content that the original game had and it's not nearly as inventive. The end of the first game was almost funny in it's attempt to shrug it's harsh content off and say "it was because we are bored". Hotline Miami 2 tries too hard with it's story and it ends up becoming a convuluted broken headachy mess.
My last sentence sums up Hotline Miami 2 for me quite perfectly. It feels like a game trying too hard to become another classic without knowing how it became one in the first place. The addition of too many firearms, bad level design and convuluted story make this extremely difficult to recommend.

Very pleasantly surprised with this title. I thought I'd pick this game up, maybe convince a friend to get it, and it'd be that '40k chess thing' we'd sometimes play now and again.
This game has me hooked, though - I have absolutely DEVOURED the campaign, and playing in multiplayer is a blast. I would favorably compare the Regicide mode with a good turn-based tactical game along the lines of the battles in King's Bounty or Might and Magic (though it's a chessboard, not hex tiles), though battles take significantly longer (avg. 1 hour to complete a match, I had one last night go for 2 hours)
Thinking of Regicide as '40K Chess' is a completely inadequate description. If this had merely been Chess with 40K units (and there is a 'classic' mode that is just that) I wouldn't be able to recommend this title over, say, just getting a free or paid account at
.
But the titular 'Regicide' mode is its own unique creation and plays completely different from how you would expect a chess match to go. During each turn, there will be a Movement Phase and an Initiative Phase - the former is what you'd expect, with pieces moving and being able to capture like everything you know in standard chess.
However, the following Initiave Phase allows you to spend Initiative Points:
If you play in a chess mindset, this can have disasterous results for you. Want to take a pawn with your queen, pinning an enemy rook for capture next turn? There is a very real possibility that all of the surrounding enemy pieces will shoot your queen into slag on their turn, so be careful.
Pro +
Neutral ~
Cons -

While GW/Warhammer 40k videogames are often a bit of a chancey investment, Regicide is one example that hasn't left me disappointed at all. I was expecting 40k Battle-Chess, and indeed the Classic mode is exactly that. Regicide Mode, however, is actually a properly clever, inventive meld of chess and an Action Point system similar to the one from Space Hulk. There's even a Campaign-mode with small-scale set engagements, specific victory and defeat conditions, and a reasonably well-scripted voice-acted narrative that ties the campaign together.
The movement rules come more-or-less directly from Chess, with one move per turn, but after moving your piece you can perform a number of other actions with any of your pieces, including the one you just moved. Pieces can either be 'captured' (like taking a piece in Chess - an instant kill) or damaged and killed over a series of turns or attacks by ranged or melee attacks from nearby pieces. Some pieces have less health, making them more susceptible to ranged attacks. Such attacks have a percentile chance to hit, modified by range, taking cover, aiming etc, and inflict varying amounts of damage depending on what weapon and how many points of armour your piece has.
On the more critical side, the interface system is mostly good except for some irritating details - for example there's no clear way to deselect an action if you decide you'd actually rather not (although clicking on an empty tile does the trick, it's not intuitive to click forward to go back). Also, optional vanity sales and paid-for content once again defile the game industry, with this offering including a range of 'unlockable' alternate Chapter liveries, and (assuming Regicide is a moderate commercial success) will probably eventually include DLC packs for Chaos Marines and other Xenos species (at the moment it's just Orks and Space Marines). The good news is that if you play enough, you can earn enough experience points to unlock most of the vanilla content anyway, and playing daily boosts an XP multiplier - but only by 0.1x per consecutive day. Considering all you're really getting for your efforts is a custom aesthetic option, if you're like me, you'll probably just ignore these options until you happen to notice one day that you've accumulated enough XP to unlock something. On the other hand, if you're wealthy enough to throw money at games developers for what ought to be included in the retail price, I suggest you donate your wealth to me instead - it's a better use for it, plus it makes me happy and keeps me in cookies and cola.
To sum up, this game will teach you the basics of chess while also showing you what happens when a Librarian explodes someone with his brain, and if you play the campaign it'll tell you an interesting war-story too. Since a decent tabletop chess-set will set you back at least £20/$30, the store price for Regicide isn't too steep - but God-o-God do game developers need to stop demanding we pay for the privilege of opening the 'options' menu.

-First Playthrough Review- (SPOLIER-FREE)
Before I begin this review, let it be noted that the current vanilla and un-patched version of the game has resulted in a horrible PC-Port, the main issues that come with the port include FPS limits, limited graphical options, poor mouse support and a very cinematic yet annoyingly painfull letterboxing feature.
Luckily however there have been several console commands released on sites such as PC Gamer that provide a means to unlock the FPS and remove the strange letterboxing, however doing so will decrease your FOV and possibly cause some glitches in the game.
Now as for the game itself, I am currently playing through The Evil Within for the first time on the "Survival Difficuly" which makes enemies tougher, supplies harder to find and generally just makes the game provide more of a challenge, there is a previous "Casual Difficulty" for an easier playthrough aswell as two locked difficultys which I assume are unlocked after completion of the game.
I will admit that during the begging chapters of the game (Chapters 1 - 3) I was very critical and judgemental about the game, I jumped right into the game believing it to be a "Jumpscare Freakout" similar to Outlast or Amnesia, but that is not what The Evil Within sets out to be, infact if it is to be compared to any game it should compare to Resident Evil.
The game focuses less on character development and explaination as to the events that occur and instead focuses actual gameplay and "Survival" as the majourity of time is spent collecting enough resources to sneak or blast your way through the next area of grotesque abominations that act as your enemies.
When talking about the enemies in The Evil Within I first have to consider "Which One?" as much like in the more recent Resident Evil games, the enemies will differentiate depending on the current location, unfortunatly this only really applies to the visual look of the enemies, as many of the zombie-like creatures in this game share similar statistics and you can judge them based on their "Build" ie: Larger Enemies will have more health.
I have to say that the art team behind The Evil Within have really done a great job making enemies look disgustingly horrid and creepy espically when it comes to the more signifcant enemies or "Bosses" these characters tend to have special attributes and a unique look and sound to them which makes each encounter with them just that extra bit more terriying.
I'm not going to talk much about the story or "Plot" of The Evil Within, mainly because I am still playing through it and don't want to make any judgements before I know the true ending, what I can tell you however is that the plot goes all over the place, during the course of my current playthrough I have had to stop and question myself as to what just happened and where/what I was doing previously as the game throws you through loop after loop of confusing segways and plot twists, I hope that the majourity of my questions will be answered by the time I reach the ending of the game as currently I am having to gather my information through in-game notes/journals and The Evil Within Wiki.
Overall I will admit that after all the port-issues and the confusing plot-journey I am still very much enjoying this game and although it is not a great game by any means It is still fun, enjoyable and a nice change from the usual "Indie Horror" games that seem to flood the marketplace so easily, I will advise though that If you are going to play this then remember that it is, in all of it's traditional ways, a Survival Horror Game!

So there we were on our merry way to South America by way of the Straits of Gibraltar when the Sonarman picks up a contact on the hydrophone. A fleet of enemy warships are closing in and are unaware of our presence. "Easy prey" me thinks, so I order the sub to snorkel depth and have a looks about. Sure enough, a whole convoy has just sailed into my path. I ready the torpedoes and aim for an easy target. I fire four of them, thinking I will hit more than one ship. Two torpedoes are duds and a third misses entirely. The fourth one, however, is a brave little torpedo and he keeps chugging along. He misses the majority of the convoy and it looks like mission failure. But a little past the convoy is another ship that happened to stray off from the others. My brow is sweating in anticipation as I watch. It's quickly closing in on the target, but too close to tell if it will hit. Then it happens. The enemy vessel explodes in a cloud of smoke and fire as the torpedo strikes it on the starboard side. The ship is destroyed instantaneously.
What was that? Suddenly our sub is rocked by something big. The hull is breached and water starts spraying through the rivets. The engine room starts flooding. It appears that the rest of the convoy has discovered us and are bombing our location. "Dive!" I scream and the crew reacts immediately. "Give me more depth!" The sub slowly starts descending to 65, 70, 75, 80, 85, 86, 87, 88 meters. "Stop!", 89, 90, 91, 92 meters. "Why isn't it stopping?" I yell. "I don't know" the Chief Engineer replies, "We can't control it Captain!". Rapidly we decline, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100 meters. It looks like we're about to sink, but by some strange miracle the sub starts to steady itself at 101 meters. The crew and I wait and listen to the bombs being dropped from above and echoing off the hull. The engines are stopped and the crew works around the clock to stop the flooding and fix the hull breach. Everything is starting to look good and we wait.
Hours slip by and the enemy fleet has not eased up on its relentless pursuit of our sub. We have in affect♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the entire Royal Navy. The Sonarman is continually reporting contacts and it appears that they are circling our location. We start up the engines on battery power and rig for silent running. We release decoys and make heading for the nearest friendly port in a desperate bid to escape the attacking fleet. It's no good. The enemy can track us anywhere we go. The ship is stable and the leaks have been fixed, but our batteries are running low. It would be suicide to surface with the enemy circling us like sharks at a feeding frenzy.
The batteries finally give out and the sub sinks to the depths below. There is no good ending to this heroic tale. Somewhere in the Mediterranean sea, beneath the murky waters, lies the brave men of U-Boat 260.

Now that Steam has fixed its issues with Achievements, I'm enjoying seeing what I didn't realise I never knew about Wakfu. I started with Dofus, and gradually made my transition to Steam where I discovered more resources and a larger fanbase of my favourite games.
Wakfu, like its predecessor, is a player-controlled environment where the ecology and economy of the world are entirely dependent on the users. While that seems simple enough, the game goes slightly further, allowing players to be elected as the governing rulers of an entire area of the map, dictating how money should be spent, and how the environment should thrive. The downfall to the above is that 100% of your item profits are from users. There are no NPCs to whom you can sell or trade items from your inventory.
With a large collection of classes, Wakfu (and Dofus) has ensured the general availability of most preferred character archetypes, and has done extensive work keeping all the classes fairly well balanced. The tutorial is only generally comprehensive, so it's strongly suggested that trying a new class is done in the Incarnum world where everything is easy enough to not concern oneself with the dangers of durress. I personally prefer playing support roles, and have found that the highly acclaimed Eniripsa is fun, but the Eca and Xelor make healing very different, and definitely a lot more worthwhile in the aspect of overcoming challenges.
Leveling is tedious, and the quests aren't very well thought out, so once you're finished with Astrub, prepare to grind. The maximum level takes a while to reach, especially since it's primarily done by grinding the entire way after LV20. Max level is 170 at the time of this writing, so there's a bit of perspective. The dungeons are awesome! when you can get friends to tag along, especially if you're following the difficult to locate storyline. I've read the manga and watched the anime, so seeing the dungeons and being part of the story is definitely a great deal of entertainment for me.
If you're having a tough time getting through an area or quest, and haven't made friends on your server yet, no problem; Sidekicks are available in the market for Ogrin. If you're from Dofus, you know Ogrin can be purchased with Kama (in-game money), and thus is possible to acquire at no cost (for those who prefer not to pay). As a long-time subscriber, I highly recommend you give Steam's monthly options a try. I'm used to getting a pet or piece of gear with my Ogrine each month, but Steam goes a step further including more items that are only available through the now gaming giant.
My final, most important factor to playing Wakfu is this: It's adorable! I love cute, and Ankama has done a great job at giving exactly that to me. Have fun, everyone, and feel free to join me on Nox or Remington. Just let me know you're coming.

Where the predecessor gives me satisfaction, this game gives me frustration. Hotline Miami 2 is a failure compared to HM1.
***GAMEPLAY 5/10
The gameplay is the same, but the developers made the game considerably harder by some kind of poor level design combined with sniper enemies AI. It is frustrating to be killed by enemies that are out of the screen, who see you because you're passing in front of a window, which is out of your view as well. The shift key that allows you to drag the screen to see more of the map isn't enough to be aware of those enemies 2 times out of 3. Basically, I ended up finishing levels out of pure luck rather than skill, which is the exact opposite of what happened in HM1.
After 3 hours of "Press R to restart" I decided that I have better games to play.
***STORY 7/10
The story seems to be about different characters from different times, some from the 80's, some from the 90's, etc. I wrote SEEMS because I couldn't follow the story very clearly, the bad things of the gameplay ruined this aspect as well for me. When I don't enjoy playing a game it's difficult to enjoy the story. I'll give a 7/10 only because, for the little I've seen, it didn't suck as the gameplay.
***GRAPHICS
I wont' consider this aspect as the others. I'll just say it's the same as HM1 and it's fine, but it's clearly not one of the main features of this game, even though it gives a good 80's/90's arcade feeling.
***SOUND 7/10
Music is good but not great. HM1 had a better soundtrack in my opinion.
Overall score 6/10  - This doesn't mean GOOD, it means BARELY PLAYABLE

After throughly enjoying Hotline Miami I decided to go balls deep into Hotline Miami 2. I had read such negative reviews and after only playing through a few levels, I too, was a little let down that not a whole lot had changed. The style was still just as great and the music is very appropriately infectious. The storyline was a little bizarre but I came around to really enjoying it after playing through it multiple times. Completing the storyline was what changed my entire opinion about this game. I realized it was definitely more difficult than the first when it comes to getting the achievements. Yeah, there were some bugs and annoying door glitches that ruin your big combo streaks, but it was just as satisfying to get that nice replayed round as it was to be off by a split second shot and have to restart over and over and over again. I was reminded of a quote from the first one "don't be afraid to die". This game exploits that rule to a whole new level with the additon of hard mode and some pretty time-consuming achievements. Hotline Miami 2 has brought me hours of satisfyingly frustrated entertainment and is worth a second shot if you gave up on it or a first try if you're still curious.

This is "strategy lite" and kind of feels like a mobile game. Nothing wrong with that, though.
Anyways, gameplay is pretty simple. You on one side, enemy on the other. Build resource gathering ships, spam fighters of various types, upgrade some ships, and occasionally use a race specific special move. Hopefully your ship spamming was more successful than the other side and you manage to push back their fleet, and take out their mothership.
There are three races, each with their own ship types and special abilities. Each race also has their own mission mode. These missions throw some minor variable at you of various difficulty, but it usually comes down to spamming the right ships as well as spending upgrade points earned in previous missions or freeplay.
Is this game hard? Not really. Is there a lot of strategy involved? Not really. Is it kind of enjoyable? Yeah.
BTW, widescreen appears to be broken in the settings.

Oh boy, This one is a dewsy.
Let's recap some porting history first;
DC>GCN>XBLA/PSN>PC
This makes this particular version of the game a port of a port of a port, with that there are some obvious technical issues I really have to address, given that the devs literally had years to fix before this review. I'll have to start with the cons.
Jankier controls, Control on the DC and GCN versions weren't bad, but now at a pinch it feels more like controlling at the game than direct response.

Sonic Adventure 2 is overall, a decent game. I don't think of it as THE best game in the series as a lot of other people do, but I still enjoy it. The high-speed platforming stages with Sonic and Shadow are pretty fun to go through. The mech-shooting levels with Tails and Eggman and the treasure-hunting levels with Knuckles and Rouge, while not as good, are still somewhat enjoyable. I don't spend much time in the Chao Garden, but I can see how it would be appealing to a lot of people. This was also the first Sonic game to rank the player at the end of stages. However, I can tell when a game has aged, and this game has definitely aged. For one thing, there will be numerous occasions when characters talk over each other in cutscenes and when the music will drown them out, which is very distracting (at least the music itself is great stuff, with Escape From the City and Live and Learn being my two favorite songs). Another thing that bothers me is that some of the voice actors read their lines in cringe-worthy ways. No offense to Connor Bringas, but this is especially noticable with Tails. I don't think that the game suffers overall because of these flaws, but I wouldn't call this aging smoothly. As for Sonic Adventure 2 as a whole? It's aged, but I still consider it to be a pretty good game. Best Sonic game ever? No, but I admire some design choices here.

can be easily summarised as Battle Chess set in the Warhammer universe. It follows the basic rules of Chess while expanding on these with other tactical mechanics to mix up the game play.
Although there is a classic mode
, my play time primarily consisted of the single player regicide campaign which includes three acts of 50 tailored scenarios
. These offer specific challenges which are made interesting by specific board obstacles & unit layouts - no two levels play out the same. There is an overarching story played out with voice acting between scenarios, but personally I didn't find it all that engrossing so usually found myself skipping these sections to read the primary & secondary objectives.
Campaign levels are more strategic or puzzle like as they play out, with many needing multiple attempts to conquer. This can simply come down to poor choices, but can also be due to 'bad luck'
. Each turn allows you to move one unit on the board, plus an initiative phase where you can use points to activate special abilities. These are mainly unit specific, offering both offensive & defensive abilities depending on your situation. Points are limited so you need to use them wisely in order to win. This double mechanic works rather well and for the most enhances the usual chess rules. Most of the basics are explained in regards to the mechanics & abilities, but found myself with a bit of a trial-by-fire often making stupid moves because I didn't understand all the possibilities until I reached around Act II. Some may find this frustrating.
Sound quality and graphics both are good, UI can get in the way a bit sometimes unless you move the camera or zoom out. Once selected, applying an ability to a specific square on the board can sometimes miss click and hit an adjacent square if you are not careful. The executions are certainly a highlight offering the expected brutality & bloody finishing moves you would expect from a Warhammer game. Regrettably, these are rather limited only offering one variation per unit combo, with some not seeming to have any! Entertaining for the first dozen times you see it but quickly found myself mashing the space bar to skip and speed up the game. Barriers also tend to get in the way blocking your vision of these animations due to the fixed camera angle. Being a strong selling point of the game I would have liked to see better camera work and much more variety.
The strong puzzle like nature of the campaign kept me coming back regularly to play this through, the challenge was well balanced on the difficulty scale, although the random nature of the rolls often frustrated the hell out of me! As I mentioned earlier, what seems like bad luck rather than good strategy more often than not can ruin your game. Each action has a percentage chance to hit, with a number of modifiers such as critical hit chance playing a role. This probability means you can get a string of bad rolls that devastate your squad, regardless of how good your overall strategy is. This takes the skill out of the game in my opinion & just leads to rage-quitting.
There have been many times where I felt like I was playing with loaded dice, where one unit regardless of the number of times you use their attack will miss vs another specific unit/square. One recent time in Act III
, I experienced
in a row trying to kill of the final Meganobz (rook)! This highlighted clearly there is some issues with the randomness/chance element of this game.
One other limitation I found was that the AI will always follow the same moves based on the board & unit layout. This makes it predictable on multiple retries of a scenario.
An online external account is needed as it doesn't use your Steam account to track progress. This is primarily for the multiplayer aspect of the game, so if you want to only play the campaign you can still play without registering, but regardless something people should be aware of
. As of the time of writing this review the devs, Hammerfall, are still updating with balance changes & improvements, along with community 'Double XP' weekends to encourage replayability.
A few improvements in the chance rolls
would be great along with an option to play the game in 'fast mode' avoiding the animations instead of having to mash the space bar
. Likewise, I would love to see a simple scenario editor included with Steam Workshop support to share your own challenges with the community once you have got through the included campaign. I think that could add much more replayablity in the long term.
Despite its few detracting points & some room for improvement, I still found
to be good fun, & something I regularly picked up for a quick 30-60min session over the past few months.

Let me start by saying I bought Warhammer 40,000: Regicide as soon as hit hit early access and it was playable then. More a proof of concept that slowly developed over time but it was playable. Now it's not even that.
I love the idea of 40k and chess. I enjoy both the concept behind regicide and classic chess with all of the wonderfully violent executions when pieces are taken.
However as of the date of this review the only recommendation I can make of this game is to stay away. I've tried close to 20 different games of both the campaign and skirmish regicide against the AI (Not a fan of online play and from the bug reports I've seen online is plagued with its own issues) and every single time in classic mode the following happens:
The weird boy makes a leaping move animation and then freezes before landing on the square he's supposed to land on. Sometimes I can move, sometimes it's stuck on the AI's turn until I give up waiting and end the game.  Or sometimes my librarian or assault marine will make an attack and then freeze there after the animation not allowing the AI to move. These aren't issues of the game crashing and sending me to my desktop as I can pull up the menu and reset the board and it all goes fine until one of these happens again.
Every single time I down the first ork in regicide I'm stuck unable to do anything and the game is over. I have to quit and start over and kill the first ork again.
This breaks the game and makes it unplayable and it is NOT acceptable for any game that proudly proclaims it has launched.
The sad part is I really want to like the game. It looks beautiful the textures are nice the view surrounding the board is very enveloping enough to were it almost seems like the perfect balanced version of 40k tabletop everyone wants to have. I've even recognized GW terrain pieces. But if I can't play the game then no matter how good it looks or sounds I can't judge the rest of it. I don't know how the rest of the campaign progresses if I can't get past killing the first ork. I don't know how good the AI is if I can't get past barely devloping my board before the game gets stuck in a bug again and i have to reset the board again.
If you want a 40k themed chess set buy a tac squad some boys and look on ebay for the remaining pieces and throw them on a chess board. At least you can play the game to its end.
Avoid Warhammer 40,000: Regicide until it can fix the key bugs that make it unplayable.

Okay after paying this game for six hours now I will give an honest opinion not just a first thought.  The Evil Within is clearly a Console game that was ported to PC as a cash grab.  This game is not ready for primetime PC play and I'll list why in a moment.
1. The Story- The story can't seem where it wants to go, and at times the game struggles to keep the tension up.  This could be to give the player a breather or they just didn't really have a plan as to how the story would flow.
2. Voice Acting- The voice acting is on point and well done and lip syncing is perfect.
3. Sounds- The sound is well done and very immersive, I would recommend 5.1 or a really good set of headphones.
4. Controls- Using the keyboard and mouse there are a few points where it can be a pain but once you learn all the key biddings it shouldn’t be an issue.
5. Graphics- Now some players claim that graphics don’t matter and that maybe true but in a game like this they do.  If your rig can run this game at high levels the graphics are amazing and very indicative of next generation games.
6. PC requirements- Trust me if your system doesn’t meet the minimum requirements skip this game for the PC.  However if you do it will run fine once you tweak it to run at optimal settings.  If you have NVIDA use the GeForce Experience to set it up.
7. Bugs and problems- It took me a full day to get this game to run as it should and that is not acceptable for a $60.00 game.  The game wanted to start in a windowed mode and when it was switched to full screen the picture was zoomed in.  I run a 2560 X 1600 screen res so to make the icons a little bigger I had the magnifier tool to 200%.  I have never had an issue with this until The Evil Within, once I put the magnifier to 100% the screen issue cleared up.  Next having to use a prompt menu to fix letterboxing, and FPS makes no sense.  It is almost like the developers said oh screw it we’ll just have the player do our job.  I hope for a patch that will fix this but I am not holding my breath.
8. Final thoughts- This game is worth the money if you go in with your eyes open and have a system that will run the game.  I noticed no real graphic issues with a 2 GB card though they do recommend a 4 GB.  If you like games like the first Resident Evil or FEAR you will likely enjoy this 18 chapter game, after 7 hours I am half way through so it gives you plenty of game for the buck.  Just be prepared to have issues with install, bugs, and have an above average rig and you will enjoy this game.  So I rate this game a 6/10 it is a good game sadly the tech issues really cost this game in my eyes.

I know this game gets a bad rap for being short and having a lacking story, but I found it easy to get into the story and keep up.  It's something you have to pay attention to. (I'm so used to shooting my guns that I don't know if I'll use the powers much.)
I also liked that the main focus, water, had life to it.  It wasn't just something that was everywhere and utterly useless, you could actually use it to progress in the game.  Need to go up one level but no stairs/ladder/etc?  Can't go through a door because there is a fire right in front of it?   Shoot a wall and ride the flood.   Need to get to the next part of the story and don't feel like killing your way through a group of 10 guys?  You guessed it, OPEN THE FLOOD GATES AND SHOOT DOWN SOME POWER LINES.
Too many indie developers go for generic, popular themes such as the ever popular Zombie shooter or some post-apocalyptic world that has little to no back story as to how things happened (or it takes forever to know the full story).  It's refreshing that they did their own spin on a futuristic dying Earth where the problem was over-population and not some catastrophic apocolyptic event.
For $5($0.49 during steam sales), this game gives you your money's worth and 8 times out of 10 you'll enjoy playing this for a few hours.  I got this through a Humble Bundle, so I didn't pay more than $0.10 for it, therefore take what I say with a grain of salt.

It's an indie game and you can see it was created on a tight budget as the ending feels a bit rushed for my taste. Nevertheless is it a surprisingly good game with some interesting approaches to gameplay mechanics e.g. hacking terminals and of course the phantastic water. As you'll do a lot of platforming it is worth mentioning that the movement controls are solid. As Hydrophobia was first released on XBLA it supports Xbox controller although playing with keyboard and mouse is no problem at all. What you get on steam is a reworked version of the game with better graphics and one different character model with new voice acting - I like the original scottish accent better. Please compare Xbox vs Pc version on youtube. The game code feels not very optimized for Pc . I play titles like Metro Last Light or Crysis 3 with ease in max settings in 1920x1200 while my HD 7950 doesn't get noisy whereas Hydrophobia seems quite taxing in max settings. Wakfu.
The name alone makes people cringe like, you don't even want to go there.
In the beginning there was Dofus, and I'd be lying if I said all was well.
Dofus was the first of its kind, back when Steam actually made games and we were all little younglings playing 'Gunz: The duel'.
Dofus was an interesting beast because unlike conventional play to win games at the time, Dofus was an over glorified demo of an MMO back when other MMO's thought they could actually stand up to the likes of Everquest and World of Warcraft.
As time went on, many of us old guard who rememered the awful, oppressive treatment at the hands of Anakama had moved on and seemingly so had a large enough portion of the playerbase that a sequel was in order!
A strange move indeed, making a sequel only a few years after your base product had launched. Wakfu of course is that sequel.
Well it was announed years before it arrived and that signalled only the beginning of its issues. Not as late as Duke Nukem Forever but late enough to miss its own funeral because Wakfu is effectively dead.
I say effectively because the servers seem to still be online, probabaly with the funding from the first game and piggy backing on those servers too no doubt.
Dofus became a franchaise even having its own cartoon series over in France and its nice that we have a game filling this cutesy on the surface but brutally difficult when you play niche, but Wakfu is an MMO and with so few people around to play with, it just falls apart.
But lets go back in time! What about when there WERE people to play with? Dofus was still a better game! Its like they took out all the things in Dofus that demanded teamwork and made Wakfu a 1 player game with online connectivity.
Some people may like that idea but remember that this game was born from an MMO; it is akin to World of Warcraft having a World of Warcraft 2, still set in Azeroth only now its a one player twin stick shooter. It might be good on its own merits but we can't ignore the dramatic shift and we know the old crowd, the ones most likely to even want a sequal are going to feel very alienated.
That is Wakfu. Welcome to Wakfu.
Now all that aside is the game even good? Well the animations are fantastic, no really they are a joy to look at! The music...Well it exists. Yeah no one track really adds much which is a shame. The graphics are once again top notch like the animation and looking at the world around you isn't breath-taking like in Dark Souls or anything like that but they look great. Real dediction went into every art asset.
Wakfus biggest failings are not even its own fault. Communities grow and wain as new products come out to tempt the crowds. Anakama are terrible at customer support but that is more of an 'outside of the game' issue. The music might lack pepper but that is very minor indeed. Really I don't recommend Wakfu but only for 1 reason and that reason is that its old!
I don't mean old games suck, not in the least but what I mean is the community is effectively gone, its like Guildwars, which is a fantastic game, but going into Lions arch and having no one to play with, well it is the death kneel for an "MMO" and while people are playing Wakfu, the vast community has long since moved on and when I played I found barely anyone to interact with, even my screenshots were barren of life when I took them.
What a shame.
If you and enough of your friends can populate the game, you may have fun. If however you are looking to play this game in order to make new friends then move on, their is nothing to see here.

This is a very mild recommendation - get this game if it's on sale, but don't bother at full price.  The game is interesting and engaging, but once you've completed the campaign there's really not much of anything to do.  Getting to 100% is a mind-numbing grind and replayability just isn't that fun.
Pros:
- Campaign is fun
- Each faction is unique and fun to play
Cons:
- There's a huge bug where your upgrades like auto-mining and auto-energy generation don't work at all.  I'm not sure, but this could also mean that all other Gear-related upgrades don't work either - the mining and energy related ones are the only ones that give a visual indicator of whether they're working or not.
- Due to the above, your only chance of beating the "Hard" AI in skirmish mode is to rush them.  Then one of two things happens: You win(yay!), or more likely the enemy starts spamming energy skills which makes it impossible to beat them.  "Hard" AI seems to have an unlimited amount of energy or generates energy extremely quickly - you cannot compete if it starts using energy skills.
- You need 360 Gears to max out all upgrades.  You can earn maybe 4-7 in a "Medium" AI skirmish, and 5-7.  So you're looking at probably 70-90 rounds.  After doing the campaign and some skirmishes, I'm sitting at 34 wins, 0 losses, and nowhere close to finishing all the upgrades.
- Replayability just isn't fun.  You spam the same build orders, upgrade chain, etc.  Once you find a good starting order of things, it's just the same thing over and over and over and over and over.  With the goal of 360 gears in mind....it's just too much.

Boson X is a fantastic game.  It's a little endless runner where you don't gain anything by progressing, you have to run on specific blue panels to gain score.  There are three buttons involved (jump left, jump right, and jump), and online leaderboards.  That's it.  No gimmicks.  No 'XP'.  No collectables.  Just you, three buttons, eighteen increasingly difficult levels, and a few thousand other people who are better than you at all of them.  Sure, the music is♥♥♥♥♥♥  Sure, the graphics are nothing special.  Sure, the stages do start to get a bit artificially difficult towards the end (the Dark X Boson, where everything is in wireframe to make it deliberately difficult to tell what's going on is the worst offender here).

Warhammer 40,000: Regicide is a new perspective within the world of chess, and the Warhammer 40,000 universe, creating one impressive game. I will add a TL;DR at the end.

Warhammer 40,000 Regicide contains Classic mode which is a normal chess game with Warhammer pieces and Regicide mode where you have a movement phase followed by an initiative phase. Elaborating more into Regicide mode you can still destroy enemies just like in a normal chess game, but the addition of the initiative phase requires a whole new strategy as different units have different abilities, and you are limited to a sense action wise. It will have you adopt a brand new strategy to defeat your opponents. You can unlock more abilities as you play and can choose between the space marines and the orks. You can choose to skirmish or play multiplayer with either gamemode or play the Regicide campaign. There are double XP weekends, daily bonuses, skin for space marines or ork, and fun to watch execution animations.

The graphical aspect of this game is highly detailed and well-made and the music helps you focus on the task at hand while you play. The executions are definitely a factor within this games appeal, but I found execution animations only worked with certain characters on certain characters.

+ Two different ways to play
+ Great for chess and have the option to disable the executions if you want
+ Librarium will help you identify roles of each units and the basics or chess
+ Reskin of pieces are well made and maps/chessboards are detailed
+ XP boosts, ability to get more abilities, and daily rewards
- Execution is limited to certain characters
- This in the end is a chess simulator, nothing more
- Chance aspect in initiative phase of Regicide can be highly frustrating

While I may not know the Warhammer 40,000 universe that well, I am happy to say this has become a great chess simulator which I will be able to play whenever I am bored, or want to play chess with a little bit more.

Warhammer 40,000: Regicide is a great chess simulator with added aspects to add to its charm. Regicide mode is fun although the chance aspect of it can be quite frustrating. The execution animations are beautiful, the music helps you keep in the game, and it’s very well developed. In the end it is simply a chess game with some added features in the Regicide versus the Classic mode, but overall very enjoyable and recommendable to anyone who likes chess and the Warhammer skin it has.

Pretty fun co-op action game. If you feel like you've played it before, you've probably played Left 4 Dead. While it does borrow several elements from L4D (four player co-op, fending off waves of a horde (rats), special buff monsters (see tank rat), objective based scenarios), it does manage to change up the formula a bit. The biggest difference is its focus on melee combat, which is executed fairly well. Swinging a weapon into an enemy manages to feel satisfyingly visceral, not unlike something you'd experience in Chivalry. There are still ranged weapons, but they are definitely downplayed in comparison. Other differences include class based characters, each with their own set of unique weapons, as well as some minor RPG-inspired mechanics. These are mostly restricted to loot-based weapon quality upgrades and upgradable weapon traits (a chance to heal on hit, for example), however they bring some welcome customizability to the game.
Overall, Vermintide is a pretty good co-op experience. The RNG for loot can be annoying, it's supposed to encourage you to try multiple classes, but if you like to stick to a class like me you'll feel cheated by it a lot, as it dumps gear for mostly other classes on you. It's a relatively minor annoyance though, all things considered, and the game is definitely still winnable without the highest tier loot. Definitely recommended if you are looking for a slightly more difficult and varied Left 4 Dead experience.
