This was my first Dirt game. I usually go by reviews, and that would mean going for Rally instead, because 4 has taken a real beating in the reviews from series fans saying that D:Rally is a better game. However, a friend bought D4 so I did too, on account of multiplayer.
I enjoyed the crap out of D4, so when Rally went on sale, it was an obvious choice to pick it up. Here's my take on the complaints I've seen the most from the people recommending D:Rally over D4.
The rally courses are the one criticism I agree with most. The maps in Rally are authentic and deliberate, with some great scenery to take in. In D4 the jigsaw maps are a tad lifeless by comparison, being deliberately neutral so that they can be generated from components. I believe this also explains a lot of the "graphical downgrade" complaints I've seen; the games are about the same in terms of fidelity but D:Rally's environments are generally more pleasing to look at.
I also found the streamlined career mode in D:Rally to have a slightly more logical progression in terms of difficulty, forcing you to start with older cars versus D4's heavily modern roster, where even a lower-tier souped-up Ford Focus can still be a bit too much car for a complete amateur.
On terms of handling and feel, on a G920 and full-simulation mode w/ no assists, they really feel about the same, which is to say, great, and I can bounce between the two games without preferring one over the other.
With that being said, Dirt 4 has a lot of unsung features that I think deserve a LOT of credit.
Dirt Academy is very well-considered and highly interactive in D4, versus the sets of videos in Rally. They did a flawless job of not only demonstrating driving principles on-track for the player to ride along and absorb, but then immediately putting it on the player to follow through with the lesson in a scenario that emphasizes the technique of focus. I'm a hands-on learner, and have somewhat poor retention if I'm merely watching and listening, so I found this extremely favorable and informative. I can understand why series veterans didn't give this much thought, since they already know how to drive, but as a total beginner I found it invaluable.
An extension of Dirt Academy is the "Dogfish" free roam area. Being able to drive free-form is a great way to get a sense for the limitations and strengths of each vehicle type, laying bare characteristics that would be hard to notice while bouncing around a linear path at blistering speed and hoping to god you don't smack any trees.
Another feature that I'm crazy about it Joyride, which is generally split between two types of challenges: time-attack on laps with icons floating around that either add or detract time when "collected", or smash attack, where you're expected to hit as many boxes as possible under a time limit. These are both a great deal of fun, and for as much as they can throw some really extreme circumstances at you (multi-story catwalk paths, anyone?), it's comparatively stress-free and a great way to continue honing driving skills that translate directly to race events.
I haven't spent much time with the new disciplines since I'm taking on one thing at a time, but they're certainly able to claim variety and a completely new set of challenges to overcome. The stadium trucks in particular are a blast to throw around the proving grounds.
I realize this is already long so I'm gonna sum this review up as such: I play Dirt: Rally for rally racing when I'm feeling serious, and D4 for everything else. At present, I give a little bit more time to D4 because it offers a lot of fun takes on the driving experience. I recommend owning both games when the price is right, neither one makes the other unnecessary.

Wakfu is a game I would like to enjoy. The art style is unique and a well made turn-based combat is practically non-existent in MMOs. But there are some glaring issues that can keep you from enjoying the game. Grind being the biggest one.
With a good group, however, the game is much more enjoyable. Try to lure in a few friends if possible.
If you want to see how a turn-based MMO might work, I'd recommend trying Wakfu. Even if you didn't stick with it.
- Art style is beautiful,
- Combat is, at it's best, an absolute joy,
- Unique and interesting world with economy ran purely by players.
- There is barely any info for new players on what to do,
(I was 13 hours into the game and still clueless on so much)
- The Grind. In action MMOs I can accept it and even enjoy it, up to a point. But in a turn-based game it becomes so mind-numbingly boring to constantly repeat the same process over and over. Quests the usual grindy MMO fare,
- Party tools. Ways to easily find and party up with other players are missing or at least I wasn't informed of any during the first 13 hours. This is a pity as the most challenging fights could be great due to the variety on combos and tactics available.
Overall I can't recommend this unless you happen to have a group of friends to actively play with. Taking on considerably higher level enemies and coming out on top is a great feeling and the fights can be real challenges sometimes. But the game's just too obscure and the progress too slow for those few instances to be worth it.

I love Resident Evil and Silent Hill and was really excited for this game but good god what a disappointment.  First off, most will be familiar with the black bar and 30 fps lock issue.  These can be solved with a few console commands provided by Bethesda.  However; even with these fixes the FOV is abysmal. Trying to aim with your weapon will make the screen zoom in almost comically far to where you can't even see your weapon.  Trying to turn your character to the left or right feels like I am trying to back a semi-truck into a parking space at Best Buy on black Friday. Combine this with horrendous screen tearing and minimal set of graphics options and you get a game that wants to be great but is hampered by technical issues.  The sad thing is, if they had allowed a full set of graphic adjustment options I feel like this could have been a GOTY contender. Obligatory pro and con list below:
Pros:
+Great graphics, especially with rain and particle effects
+RPG like elements which I enjoy
+Silent Hill esque atmosphere
+Decent story so far
Cons:
-Character movement is terrible.  They clearly modeled the game after RE4 yet a game that is 10 years old handles movement much better than this game
-The FOV is inexcusable.  I get having a tight camera to make a tense feeling but this is so bad that if you are trying to fire your weapon at an enemy up close the camera doesn't know what to do and you end up dying as you can't see a damn thing
-Complete lack of graphical adjustment options
-Poor performance even on a higher end system
I really hope they patch this game.  As it stands right now, this game is nothing but squandered potential.

I'll preface this review with the fact that I'm not done yet, I'm probably a little more than half way through the game and my opinion will likely become more cynical as I progress.
The Evil Within is a game which has a lot of potential but drops it, repeatedly. What should've been a Survival Horror reimagining ends up retreating old ground before deciding that it wants to go into the modern day Survival Horror stables of... well, not really existing all that much.
I'll avoid the technical issues, the framerate, etc. Those are issues which one can learn to look past. I'll approach my personal grievances with the actual game.
The game begins right, it's a confusing jumbled mess but you're somewhat terrified of being grabbed or spotted by the nearest enemy and being killed. I've escaped reloads by using the many scattered environmental stealth cabinets/beds and the feeling of looking at the enemies walk into the room was pushing all the right buttons.
That was until I realized how simple the enemies were. Maybe I'm just disappointed because I finished Alien: Isolation not too long ago but the fact that enemies won't search the room and simply return to the environment which they usually hang out was soul-crushingly disappointing.
Hiding under the bed when the entire room has no windows, no closets and the enemies saw me walk into the room should be silly. It shouldn't work that way. This stealth system is poorly implemented if it's going to last the entire gam-
Wait, no. That's the biggest offender right there. Stealth becomes irrelevant not even 1/4 through the game. As your arsenal expands, the enemies grow weaker in the sense that they're not as intimidating as they were anymore. The first few enemies wielding knives and being all disfigured was intimidating, I didn't want to fight two of them in close proximity but soon enough, you'll end up being swarmed by hordes of them and not even flinch.
"Surely there's more enemy than knife-wielding zombies, right?" you may ask. And you'd be right but this is the core of the problem. The way to balance out your growing arsenal was giving the enemy more of an arsenal, knives and axes slowly phase out and are replaced with guns. Any element of survival horror which the game established becomes thin at this point, only showing up when the story deems it necessary before throwing you into another action sequence.
The amount of times which I'm thrown into an action sequence with little to no ammo and cannot progress unless I kill everything frustrates me, you're telling me to use everything so I've got nothing to use in the next scene and it creates an exercise of frustration where you're trying to melee the enemy and avoid their ridiculously easy to dodge pattern but it isn't fun.
Perhaps the sense of terror will return, perhaps there's some semblance of the game which the first horror had shown me can exist in this action shooter with zombies affair. However, until I witness it, I'd say no to The Evil Within.

I'll update this later after more gameplay but wanted to address some potential issues right away and give some initial thoughts.
CPU INTENSIVE:  I have an i5 64 bit core, 8 gb of RAM and a Radeon graphics card with 2 gb dedicated memory.  This is enough to run 99 percent of games just fine; however, I did have to dumb down the graphics setttings on this to get an adequate frame rate.  To my perspective, the graphics still look great, but I know that some people will dislike this.
FRAME RATE:  A lot has been said about the game dropping frame rate, but in 2 hours of play I have not had that problem.  Of course, I did, as I said above, dumb down the graphics a little.
ENEMY AI:  This will irritate some people because the enemies follow you around when they have no reason to.  You finally escape one room, and the bad guy just follows you into the next one even though he didn't see you.  Now you go about escaping the same guy again.  Make it to the next room?  No worries.  He decides to follow you there, as well.
CONTROLS:  The controls are very basic.  The only problem I had with them is that the CROUCH key is also the same as the HIDE key, so while sneeking around I did on a couple of occasions accidentally hide.  I strongly suggest going into the settings and changing crouch to toggle so you don't have to hold <L Control> all day.  One more thing on the controls, I have yet to throw a bottle and stun an enemy.  I always miss.  The aiming for this particular feature is a bit bizzare, so I just use the bottles to cause distractions.
GAMEPLAY:  Well, there's a small intro section and then you are thrown right into it, hiding and running from a chainsaw wielding gimp.  The gameplay is very challenging.  You will die, and you will spend a lot of time hoping the gimp will turn around and go elsewhere, and then hobbling across rooms in the split second he's not looking.  Definitely a traditional third-person horror experience.
OVERALL:  So far I am enjoying the game, though I've been a bit nit-picky above.  So far it seems like a buy if you like third-person horror games with a lot of stealth features.

The storyline follows Detective Sebastian Castellanos and his two partners that are sent to investigate a mass murder. Once at the scene, they witness supernatural events that catapult them into another dimension and further into madness.
Telling you anything more about the plot would ruin it.
It plays like a mixtape Shinji Mikami put together for his loved ones.. except his loved ones exclusively like survival horror video games. It amalgamates elements all across the board all-the-while creating it's own atmosphere and story from scratch. The Evil Within is without a doubt a challenging, yet satisfying survival horror, however the mechanics aren't anything we haven't experienced before...With that being said it's not by any means a copy and paste, but this game's execution does overall feel familiar, especially to veterans of the genre.
The overall presentation feels like a spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4 that's amped up on steroids. It's got a consistently tense and grotesque atmosphere, but it's not pause-button frightening. A lot of narrow corridors with enemies and traps cutting off your exits left and right.
It does have some outdoor and larger area level designs, which are a genuine pleasure to play.
The mechanics feel adapted to more recent titles like The Last of Us - giving us a sprint, a sneak/crouch, a hide button and a weapon wheel.
The paranormal aspect feels most akin to Silent Hill's franchise in my personal opinion - with the player being right in the middle of changing landscapes and hallucinations adding to the hazards within the game, which are in the form of bear traps, falling spikes, trip mines, and more.
Each enemy has the potential to come back to life unless completely decapitated. Another way to eradicate them permanently is to set their corpse on fire with a match in your inventory or a torch you picked up along the way.
You have four inventory slots you can assign weapons and items for quick draw and you can upgrade your abilities as well as your weapons from collecting green plasma in mason jars.
Once you complete the game, new game plus will unlock as well as harder difficulty options.
However in the spirit of oldschool titles, it only carries over upgrades for that same difficulty level. So you'll have to go into the nightmare bare bones each new difficulty level.
*Highly talked about information*
*FOV: The Dev's decided to have a slight zoom in on the left side of the camera when the player aims to shoot enemies. This causes the left side of the screen to be filled up by the players body, while giving you focus on the reticle and enemy in front of you. It can be a bit distracting at times. But then again, it all comes down to preferences.
*This game can run at 30 FPS and 60 FPS with v-sync locked.
I love this game immensely and am currently enjoying my second playthrough.
Setting corpses on fire and damning them back to hell hasn't been this satisfying since Gamecube's RE: Remastered. Also directed by Shinji Mikami. Coincidence? Not really. He's the Grandmaster of survival horror.

This is a game modeled after the mods for the RTS sub genre typically found for mods of Blizzard games called "Tug of war".
I wanted a game like this that I didn't need to run Starcraft 2 or Warcraft 3 in order to play, but I have to say that I'm quite disappointed. If you don't know what a tug of war game is, let me explain: A tug a war game is where you typically have 2 teams. Both teams have to build a structure which represents a unit which will continually spawn after set times in waves, those units will (usually) all spawn at the same time and without any control from the player, will run towards the enemy base, attacking your enemy's army as it encounters them. As time progresses and you farm more and more resources, your army gets bigger and so does your enemy's. Certain units counter certain other units so it's really up to the teams to figure out how to counter their enemy and destroy their base first. It's a huge amount of fun and very addictive.
Unfortunately, this game just has no heart at all. It's a 1v1 tug of war which will basically wear out your left mouse button as all you do is click repeatedly to create a unit. It's created instantly and there are no waves. There is, however, a spawn cooldown. It's short but it's there, which means rather than armies pushing each other in waves, you get long strings of individual ships which may or may not gather up if they stop to fight. Ships will not automatically spawn either; you click on their build icon and they spawn there once and that's it.
Incredibly boring and nothing compared to the custom mods you get in those games. I would say that if you have never played a game like this before, this might be a nice cheap (if you get it on sale) place to start. If you have Warcraft/Starcraft and want something similar to Desert Strike or Black and white, don't bother; this can't compare.

Aeon Command can be thought of as a remake of the old strategy game "Rescue Raiders", albeit, in a sci-fi context. As a result, the commands are vastly simplified, and combat is fast. The problem is the AI relies on timing. If you build your ships in the wrong order, you're likely to lose and have no way to recover other than to die and start over, at least against AI. On the other hand, the multiplayer capability makes games a bit more unpredictable. All in all, you should at least give this game a try.
The combat in Aeon Command is simple: you do NOT give orders to your ships. They know to engage the enemy. Instead, your job as commander is the build the units and/or deploy special abilities such as EMP, repair, and so on. There are variety of units, from simple fighters to long-range bombers to shield-bearers, and a few other units.
You don't group ships yourself. Instead, by building them together (close in time) they will congregate and fight as a group themselves. However, this means you have to let resources accumulate to the level when you can build them in quick succession rather than building them one at a time but somehow hold them back until your signal.
You do need to gather some resources, which are some asteroids near your mothership. You simply build a few miners (usually, one per asteroid, with one or two spares to account for travel time) and they'll do their jobs. The problem is, when enemies get too close, they will shoot at your mothership and the miners, and if you lose the mothership it's game over. And there's no way to repair the mothership should it suffer damage (but repair works on the small crafts).
The overall objective is to conquer the map by destroying the other side's mothership, of course.
The main problem with this game is while it plays fast, after a certain point the game's already won or lost, and there's little point to force it to continue. In other words, if you already look like you're losing, then you indeed are and there's no way you can "dig" yourself out of a huge hole.
With multiple factions (each with some unique abilities), dozens of battle scenarios, multiplayer, Aeon Command is an interesting take on the space strategy genre with inspiration from old classic. If you value a simple and fast tactical strategy combat game, Aeon Command may scratch that itch. it's not complex, nor does it pretend to be.

I had such high hopes for this game after the amazing Dirt Rally. "It's based on Dirt Rally, but MUCH better" said the Devs in pre-release interviews. And in many ways it has improved some core areas - the graphics are excellent and the weather effects superb, the feel of a rally event is much better than the "rough around the edges" Dirt Rally.
However for me the key selling point was the new dynamic route creation - allowing an almost infinite amount of routes to keep you keyed in to your co-driver at all times. Having to go in blind and drive to the pace notes, as rally should be.
Except rather than some ultra clever system of random splines routed over a large generated (or even pre-built landscape) we got... tiles! Yup, tiles that bolt together like a 1980's Games Workshop boardgame. But they give you a lot right? So there won't be too much repetition? Nope - if you drive anything more than 3-4km (and you can create routes up to ~12km long) you will see the same sets of corners twice, three times, or more.
Added to this, the tiles have their own pace notes. Which works until you have a long straight at the end of one tile and a sharp corner at the start of the next tile, so the co-driver doesn't tell you about it until you're already in the trees. This has happened to me SO many times and it ruins the "trust your co-driver" mindset that is essential when rally driving.
And all of this in only 5 locations, which become tiresome very fast.
I won't go into the handling too much as this has been done to death everywhere else. For sure the aero is much better, and you can tune the cars to be more oversteer'y than default, however there is something very broken when the same set-up in the Dirt Fish test area drives perfectly and then understeers like mad on the rally routes.
My suspicion is that the aracde "helper" system is the root problem of all of this. They couldn't create a system that could make the arcade driving easy whilst maintaining the correct set up for the simulation so they fudged the grip levels so the arcade mode could be stable. Just a theory, but something somewhere is badly broken in the handling. Something that isn't the case in the Rally Cross mode - which I have to say is brilliant all round - however I bought the game to drive rallys, not to race on a circuit.
Add to this the lack of VR support, one of the things that made Dirt Rally so popular, and although again a bit rough around the edges, the first VR game that made me drop my jaw as I sat IN the car and drove it like I do a real car (albeit a LOT faster!)
I think I have given this game ample chance - 116 hours of play and 5 months of waiting and it's pretty clear that the devs have written it off and moved on. The last mention of any patch was to do with adding support for clubs! Nothing about the handling, nothing about the repetitive route tiles.
Oh and finally, they added a checksum to this for the game files so you can't even mod in car reskins of your favourite historic liveries as the game will never save - not even in single player mode.
Dirt Rally has it's flaws, but I am very sad to say that as it stands it is still head and shoulders above Dirt 4 and I will wait for a LOT of reviews before I ever look at purchasing a Codemasters game in future. Once bitten, twice shy.

Verdict: worth the current 5 bucks just to experience some neat water effects, and you get a half decent third person adventure with some interesting controls in the mix.
Forget whatever hyped game critic reviews you read; you'll likely be disappointed, for several reasons listed further on. But if you take this as a cheap game without preconceptions, it has enough content to entertain for the price, and showcases elements that other games could benefit from.
Positive:
- Female protagonist. We don't get nearly enough of that, so that's always a plus. Don't expect the typical boob and skin show: both body shape and attire are kept reasonably modest and realistic, if maybe not the most practical. Her face could have used a bit more lifelike expression, but since you play in third person from over the shoulder, you only really notice this in the cutscenes.
- Water graphics and physics. This is one of those games that was obviously built around a specific gimmick, and in this game the gimmick is water. Lots of it. Beautifully animated and visualized, and it actually plays a role in progressing the game. This is done in regular ways - swimming, diving, breaking falls, putting out fires, moving objects - and unexpected ways - the protagonist gets to directly control water through powers of sorts.
- User interface. FPS-like controls combined with augmented reality type of gadgets add interesting concepts to the game and give it enough to stand out. Personally I hope to see some of these elements used in new games.
Negative:
- Protagonist background/development. Essentially, almost none. The game doesn't really need it, mind you, but since it has a definite adventure-ish story and play style, it could have benefited from a more personal bond with the main character. The log fragments you get to read along the way are a nice touch, but mostly they just unnecessarily repeat confusion at what is going on. There are hints she has some type of trauma about water and drowning... but the story never really makes much use of it. Missed opportunities.
- Imprecise controls. The game adds platforming and shooter elements, a bit in the style of Tomb Raider, but makes things unnecessarily difficult at times due to imprecise controls. There is no fine movement, so simply turning to face around can already make you step over the edge if you aren't careful, and she seems to always add a step or two after jumps and running. Gun aim suffers in a similar way. You get used to after a bit and then with an exception or two it's not much of an issue anymore, but it could've been better and will probably annoy fervent FPS players.
- Water physics underused. The story progression does hide this a bit, but in most cases you really just seem to be trying to find keys to open doors. They used the water physics to block/unblock doors in only a couple of cases... which is a pity, especially since that seems to be the game's main gimmick anyway.
- <Booming Genie voice>"Phenomenal cosmic Water Powers"... teeny little opportunity to use them. The regular water physics are a nice gimmick, but the special water control powers the protagonist gets at one point could've really made for some entertaining game play and story elements. Unfortunately, you only get them at the very last part of the game, and even then you could pretty much do without them right up to the last fight. Huge missed opportunity and frankly very disappointing.
- The End?! Biggest disappointment is by far and large the very sudden ending. You get to a fight, which granted is quite more difficult than anything previous to that, but when you finally beat it... you get a cutscene that gives no further explanation and it all ends. All the build up to the grander background story plummets into a void. It feels unfinished, and unsatisfying. Unfortunately, since the developer is out of business, there's not much hope for a continuation.
For 5 bucks, or less in a sale, Hydrophobia gives a good enough bit of entertainment, and showcases some UI and physics elements that I hope will come back in one form or another in future games. The story is left with an unsatisfactory ending, but it entertains up to that point, and with the exception of the very last fight, gave me a solid bug-free performance.

The storyline follows Detective Sebastian Castellanos and his two partners that are sent to investigate a mass murder. Once at the scene, they witness supernatural events that catapult them into another dimension and further into madness.
Telling you anything more about the plot would ruin it.
It plays like a mixtape Shinji Mikami put together for his loved ones.. except his loved ones exclusively like survival horror video games. It amalgamates elements all across the board all-the-while creating it's own atmosphere and story from scratch. The Evil Within is without a doubt a challenging, yet satisfying survival horror, however the mechanics aren't anything we haven't experienced before...With that being said it's not by any means a copy and paste, but this game's execution does overall feel familiar, especially to veterans of the genre.
The overall presentation feels like a spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4 that's amped up on steroids. It's got a consistently tense and grotesque atmosphere, but it's not pause-button frightening. A lot of narrow corridors with enemies and traps cutting off your exits left and right.
It does have some outdoor and larger area level designs, which are a genuine pleasure to play.
The mechanics feel adapted to more recent titles like The Last of Us - giving us a sprint, a sneak/crouch, a hide button and a weapon wheel.
The paranormal aspect feels most akin to Silent Hill's franchise in my personal opinion - with the player being right in the middle of changing landscapes and hallucinations adding to the hazards within the game, which are in the form of bear traps, falling spikes, trip mines, and more.
Each enemy has the potential to come back to life unless completely decapitated. Another way to eradicate them permanently is to set their corpse on fire with a match in your inventory or a torch you picked up along the way.
You have four inventory slots you can assign weapons and items for quick draw and you can upgrade your abilities as well as your weapons from collecting green plasma in mason jars.
Once you complete the game, new game plus will unlock as well as harder difficulty options.
However in the spirit of oldschool titles, it only carries over upgrades for that same difficulty level. So you'll have to go into the nightmare bare bones each new difficulty level.
*Highly talked about information*
*FOV: The Dev's decided to have a slight zoom in on the left side of the camera when the player aims to shoot enemies. This causes the left side of the screen to be filled up by the players body, while giving you focus on the reticle and enemy in front of you. It can be a bit distracting at times. But then again, it all comes down to preferences.
*This game can run at 30 FPS and 60 FPS with v-sync locked.
I love this game immensely and am currently enjoying my second playthrough.
Setting corpses on fire and damning them back to hell hasn't been this satisfying since Gamecube's RE: Remastered. Also directed by Shinji Mikami. Coincidence? Not really. He's the Grandmaster of survival horror.

This game was a wonderful surprise. Give credit to the developers, the promo vids say it all.
Poured 15 hours into it. A huge amount of fun. The constructions people will make will be truly incredible. It boggles the mind when you realise after a few hours tinkering what could be possible, and the FUN you could have with friends. It forces you to think - sometimes you’ll just sit staring at your object as your brain melts - but at the same time is rewarding just to strap a few boosters on a chair to see what happens.
I've spent hours alone on buildings and rooms, let alone the vehicles. If you like the graphic style there's enough content to build a great looking workshop, warehouse or cabin in the woods. And basically enough mechanics to turn your house into a walking robot, if you have the time, skill and patience.
Currently with creative mode only, you make up your own goals. The ambitious or creative mind of a mechanic is spoilt here. You realise the value of suspension, tune the engine, figure it might go faster with boosters, then make it fly, then balance the weight, make it float with sensors, then add a co-pilot, laughing the whole time at the disasters, then you watch a YouTube video and realise you've barely scratched the surface: You could literally create a flying warship with a manned bridge!
Not that there’s any war yet.
Please can there be war?!
And you look back at the bizarre creations you’ve cluttered the world with, with both fondness and failure. Occasionally stumbling over one that went rogue.
At the core of it, for me at least, it’s the construction mechanics that make it great. Whilst not perfect, the build controls are still slick, fast and intuitive. Much more than I initially realised. It pays you to get to grips with them fast.
Multiplayer has worked well (for me at least). My girlfriend kept building milk floats, so I secretly turned the roof of our house into a rocket platform and invited her up there to press the button. No falling damage implemented yet, but still, for some reason, the funniest thing I've witnessed this year. And now we have a twinkling star up there in the atmosphere, constantly reminding me that I need to build a flying craft capable of getting out roof back.
As for PROBLEMS:
- Ran smooth enough for 10 hours till I experienced the odd crash. That could be down to me now building a mega structure, so maybe I'm pushing it a little. Quick crash, quick restart, saves every few seconds as far as I can tell. Annoying but not a problem.
- Get some odd ground vehicle movement in some areas of the map. It might be my design, but I think more likely the world bugging out slightly. Slightly annoying but not a problem.
- Occasional bit of slow down or stuttering.
- CPU running a little hot. I have an above average machine.
- Cannot keymap certain keys. ALWAYS frustrating for me as I hate using WASD. AutoHotkey sorted that out so all good.
- Lots of stuff needs tweaking, obviously.
Overall pretty damn solid for an EA game, and I feel like I’ve had my monies worth already!
Those that aren’t having the same experience as me I would imagine £15 a little steep. But I guess we take these risks on EA. Especially day 1.
£10 might be a fairer price, but I will happily pay a little extra to support the devs. That is after all what you’re doing when you hit the Purchase button.
Devs, please keep this up! I know you know we know you’ve got a gem here. Polish it!!!
And give me missiles!
Random tip: When working on a huge structure, use the vehicle lift as a motorised scaffolding. Put it under a light floor and jump on. Bit easier to reach high places!
EDIT: 50 hours in. Multiplayer experience is amazing with friends (connection through Steam is seamless) AS LONG AS it runs well on your system. We all need fair machines to play it due to lack of optimization.
The biggest problem is the frame drop when certain physics take hold. Basically big, heavy structures. Especially when they are resting on servos or suspension. You can have a HUGE amount of creative, collaborative fun, but don't think too big just yet...
Ohh yeah this is going to be fun. I love everything about it :D

The visual design is great, first of all. Catacombs, hospitals, villages at night, all look great and are designed nicely both from the level design perspective and the visuals. The amount of work that was put into designing enviroments and enemies is stunning and if you like pretty games, check this one out, because it's one the best grit and rust fueled videogame nightmares out there.
The gameplay is basically Resident Evil 4 with a dash of stealth and a clever fire mechanic. It's also considerably harder, since ammo is pretty scarce and the zombies are tough SOBs. And this is just your normal mode, game features hard and even insane mode, which are not just punishing, but probably the hardest thing you ever played! Oh and it also comes with NG+ and a bunch of unlockable stuff, so you can blast your way through after completing the game one time!
The story is pretty clever and i'm glad nobody is spoiling it, since i'm actually excited to see it through. So far, it's surprisingly coherent, not in your face and feature a lot of imagery that intertwines with the main theme of the game. It's pretty subtle overall, where reality and nightmare come crashing down on each other and the understanding of the story is completely on your shoulders, nobody will sit you down in a cutscene and explain it all.
If you want a new survival horror game that is well paced and fun, get it. You may want to wait a bit to see if they'll release some kind of patch, but it's mighty playable as it is. Weird aspect ratio is not that obnoxious and you get used to it just as you get used to FoV in Dead Space.
P.S. You can unlock aspect ratio, FPS and even tweak some visuals, just take a look at the Steam Guides.

So even if you can't complete a level initially if you keep at it chances are you'll recognize a pattern and eventually overcome it. The routes you have to run are varied and new obstacles are added at every point in the game which makes gameplay fun. The controls are simple (arrow keys) and easy to use as well.

The soundtrack is good. It is upbeat and fits with the art style which is also interesting and intuitive. The way the score is displayed is fantastic and fits well with the particle physics theme.
The one bad thing I have to say about this game is that there is a lot of flashing lights and the visual style is very hard on the eyes. This makes it hard to play for more than an hour or so at a time.
If you enjoy platform jumpers you'll enjoy this game.

This game is terrible. Lets start with the bad things about it because I don't want to forget all of the things that are bad. First of all, the campaign/war mode is completely unbalanced at every turn, I know it is supposed to be "realistic" but there comes a point where throwing you into a battle where you have 50 lives for a team of 18 people and the enemy has 1200 lives, and vice versa, that it get boring. It seems that the only way you can win the game is good communication with your team, there is no ingame voice chat, there is a primitive chat window which reminds my of minecraft or League of Legends, and when you try to find a team to play with there is a plethera of problems. First one is that the forums to find clans are dead except from communities and clans thats barely play the game in the first place, the ones that do play the game have zero American teams, making it not fun whatsoever to play American, and the ones that are American clans have age restrictions from 20+ so a mature, younger player seems to be out of luck (no offense to the clans themselves but it is just rediculous).
Another complaint I have about it is the balancing and purchasing of weapons and vechicles. First of all my favorite WWII era weapon, the M1 Grand which fires a .30-06 Springfield round acts like a BB-gun. It takes on average 3 rounds to kill a full health enemy with it and the German and Russia equivalents of it seem to be 1-2  shot kills (with exceptions from headshots which are only 1 shot kills for every primary). I know that the Russian and German guns are bolt action but they can easily get one shot off to kill a person with the M1 before the American is able to get 3 shots off. Oh ya, russians have a rifle that can one-shot anything. Now on to the purchasing system, it turns out you already have and M1 Grand varient when you start the game but it didn't tell me until after I bought another M1 Grand that I had it in my inventory, in fact it didn't let me access my inventory until I had wasted my in game currency on the new Rifle and there is no tutorial to show you around so, in case there is a way that I had not discovered in the 30minutes of looking around the interface I was screwed either way. Then when I saved up to buy a jeep with an MG on the back I guess it glitched and bought it twice, therefore I spent twice the in-game currency on sometime I am never going to use (I am one person I don't need to be drive and maintaining two vehicles if they do the same thing as one another).
Apparently there is about 25,000 people logged on the game and fighting in a war at a time but that doesn't stop the 5-7 minutes queue times that occur before every match. Even in Skirmish battles there is still 2-3 minutes I have to wait and only get into a game with 7 or so people.
OKAY now the good stuff abuout this game. I have not encountered obvious cheaters/ hackers yet which is suprising considering it is a free to play game. It is a "I bought a sniper I win the game" sort of game which deprives the communities of many trolls, or people in general. Takes a good grind to level up so long sessions are often needed, unless you buy their veteran pack which costs a monthly subscription and it seems that people that have this win the game more (I can not 100% comfirm but I have a good feeling about this probablity).
REFLECTION overall -
Mildly addicting but a bad game that needs a lot of work to hopefully make it better than what League of Legends have become in the last few years.

!UPDATE!
After playing the new updates I will re-review the game and keep my old one posted at the bottom. The last time I reviewed this was prior to the MAA release and at a time when development seemed dead or stagnant.  It seems the devs are more coordinated now with more updates lately then in the last few years, so that is a positive.  Hopefully they got rid of anyone who was hindering the progress and kept the talent.
So PVK II finally has the men-at-arms.    Well I am happy the guys have finally sorted that one out after some years and I do enjoy the character.   He is what I would consider an all around character.  He can fight/defend well and has a crossbow for ranged attacks.  I would say he doesn't necessarily shine at anything but he is solid on all fronts.  I enjoy the wacky voice for him but some may find it annoying.  A new mechanic was added which is a roll/dodge.  Now I am glad they added a new mechanic and it shows they got some new ideas pumping through their heads.  I personally find it not practical(imo) to use in a fight because it slows you down tremendously and leaves you open for attack as you exit the roll.  I still think its more effective to keep your speed up and jump around but I do enjoy the choice of having it. You can also kick now, which I enjoy a lot because it's to much fun to kick someone to their death in pvk.   I enjoy the new parrot colors, thats was a good idea on their part.  Also alot fo classic maps have been revamped which is a good thing.  (The knights have a spawn now in Island!)  My favorite one is the new SDK update for the game which was widely anticipated because of the general overall improvement it would have on the game.
I know I was harsh towards this game but I reserve that right.   I am glad they are working on it more again and I hope to see it finish one day.  The game has a low playerbase but we could always use more people t join us.  You may look at this game and think it looks strange but no matter what bad I could say it is still my most played steam game ever(possibly more than anything else I have ever played too) It's like an addiction I can't shake,  I always come back.   So I will upvote it for now because it seems like they are rolling the wheels again in the right direction.  Now lets hope a few years don't pass and nothing happens ;)

Swords, axes, crossbows, and rifles. You have three classic teams of old times, Pirates, Vikings, and Knights. The Pirates have their speedy skirmishers, tough captains, and a gun-happy sharpshooter. The Vikings have their insane yet fast berserkers, the powerfully defensive huscarl with his two handed axe and shield, and the gestir that pokes people with a spear. The Knights have your standard archer with both a longbow and a crossbow that's not quite so strong but is very quick, and they also have the heavy knight with his two handed sword can take out most enemies in just two or three hits.
This is a great game for up close melee, but you do have to deal with the ranged classes and they can be very annoying from afar. But with your speedy sword swinging teammates, taking them down can be very easy depending on who you're fighting. Sure you have people that love to run away, and that's when it's best to have a ranged weapon to take them out from afar when they have their back turned trying desperately to run away from you.
It's a great, fun, and crazy online game to play. It takes a while to master your sword swinging, parrying, and gunslinging, but it's well worth it when you're finally able to take down those really tough opponents. It's an all around enjoyable game that's not without its flaws, but still a great game especially for free. If you have the time to download it, I say get it. I rate this game a 7.5/10. Sure I want to rate it a 9/10, but I do recognize some of the game mechanics flaws particularly in balancing the three teams. Still I definitely recommend this game!

DIRT 4 can be best described as a really good idea executed horribly. i have been a rallying fan for more than a decade and i'd like to think i am fairly well acqainted with rallying, eventhough this is one of my first rally games that is a simulator type that i bought a racing wheel for.
I have been trying to get the hang of driving a rally car in DIRT 4 for a while now but the longer i play the more i notice that the car tends to respond unpredictable, even when using the same amount of throttle, steering input or braking. the physics can only be described as a bad attempt to cater to both hardcore fans who came straight from dirt rally and the 14 year old kids who just bought this game after going to see their first rally. cars tend to lose and regain grip whenever they want to, not relying on the drivers inputs to control the car but rather pure luck as to what the car will do next. its almost as if alot of the calculations made in the physics engine are being done by a random number generator. this unpredictablity and bad physics is my first problem with the game.
Secondly, the AI stage times are incredibly inconsistent. i have tried multiple difficulty settings but they all seem to suffer from the same problem. sometimes i win a stage by beating the AI who came second with 20 seconds to spare, and sometimes i am full-out max attacking a stage and driving perfectly (which is a pain already because of the unpredictability) and i get absolutly stomped by getting 8th place with a 17 second deficit. its almost as if DIRT 4 tries to match the AI's difficulty setting to your own skill level by trying to increase or decrease the difficulty of the AI according to your own stage times, but overcompensating everytime. one thing in particular that makes me mad about the bad AI is that at a rally start, the AI almost always gets an incredible start giving them a lead by atleast a second or two. even if my own start could not have been faster. this does not depend on what car or class they are driving, since it happens irregardless.
The generated stages are a really good idea, considering real rally drivers do not know the road ahead. this is why its such a shame its been implemented in a rather weird way. Instead of actually generating every career stage each time you partake in an event, they use a set of pre-generated stages using the exact same generation as every customer gets. meaning that you are stuck with the same stages eventhough they are no different from completely random stages you can generate yourself. this really shortens the re-playability of the game down to what every other rally game without generated stages would have had. if we take a closer look at the generation engine it actually does quite a good job for the first rally game to do this. setpieces are neatly stitched together to the point that you don't notice the transition from one set piece to the other. the only small problem i have with the generation is the rather small amount of setpieces in the game as of this moment meaning that you will frequently see the same turn multiple times during an event.
those three points are what makes DIRT 4 a game that did not live up to my expectations. a big shame because DIRT 4 does a lot of things really well. For example, the whole team management is done in a simple yet very complex way. you get alot of wiggle room to create your own team while still being simple to manage. sadly though these smaller very well done parts dont really cover up the badly done parts, cause driving a rally car is what this game is supposed to be about.
I was very close to recommending this game, but i decided not to. Hopefully DIRT 4's sequel tries to please the fans of Dirt Rally and ditch the whole arcade idea.

Aeon Command is one of those games that's fun in small doses, and with its low price it's actually worth paying for those doses.  The graphics are certainly more than adequate to do the job, and the audio fits the art style and theme of gameplay.
The gameplay, however, won't win any awards for depth or breadth.  You spam numbers/clicks to build ships, use different keys/clicks to use special abilities, determine which ships to unlock and/or upgrade, and click on icons in the combat window to get resource, upgrade, or energy bonuses.
Likewise the campaign is nothing to write home about.  You get a set number of missions which each introduce a new ship or skill, do the same number of missions for each race, or game mode, and that's it.  The campaign is little more than a tutorial for skirmish games.
Skirmish, on the other hand, is where the game both shines and shows its worst flaw.  You get to play with all the races, all the game modes, all the range options, and even mix things up so that you and/or your enemy get a random assortment of ships and special abilities.  You could, for example, get the mining craft from race A which costs 8 resources to build (the others cost 10), a healer ship, a chain lightning ship, a railgun ship, and so on.  It will never randomly assign ships outside of their assigned slot so that you'll never get 2 or 3 ships normally in slot six, but it suffices to provide some variety in gameplay.  The game also provides three "difficulty" modes, and that is where the game's biggest flaw comes into play.
The AI cheats, at least on Hard difficulty.  It doesn't cheat by being "smarter" or by reacting faster to changes than a human can, nor do AI-controlled ships do any better when run by an AI player than a human.  Instead the developers opted to give the AI bonuses to resource acquisition.  Either it gets a steady stream of the crystals and energy or it gets a significant boost to how much it gets when it gets it.
This isn't a case of me being a bad player and blaming it on the game, nor is it a case of not understanding how the game works.  It's simply a matter of observing the facts.  When the AI is producing more ships than I can despite having the same number of collection ships out, and when the AI can use 55 energy skills/powers before I even have 1 energy, the AI is, in fact, cheating.  Edit:  I found a perfect example of the sort of benefits the AI gets over players.  As a player, I only get energy from killing enemy ships, but despite the AI having destroyed none of my ships it was able to pop off two EMPs and a Repair, total cost around 100 energy, at a time when I had only 17 energy, and this was less than four minutes into the game.
Over the course of half a dozen games against a Hard AI using the Cyborg race I had one of my first three combat ships mind controlled when I had 0 energy, the ship had just been produced, and while it was in range of my base ship and thus nowhere near enemy lines.  Furthermore, during my last play session I used Cheat Engine four times to bump my credits up by 1k, 1.5k, 2k, and 2.5k, and the first three were not enough to build and upgrade enough ships to give me a fighting chance.  It wasn't until I did the 2.5k bump that I had enough, and enough upgrades, to fight the AI with some degree of parity.  Eventually I won by spamming the slot 6 ship which, more often than not, can be an "I win" button for each race if you get a large enough swarm of them going.
This sort of cheating doesn't completely ruin gameplay, but it does make me want to avoid playing against Cyborgs or playing as Cyborgs on Hard.  Still, at $2.99 I'm more than willing to cut the developers some slack on shipping the game with a "difficulty" option that, at least for me, makes certain race/gameplay/side combinations absolute no-nos.  It's still something that should be considered if that sort of thing really irritates you.  The game is still quite fun up until Hard, and even on Hard as long as I play Human or Exile it's still quite enjoyable and winnable.

At the time I'm writing this review, I have a little over 300 hours invested in this game as a F2P member of the community. I have played the vast majority of this game on one character, a German Infantryman, that I swap to other classes once in a while to change it up, and then swap back to infantry afterwards.
The following details my lack of general satisfaction with the game and explains my opinion of it being mediocre. Let it be known that when I refer to the community in a negative light, I am not referring to anyone in particular or the whole community - only the select few that bring the group down. Although fun with friends, this game brings nothing new to the table and is just another reskin of your standard F2P FPS model.
This game is highly repetitive, slow to add new content, and mostly a zerging experience due to lack of coordination in a match even in the presence of a squad leader. There are no voice comms, which would be a downside, but due to the overall cancerous chat I've encountered in nearly every game and everyone wanting to be the hero (placing blame, etc.), I'm very grateful that this is the case - voice comms would be unbearable. This game resembles teamwork and even emulates it sometimes, but unless you run with an outfit or a group of friends, you might as well be playing alone.
Although friendly fire is present, it is inconsistent. You can be killed by teammates' grenades, vehicles, bombing-runs, and mines, but not from actual bullets. This, again, lends to the reckless zerging mob that rushes capture points.
The reporting system is exploitable and never there when it is truly needed.The current system consists of a three-tiered flag - green, yellow, and red. You need at least two flags from one game to be demoted from green to yellow tier. The next match, you need to receive three reports, or three yellow flags, to move into the red tier. The red tier, which activates in yet another match, gets temp-banned after another two reports. The official wiki states "Green flags are not transferred from match to match. Yellow flags are removed 1 for every match you complete with a score above 5 and no Red flags. Red flags are removed 1 every 48 hours." I have seen people exploit this mechanic blatantly, and nothing can be done with the current setup. Multiple times I have been the victim of this explotiation - as long as the griefer doesn't cross into the red, they can kill you much as they want, take a break, and then resume after the yellow flags are removed. The yellow flags are easy to remove, as long as you have more than 5 XP from the match, and you can get high as 200 XP just from being at a point while it's being captured. You only lose 10 XP for team-killing. At the end of the day, they need a system that recognizes trends or something similar to PS2 where the player cannot fire their weapon if they have a certain number of grief points accumulated from damaging friendly players.
The game has a built in filter for suicides. Suicides delay your respawn by a considerable amount. Methods for suicide include being killed by your own grenades, vehicles, jumping out of moving vehicles, bombing-runs, mines, and falling. I understand the mechanic - it is there to encourage safety and discourage recklessness. I feel like the word "suicide," though, really communicates something different altogether. I have never intentionally killed myself in this game, but I have had accidental deaths. I feel like the vast majority of people don't kill themselves in this game. There is no benefit that I can think of to suicide in H&G. Staying alive and walking to get whatever you need is always a better alternative. If you want to die, all you have to do is stand still in a capture point in the open - someone else would put you out of your misery shortly. Better yet, go look for trouble by walking into the enemies' spawn. Either way, this system is more annoying than anything else. My suicides in this game consist mostly of walking off a ledge about tall as my character while on low health and grenades. Keep in mind, I'm not saying that the suicides should be removed or that you shouldn't be able to accidentally kill yourself - those have to stay for the game to work. I'm saying that suicides for something like walking off a six foot tall ledge shouldn't count as a suicide. You wouldn't even need to check how far the player fell to rule it out. Have the server check the circumstance in which they died - did the player kill themselves or were they killed by another player? If killed by themselves, check the damage done to the player - should it be under a certain threshold to health ratio, let it be ruled a plain death instead of a suicide. Have weighted options for each circumstance surrounding the death (i.e., different damage thresholds for the circumstances). The logic is there, the rule is simple enough to add - it's just a lack of concern as far as I can tell.
Although at the time of this review the devs have gone to respectable lengths to implement anti-cheat systems, I still encounter the same cheaters, cheats, or exploits nearly every game. For the sake of the game, I will not list these exploits publically as I don't want the servers to get any more polluted. Although I understand the lack of a report system within the game itself as it would be abused, it would be nice if there was a more dependable way to report players exploiting the game. Again, I understand the difficulty behind this, but it really does dilute my fun.
Although the models for the weapons, vehicles, uniforms, and sounds are spot on, the realism stops there. Beyond the aesthetic, this is just another FPS where stats matter more than common sense.
I don't think that this game is pay to win. I do think that players that pay for memberships or buy gold are more apt to have an easier time leveling and acquiring weapons. Your paygrade scales with level, your required experience scales with level. After each match, the player has to pay to refill ammo for any weapons used, pay to repair any weapons or vehicles used. The price increases with the more modifications per weapon for both payments. On a losing match at the top of the leaderboard, I might net 5k credits for use in the shop. On a winning match at the top of the leaderboard, I might net 7k credits for use in the shop. The two weapons that you would spend the most time with as a German Infantry are the Bolt Action Kar. 98 and the MP40. I can't speak for the Kar. at the moment, but the MP40 alone costs around 128k to purchase. For a new player, that is a very long road.
The anti-tank rockets, such as the bazooka, cost 700 credits a shot. It takes at least two shots to destroy an enemy tank. Over a 30 minute match my side is winning, I might be able to destroy 5 tankers before dipping into my savings. These weapons are given to the new players at level 2 without providing this information - you have to go to the wiki to know many of the repair and refill prices - to wipe out any savings they might have had and coerce them to buy gold or a Veteran membership.
I have 750k saved up and am currently level 13 basically from min-maxing. I don't use modified weapons. I don't use grenades or vehicles beyond a certain threshold. I work the objective.
All this said, though, I still don't think it's pay to win. I feel that a large amount of this game is in general knowledge of stats, maps and locations, trends, and practice. I'm not saying that you need to be particularly skillful to outperform anyone, just know more than the guy you're shooting at.
Can't recommend it. Too grindy with too little reward. (Also, text limit here. Sorry.)

I honestly don't know whether to recommend this game or not. So here is the pros and cons:
PROS-
1) The combination of RTS and FPS is wonderful.
2) The amount of guns are wonderful, and are plentiful and unique to all sides.
3) The maps are wide, for the most part, and are very detailed.
4) The rank system is very wonderful, and the perks that come with it.
5) The classes are an added plus.
6) Team isn't composed of jerks.
7) Highly addictive.
8) Smooth gameplay (For the most part)
CONS-
1) The games are not extremely balanced. Its kinda like a rock - paper - scissors kind of system. Only - Germany trumps Amercia and America can trump germany, and Soviets trump all 85% of the time.
2) The guns have weird adverse effects. To germany's and the soviets' advantage. The Thompson M1A1 has a large spread. The spread stays the same even at close range, even though it should be more accurate and faster at close range. I jumped into a a small space with two guys, one guy directly in front me without moving. I can tell you right nw, not one bullet hit them, but their PSSH sprayed me and killed me in less that a quarter of a second.
3) Snipers. Snipers are way too over powered. They can shoot from across the map, and headshot you. Even if they cant see that far. They will camp in one spot, with a perk that gives no way to find them, unless you somehow stumble upon one. Doesn't matter if the condition is foggy or not, hills or not, tanks or not, flying through the air or not, they WILL headshot you. Wanna know who's a sniper? Their K/D is usually 37/3.
4) Maps. Although the maps are wonderful, and detailed. There is NO variations to the maps. its the same 9 maps. No variation based on area or spot. Its either a factory, airfield, or small town. Very easy to memorize each map, making it harder for enemies or you to stay on your toes, constantly in a tug of war with the enemy.
5) P2W. You can get far without paying, although expect loooots of hours of playing. Over hundreds of hours. The new update i heard reduced how fast you get promoted. Definitely slower than before that update. P2W guys top F2P anyday, gladly, there are more F2P than P2P.
6) Money is hard to come by. Practically improbable to buy other guns besides the base rifle and base SMG. It took me a long while to earn my Thompson M1A1.
7) Prices are off set. I would understand for vehicles, but for guns? Thats outrageous. 160,000(?) Silver for 1 Thompson M1A1? That is a ton. If you play, you know. In WW2, that was the Standard Issue SMG, if i am not mistaken.
8) Highly Addictive.
9) If you wanna play russian, thats a plus. They are the most Over Powered faction out there.
10) If you're squad leader, no matter what your objectives are, your squad will wander around the map alone.
Final rating?
7.5/10 -

DIRT 4 can be best described as a really good idea executed horribly. i have been a rallying fan for more than a decade and i'd like to think i am fairly well acqainted with rallying, eventhough this is one of my first rally games that is a simulator type that i bought a racing wheel for.
I have been trying to get the hang of driving a rally car in DIRT 4 for a while now but the longer i play the more i notice that the car tends to respond unpredictable, even when using the same amount of throttle, steering input or braking. the physics can only be described as a bad attempt to cater to both hardcore fans who came straight from dirt rally and the 14 year old kids who just bought this game after going to see their first rally. cars tend to lose and regain grip whenever they want to, not relying on the drivers inputs to control the car but rather pure luck as to what the car will do next. its almost as if alot of the calculations made in the physics engine are being done by a random number generator. this unpredictablity and bad physics is my first problem with the game.
Secondly, the AI stage times are incredibly inconsistent. i have tried multiple difficulty settings but they all seem to suffer from the same problem. sometimes i win a stage by beating the AI who came second with 20 seconds to spare, and sometimes i am full-out max attacking a stage and driving perfectly (which is a pain already because of the unpredictability) and i get absolutly stomped by getting 8th place with a 17 second deficit. its almost as if DIRT 4 tries to match the AI's difficulty setting to your own skill level by trying to increase or decrease the difficulty of the AI according to your own stage times, but overcompensating everytime. one thing in particular that makes me mad about the bad AI is that at a rally start, the AI almost always gets an incredible start giving them a lead by atleast a second or two. even if my own start could not have been faster. this does not depend on what car or class they are driving, since it happens irregardless.
The generated stages are a really good idea, considering real rally drivers do not know the road ahead. this is why its such a shame its been implemented in a rather weird way. Instead of actually generating every career stage each time you partake in an event, they use a set of pre-generated stages using the exact same generation as every customer gets. meaning that you are stuck with the same stages eventhough they are no different from completely random stages you can generate yourself. this really shortens the re-playability of the game down to what every other rally game without generated stages would have had. if we take a closer look at the generation engine it actually does quite a good job for the first rally game to do this. setpieces are neatly stitched together to the point that you don't notice the transition from one set piece to the other. the only small problem i have with the generation is the rather small amount of setpieces in the game as of this moment meaning that you will frequently see the same turn multiple times during an event.
those three points are what makes DIRT 4 a game that did not live up to my expectations. a big shame because DIRT 4 does a lot of things really well. For example, the whole team management is done in a simple yet very complex way. you get alot of wiggle room to create your own team while still being simple to manage. sadly though these smaller very well done parts dont really cover up the badly done parts, cause driving a rally car is what this game is supposed to be about.
I was very close to recommending this game, but i decided not to. Hopefully DIRT 4's sequel tries to please the fans of Dirt Rally and ditch the whole arcade idea.

Hydrophobia: Prophecy is an odd mixture of a third person shooter and a platform game about Kate, an engineer working on the greatest ship of the ocean, the Queen of the World, in a futuristic setting. The game takes place during an unexpected terrorists attack on the ship, with Kate trying to survive the whole ordeal as the ship is filled with water and other environmental hazards. Notice that Hydrophobia was originally released as an Xbox arcade game and was tweaked/remade two times before being reborn as the version you can buy here on Steam, Prophecy.
The main objective of the game is to navigate the Queen of the World while trying to survive the rampant hazards within (water floods, fires and electrical sparks): Kate is able to jump, swim and move on ledges, as well as to carry around items to clear her path. An important tool for the exploration is your hacking tool, which can be used to unlock doors and see through the eyes of the security cameras. Truth be told, the whole level advancement does feel repetitive and, beside the varied platforming sessions, you are mainly tasked to find the next code you can use to open the door blocking your way.
Hydrophobia also features firefights against the invading terrorist forces. In this regard the games plays out as a typical third person shooter, with your only available gun being a LP 4 sonic pistol, which can be equipped with several kinds of ammos. Truth be told, however, the stock sonic bullets will be the only things you'll ever need to clear Hydrophobia and, unlike the others, are infinite. Something I'd like to point out though: it's really hard to actually get where your enemies are coming from, which can quickly lead to frustration as you die for the third time because you couldn't get to your attackers in time.
The title has also some collectables in the form of documents or logs scattered around the levels (with some being less obvious than others to find) and medals, which pretty much counts as in-game achievements. There is also a challenge mode, which isn't very notable.
The main problem I have with Hydrophobia: Prophecy is that, despite the great presentation and the well crafted environments, they hardly make up for a very short game (I clocked it around two or three hours) which doesn't make good use of the many interesting elements it puts on the table. I'd advise to try it out only if you get a really good feeling from it

AdventureQuest 3D is a game based on the popular web browser game AdventureQuest World. I am a long time player of Artix Entertainment since the first AdventureQuest. Athough most, or should i say, every single one their games are heavily money based, pay-to-win type game, and basically are just a grindfest, i can still thoroughly enjoy their game. I love on how the developer are really friendly and really in touch with their player and i can say that they are one of the best developer out there. So, yeah, naturally i am excited when they announced that they are releasing AQ3D.
I want to reccomend the game, I really do. This game looks promising since the first they announce this, and i have a soft place in my heart for AE team. But at this current state, no. I cannot recommend this. They made little progress since the alpha state, the controls are bad, it's just as clunky as ever, gameplay are just boring and nothing really worthwile, it's basically just AQWorlds (to anyone who never played it, it's basically just a grindfest simulator) made into 3d with clunkier control, animation are terrible, a lot of bug here and there, occasional lag here and there and what not. Graphic are mediocre, borderline bad to be honest.
At this current state, this game is unplayable. You didn't even make a significant progress since the alpha state mechanic-wise. You guys, i mean the dev, are way too focused on the content, on how much equipment you could put into the game and seems like didn't really care about the gameplay mechanics. The amount of content doesn't matter if you could even barely play the game. It's like, a sea with million miles wide, but an inches deep.
Pros (+)
* It's Adventure Quest in 3D!
Cons (-)
* Bad gameplay mechanics
* REALLY clunky control
* A lot of bugs
* There's not much of a variation in gameplay. It's basically left-clicking simulator
* Graphics are meh
* Grindfest combined with clunky control, it's probably one of your worst nightmare
* In-game currency
* Story are boring
CONCLUSION:
I cannot reccomend it to anyone because it is unplayable at its current state (nor that i would actually recommend it to anyone even on the full release because their game is pretty exclusive, as in i doubt that anyone could hardly enjoy it except if you've played their previous game (which is why most, if not all, of the good reviewer here are their loyal fans)). There's not much to offer in this game, except for heavy grinding and a lot of bugs. The only content they could offer is just a hefty amount of equipment and that's all. Gameplay are not engaging, quests are basicaly just a grindfest, kill this, deliver that, get a sums of money and so on, and the story is basically just a common "hero-who-saved-the-world" trope.
I know you guys could do better than this. I understand that this is still an early access, but come on. There's not much of an improvement since the alpha except for the content.
Also, asking for the players to spend money for in game currency in a nearly unplayable game is just insulting man.

Some people thumbs this game down for not having survival mode yet and/or not updating frequently/substanitally enough. What they don't understand is that when we get those smaller udpates (that really aren't that far out, anyways), the devs are ALSO working on survival mode. Anyone that has any clue regarding game development would be impressed by the level of polish from these devs and the hard work involved in adding a survival mode to a physics game such as this. It's ok to feel like you should wait on this game if what you really want is survival mode, but don't crap on the game because you simply don't know what you're talking about. Also, if you already own this game, stop thumbing it down because you couldn't be bothered to read the minimum specs required and/or don't understand what Early Access is.
Owning just about all of the physics-based bulding games on Steam, I can honestly say this has been one of the best purchases I've made of ANY game. Many will make comparisons to other games and while those games have their own strengths, in terms of just the foundation for physics-based building, this game surpasses them. Games like Garry's Mod, Space Engineers, and Besiege all have more "stuff", but they've also been around longer. The core of this game just gets everything right: the block building mechanic is intuitive, the physics are very well done, the art style looks fantastic, and it already has multiplayer out of the gate. I think any sandbox builder, enginner, or tinkerer owes it to themselves to buy this game.
+Physics
+Not limited to just one thing - you can build vehicles and bases, sure, but so much more, as well.
+Looks Great
+Runs Great (there are some rare exceptions, but it mostly boils down to people that can't read and/or troubleshoot a computer)
+Already has multiplayer
+Devs are eager to help and communicate (Mostly via Twitter)
-It's a shame we can't wire up specific keys to specific things (other than the number keys). The driver's seat always stears bearings with A and D, but I'd rather be able to wire any output to any input, such as a thruster to any WASD key.
-I'd like to see a server browser instead of the current invite system
-Certain things need more customization, such as certain instances I'd like to have more speed using controllers.
-They added a basic logic gate, but I want to see more parts and features that revolve around logic and directly controlling contraptions.
8.5/10 - and only because I demand more options out of building games having spent over 3k hours in Gmod alone. This score will probably go up as more features come out and survival mode is added.

I've spent just under 100 hours at the time of this review, but I'm sure I will easily spend twice that amount soon. The game is easy to pick up quickly, but one issue is that once you start a mission you are committing to completing that mission regardless of how long it takes. All the reviews I can find on Steam seem positive for this game, which is clearly marketing bias.  I'm an avid gamer and I like difficult games, and indie games, and this type of design.  But this game is atrocious.  I can't be the only one who thinks so?
This game is a hipster-hype nightmare.  The gameplay the boring "test your reaction time" type, OK, fine.  I'm already not that enticed but whatever.  I gave it a good few plays, on multiple occasions, and I wanted to love it.  Then I just wanted to LIKE it.  But it's one of those games that has some tricky mechanic which seems unfair - in Boson X's case, you jump platforms - but the thing is, after a level or two platforms start randomly dropping off.  But there isn't any indication of when this happens, at least that I could tell, and it is just too hard to determine your vertical position - there isn't any ground or reference area to be able to tell if the platform is dropping - it starts to drop, you jump, but you're too low to make the next platform, and the game says Ooopsoe!  Try again!  But.... it doesn't feel like my fault, like I could even do anything about those deaths.
So the end effect is that I start the game, play an easy level, think "ooo, I may like this". Next level, I'll jump to a platform and be too low to land it.... but.... what?  I didn't even know I was dropping.  So I try the tutorial, which is of the modern, very hipster, minimalist school of tutorials where it has to be self-righteous about its hyper simple core gameplay, emphasising how "clean" and "simple" the gameplay is.  But it doesn't even mention these dropping platforms!  How do I deal with them?  They seem unpredictable and random, and every time you die from being too low it seems really cheap to me.
I search online, and of course, you just hear people bragging about how amazing they are and how easy the game is etc..... I dunno.  For my money (and I did pay money for this game!), it's an overhyped game which treats its players with disrespect.  I love a game which punishes - but it has to feel fair.  This game feels like it throws me under a bus, and I didn't even know the bus was coming, and I didn't even see the bus until my face was plated firmly in the bumper.  I wish I could at least find info on how those falling platforms work, but all you can find is over-hype and people bragging about how awesome they are, or how amazing the game is, etc.  Honestly - overhyped, boring gameplay, and the design is too noisy and trendy/indie/bleh.  And this is coming from an indie games NERD.

This is a very well-made endless-runner game by a couple of indie developers.
The basic idea is that your character represents a particle in a series of 3 particle accellerators, and you need to get your particle up to a certain energy level by standing on the blue platorms. If you hit anything head-on or fall down you have to start over again. As you get more and more power you start to move faster and faster. Once you get to 100% you can either collide with something to discover a new particle or you can continue on to get a high score for your power level.
That said, the game technically does have an official endpoint. The game is named "Boson X," and one of the "particles" you can discover is the X Boson, you could say that's a good spot to end off if you don't want to go for 100% completion.
All this is made more difficult by the fact that the levels range from easy to begin with to extremely unique and difficult in their own regards. An example of one of the levels:
There is no real plot to the game, though the characters are quite cool. There's a man, a woman, and a robot. Personally, the robot (Keiro is its name) is my favorite to play as.
The controls are tight, responsive and easy to get used to. You only need 3 buttons: left, right, and up. Hold the buttons for longer, the longer you jump, and if you press a direction key you'll move a lane over in that direction. Different levels have different numbers of lanes too.
The graphics are quite nice, they're not complex but they're eye-catching and nicely stylized. There are no actual quality or graphics options though you have the option to lower or mute the audio, to play in fullscreen or windowed. The game is not very resource intensive at all, and you can run this at 60fps 1080p on fairly low-end hardware.
I also like to listen to my own music while playing it, which seems to improve my performance a bit, the soundtrack in the game isn't that great.
