Honestly, a cash grab. It's Dirt Rally with worse physics and some no-effort "game mechanics" like sponsors and race crew. Your race crew doesn't affect your car that much as long as you know how to drive, and your garage slots are arbitrarily limited to try to give a sense of "progression," something that's been achieved in other Dirt games by you going to more and more important races.
The physics, especially on roads, are awful. For some reason the cars are barely controllable.
In the Rally stages, other cars aren't represented on the track - they have a set time that's generated depending on which car you choose. This leads to some horrible AI times, which are either literally impossible to beat (AI taking hairpin turns at 120mph) or so difficult to lose that you could drive backward for half the race and probably take first. This also makes it impossible to play some cars, like the BMW M3 - probably my favorite in its class, which is totally unplayable in this game thanks to the shoddy AI.
This isn't the perfect mix of realism and arcade, like Dirt 2 and 3. It's a blatant cash grab in the form of a rushed conversion of another game. Sadly, you can't buy Dirt 2 or 3 anymore, but I can tell you this; don't buy this game. It's awful, and a horrible dent in my favorite racing game series.

If you buy this game, be prepared to fight two wars at once; one against the British and the other against the game controls and interface. The latter seems to pose the greatest threat.  Silent Hunter 5 reeks of a game that has been rushed out the door in order to meet a deadline. The game is no more finished than an early beta release, but is being sold as a completed project. That's unfortunate because this game could have been a gem.
Missing are some of the basic controls you would expect in a submarine simulator. For example, you have no way of checking your depth under keel. This remarkable oversight would have sent every sub in WWII to the bottom, literally. There is no way to adjust game controls such as mouse tracking speed. This is incredibly frustrating since the tracking speed while in first person is incredibly slow.
The AI is unpredictable and often just plain stupid. The safety of your home port is the most dangerous place in the game, as friendly ships will slam right into you with no attempt to avert the disaster. This is especially prevalant while time warping. You have to always save the game before time warping, otherwise you will find you ship destroyed due to the game's failure to pull you out of time warp when there is a danger (as it is supposed to do). Rightclick on SH5.exe then choose Compatibilty Tab then set the X on "Disable scaling on High DPI) worked like a dream. (just for good measure I also ticked the box about "run as admin")

Many were unsatisfied, including myself, with such an obvious and, quite frankly, disappointing twist to what had otherwise been a masterful crafted tale. Many believed that Ohtani was far better than this and sent out to dig deeper into the previous entries to derive the true meaning of Find Myself.
The biggest clue was when Ohtani mentioned that he had made a major revision to Find Myself upon learning that it would become a credits stage. Now why would that be? Ohtani had, up to now, made no concessions for Sega’s bull♥♥♥♥♥♥ He had kept true to his story and refused to let his superior get in the way of telling it.
And that’s just it, it wasn’t in the way at all. In fact, it was just what he needed.
The credits themselves would be the multiple personalities of Knuckles, the friends he had come to love and cherish over the years he spent with them, slowly disappearing from him as he slipped more and more back into reality as he cruised down the mountain. Knuckles would never face the camera, he would never look back until the game was over. There, in fact, most likely were NEVER to be any lyrics, an eerie silence juxtaposed next to nearly two hours of nonstop monologue.
The game would end with a cut to black and complete silence as the Sonic Team logo came up for one last time and simply hung there, waiting for the player to provide input for the game to continue.
The player themselves would have to cast away Sonic, not only a character that gamers around the world have known and loved for decades, but also the last and only true friend Knuckles had ever had, even if he was imaginary.
The player themselves would have to pull the final plug on Knuckles’s warped reality and finally set him free.

As someone who was in love with the original Hotline Miami, it is with a heavy heart that I cannot recommend this game. In it's own right, it might be an alright game, but as a sequel to Hotline Miami? This is a tremendous waste.
It is as if the developers did not understand what people adored about the original and just increased the wrong areas/ideas of the game. The first game was endearing from the lack of what was given away in terms of the story, it was really minimalist in this sense and let you fill gaps based on what you'd experienced as the player. Hotline Miami 2's plot is a mess. A mix of flashbacks and nonesense.
The difficult has been ramped up, but, and this is very important, in all the WRONG ways. TOO many enemies on screen, TOO much potential to be shot by an enemy unseen. Bigger maps but somehow worse level design. They've increased the 'fustration' and very little of the sense of being rewarded. Hard work nets you a cheap death. Hotline Miami 1 always struck me as fair, sure you'd get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when you died, but you were annoyed with yourself, not the game. I frequently find myself, totally the opposite, completely angered by the game with the sequel. Being shot by an enemy you cannot see is cheap, and boy does it happen a lot.
As a standalone game, it's alright, but it will always sit in the shadow of the original, which is an absolute must-play. My own personal lack of enthusiasm  with this game led me to refunding it.
tl;dr/final takeaway: Play the original Hotline Miami, skip this.

A 3D endless runner with a slick and clean aesthetic and a mobile game through and through. If that sort of thing isn't your cup of tea then this game really won't change your mind. I'm personally not really into these types of games myself, but for what it was i thought it was pretty enjoyable.

Set in a particle accelerator, in some sort of metaphor for the scientific method, you play either a scientist [male], scientist [female], or the better third gender - robot. It is a nice touch that they added the ability to pick your gender, but it doesn't really affect the gameplay beyond the footstep sound.
The game is what you could call 3D, however the main running is along the x axis, you jump on the y and instead of moving left/right to avoid obstacles or jump gaps, you 'rotate' around a predefined polygon. This was an interesting game mechanic, and I felt the game executed it very well.
The different levels generate randomly but each one has its own signature features, from platforms that move or drop out beneath you to the various structures that they make up. This is good, because it prevents you from just learning the tricks to the first level and burning right through the others.
The style is very minimalistic, and it manages to pull it off well. With the exception of one level and its 'wireframe' look [which is completely impossible to play, as far as i'm concerned], the various styles to levels work nicely. Some of the music is good, but overall it was OK. The world you run through doesn't require the music [i.e. it isn't generated according to the music], although it would be a nice addition if they made that so.
It can be played with either the keyboard or controller, and both work equally well for this game. I didn't have the game crash on me at all, and there were no installation problems. Some screen tearing, but that is easily solved.
Boson X is a very fast-paced runner game that seems in many ways similar to Super Hexagon. If you liked that and want to try a runner, then you should play this.

I'll review this as a single player game as multiplayer seems dead as a doornail.
The ability to hot-seat is likely to be a great benefit, however.
At its simplest, this is Battle-Chess. In "Classic" mode, you can just play chess against the computer or another player - using your Warhammer characters. Each piece is taken rather violently with whatever weapon the character has to hand. To be honest, if you enjoy chess, this is a lot of fun.
The "Skirmish" mode is similar, except each piece has weaponry and can take a certain amount of damage. It's not chess, but it does add a new wrinkle to the game, which makes for some interesting play.
The campaign mode has a lot of playability. You progress by completing chess-type scenarios, with warhammer characters that correspond to chess pieces. They can, however, capture pieces through moving, or damage/destroy them with weaponry. The board also has barricades on it to spice things up, and there are different victory conditions which alter how you play.
I'm really enjoying this game... but you probably need to have an appreciation for chess and, at the very least understand how the pieces move.
If you go into this game thinking it's a regular turn-based strategy game, you may be frustrated at not being able to move your tactical marine (read: Pawn) to the left, or capture the piece in front of you... and you may be annoyed that the heavy-bolter marine (read: Bishop) can only move diagonally.
If this isn't a problem for you, then this game is a great addition to the Warhammer 40k universe.

While this game ticks all the boxes for me, in terms of a zombie shooter, and is probably one of the more unique ones I've come across, in that its atmosphere and mechanics make it plausible that a roving horde of zombies could overwhelm somebody who isn't paying complete attention to their surroundings at all times, it's best played with multiple people.
Unfortuantely, not many people know about this game and, while it doesn't have a hefty price tag like a more contemporary game, people just haven't picked it up all that much.
It's fun, tense, and in some cases absolutely nerve-wracking, and I recommend it if you think you can fight zombie hordes all by yourself.
One negative about the game is that the absolutely sprawling maps can be a slog to trudge through, although this seems intentional on the part of the developers, giving players ample opportunity to get separated (and therefore more easliy killed by zombies) exploring for weapons, ammo, and tools. On the downside, if you (or your team) get stuck in one particular area because you don't have the tools to proceed, it can be downright boring trudging backwards and digging through abandoned buildings to find a pair of bolt cutters or a particular keycard.
All in all, this game is very solid and is only truly lacking the kind of following a Left 4 Dead game garners. And a story mode.

Similar to how the tower defense genre distills the RTS down to its immobile defensive elements, Aeon Command simplifies the RTS into a 1-dimensional clash of mobile offensive units.
There is simplified resource gathering, there is a simplified research tree, but mostly this is about spending your resources wisely and, most critically, TIMING and COMBINING your deployments for maximum effectiveness.
If you find RTS games a little too overwhelming, if you like tower defense but need a change of pace, or for that matter if you like Gratuitous Space Battles but want to be slightly more hands-on, this is a light and fun game with a decent amount of replay value. I'll be coming back to this game periodcally for quite a while.
Short learning curve, lots of tactical variety, perfect lunch break game.

A very good space RTS game given the $2.99AUD price tag or the equivalent in your area! Like it says in the description this is a 'tug of war' style game where you gather resources and produce units to proceed towards the enemy mothership (base) and destroy it, engaging any enemy fighters along the way. You do not have direct control over your units, however you can turn the tide of battle with abilities which cost energy points to use that slowly regenerate automatically. These include abilities that can heal your ships, stun enemy ships, or nuke a small area. Graphics are pretty unsurprising given the budget and it looks like a glorified flash game, however thankfully for a strategy game graphics are easily forgiven, not to mention expectations are low at this price point. Games are short (~5-10min) making it the perfect bite-size RTS, you will not find a huge amount of depth here and some strategies can be exploited to easily win matches against AI but it even includes a multiplayer mode to play against your friends! A great value game, despite its shortcomings. 7/10

I loved the Silent Hunter series, and I was excited to play this title when I first heard of it. Sadly, this game does NOT live up to the high standards set by its predecessors.
The main flaws include the following:
Uplay DRM to play the game.
Game-breaking bugs and flaws that will sometimes prevent you from even progressing, or on occasion, will reset your progress to a much earlier point.
-Examples of this include:
-When opening the periscope view the game instantly crashes to desktop with no crash dump, report, or warning.
-Some enemy units will disappear in full view of the player without explanation or warning.
-Certain story objectives are not acomplishable due to the game not tallying kills properly.
The main reasons to enjoy your time in this game:
All gamebreaking bugs aside, the game looks beautiful, and is a good platform for mods (assuming you are allowed to, I wouldn't know as I have only played the stock game).
The mechanics from the old Silent Hunter games are somewhat present, but the game is much easier than it's predecessors.
Overall:
Don't buy this game, buy Silent Hunter IV or Silent Hunter III

I have no idea why I keep seeing so many negative reviews... This game is awesome in my opinion.  It's a very niche game. It's really only going to appeal to a certain crowd.
If I had to describe the game quickly in a manner it's understandable, I'd have to say that it's an attempt to make a somewhat more realistic warfare in terms of bullet damage & kill times, set in WWII. Now for the lenghty summary...  In terms of all out chaos & full on action packed battles like Battlefield, you're not really going to find that here. This game plays out more like real life would. You have a few guys hiding behind cover taking pop shots at each other until the stupiest one stands out in the open to long & finally gets picked off. Headshots are always 1 shot kills & depending on the gun & type of ammo you're using, 2-3 body shots & you're down. SMG's & pistols require more bullets obviously, but you get the general idea.
That being said, there ARE action packed moments! You'll often have a little skirmish with 5-10 people involved fighting over the objective, it's just unlike Battlefield where it takes a while to down your enemy & you can move around stupid fast, this game you die quick & you move slow, so the little battles don't last as long & aren't AS crazy as they are in Battlefield & other games.
Yes it's Free to Play. No it's not technically pay to win, however... You can pay to get ahead. To be perfectly honest, you start out with probably the best guns in the game right off the bat! Team USA gets the M1 Garand default, Russia gets the SVT-40 & Germany gets the Gewer-43. These Semi-Auto Rifles are the most accurate & hardest hitting aside from the Sniper Rifle. Throw some Match Grade ammo in them & learn the recoil patterns & you can drop people really quick! OR, you can fork up some real money to buy the games premium currency & unlock guns & vehicles early. You can unlock the weapons later in the game & purchase them using the games freely provided currency, but as F2P games goes... Everything is really expensive & it takes FOREVER to stockpile the money. SO it is kind of pay to win in that regards, it's just that none of the other guns really out perform the default guns all around. The excel in one area or the other.
I highly recommend this game. It's fun, it's a super change of pace if you're getting burnt out on the super soldier BS from modern shooters, it actually takes SKILL to be good at. You "CAN" camp a corner, but you're going to get very few kills that way, so it's not advised & hardly anyone ever does it. Give it a try. It's free so you have nothing to lose. Who knows, you might like it.

Oh Boson X, how you anger me so. But seriously, this game is fun.
Game mechanics: this is an endless runner where you press left to jump left, press right to jump right, and press up to jump forward. Hold these keys longer for longer jumps. Don't fall, or hit the platforms/walls.The context that they put this game is interesting: you're a physicist trying to discover new particles. Your objective is to land and run on blue platforms and increase your particle discovery to 100%. Red platforms fall (and try to screw you up). You can go over if you want, but that's just for a high score. When you hit 100%, you can discover new particles. Be careful, you go faster as you approach 100%, with a significant boost in speed after hitting that percentage. Each level has certain repeating units of platforms, which allows for a learning curve.
This game can get hard quickly, but as I said before, there is some predictibility with platform within the levels, so you can learn the layout and get closer and closer to 100%. The satisfaction and exciting gameplay is the reward that overshadows the sometimes big frustration.

It is a simple game, so there is not much to criticize. Perhaps, longer music loops for the levels (it can get quite annoying).
Buy it now; it's price, whether full or discounted, is cheap.
A simple and charming procedurally generated platforming game about pattern recognition and tearing your eyes out when you botch that one jump while you're at 99%.

The first thing that is immediately apparent is the sheer presentation of it. Animations, sound effects, music are all fantastic. The interface is sharp and responsive. Each race and unit has their own animations, sfx, and voice-acted banter of what you would expect of a 40k game. Such as always amusing ork slang and banter. Can never have enough dakka dakka.
In addition of the traditional chess mode, called 'Classic', the meat of the game is definitely in the 'Regicide' mode. Essentially, 'Regicide' adds an action phase after movement where units can use range, melee attacks, or use special abilities at the expense of action points. All of the conventional chess moves and attacks are present, of course, in the movement phase of your turn. With the addition of ranged, special attacks/abilities you definitely have to consider strategies outside the chess norm. Which is quite refreshing.
In addition to conventional play, I was astounded to find that a voice-acted campaign mode was in the game. It's certainly presented simplistically, namely voiced transmissions before each mission and a smattering of cutscenes, but definitely a welcome feature. The devs could have easily just made a chess game, dress it up in 40k skivvies and kicked it out the door.
Usually, when you encounter games like this they are cobbled together with little concern other then getting it out the door to capitalize on the brand. You just really don't expect this level of quality. While it does have a few wrinkles, such as questionable AI at times, and my want for quicker gameplay, I am hard pressed to find negative aspects or faults with the game.
Hopefully, whatever wrinkles exist will be ironed out and we'll see more additions to the game such as armies(tau pls), features, Definitely worth the price of admission.

Although my laptop has heat problems with this game (and with many others, unfortunately), I may as well review what little I got from my 40 minutes of play-time. As you might know already, the game is essentially a combination of chess and Warhammer 40,000. Having not played a whole lot of warhammer, I can't say much about what chess adds to it. I have, however, played quite a lot of chess, and the addition of certain warhammer mechanics makes me see particular board positions completely differently to how I might see them in chess.
Basically, even as someone who hasn't played warhammer very much, Regicide provides a refreshing mix of the familiar and the not-so-familiar.
Nice take on classic Chess. Very easy to beat using Chess rules, but much more challenging in Regicide mode...

Aeon Command is a streamlined space RTS.  You start with a mothership and are tasked with collecting resources to build space craft to take on the opposing mothership.  You really just have one collectable resource which is metal.  You also have eneregy to use abilities but that is automatically generated over time or collected as power-ups from the wreckage of defeated enemy ships.  Once you get some resources flowing you can start to build ships to assail your enemy.  Once built your ships will automatically seek out and attack the enemy.  You can't directly control combat but you can influence the battles using special abilities to buff your troops or debuff and even damage the enemy fleet.  The trick comes down to what ships to produce when and what improvements to research.  You can research better ships and improve your ships armor and weapons during play.  You can also permanently augment the ships and abilities of the three different playable factions by spending upgrades collected in the campaign and skirmishes.
Aeon Command contains a single player camaign and a skirmish mode.  The campaign is a tutorial and campaign in one.  The campaign is pretty easy with a difficulty spike at the end.  Once you start to really understand resource management and research you'll dominate the campaign in no time.  I have not tried the multiplayer but I imagine it would be pretty fun to battle it out with a friend.
Overall a fun game.  It probably won't occupy you for too long (the campaign can be beaten in a couple hours) but for a few bucks it's a pretty fun space game.

Straight up, I don't recommend this as a game. This is one of the most average third person shooters I have ever played. It's not necessarily a bad game, but it's not worth playing if you aren't going to buy it for the water effects/physics. If you are okay with a tech demo, then consider getting it.
Hydrophobia: Prophecy was developed by an indie company, so straight away you know that it won't easily compete with the best TPS games out there.
If I had to compare the entire game to other games, I would say that they took the climbing mechanics from Tomb Raider/Uncharted and made the sinking ship level from "Tomb Raider: Underworld" into a game.
The game was made for almost no other reason than to show off the engine. It has dynamic water with physics that are incredible. You can shoot out windows to flood rooms even more and the water can either help you in combat or it will just make things more difficult. Unfortunately the game is short and doesn't really speed up. The game is apparently the first in a series, but when you are playing a 4 year old game, you know that there won't be a sequel any time soon.
The gameplay would be far too unacceptable if it weren't for the water mechanics. It's essentially a corridoor shooter with an upturned bucket of water over it. Most of the time you'll die because you didn't know what the game wanted you to do. The waypoints and tips from your work partner who is known as "Scoot" are overdone as they literally tell you how to get through each section of the game. The character development is so weak that it shouldn't have even existed.
The controls are okay most of the time, but the camera does not want to go under the water, so it really limits how far you can look up or down, which is really annoying when there are 3 metre waves flying everywhere.
The story is just a lame excuse for a giant city on a boat to start sinking. Basically a bunch of terrorists claim that in order to save the world, they need to kill everybody on board. The story is weak as anything I'm afraid.
The water is definitely the main focus of the game, as waves crash against you and send crates floating in all directions. I especially love it when you open a door and the water from the room you were in slowly seeps through. The water can appear almost gel-like at times, but since it was an innovation that literally tested the water (heheh), I can forgive it.
This game could have shown how water can really change up the gameplay of a game, but unfortunately, they didn't make the mechanics good enough for it. The potential was there, but the presentation was sub-par.
Unfortunately, no other games used this engine and other engines are starting to produce better effects, which is making this game even more obsolete and mediocre. Some things just don't get better with age.

Contagion is an Indie, cooperative, multiplayer, Source-based, zombie survival horror, first person shooter PC Game developed and published by Monochrome LLC. It is the spiritual successor to Zombie Panic! Source. The game was funded out of pocket for nearly the entirety of its development, but with the support of others via a successful Kickstarter campaign, it was able to be released on Steam as an Early Access title. Contagion released on October 25, 2013 as a Steam Early Access Indie title and was published as Full Release on April 11, 2014.
Contagion is a multiplayer focused game with 3 different game modes; Hunted, Escape, and Extraction. There is also a beta game mode called Flatline.
Hunted, which supports up to 16 players, is a free-for-all "deathmatch" game mode in which players fight each other, while A.I.-controlled zombies wander the level and serve as an environmental hazard. When a player is killed, they respawn as a zombie and can participate alongside the A.I.-controlled zombies in attacking the surviving players. The goal of the game is to be the last living player.
Escape is a cooperative game mode in which a team of up to 8 players is tasked with progressing through a level, fighting through zombies while completing various mission objectives in a linear order with the ultimate goal of escaping the map.
Extraction is another cooperative game mode in which the goal is to explore an area and rescue a number of A.I.-controlled non-player character survivors.
In both game modes, when a player is killed they respawn as a zombie and are tasked with helping the A.I.-controlled zombies hunt down the remaining human players. Player-controlled zombies are faster and more maneuverable than A.I.-controlled zombie enemies and therefore present a greater threat to human players. Both Escape and Extraction can be played off-line by a single player, although they are geared towards multi-player gameplay.
Flatline is a multiplayer-geared wave based survival mode. The player starts in a singular location, where new parts of the map open every few waves. At the end of a wave, players who died the previous round are resurrected and all players have the option to visit a shop/safehouse and get better weapons/equipment.
Contagion is distinguished from other similar games in the genre in that it features "Romero Zombies" (zombies akin to those seen in the Night of the Living Dead series of films by director George Romero). Resources such as weapons and ammunition are scarce, encouraging more precise and methodical gameplay. Unlike other games in the genre, Contagion does not feature zombies with special abilities, with the exception of a rare riot cop zombie wearing body armor that can survive significantly more damage than a regular zombie.

I'm not devoted enough to this game to know the ins-and-outs in order to give a surefire recommendation, but boy does this game have, at the very least, potential, and even decent delivery.
For one thing, there's a truckload of playable character classes with their own abilities, all of which not just have their own compelling gameplay identities, but three different proposed styles within them that allow you to 'build' one the way you want. And all of those abilities take, like, no time at all unlock. Streamlines the process in a way I don't mind, as from then on really all it's building up to is making those abilities more powerful, and even that's made as easy as possible without taking the grinding out of it. Various effects and damages scale with bonus damage provided by items, and every now and then if you're no happy with the level of your abilities, or the way you've allocated your stats, you can just re-do it (albeit only once a month for whatever wierd reason).
And then I guess second is the turn-based grid-based pseudo-strategy approach to combat. Fresh breath of air, and it works well, though this is one of those wierd MMOs where you have to do not-combat things, but they still use the combat system for whatever reason and it looks incredibly out of place and is unnecessarily complicated. Only those things though, actual battles are just fine.
The english localization is kind of a bang-up job, as all these types of games tend to be. And certain systems being as complicated as they are means this doesn't help learning the game very much. It took me about halfway in to my current playtime to realize what Lock and Dodge even did, so either I can blame that on the game or tell you to do what I didn't and go do some research.
There's also buddings of a Runescape-lite kind of thing going on where you have different crafting and harvesting skills and using them levels them up. This is not a bad thing, I like Runescape, and it's nice to make it feel like you don't need to invest in combat to see most of what the game has to offer, but going the whole hog and having freaking full-on ecosystem management puts player-to-player trust at arms. Everyone can plant the seeds of the things they just cut down to resupply for anyone else who wants to cut them, but there's nothing going on to say you must.
EDIT: Playing it again after putting it down I did remember one other problem with it. Most of the game's dungeons say they're supposed to be done at certain levels, but you can only do them that way if you have a party of friends with you. It makes no concessions for solo players, and it's not exactly the best environment for finding people to help you out.

This game is dope.

Pros:
* The best pre-firearms fighting system bar none in any game. There is nothing quite like lancing an opposing cavalryman and seeing him dehorsed and dragged through the mud, or in planting a perfect headshot from far away with a bow and arrow. But where this game really shines is in its system of directional melee combat, which takes an hour to learn but a lifetime (or at least a few hundred hours) to truly master. There are no real glitches that you can exploit, as in a game like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare; in a duel, it is almost invariably the better man who wins.
* Its sandbox nature means huge scope for RPing and going your own way about Calradia. Start life as a male noble, with substantial money and renown already to your name, or make it more challenging by starting out as a peasant girl. Make money as a trader, enterprise owner, tournie jockey, or manhunter. Fight as a freelancer, a sworn lord, a mercenary, a sellsword accompanying another lord's army (mod-only), or as king of your own empire. Use combined arms - e.g. Rhodok Sharpshooters, Nord Huscarls, and Swadian Knights - to maximize your army's combat effectiveness (though there may be morale problems if you combine too many units from different countries). Win wars by charging the enemy or storming castles with yourself at the head of your own army, skulking away at the rear with your archers, auto-resolve battles (and have half your elite Huscarls die and Jeremus get wounded against a bunch of peasants), make your sworn lords do your fighting, or persuade enemy lords to defect to your side.
* Huge variety of mods, many of which fix Native's inadequacies (e.g. Floris, the Native Expansion), provide new historical (e.g. Brytenwalda, AD 1257, Gekokujo, and the paid DLCs Napoleonic Wars and Viking Conquest) or fantasy (Prophecy of Pendor) settings, or make for an enhanced or different MP experience (e.g. neoGK, cRPG, Full Invasion). If you try nothing else, I really recommend Floris. After that, Prophecy of Pendor and Brytenwalda. Buy Napoleonic Wars if you enjoy the idea of having cannons, colorful uniforms, and muskets that can't hit the side of a barn from a few yards away. Although Viking Conquest has the potential to be good - its creators are the same guys behind Brytenwalda - it is just too bug-riddled to justify buying right now. Maybe (hopefully) in a few months.
Cons
* Quite a few, actually. Sieges are one-dimensional: Walk (not climb) up a ladder, bash some heads, survive a number of new enemy spawns - sometimes with you right in the middle of them - and capture the castle (though the MP mod neoGK, which is used on the Golden Kingdom servers, does add siege engines and boiling oil cauldrons to the mix). The combat AI just isn't that great; only other humans can truly pose a challenge. I have some issus with the movement and combat options: No running (you kind of waddle quickly instead), no crouching, shields are like a magic magnet for arrowheads, no shield bashing (except in mods), no dynamic blocking, weapons have no momentum value (a flimsy falchion can still stop a downwards blow by a Long Great Ax). Tournaments get repetitive and boring quick. A clunky management interface is compounded by an excessive requirement for pointless micro-management (though there are mods that greatly alleviate this, such as Floris). MP is great, really dynamic and almost entirely free of hackers, but is really hampered by the lack of ingame VOIP, forcing you to rely on chat or TS instead. And there a number of explicit bugs that haven't been fixed even after many years. Still, it's a great testament to the underlying strength of the game that all these cons barely make a dent on my overall rating.

A great concept executed poorly. Ace of Spades began as a cult-classic browser shooter that garnered a small, but loyal community. Ever since Jagex, however, picked up the rights to the title, it's all gone downhill. A drastically redesigned class system, terribly-designed maps, and a by-the-numbers list of gamemodes seems to complete the new Ace of Spades. The only "plus" to this mess is the mining and terrain destruction. Prolonged carnage on certain maps leave the land radically changed, forcing players to adjust their tactics. Another good use of the mechanic is as the Engineer, blasting your way through fort walls and bases with your Drill Cannon and your dynamite charges.
Unfortunately, that's as far as the fun goes. The rest of the classes are either terribly overpowered, or too weak to overcome their opposition. You're better off trying to find a website hosting the original browser-based version, because the "new and improved" Ace of Spades just isn't enough fun to warrant prolonged use.

I was looking forward to this game, but as soon as I hit play I was disappointed. The aspect ratio is way off and to put matters worse my FPS still dips even with the 30FPS lock. What I find really funny is even if I try to unlock the FPS its still staying around 30 FPS AND still dips below that! That should not be possible with a Radeon R9 290X, I can run Crysis 3 on average of 80FPS and that puts The Evil Within graphics to shame.
Added Note: This is strictly a performance review, I figured we would all be smart enough to realise that but I guess only some caught on. That out of the way after more testing it would appear my FPS was struggling only when I'm outside but as soon as I went indoors everything was where it should be, about 80-100FPS and I'm ok with that. I notice though my game would randomly lock up for a few seconds and everything would be fine after until it locked up again but it is a new game and that can be expected to happen on release.
Now just to make those who wanted more than just a performance review happy, I did play through chapter 1 with the recommended aspect ratio and it did seem like I was watching and playing a more interactive movie approach, which was interesting. However atleast through chapter 1, I didn't feel like I was getting immersed into the story of the game, maybe because I didn't feel like I had any full control on my movement. The story doesn't really make since, atleast not right now in the early game but so far it feels like I'm watching a cheesy horror flick where one minute I'm injured but the next scene I'm fine?
After reading through some comments and gave more thought to it, I recommend to tread carefully with purchasing this game. If steam had a third recommendation option I would have chose that one but alas they don't so I'm still sticking with not recommending. Since I've only played through the first chapter I have regained some hope for this game and hoping the story starts to make more sense and maybe even become immersive.  We shall see.

Warhammer Vermintide is a game you will Love and Hate. And let me explain why.
Pros:
-Excellent developer support with regular patches, listens to the community, free DLC and events such as double XP weekends.
-The game looks great. Animations on the enemies look and feel natural. The weapons and armour all have great detail. Textures rarely pop in.  The environments look and feel perfect for the lore and time period they are set in.
-The sound design is also very good. The Skaven chatter and screech like you would imagine a giant rat man would. Very atmospheric sounds.
-The characters all feel completely different from each other.
-There is lots of loot and customizability.
-Impressive crowds. You will see possibly hundreds of rats running at you at a time and it does look amazing.
-The dismemberment is really visceral and really pulls you into the game.
-The game is now quite well optimised compared to it's shaky launch.
-The Forge and Shrine mechanics are great additions. These let you unlock upgrades for your weapons. They also let you salvage weapons you dont want for a chance to get one you do.  This game has four tiers of weapon rareness. White, green, blue and orange. Got five white weapons you dont want? Change it into a green one that you do!
-If you are a fan of the Warhammer Fantasy lore and world (before the age of sigmar) then you will love this game. The developers have taken great care with the IP.
Cons:
-There is a missed opportunity for a proper story. The story is given in small talk between the characters but as a fan of the lore on which this game is based it is a little disappointing.
-Unfair situations. Sometimes when playing you may be two people down. The AI does not account for this. It will still send hundreds and hundreds of clanrats against you and perhaps four assassins and two poison rats for good measure. There is no balancing for when the players are severely outnumbered.
-No checkpoints. If you come into this thinking that it is like left for dead. Well, you are right and wrong. The main missions take around 30-60 mins each depending on your team and skill level. If you all die at 55 mins in, that's it. No checkpoint earlier in the level. It's an instant reset. This used to be even worse when you would get no reward for the hard work. Now you get a measly bonus. Prepare to get frustrated when you have a bad team.
-Constant specials. This game has special rats. These special rats can incap a team-mate very easily. Unlike left for dead there can be more than one of the same at a time. One time i was playing and two assassins, and immediately two packmasters, grabbed our team. All four of us were grabbed and couldnt do anything. Instant failure. It seems unfair when you have 100 rats barreling down at you, and a gatling gunner shooting you, then an assassin jumps on you whilst being poisoned. Prepare to get frustrated and what feels like cheated. Just pray a rat ogre isnt thrown into the mix.
-The missions quickly run out. They become stale and boring after a while. There are quite a few missions but only half are proper 'full' missions. Others are smaller objective ones. You will be replaying the same levels over and over again.
-The dice loot system makes you cry. When doing the longer missions you have the opportunity to pick up Tomes and Grimoires. These give you extra dice at the end of the level. At the end of the level you roll a certain amount of dice. How many face ups you get determines how good the loot you receive is. Normal dice is a 2/6 chance. Grimoires guarantee a face up symbol, but cut your health down 25% for the rest of the level (all players). You can get two of these. Tomes take up your health slot. They just give you an extra dice to roll with a 3/6 chance of getting a face up symbol. There are 3 of these. The harder the level, the more dice you get for it. I have once grabbed all tomes, grimoires and completed it on hard (which is not easy) and only got 2 face-ups (which were because of the grimoires). Your hard work means nothing and the reward is all luck based. No matter how you perform. Killed the most? Took the least amount of damage? No bonus. It's like playing 2014 destiny.
I do like this game (see hours played) but i also hate some of its design. This game is fun with 4 friends when you can communicate. A lot of the time you will be getting frustrated with the constant barrage of enemies and the lack of reward from an hour of your time. I do recommend you pick this game up. It is a fantastic little gem of a game. But also take in what i have said. The pro's outweigh the cons most of the time.

All I can say is wow!
This is an amazing zombie survival game to say the least! It has the nice and classic styles of Left For Dead along with superb realism. Combined, this makes the game fantastic. With a variety of guns, melee weapons, and more, Contagion is not something you want to miss out on.
Some of my favorite aspects of this game are the abilities to hold a base instead of just wandering around in the streets. You can find nail guns, nails, wooden boards, and more to help board up a home so that you and others can stay there, away from the zombies. I also love how the zombies are not just some old "shoot em in the chest a few times and done" type of zombies. You will have to load at least a full clip of your pistol or whatever gun you have to kill them. The best way to bring down a zombie is to aim for the head. I like this because it gives you a new perspective on zombie shooters and can make you feel very powerless at times, which is what should be protrayed in zombie shooter games, since they are zombies after all.
Another very good thing about this game is it's stability. I was able to handle this game on medium-high settings and I have a low end computer. Definitely good for players who love games but cannot find things that their PC can handle.
Summary(Some things in the summary were not mentioned earlier in the review):
-Item Variety
-Weapon Variety
-Unique Medkit Animation
-Amazing Realism
-Sense of Helplessness Around Zombies
-Objectives and Hints Found in the Phone
-Nice Shooting Mechanics
-Lack of Holdable Rounds (Directs towards the sense of helplessness while around zombies, since you cannot hold many rounds in your guns)
-Very Light but Great Detail
TOTAL SCORE: 10/10 - Great game to play with friends and amazing in all aspects!

I like Dirt 4 but it has some fierce competition from the likes of Dirt Rally and WRC 7.
Cars are fun to drive. But the handling feels a little lackluster. The connection with the car and the road is poor. Cars tend to float through the stages. You only need to slow down for the hairpins. You might just fall asleep at the wheel.
Stages in Dirt 4 are auto-generated. So they tend to feel a little stale and lacking in variety. There is just not enough elevation in the terrain. The feel of a handcrafted track is sorely missed in this game. Co-driver calls are sometimes out of sync. Whatever you adjust in the options menu the outcome is the same. You won’t hear that hairpin call until it’s too late. That really hurts the driving experience but it's still playable.
The music is good which is very rare in a racing sim. Catchy vocal tracks play in between races and during the replays. Dirt 4’s use of music is very bold and really sets it apart from other similar games in the genre.
Graphics run well but they are nothing to write home about. Very drab with plain colours throughout the stages. Where are the lighting effects and intense lens flare? Car interiors are perfectly functional but the instrument panels feel bare at times.
If I could give Dirt 4 a "maybe" rating I would. For me it's delete and forget. For you it may be something special. Either way I wish you all the best.

My initial review was negative and given without much thought or playtime with the game, and for that I am sorry. On a further note, after playing the game for over 25 hours with plans to keep playing for many more hours, my entire review of the game has drastically changed to what it shouldve been originally.
I played through the game on survivalist difficulty I believe, and while it didn't offer up that big of a challenge, the game was incredibily enjoyable. It took me around 13 hours to complete the game, having spend a large amount of time exploring the mostly linear map, which provided a lot of background on the games story and a lot of intersting and unique settings that one might miss their first playthrough. I also spent a large amount of time playing around with the game mechanics, seeing how many ways there were to get through each chapter, and although the game is relatively linear, there are a good amount of paths to take. While I never felt like I was low on ammunition, or facing an enemy I couldn't handle, there was a good deal of suspense that most games lack. Overall, playing the game through on the hardest difficulty available at the start is enjoyable but not as challenging as one might expect, at least if they have played a good deal of shooters.
The gameplay mechanics themselves are decent, offering a couple of different ways to take out enemies, whether it be stealth, guns, the environment, or the agony bow (Which is by far the most enjoyable weapon to use). The gun play is not bad, one complaint I have is that it seems as though the bullet fires out of the crosshairs, rather than the guns themselves, which causes a loss of accuracy. The stealth is great for a non stealth oriented game, enemies are decently hard to sneak up on (Especially on Akumu which ill get to in a second) and stealth kills are rewarding and fun to do. There are a good deal of environmental objects that the player can use to kill enemies or distance themselve from them, although these can also work against the player. Some of the traps are a bit oddly placed, mainly the explosive traps which often don't make logical sense as to why theyre there in the first place. Leveling up all of the players traits, health, melee, sprint, weapons, how much ammo you can hold, ect. is a great feature to add to the game that really comes into play on further difficulties. Overall the gameplay is fun and relatively new, especially the agony crossbow, which allows the player to strategically handle hoards of enemies while feeling powerful.
The game really shines after the initial playthrough. The player will unlock a machine gun, three different game difficulties, and a model viewer (Similiar to the RE4 one, although there is no minigame to unlock them). The difficulties include nightmare, which I have not played, and Akumu, which I am currently halfway through completely, along with a continue+ that lets the player carry over their upgrades and weapons into a new game. Akumu difficulty is one of the most difficult difficulties I have ever played. The player will die from one hit from ANYTHING, which (trust me) will leave you starting over checkpoint after checkpoint. It also takes enemies the player would normally see later on in the game, when they are more equiped to take them on, and puts them in earlier chapters. This drastically changes many portions of the game and increases the difficulty to an insane perspective. The thing with this difficulty is that it actually is enjoyable to play, at least for me. The very first encounter with a large group of enemies took me near an hour to get through, yet I still had fun doing it. All of the gameplay mechanics really shine on this difficulty as well. Players will be forced to survey situations before they go in, think about what weapons to use, know the environment and where traps and other items can be found, and think about who to engage and when to engage them. It is by far one of the most challenging yet fun difficulties I have ever played in a game like this, one that I recommend you play immediately after completing the game.
Overall, I would give this game a solid 9/10. I can't wait to play the DLCs they release, and I can see myself playing through the main story multiple times in the future.

Don't expect anything fancy from graphics or sound - they do the job, but that's it. As for so many Indie games, this one is all about the gameplay.
Basically, this is a tower defense game: you have to gather resources (happens automatically), build ever more powerful units, and research upgrades for them. With these spaceships, the goal is to reach the mothership of your opponent, at the other side of the playfield, while at the same time defending your own mothership against incoming attacks.
Since there is only one path between the two bases, most of the time the two opposing fleets meet somewhere in between, slowly (or faster if you're good) progressing towards the enemy's side. There is not much more to it: the core gameplay is dead simple, but it has something about it that keeps the attention going. One does have to make important and micro-strategic decisions: does one invest the resources gathered into new ships, or rather into upgrades? And there is a neat supra research-tree, which allows you to spend resource points that affects all or any of the three factions in the game.
Part of the attraction of the game surely lies in the excellent way it is embedded in the Steam cloud, with achievements, trading cards, multiplayer options, rankings, etc. Name it, and this game has it. So for the moment I want to try going up on the ladder, or win my first multiplayer. It's a simple game, but it does what it wants to do pretty good.

This game was surprisingly fun and addictive. The campaign took over 3 hours in total, and the three factions kept me interested until the end.
It's a bit like Swords & Soldiers in space. The map is a long, 2D battleground. You build units who you do not directly control, but who automatically fly to the other end of the map and fight each other. The objective is to destroy your opponent's mothership. Often, it's a war of attrition - you just try to outbuild your opponent, trying to balance that with buying research to improve your ships in the long term. However, there's a decent variety of units and special powers (all unique to each faction), so there's plenty of room for strategising and countering your opponent.
Outside each battle you can spend upgrade points, to do things like improve specific ships, or increase the rate at which you gain resources.
Once you've finished with the campaign, there's a skirmish mode, or multiplayer. At the current price of $2.99 I can say it's definitely worth it.

The point I’d like to express is: what you don’t feed does not grow: you  m i g h t  be rewarded for whichever investments (hence buying equals supporting the game, in this case), but surely you won’t be paid back if you don’t “invest” at all …. shouldn’t the devs be motivated to act fast, if the profit from D4/WRC7 was …motivating ?
That’s what looks like to be happening: we claim fixes for a niche game which allegedly has sold little and received so many negative contemptuous opinions: do “we” deserve, did we support their effort and time ?
We claim to receive a hardcore perfected game (without buying a Hyundai WRC and traveling to Australia :-), for 30-50€….as a matter of fact, very likely, that won’t happen
Just look at hardcore flight simulations prices listings (DCS, FSX, Prepar3D, X-Plane), a world which, after almost a decade of void, has literally exploded in every kind of accessory:

if the answer is no, there we have what we “invest” for: to stick with Dirt4 and its flaws and no dlcs; and, maybe, for the next years, D4, RBR, WRC7, DR might be the only best companions for rally enthusiasts

I really wanted to like this game, and I enjoyed parts of it for a while. But this game really has too many flaws to overlook the good things about it. There is definitley something of a p2w aspect, while it's overcomable on the Heroes side with skill and some luck it is much harder to excuse the p2w aspect when it comes to Generals. It takes forever to grind from Rank 1 to a Rank where you can turn your character into a General (look at my played hours, I still didn't get enough XP to level a General, but I got one single command point so I can control 35 Infantry). Or instead of grinding for hundreds of hours, you can just buy a General.
Some other issues I have with this game:
-When you're trying to join a match you can't look over your character build or change anything. You can't do anything but chat, and sometimes the queues are obnoxious.
-Matchmaking is funky. There will be matches where too many people spawn in tanks/planes or everyone is infantry even though there are tanks and planes avaliable to your side, and then the enemy is evenly outfitted with a good mix of armor/infantry/air.
-Matchmaking wouldn't be so bad if you could more easily change characters in a match. Mostly I say that due to wanting to bring an anti-tank character into matches where we just get overwhelmed by top-tier tanks and the rest of the team is full of new players.
-Matchmaking doesn't always mesh well with an RTS strategy of blocking certain lines because one side will have been matched to a game where they have 35 spawns from the attempted block and the other team has hundreds. Winnable? I guess, but it's like fighting as Sparta in 300.
-Spawn camping can be an issue, like most games. Spawning on top of enemies/enemies spawning on you is also an issue.
-Level design is average, because it has some fairly well designed stuff (like the Town overall is well designed), and then some not so well done stuff (like the factory level which they may be changing in the future). Their first Airfield map is fun, but suffers from too much open space where you're forced to use vehicles (so if your team is full of new people you'll be stuck with bicycles and old pickup trucks to get around while the other team will have motorcycles, jeeps, and APCs, possibly even tanks and planes!)  More trenches and/or fox holes would be both a welcome change and more realistic.
-Lack of a good tutorial level. The one they have is singleplayer and teaches you how to shoot/move, doesn't teach you about other gameplay basics from multiplayer. No tutorial/shooting range for tanks or planes so any person who grinds for a tank or a plane has to go into matches to just figure out the controls. The tank controls are fine, but the plane controls take some getting used to.
-Two Map Types. I don't really like King of the Hill type matches in general, so I don't really play those much. Their assault/defense maps can be interesting, but suffer from a lot of noobness due to the lack of a proper tutorial.
-Shooting people coming out of a vehicle takes practice because the animations for the transition between in-vehicle and stepping out of it aren't that smooth yet. (That's what I remember at least)
-Not enough sprint for the map sizes.
-Melee hitboxes need to be bigger
Did I have fun in this game? Yes.
Is is flawed? Definitely.
Other than the flaws it is a game I enjoy because, while it takes some getting used to, I think it's a good WW2 FPS that feels more realistic than COD.

As someone that loves Warhammer 40k AND Chess: This game is absolutely addictive!
- Classic mode
It's just like chess. But with awesome kill animations and of course the Warhammer 40k vibe. Pretty standard but refreshingly artistic.
- Regicide mode
It's chess. With Blood Angels. And Orcs. Chainsaws, Grenades, Lasers! And the best is: For every single unit matchup (Pawn vs Pawn, Pawn vs Bishop, and so on) there is a new "fatality" animation if you kill the unit with a regular chess move. Pretty fun and can be really tricky with all the skills and player abilities.
- Campaign
The Orcs are spreading like a disease. You are the cure. I don't want to spoiler anything so let me just say: You kick♥♥♥♥♥and live a story while doing so - what's not to like?
Pros:
+ It's Warhammer 40k!
+ It's Chess!
+ No seriously, the combination is absolutely fantastic.
+ A lot of animations for each piece matchup (Pawn vs Pawn, Pawn vs Bishop, and so on).
+ Gameplay is great, tutorial does all it should. I think it's fairly easy for chess newcomers to get used to it.
Cons:
- The biggest con for me (have been playing chess for 20 years now): the AI sometimes do stupid mistakes that make a game ridicilously easy. At least during the first 10 missions of the campaign. But I hope the difficulty grows with the story.
- Campaign story is (so far) only told in text and voice. I would've loved some cinematics or more animations. (Just did the first 10 Missions, I'm sorry if they come after those!)
- ...I love tyranids (insert random other Warhammer 40K Faction besides Space Marines & Orcs). I need them. Hoping for an addon!
Conclusion:
I say the 15€ were well spent on it. I didn't regret it so far and I cannot imagine that I would regret it later on. If you enjoy chess and / or Warhammer 40, you should absolutely check it out.

WH40K Regicide combines the best elements of a grid-based combat strategy game and the classic board game chess.  Like any grid-based combat game, you try to advance your squad across the board and dispatch enemies.  Each unit is assigned a class based on the traditional chess pieces, which determines their movement.  You can also instantly eliminate an opposing piece by moving onto its space in a traditional chess capture.  It is not simply a 40K reskin of chess, however, because each piece has unique abilities and added attacking options, allowing each piece to attack at a range from its square.  In all, I find it to be a delightful merger of two different, yet compatible games.
And in keeping with the grimdarkness of the 41st Millenium, there is a delightful number of over-the-top execution animations and blood-spilling.

Sonic Adventure 2 is a good game! My only problem with it is that only the Speed Stages are really all that's fun, that's just me of course, I'm sure there are many others who feel differently. There are two sides, Hero and Dark, but all for the same, exciting story!
The Speed Stages are full of thrill and excitement, from being chased by a truck bent on trying to kill you to skateboarding straight down on a wall, the high speed and adrenaline will keep you going to the finish!
The Treasure Hunting Stages really test you and all your tracking skills, they are yet very frusturating and hard to beat. Luckily it has hot or cold type gameplay, there's a little radar that will tell you whether you're far away from the object you're looking for or right next to it. Or anywhere inbetween.
Then the Mech stages, they are unfourtanetly very forgettable. Not that fun either, it's more like Speed Stages than Treasure Hunting though, sure, there are some fun ones, but mostly very very boring ones.
Also, there are multiple missions for each stage, which let you explore around the stage some more or simply get a certain number of Rings.
There's a really great soundtrack too! Most of it adds some adrenaline to the level, except for the Treasure Hunting levels, at least, not on the Hero side.
Overall, 6/10... really great in some parts, but in other parts, *raspberry noise*. I don't really know if I would reccommend it to anyone.

This game is excellent, but not for everyone. The start can be fairly slow, and it takes a bit of time before you can really get into the huge battles and sieges. The realistic mode of no quitting without saving adds a HUGE amount of challenge as you can lose a large, high built army very quickly, so I would suggest that new players use the setting "allow me to quit without saving".
Now with that said, Mount and Blade Warband is amazing. The modding community is huge, and you can find just about anything, from fantasy to sci-fi mods, and if you get over the initial starting bump, the rest of the game is a blast.
Unit trees are fairly well fleshed out and the combat, while not exactly flashy or cool like Witcher 3, is weighty and deadly. Mounted combat is also well designed (though watching two galloping horses instantaneously stop upon impact is a head-scratcher). The diplomacy and economic management in the base game is bare bones, given that the most diplomacy you will ever perform as king is "Join my faction, surrender, give me back that fief or watch my Rhodok bolts darken the skies".
Factions are stacked to be amazing in one department, decent in a few departments, and absolute garbage in other departments. Case in point, the Khergit Khanate: their brilliant horse archers make open field combat a nightmare for the opposition, but they are about as effective as a wet noodle in sieges. Rhodoks: no cavalry makes open field combat dicy at best, but good luck trying to climb siege ladders with Rhodok crossbows tearing all of your troops apart.
The best part though is the mods for this game. By a long shot. Gekokujo, A Clash of Kings, The Last Days of the Third Age, and L'Aigle are my personal favorites, dealing with feudal Japan, Game of Thrones, Lord of the Rings, and blackpowder Europe, respectively.
I personally have not played the Napoleonic Warfare DLC as it is just multiplayer (which is an absolute crapshoot if you haven't dedicated hours to relearning combat to play online) and the Viking DLC didn't seem worth it since I could most likely find a mod along the same lines.
TL;DR Probably one of the top ten games on steam, potential for hours of play and multiple replays, non flashy combat that functions decently enough, and plenty of mods to scratch whatever itch you happen to have at the time.

It's been ages since I played this back on the Gamecube and I must say it's a lot more solid than I remember. Game play is fun and the levels are designed well enough with alternate paths to add challenge and reward for going out of your way to explore options. All chracters feel great and control decently. And the story is pretty good and at kept my attention throughout. The chao garden is a major plus as well, lots of extra post game content to focus on. Getting all the emblems and completing challenges can keep you going well past the 5-10 hours the main story will get you.
That being said, there are issues. Hit detection and physics are where this game gets into trouble. Sometimes you'll fall through things or the homing attack won't take you where it should. This is especially noticable in the extra missions on each stage that have you completing different tasks than the simple get to the end. Eggman and Tails stages have the these issues most obviously but I still enjoy their levels. Though I do not enjoy them nearly as much as the other characters stages and game play styles. These issues don't hinder my experience overall, just a few minor frustrations. The game is over 15 years old at this point so that is something to keep in mind.
The story is decent but not stellar, some things don't make sense and I'm sure you've heard it before but really the story in a sonic game isn't too important. It's a fun little weird story that tries to be super epic and I find that funny. The English voice acting and sound mixing are noticeably bad though. Once again I find it more hilarious than frustrating but take that with a grain of salt.
The level for the Last Story is also not great, I had to use a guide to figure out some parts because it is really not obvious what you have to do and not well explained. Most of the other levels are fantastic though so don't be discouraged if one or two stages are annoying or difficult. When this game is fun it is extremely fun and very rewarding.
The Chao garden is a god send for extra content in a video game. From raising stats to afk aging your chao to breeding different colors and stat grades this is the part of the game I spend an unhealthy amount of time on. This is a fantastic addition to a good game and I wish more games had extra content like this. It's not even separate from the main game as stuff in the levels help you in the Chao world. HOWEVER, I will say that this mode is only really playable because of a certain glitch that allows you to re-use animals to level up your chao's stats. Look it up if you don't know. If this glitch was patched or non-existent I definitely wouldn't spend so much time on this mode. It's still fun regardless, it just kinda stinks that a glitch is needed to get the most out of the feature.
After 15 years I still recommend this game. Score would be a decent 7. Definitely pick this up if you're a Sonic fan and if you like gimmicky RPG mini games, pick this one up anyway and research the chao garden.

This game is a lot of fun, for the most part.  There were a few elements I didn't care for but, overall, it was very well done and very entertaining.
The Good:
-- Very engaging story (except towards the end; see below).
-- Huge map with tons of opportunities to explore; lots of extra hidden goodies to find.
-- Great combat...99% of the time (see below).  Lots of stuff to blow in the environment such as propane tanks, oil drums, ammo dumps, vehicles, etc.
-- Lots of cool weapons to unlock as you go, with plenty of nifty attachments and upgrades to be had.
-- Tons of vehicles to drive...and crash.  There are gunboats, motorboats, jetskis, trucks, jeeps, cars...even hang-gliders!
-- Lots of entertaining side quests/bonus missions.
-- Lots of crafting of medicine, ammo bags, and other useful gear based on what you find around the map.
-- The digital camera your character carries allows you to tag enemies, which is VERY helpful in tracking their movements, and for getting headcounts to estimate the strength of the enemy force before launching your assault.
The Meh:
-- The stealth mechanics are iffy.  I mean hiding in tall grass and bushes seems to work great, as does hiding behind obstacles (rocks, oil drums, vehicles, etc).  But enemy line of sight is odd sometimes.  And the ability to throw rocks to distract enemies is pretty useless for the most part.  I mean, 99% of the time when I'd throw a rock, the enemy would hear it, look around, and say something like "What's that?  Did you hear that?", but they'd rarely move in the direction of the sound to investigate.  In fact, on the rare occasion they did move, they usually moved a very short distance AWAY from the sound of the rock banging on the wall (or whatever it happened to hit) in an apparently random direction.  So using rocks as "distractions" was rarely helpful in any way.  Stealth seemed to work well enough on levels where it was mission critical (indeed, in these situations the AI sometimes seems to even help you.  In other words, you'd have to try pretty hard to botch it).  But in instances when you're trying to be optionally stealthy, it doesn't work very well.
-- The physics for falling were kind of weird sometimes.  I mean, I would jump to the ground from a 10 foot tall roof with no ill effects.  But stumbling down a 3 foot embankment while running would sometimes kill me.  I mean, really?!?  This didn't happen very often...just often enough to be annoying.
The Bad:
-- Boss fights are not really fights.  They are just cinematics with lame QTEs.  Press the button when it tells you to and, presto, you won the fight.  Pretty disappointing and irritating.  And at least one of them (the one where you fight the bearded Australian guy...can't remember the character's name) is glitched and is missing one of the prompts.  I had to look on the internet to see what I was supposed to do.  When I pressed the right key at the right time (based on what I saw on the walkthrough) it resolved the QTE...but it never did show the prompt like it was supposed to.  Fortunately, there are only a few of these "fights" in the game.  Most of the combat in the rest of the game is straight up FPS run & gun, which is a ball.
-- At the very end of the game, I thought the last part of the story was a little bit far-fetched (even for a video game).  It gave me two choices for the ending.  I chose the one that
That ending turned out to be rather anti-climatic, in my opinion.  The save system is such that there doesn't seem to be a way to go back to just before the ending and choose the other option, so I'm not sure if that's a better ending...but, honestly, I don't see my self replaying the entire game just to find out.  I guess I could just look it up on YouTube or something.  Anyway, in short, great story for the most part...I just thought the ending could have been better.
-- A few small bugs/crashes.  I had to verify the game file cache a couple of times but it seemed to work itself out and allow me to continue with no hassle.  Still, it's something to be aware of.  One other annoying glitch was with the land mines -- basically, they never worked.  I'd drop them right in the middle of a hallway, right in front of a doorway, and in other impossible-to-miss-locations, and the enemy would walk right over them...but they'd never detonate.  I didn't get them to work one single time the entire game.  The other explosives like C4, grenades, and Molotovs all worked great, so the thing with the mines wasn't game-breaking in any way, just annoying.
To sum up:
I felt the good far outweighed the bad, and the game provided me with lots of fun.
8/10

Note: presumably, playing this game means you've played Hotline Miami 2, so I will discuss it as such. HM2 will make little sense in terms of mechanics, story, or pacing without at least some familiarity with the original. That being said, HM2 has little to do with the first.
Mechanically, Hotline Miami 2 foregoes the wide range of choices previously allowed to the player. Ability-granting masks are largely made irrelevant to gameplay as you will almost certainly need ranged weapons to survive the levels. This is, in large part, due to the massive quantity of windows hiding gun-toting enemies, usually off-screen. In effect, the huge levels combined with so many ranged weapons turn the game into a cover shooter. Having been used to melee-heavy gameplay in the original, I found this nearly forced gameplay aggravating. Furthermore, I could not justify the change as being supportive of a different method of story telling, which is when I'm willing to forgive such a drastic change in player choice. The long levels are often endurance tests necessitating multiple tries. You're not given any sense of the length of a level before you start it and there is no in-level saving, so unlike the arcade gameplay of the first game, you'll have to block off some time to make progress in the storyline. Whereas the first game made a spectable of the gratuitous violence, HM2 makes it a slog with little sense of variety and just enough randomness to make your victories "allowed" by the game rather than fairly won.
As for story, good luck... You'll play as a dozen or so people across two dozen levels. Many characters are worthless to the 'main' story thread - a story heavily reliant on the first game. Be prepared for unsatisfying dissolution of plot lines and only weakly interwoven threads.
The soundtrack is mostly very good. You can find the whole thing on bandcamp and elsewhere, so you really don't have to play the game to enjoy it. That being said, the length of some levels (>30 minutes) can lead even the best tunes to become annoying reminders that you're sweating tears to finish a game weighted heavily against you.
So who is this game for? Playing this game without having played the first would likely feel supremely disorienting and challenging. Playing the first, you're likely to be let down by the structural changes to the mask system and character-driven storytelling. You could argue based on the numbers that HM2 is a superior game to HM: it is longer, levels are larger, the AI is smarter, there are more weapons and characters.... But simply throwing good ingredients together does not a good game make.

I'd say it's about worth it's current price on steam. Short story/campaign. Decent graphics with some interesting and unique gameplay. The story just kinda throws you in, you don't really understand much about the character. If the game was just a "tech demo" for water physics, it fit it's purpose, although you don't really see it completely until the end. Having said that,  Dark Energy Digital steamlined the dynamic water in and made it part of the gameplay aesthetically well.
Some pitfalls is the very unintelligent AI which gets stuck swimming into walls, and almost always knows where you are no matter what—and sometimes they can shoot through objects you're using for cover. The game has some lack luster controls, and the heroine is the most annoying I've ever encountered aswell—having a distaste for her within the first few sentences she said. At the end of the story her "partner", or whomever, had said something about the terroists being there, but other than a few seconds in the beginning of seeing him, he becomes just a voice in your head like a Cortana. Not making him more important to the story, or his death more part of the story really bugged me. He just eventually stops talking to you. They could have done that so much better.
Amazing water effects aside, it felt very broken at certain parts, but it's an aging title(3 years+). I've played better in that time, but for it's price it was something different and entertaining to play despite some minor frustrations.

*First 2+ hours (just hit chapter 3):
Really enjoying this so far but bear in mind very, very early days.
The visuals are very stylized and have a gritty / snuff movie feel to them, (like Alien Isolation (AI)) this isn't pretty in a Far Cry or AC Black Flag kinda way but it works and the shadows and dynamic lighting give it that 'now' gen feel. The borders are jarring at first but you soon forget them although I'm at a lost as to why there so big as they take up a lot of screen real estate for artistic impression (at least I assume that's what it's for) but again for me no biggee.
This game is tough! But so far in a good way as although I've died a few times I was able to (and allowed to much like AI) figure things out for myself although this may be borderline further on but it's nice to have another game that doesn't hold your hand (two in a row in the same month, awesome!). Also ammo is at a huge premium thus far so being accurate with it was not advertising hype, it's very precious also like Alie...ok you get it already.
The game controls well (I'm using an XBOX controller. I'd recommend setting the sneak to toggle to save your finger from cramp due to having to hold the LB button for long periods in order to stay crouched) minus having to be facing the right point and position to pick / interact with things. Getting a head shot in this has a very satisfying pop (RE classic style) and gib effect that combined really are second to none.
The camera has it's moments but this is mainly to having to pivot Sebastian so he's facing the way you want to view and is otherwise solid. The camera also allows you to look around corners which is going to and has been very handy. I think I experienced a glitch with a stealth section that caused me to be seen when I shouldn't have been but I'm not sure if that's the case however it was the first and only instance that it appeared to occur.
Overall it feels like Resident Evil 4 with less tanky controls, better visuals, more depth (stealth, hiding, upgrade system etc) with undertones / nods to Silent Hill. I haven't found it scary thus far but this may be because of AI which presents a constant tense feel to it especially with it's superior use of audio and cueing and thus far this kinda feels like a cakewalk in comparison.
Yeah, great game thus far, with this and AI we're being spoiled this month! 8.5-9/10

Is this a sick joke on PC gamers?
The game looks and performs horribly. It's just terrible given it uses the same Engine as Wolfenstein: TNO. The character models looks very out dated, the game has almost no graphical options and the FOV is so narrow I get nausea from it. Written Below
There's so much input lag that it feels like there's heavy mouse acceleration.
The take 1 step forward, and your character stumbles 3 steps always, from a single button press. Makes disarming traps hell.
The save system is punishing to say the least. There's only 1 checkpoint every 20+ minutes. Enemies kill you instantly, or at best two hits, and if they chase you I hope you enjoy kiting them for ever.
You can stealth kill them with a knife from behind, but you can never use that knife for anything else.
It takes 2-3 well places head shots to take down the basic enemy, despite them having a railroad spike through their heads, and stabbing them in the back of the head with the knife kills them.
The camera control is dire, and you can't look around corners unless you move out of cover.
Enemy pathing gets stuck, so you can't sneak by them as they're stuck staring in your direction, and they're not patrolling.
Loot that's vital to finishing chapters is horrible RNG, and the game often sets you up for failure. So then you're back 20+ minutes to your last check point.
There's also some chance of either you or an enemy partially clipping through a wall. So that enemy then goes ape as they've seen you. because of that glitch.
It's not scary, it's just frustrating, and annoying at best. The plot is nonexistent so far in the game
To make matters worse their touting of the game using the cinematic aspect ratio was a lie. I have a 3440x1440 21:9 aspect ratio monitor and I don't just have letterboxing, but I have pillar boxing.
Here's a screenshot for all to gander at.
Note folks, I did unlock the fps, and remove the black letter boxing. That's still what I get. Sadly the game is locked at 16:9, and refuses to render properly in full screen at 3440x1440.
Also using the dev console commands disables Steam's Achievements and game tracking.
Even with Crossfire and essentially two R9 280X's at that tiny window, the game has issues maintaining 30fps. It's just horribly optimized and makes you wonder just how the hell they could have gone and messed up so badly when Wolfenstein looked amazing, and ran brilliantly.
The Evil Within uses 4.8GB of VRAM on my GPU, and the usage is around 80-99% as well.
