First and foremost, it's a Connect-3 game, not a Match 3.  There are a few different level types: match X amount of Y colour, get Z objects to bottom of screen, break obstacles, match next to unbreakable sigils to deceipher codes, and reveal hidden objects only when you also match with a magnifying glass.  It's a variation on the usual theme.
I'm about 4 chapters into the storyline from about 4 hours of play.  Story runs by itself, you're just intermittently playing puzzles that mostly fit an action in the story.
Most puzzles are easy to solve, and 3 stars is usually attainable with a little effort.
I'd recommend for me, but it depends if you personally like that style of gameplay.  It's a nice little timewaster, probably best picked up on sale.

Think Chess and think W40K and you will have an idea of how the game works - built into it is a challenging story 1 player mode which is great so far - with good replay value for optional objectives.
Classic CHess mode and Regicide mode are available both SP and MP. By Regicide i mean each unit on the board is taken directly from the actual W40K universe and mapped to a chess piece - Shoota Boy = Pawn etc and each unit has abilities on top of its chess move. So you can shoot or throw a Frak grenade in the Initiative phase after movement.
Basically adding another challenge to the game - where you cant take a certain piece can you blast him into submission instead?
Great replay value so far - level up units and make them stronger.
Achievements available for those chasing a tougher challenge too.
Yet to play the mulitplayer yet but i am sure it will be just as addictive and fun

I really wanted to like this game, and I enjoyed parts of it for a while. But this game really has too many flaws to overlook the good things about it. There is definitley something of a p2w aspect, while it's overcomable on the Heroes side with skill and some luck it is much harder to excuse the p2w aspect when it comes to Generals. It takes forever to grind from Rank 1 to a Rank where you can turn your character into a General (look at my played hours, I still didn't get enough XP to level a General, but I got one single command point so I can control 35 Infantry). Or instead of grinding for hundreds of hours, you can just buy a General.
Some other issues I have with this game:
-When you're trying to join a match you can't look over your character build or change anything. You can't do anything but chat, and sometimes the queues are obnoxious.
-Matchmaking is funky. There will be matches where too many people spawn in tanks/planes or everyone is infantry even though there are tanks and planes avaliable to your side, and then the enemy is evenly outfitted with a good mix of armor/infantry/air.
-Matchmaking wouldn't be so bad if you could more easily change characters in a match. Mostly I say that due to wanting to bring an anti-tank character into matches where we just get overwhelmed by top-tier tanks and the rest of the team is full of new players.
-Matchmaking doesn't always mesh well with an RTS strategy of blocking certain lines because one side will have been matched to a game where they have 35 spawns from the attempted block and the other team has hundreds. Winnable? I guess, but it's like fighting as Sparta in 300.
-Spawn camping can be an issue, like most games. Spawning on top of enemies/enemies spawning on you is also an issue.
-Level design is average, because it has some fairly well designed stuff (like the Town overall is well designed), and then some not so well done stuff (like the factory level which they may be changing in the future). Their first Airfield map is fun, but suffers from too much open space where you're forced to use vehicles (so if your team is full of new people you'll be stuck with bicycles and old pickup trucks to get around while the other team will have motorcycles, jeeps, and APCs, possibly even tanks and planes!)  More trenches and/or fox holes would be both a welcome change and more realistic.
-Lack of a good tutorial level. The one they have is singleplayer and teaches you how to shoot/move, doesn't teach you about other gameplay basics from multiplayer. No tutorial/shooting range for tanks or planes so any person who grinds for a tank or a plane has to go into matches to just figure out the controls. The tank controls are fine, but the plane controls take some getting used to.
-Two Map Types. I don't really like King of the Hill type matches in general, so I don't really play those much. Their assault/defense maps can be interesting, but suffer from a lot of noobness due to the lack of a proper tutorial.
-Shooting people coming out of a vehicle takes practice because the animations for the transition between in-vehicle and stepping out of it aren't that smooth yet. (That's what I remember at least)
-Not enough sprint for the map sizes.
-Melee hitboxes need to be bigger
Did I have fun in this game? Yes.
Is is flawed? Definitely.
Other than the flaws it is a game I enjoy because, while it takes some getting used to, I think it's a good WW2 FPS that feels more realistic than COD.

Not a lot of people with a significant amount of playtime appear to be posting these, so let me get off on the right foot by establishing myself as a pro at this game. I've played with some of the people who go competitively, and have maintained touch with a couple of them. That being said, this game, in its current state, is... sort of fun. But don't take it very seriously.
This game used to be quite fun in its original version (which I played A LOT) because I liked the largely strategical aspect to it because of the sandboxy-minecraft element, which definitely cut down on the DIE DIE DIE DIE of traditional FPS games (like COD). The game forced you to think and be creative, as well as manage your surroundings in a manner that very few FPS's have been able to do because of their largely static maps. With completely dynamic maps, that changed everything. So for some time I enjoyed myself, sniping people with the regular rifle, cleaning out tunnels with the shotgun, mowing people down with the SMG in Hallway, etc. There were no seriously overpowered weapons at the time. Each one had its role, and gameplay was fairly simple yet very complex at the same time.
And then Jagex announced a new version of the game.
Originally, I was pretty excited. The new classes looked cool, the maps looked great, and the graphics were given a nice boost. I played and played and played, and generally had fun for the time being. I attached pretty quickly to Marksman, which was fairly overpowered from the start (no method of sights, which was fine). Jagex was very slow to do the updates. None of the original requests for balance were heeded, such as a laser dot (Not a ♥♥♥♥ing beam) like the one they have in tf2, which makes it obvious yet not completely in your face like it currently does. Minigun did a bit too much damage, and the rocket launcher was a little slow, simple little balancing tweaks to make the gameplay more even and smooth.
That is not what we got.
Instead we got a ♥♥♥♥ing beam for the sniper, which has made the class... well. Difficult to play. It requires a series finesse for quickness that most people simply do not have, and really it ruins the game because people just spam it all the time. The rocket jumper was taken directly from Tf2 and not executed properly at all. The commando was reskined to look like Rambo... Why??? The rocketeer was nerfed and replaced with a stupid class called engineer, which removed the amazingly effective snowblower and gave it to engineer exclusively... who then became a fairly worthless class at actually fighting. This did not balance the game at all!
Then came the stupid battle builder. Useless!!! Whenever you tried to place one of the larger pre-made blocks the game just lagged incredibly. It was not even worth your time to create detailed maps. They got rid of (temporarily) the server browser, and replaced it with some stupid auto-join thing that nobody liked. Battle builder maps were not popular and were never really widespread (outside of games with friends).
Don't buy this game. DON'T BUY BLOCK AND LOAD EITHER!!!

Let me start off this review by saying that Ace of Spades was one of my first games on steam. I was naive at the time, and didn't even bother to search up reviews for the game. Boy, was I wrong in doing this (although it in no way made me be turned off by steam).
Bottom line; this game is terrible, and do not expect more from it. Let me start off by saying that this game is horrid when it comes to anything, actually. More than that, there is DLC in this game, as if the fact it was already broken with various glitches was not enough. This already adds to the worst part of the game;
You see, when somebody says they want to play a multiplayer fps, I think it means with various people. It's a network that *can* hold various people, after all. But with this game, you could never be so wrong. The one time I got on a server with people - 5 people, that is - the lag and latency was so high, I had to quit.
All in all, do yourself a favor and *don't* buy this game. Get the free, online version, which ironically has more players.

If you played Hotline Miami, and loved, it, you will more then likley like this.
Some things to point out:
Its confusing, and by confusing I mean imagine HM1 (Hotline Miami 1) x1000. Thats something that will turn a lot of people off.
The first scene is something that will also turn lots of people off from this game. Its the most confusing part of the game and it is frustratingly hard (for someone just starting out) and you will see that a lot in the game.
All I can say is pay attention to the story, and you can get through it.
Okay now the start of the actual review:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number brings a whole ton of new content to the Hotline Mimai franchise. New weapons, skills, masks and much more. In Hotline Miami 2 you get more backstory on the orignal events of Hotline Miami, and more that happens in the future, after the events of Hotline Miami. As you might be able to tell, this makes the game, VERY confusing. So because its not in chronological order, you will more then likely have 0 idea what is going on a some points, but it will all (hopefully) makes sense in the end.
This game is great, although at times I was ripping my hair out, but then again thats what Hotline Miami was really all about. This game is MUCH MUCH HARDER then the first game, and once you finish the game through its entrity once, you can play on hard mode, which, well, I have only beaten the first mission with that, lets just put it that way.
Now as you might have noticed people have pointed out that there are glitches. Now I have only found about 4 of them, but unfortunitly all of them are game breaking. I had points in time where I would spend 2 hours on a mission (and yes this actually happend) and as I am walking back to the car, I go up some stairs (a.k.a. where you switch areas) and I ended up in a wall. Yes, a wall. There was no way to get out so I shut off the game and didnt try it again until the next day. I had other issues where I would go outside the normal walkable area on accident, and was stuck there (yet again, trying to go back to the car) so most of the issues are in load zones.
Besides this, I think this is a worthy sucsessor to Hotline Miami. If you like the first game, you, will probobly like this. If you didnt play the first game (stop reading this review and go buy it!) or didnt like the first game, you wont like this game.
Enjoy.

It's been ages since I played this back on the Gamecube and I must say it's a lot more solid than I remember. Game play is fun and the levels are designed well enough with alternate paths to add challenge and reward for going out of your way to explore options. All chracters feel great and control decently. And the story is pretty good and at kept my attention throughout. The chao garden is a major plus as well, lots of extra post game content to focus on. Getting all the emblems and completing challenges can keep you going well past the 5-10 hours the main story will get you.
That being said, there are issues. Hit detection and physics are where this game gets into trouble. Sometimes you'll fall through things or the homing attack won't take you where it should. This is especially noticable in the extra missions on each stage that have you completing different tasks than the simple get to the end. Eggman and Tails stages have the these issues most obviously but I still enjoy their levels. Though I do not enjoy them nearly as much as the other characters stages and game play styles. These issues don't hinder my experience overall, just a few minor frustrations. The game is over 15 years old at this point so that is something to keep in mind.
The story is decent but not stellar, some things don't make sense and I'm sure you've heard it before but really the story in a sonic game isn't too important. It's a fun little weird story that tries to be super epic and I find that funny. The English voice acting and sound mixing are noticeably bad though. Once again I find it more hilarious than frustrating but take that with a grain of salt.
The level for the Last Story is also not great, I had to use a guide to figure out some parts because it is really not obvious what you have to do and not well explained. Most of the other levels are fantastic though so don't be discouraged if one or two stages are annoying or difficult. When this game is fun it is extremely fun and very rewarding.
The Chao garden is a god send for extra content in a video game. From raising stats to afk aging your chao to breeding different colors and stat grades this is the part of the game I spend an unhealthy amount of time on. This is a fantastic addition to a good game and I wish more games had extra content like this. It's not even separate from the main game as stuff in the levels help you in the Chao world. HOWEVER, I will say that this mode is only really playable because of a certain glitch that allows you to re-use animals to level up your chao's stats. Look it up if you don't know. If this glitch was patched or non-existent I definitely wouldn't spend so much time on this mode. It's still fun regardless, it just kinda stinks that a glitch is needed to get the most out of the feature.
After 15 years I still recommend this game. Score would be a decent 7. Definitely pick this up if you're a Sonic fan and if you like gimmicky RPG mini games, pick this one up anyway and research the chao garden.

There are so many better 3D platformers out there, and a lot of 2D Sonic games that are a lot more fun than this one. It has some good aspects, but the flaws are too significant to ignore.

This game is a lot of fun, for the most part.  There were a few elements I didn't care for but, overall, it was very well done and very entertaining.
The Good:
-- Very engaging story (except towards the end; see below).
-- Huge map with tons of opportunities to explore; lots of extra hidden goodies to find.
-- Great combat...99% of the time (see below).  Lots of stuff to blow in the environment such as propane tanks, oil drums, ammo dumps, vehicles, etc.
-- Lots of cool weapons to unlock as you go, with plenty of nifty attachments and upgrades to be had.
-- Tons of vehicles to drive...and crash.  There are gunboats, motorboats, jetskis, trucks, jeeps, cars...even hang-gliders!
-- Lots of entertaining side quests/bonus missions.
-- Lots of crafting of medicine, ammo bags, and other useful gear based on what you find around the map.
-- The digital camera your character carries allows you to tag enemies, which is VERY helpful in tracking their movements, and for getting headcounts to estimate the strength of the enemy force before launching your assault.
The Meh:
-- The stealth mechanics are iffy.  I mean hiding in tall grass and bushes seems to work great, as does hiding behind obstacles (rocks, oil drums, vehicles, etc).  But enemy line of sight is odd sometimes.  And the ability to throw rocks to distract enemies is pretty useless for the most part.  I mean, 99% of the time when I'd throw a rock, the enemy would hear it, look around, and say something like "What's that?  Did you hear that?", but they'd rarely move in the direction of the sound to investigate.  In fact, on the rare occasion they did move, they usually moved a very short distance AWAY from the sound of the rock banging on the wall (or whatever it happened to hit) in an apparently random direction.  So using rocks as "distractions" was rarely helpful in any way.  Stealth seemed to work well enough on levels where it was mission critical (indeed, in these situations the AI sometimes seems to even help you.  In other words, you'd have to try pretty hard to botch it).  But in instances when you're trying to be optionally stealthy, it doesn't work very well.
-- The physics for falling were kind of weird sometimes.  I mean, I would jump to the ground from a 10 foot tall roof with no ill effects.  But stumbling down a 3 foot embankment while running would sometimes kill me.  I mean, really?!?  This didn't happen very often...just often enough to be annoying.
The Bad:
-- Boss fights are not really fights.  They are just cinematics with lame QTEs.  Press the button when it tells you to and, presto, you won the fight.  Pretty disappointing and irritating.  And at least one of them (the one where you fight the bearded Australian guy...can't remember the character's name) is glitched and is missing one of the prompts.  I had to look on the internet to see what I was supposed to do.  When I pressed the right key at the right time (based on what I saw on the walkthrough) it resolved the QTE...but it never did show the prompt like it was supposed to.  Fortunately, there are only a few of these "fights" in the game.  Most of the combat in the rest of the game is straight up FPS run & gun, which is a ball.
-- At the very end of the game, I thought the last part of the story was a little bit far-fetched (even for a video game).  It gave me two choices for the ending.  I chose the one that
That ending turned out to be rather anti-climatic, in my opinion.  The save system is such that there doesn't seem to be a way to go back to just before the ending and choose the other option, so I'm not sure if that's a better ending...but, honestly, I don't see my self replaying the entire game just to find out.  I guess I could just look it up on YouTube or something.  Anyway, in short, great story for the most part...I just thought the ending could have been better.
-- A few small bugs/crashes.  I had to verify the game file cache a couple of times but it seemed to work itself out and allow me to continue with no hassle.  Still, it's something to be aware of.  One other annoying glitch was with the land mines -- basically, they never worked.  I'd drop them right in the middle of a hallway, right in front of a doorway, and in other impossible-to-miss-locations, and the enemy would walk right over them...but they'd never detonate.  I didn't get them to work one single time the entire game.  The other explosives like C4, grenades, and Molotovs all worked great, so the thing with the mines wasn't game-breaking in any way, just annoying.
To sum up:
I felt the good far outweighed the bad, and the game provided me with lots of fun.

Updated Review (02/03/16):
Had a chance to play quite a bit more - split between Bright Wizard, Witch Hunter, and Waywatcher.
I still think this is a great game with a lot of potential, but a few things need some polish:
Overall I'd like to see it move more towards a 'tactical shooter'. Unfortunately, I found that the most effective tactic is button mashing, especially with PBAOE melee weapons (like Greatswords and Axes).
Collision detection needs to be implemented to give both enemies and players a feeling of 'weight' and 'presence' - and also the ability to do things like defend choke points, or body block.
It would be nice if attacks had even a little bit of context - as in holding a direction might change the type of attack slightly (holding right might make the attack come from the right, holding forward an overhead, etc.)
The loot system is ok, but it encourages grinding in the beginning.
The AI is terrible. Rats do little more than run at you and melee or shoot (in the case of Globadiers and Ratling Gunners). There is no tactics to the enemy whatsoever. Also, the friendly bots are terribly dumb, to the point I'd rather play solo most of the time, as they just tend to be visual clutter, which leads to my next point...
Give us the option to disable bots on solo runs. Seriously, I can't believe this wasn't an option from the start.

If you own Left 4 Dead, you're really not missing out on much here
Many claims to fame over this game involve how this game is a perfect mixture of Payday and Left 4 Dead and Chivalry, but this game ultimately fails to create a distinct and enjoyable self outside these prestated realms.
Pros:
-Well done gothic setting
-Decent enough loot system
-Rat variants enforce the idea of staying together(like the hunter and smoker clones)
-Maps are fairly long, pretty interesting enough
-Damn fine graphics
-Each character most definetly feels distinct
-Is fun with friends
Cons:
-Melee combat feels weightless and meaningless, no blow feels like a real meaty hit(needed better fx and hit animations)
-Gore system is incredibly lacking, rats lose their heads and arms, with very little splatter involved
-The very grim setting contrasts with how goofy the rats look, and not in a good way
-Ranged play suffers from the same thing as melee play(nothing feels like it matters)
-No memorable lines from any of the characters, everyone seems to be the same in that regard
With a few tweaks to what already exists here, I would totally consider rebuying this game and giving it another shot, but as of right now, it just doesnt fit the bill. The game just doesn't feel nearly as exciting to play as its contemporaries.

This is a surprisingly entertaining little distraction.  It's much like the Starcraft custom maps I used to play back in the day.  Ripping through fleets of ships is very satisfying, and the game appears to be very well balanced.  However, it isn't perfect, and the low price point is very justified.
The campaign is pretty short and mostly easy, with very difficult final missions thrown in at the end which accounts for most of the game's length.  While that sounds like a damnning critique, I still very much enjoyed the time I spent with this game, and I would love to revisit this game again if the devs decide to add some more missions.
The interface has some pretty major problems, which I'll list:
- There's no reason for the Research panel to be a huge popup window in the center of the screen, which prohibits you from picking up powerups while it's active.  The research panel should be a compact sidebar that gives you easy access to your upgrades at all times, and allows you to monitor them continuously.
- There's no way to queue up units, so this game is a bit of a keyboard masher.  This isn't horrible, but definitely inferior to  an actual unit queueing system.
- Map scrolling halts when your cursor hits the edge of the screen, causing you to "drag" the map over and over to navigate.  The map scrolling function should be free while the mouse button is held down.
- I personally do not like clickable powerups in strategy games like this (a trend that I believe gathered a lot of momentum from Plants vs. Zombies, which constantly has you clicking coins and resources until you want to shoot yourself).  I think this game can keep the powerup system, but just make them pick up when I mouse over.  It's just annoying to me, and takes away from the strategy aspect of the game, which is the game I actually want to play.
I think the resource gathering aspect of this game could use a bit more depth.  As it stands now, your miners are just something you max out early on and replace if they get destroyed, and they allow the enemy to snowball you if they get the upper hand (which is fine, a match has to end somehow).  You also can't mine into your enemy's territory, once you hit the end of your half of the map, you can't mine anymore.  Because of this, the game misses out on fun possibilities of map control.
Despite all my complaints, I like this game, and I recommend it based on the low price point.  It's a fun way to spend an afternoon on the weekend.

PROS:
Best ever game environment.  Beautiful art and style. Extensive crafting system. PVP option. Dungeons are unique and mob's are difficult to master-  they all have different abilities. Gameplay grind and difficulty creates a relatively mature player base. Can play for free if you can stand the grind punishment.
CONS:
Gear acquisition until you have a maxed out character is very punishing! If you're used to Warcraft dungeons, where you can get all the gear you need that matches your level running  dungeons, you're going to be frustrated. Dungeons AT YOUR LEVEL, are DIFFICULT for a group, YOUR LEVEL. So you're basically left with hoping you have some maxed level freinds to run you through, over and over. Which by that time, you've leveled past the gear you were after in the first place. The system really makes no sense.
Getting groups at levels other than high levels is hard. Most players are maxed and have no incentive to help you with low level dungeons. They need to introduce player scaling and rewards so high level players are compelled to play low level dungeons.
BIGGEST CON:  THE GRIND.
It's the most punishing grind I've ever experienced- even if you purchase booster packs for 3x the XP. Now I only get to play an hour or two here and there and on weekends, but I've been playing about a year and my highest toon is 115 out of 165. People get around this by being "power leveled" by high level players- which is about as fun as teasing a cat with string... You're just there for idle chit chat while they blow mobs down- for hours....
SUMMARY:
One of my favorite games ever due to art, sounds, playstyle and difficulty. But it has serious flaws with helping and keeping new players interested (grind and grouping).

TheGameSelectionz PC Review on: WARHAMMER 40K: REGICIDE
As we all know that a normal chess is by moving chess pieces in every turn after you or your opponent make the first move. In the new WARHAMMER 40000 series Regicide, I equip my knights into the midfield of battle and into reaching range of the boltguns carried by my pawns to cleanse, purge and kill the orcs.
Regicide is a two in one game. First is exactly is a chess game (as for players that don't know how to play chess, don't you worry the tutorial will teach you the basic and it's easy) but, try switching all the chess pieces from the chess board a chess game usually used to Space Marines and Orks characters from Warhammer 40,000 world, awesome right?!
Now.. let us talk about the modes available in Regicide shall we.
Classic Mode: lets you play normal chess against the AI or other humans, and while it might not be the best chess game ever made, like Battle Chess for example, the pieces animate into entertaining miniature duels that make up for basic features.The animations itself as brutal as you will expected that has been given in the setting. While playing and watching pawns blast to pulverize each other into chunks of meat plus the gore had livens up well... boring moves.. at least until you've seen them all.
Regicide Mode: This mode keeps the regular chess rules, even advanced stuff like castling and 'en passant'(in passing) captures, and adding a slice of light strategy. After each turn plays out, like in normal chess, you'll enter the initiative phase by spending points to activate special abilities. A players unit piece might gain a defensive shield, shoot at an enemy, use a psychic power, or throw a grenade. Each piece has hit points to be chipped away or reinforced it by using these abilities, but the initiative phase initially seems less decisive than in the movement phase.
The last two modes will be the Skirmish and Campaign Modes:
You could play as a stand-off skirmish against the AI with different difficulties or a human opponent online or hot-seat. Through a single-player campaign with a surprising amount of good narrative development by opening the story with a cut-scene. Each of its 50 levels has an intro, as the Blood Angels chapter of Space Marines strive to take Hethgar Prime back from the Orks of the Goff clan. These levels are like puzzling chess books, that will give you a set of pieces in an unusual way to let you find out as a challenged for you to take the queen without losing your own, or preventing your opponent promoting a pawn.
As a 40K fan recognizes Regicide as the chess variant had been played in one of the official novels while also realizing that this game doesn’t resemble the descriptions of it, but who knows the Blood Angels sometimes got into blood-drinking frenzies and maybe eat brains. As I played the campaign to see how its story going out to be the weakest part of Regicide, but even with nicely done voice actors from the Dawn Of War series would not be enough to convince the nerds that had known more about the 40K universe. Skirmish mode had it good, whether against an AI with harder difficulties or an actual player, where it feels more like Chess+ mode.
TheGameSelectionz final verdict for this game is 8/10(Great Game).

The first scene is something that will also turn lots of people off from this game. Its the most confusing part of the game and it is frustratingly hard (for someone just starting out) and you will see that a lot in the game.
All I can say is pay attention to the story, and you can get through it.
Okay now the start of the actual review:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number brings a whole ton of new content to the Hotline Mimai franchise. New weapons, skills, masks and much more. In Hotline Miami 2 you get more backstory on the orignal events of Hotline Miami, and more that happens in the future, after the events of Hotline Miami. As you might be able to tell, this makes the game, VERY confusing. So because its not in chronological order, you will more then likely have 0 idea what is going on a some points, but it will all (hopefully) makes sense in the end.
This game is great, although at times I was ripping my hair out, but then again thats what Hotline Miami was really all about. This game is MUCH MUCH HARDER then the first game, and once you finish the game through its entrity once, you can play on hard mode, which, well, I have only beaten the first mission with that, lets just put it that way.
Now as you might have noticed people have pointed out that there are glitches. Now I have only found about 4 of them, but unfortunitly all of them are game breaking. I had points in time where I would spend 2 hours on a mission (and yes this actually happend) and as I am walking back to the car, I go up some stairs (a.k.a. where you switch areas) and I ended up in a wall. Yes, a wall. There was no way to get out so I shut off the game and didnt try it again until the next day. I had other issues where I would go outside the normal walkable area on accident, and was stuck there (yet again, trying to go back to the car) so most of the issues are in load zones.
Besides this, I think this is a worthy sucsessor to Hotline Miami. If you like the first game, you, will probobly like this. If you didnt play the first game (stop reading this review and go buy it!) or didnt like the first game, you wont like this game.
Enjoy.

I regard the original Far cry, as one of the finest single player games ever made. So naturally, I had high hopes for the third instalment. It all looked very promising.
The Rook islands are a wonderful setting. The map is very well thought out, offering plenty of options to get around by obvious means, but also less noticeable ones. The developers have deliberately made traversing the map as frustration free as possible, everything is made pretty accessible. It is also diverse, with plenty of unique places and incredibly dense with points of interest and random encounters. This being [mostly] an open world game, the environment provides plenty of combat scenarios and ways to tackle objectives. The graphics looked good and were stable.
The gunplay is satisfying. There is a decent selection of weapons that are customizable and there’s always the option to execute a takedown on someone [i.e. stab in the chest]. The A.I. you’re battling are nothing exceptional, but more importantly, they are not a frustrating opponent to fight. I also particularly enjoyed a feature, where if you shoot the driver of a car (at speed), the car would usually do a flip and explode.
The original score, composed by Brian Tyler is good. But the main theme and its equally emotional variant ‘’Further’’, deserve special recognition. That theme is, in my opinion the backbone of the game. It beautifully sums up the experience and Far cry 3 wouldn’t be the game it is, without it. The overall sound design is great also.
The story doesn’t really make sense and there are a lot of weak points to it. I found the ending to be underwhelming as well, unfortunately. But the characters are great, Vaas in particular and all the voice actors give a solid performance. What bothers me though, is that it is nowhere near as good as it could have been. I’d go as far as saying it leaves you disappointed. But even with all its shortcomings, I enjoyed the story.
The missions themselves were not what I expected. I was positively surprised at times, but on other occasions they were somewhat anticlimactic; very linear and restrictive; or stuff that was straight up boring. Boss fights for example are QTEs (could have been much more creative). In between the main missions, you’ll be exploring a lot and this is where Far cry 3 shines best. I found myself liberating outposts, activating radio towers, collecting letters/artifacts and doing all sorts of sidequests out of pure enjoyment, although it doesn’t really reward the player or offer any variety after some point. You’ll use that time to gain experience, get crafting items and just expand your knowledge of the islands. All those systems were nicely implemented as well. As the main story ends, there is little else to do. You could try out the multiplayer, but it is mostly dead and the co-op mode is a repetitive grind.
In conclusion, a good game, worth your time, but underperforming in terms of its potential.

They correctly named it "Dirt 4" - it's not a worthy sequel to Dirt Rally (which I think is the best rally game ever made).
The biggest problem is that the tracks are all strange, repetitive, and boring. Auto-generated tracks was a great idea but in practice it's really terrible. Instead of a game with, say, 100km of unique track like Dirt Rally, in Dirt 4 you get 50 different 100-metre sections of track which appear randomly one after another. So you end up effectively driving a muddled-up 5km of track with a continual weird sense of deja-vu. After 5 minutes you've seen all there is to see.
Not that you would want to see more than 5 minutes of these cartoon-ishly colourful landscapes that make the game feel so unrealistic. This really spoils the whole game as unlike Dirt Rally it doesn't feel like I'm driving a real car (oh, and despite the graphics looking worse, the game runs slower). Also breaking the realism is the co-drivers' speech. It doesn't sound like they are really travelling in the car with you. I really missed the Dirt Rally co-driver's voice.
The aspect of team management, sponsorships, and buying used cars felt really appealing at first, but after 10 minutes I realised it was totally hollow, not adding any substance to the game. I am left wondering if this is game any better than Dirt 3. A quick 5 minutes playing Dirt 3 confirms, yes, Dirt 4 is better. But not by much. Maybe "Dirt 4" was not the correct name after all.

My recommendation is conditional -- this game is not worth full price. However it routinely goes on sale for 90% off (so I paid $0.50), and at that price I think it's worth it. I just finished my first playthrough which took me about three hours; I could run through it again once or twice to pick up medals/achievements I missed, and I've also unlocked a "Challenge Room" that I haven't played yet.
The mechanics are fun, and the water physics is great. In most games, water just makes you walk slower as you're moving through it -- in this games, water actually exerts force on you and the environment, so a wave of water flooding a corridor will shove you back and carry debris with it. Thanks, Havok physics!
The controls could feel a little clunky, and the story was completely underdeveloped. I thought I was fighting a mid-game mini-boss battle and then the game was over. If you somehow become emotionally invested in your character and her helpful friend, you'll get no resolution whatsoever.
Overall -- $0.50 is worth it for an afternoon of playtime with some fun water physics, but this wasn't a Game of the Year by a long shot.

Primary conclusion: Best bought for game research/curiosity and little else. It's only an average third-person shooter, with an unfortunately short-lived exploration of a unique mechanic (water manipulation, towards the end of the game). Sell a few Steam cards, nab it during a sale, jump in with low expectations and enjoy a few hours of fairly impressive water simulation whilst shooting suicidal baddies (no really, that's their whole gig, convincing people to kill themselves, you'll see it all throughout the game, not advised if suicidal).

Incomplete.
That's the word that best describes Contagion, which lingers in an Early Access state despite its official release.
From the inability to vote trolling players off of a server to underdeveloped game interfaces to the small quantity of maps to the lingering bugs, this game simply feels underdeveloped. Mind, it isn't in any way bad- in fact, it plays just like you'd expect: A slow-paced, more atmospheric version of Left 4 Dead, sans the well-developed co-op mechanics which help flesh that game out. It's the style of game which lives by its polish, its ability to maintain strong teamwork, and its variety of gameplay- and currently, stumbles its way through all those components with all the vigor of a walking corpse.
At the moment maps are simplistic, linear affairs, so there's none of that emergent gameplay that comes from a more open-world or branching-path approach. The game plays like any co-op zombie FPS, but from zombies that occasionally have 5 foot reach, to extremely inconsistant gun accuracy, to unclear progression (which is fine in open-world, not so much in linear), to..
Basically, this game works as a free-to-play prototype, or as an Early Access game, but the shallow framework it offers prevents it from being able to be considered as a fully developed game. More than that, it feels like it's not entirely sure if it wants to be a linear co-operative FPS or a more freeform open-world sim, and the lack of dedication toward either focus further hinders the game.
There's a lot of work left to be done on this game. If the devs do that work, it could be a great game. As is, it's a game that lacks any single massive negative mark against it, but, much like a victim going down under the zombie flood, is drug down by its countless shortcomings.
In sum, the development of this game may currently be rather poetically dedicated to the game's theme, but as far as attracting and retaining players, potential alone isn't enough to allow the game to survive the contagion of inadequacies it is infected by.
The same, of course, could be said for my puns.
Just think- this the wit I offer when my brain isn't addled by a zombie virus!
But if you give me just a moment to recover from this completely innocent cold I just seem to have caught, I'm sure I can find a rather funny way of giving you a hug and a kiss..
Final Score: 3/5

or, at least, that's what I thought when I began playing the sequel to Hotline Miami.
On the surface, the game is much the same: the same one-hit-kills/deaths, the same weapon variety, the same goofy AI, and the same kick♥♥♥♥♥music style and aesthetic. But, after a while, one begins to realize it is much more.
The level design I knew (and loved) in HM1 was completely changed. In HM2, gone are the floors of nothing but tight hallways and plentiful corners. While they still exist to an extent, HM2 incorporates a much more open level design, with long ranges of sight and wide expanses abound.
While the game was panned (by some) at launch for this fact, I (and many other HM1 fans) began to see the merit of the layouts. Frankly, the floor plans of HM1 were easy. They were exploitable. With quick enough reflexes and decent knowledge of AI, a “veteran” of the franchise can/could complete them with no problems. For some, this made the game what it was. HM1 would have been a far worse game if it had the same level design style as HM2. But it didn't, and the HM2 level design, while harder, less fluid, and (to some) less “fun”, makes the game what it is. In HM1, one could be a veritable GOD, easily cutting through the waves of dumb, slow henchmen. In HM2 the bar is raised.
Despite the harder level design, it is nothing if not fair. Sure, you will sometimes be killed from an enemy off screen, ending an otherwise perfect run in a frustrating manner. But, next time, you won't. Or maybe you will. Either way, it is up to the player. With decent reflexes and knowledge, you can “master” HM2 in much the same way you could HM1. It's just much harder.
Essentially, HM2's levels will feel unfair at first and, if you haven't played HM1, may seem difficult. But the same level of fluidity will come with time. It's not impossible to achieve HM1-like gameplay in HM2, it just takes more skill.
Although HM1 was known for its unforgiving gameplay, few would classify it as a “hard” game. If one played it slow enough, any level could be beaten with ease. True skill was shone in the WAY a player completed a floor/level, not in whether or not they could do it. In HM2, it is much the same, but the skill cap is quite a bit higher. For most HM1 “veterans”, the first 5-10 levels of HM2 should be fairly easy. But from there on out, new heights must be reached. Anyone who says otherwise, simply go back to HM1 and tell me it's harder. HM1 is a veritable cakewalk compared to HM2's later levels.
Enter hard mode, the masochist's way to increase playtime. Levels are mirrored, have many more enemies, and every time a weapon is picked up, its ammo is halved. Enemy reflexes are also much faster, although their AI I not much better. Hard mode, for a mediocre player like myself, is tough. There's no other way to say it. It will, once again, require you to reach new heights, and going back to normal mode (or HM1) after completing hard mode will make you wonder how you ever struggled in the first place. It will take much more time, but it is rewarding.
HM2's normal mode is significantly harder than HM1, and hardmode is much harder than both.
The music is just as good as the first. While not as many songs resonate with me personally (I will never forget M O O N's  Paris or Hydrogen, and Scattle's Knock Knock), the beats are as sick as ever, and the soundtrack is genuinely fantastic. If you even remotely liked HM1's soundtrack, I'd recommend picking up HM2's as well.
Sure, some masks were cut out, and you are restricted in some levels, but the new system is still extremely fun. Without going too in depth and spoiling any story, there are four sets of masks/powers that one may choose, depending on the level. Each has its own challenge, and overall the system is still fun, although in a different way than HM1. Let's be honest, most of HM1's masks were pretty dull in the first place, with some masks having little effect on the gameplay. HM2 condenses the system, with each mask having bringing a wildly different playstyle.
HM2 is, in my opinion, less replayable than the first. I'd often load up HM1 to just play a few levels and revel in fluidity of the run, and put at least 100 hours in, beating the game multiple times (I played on a DRM free copy before being given the game on Steam, hence my lack of hours on here). However. HM2 is still well worth the money. As a fairly experienced HM1 player, It took approximately 5-6 hours to complete the game on normal, and around 8-10 hours on hardmode (One level (not Dead Ahead) took around 2.5 hours). Some may complete it more quickly, other more slowly. Either way, I consider it worth the money considering the amount of content you receive, especially with hardmode.
Overall, HM2 is a fantastic sequel to HM1. It is challenging but fair, frantic but tactical, and, above all, fun. I'd 100% recommend  to anyone who's played the first game (I'd recommend HM1 first to anyone new to HM). It may not have had the warmest welcome on launch, but in this HM fan's eyes, its flaws are easily overlooked.
Hopefully this review was helpful. Feel free to add/comment to ask any questions. I'd be glad to help anyone enjoy HM as much as I do.

(+)    Big levels
(+)    Nice level design

(+)    Tons of enemies
(+)    Voice acting/ good Voice interaction (like: dwarf heals the mage and says something specific to that mage character, not only “here is your health portion” but more like “hey wizard woman, there you go, your bandage”)

Although the devs promised next level melee gameplay, I feel like there are some things missing older games did better. Dirt 4 gets a lot of hate online because people were expecting Dirt Rally 2 - i.e. a simulation experience of rallying. As a gamer who played Dirt Rally (and loved it), I'm the odd one out here as I think Dirt 4 is awesome. Bare in mind, as you read my review though, that I'm the sort of crazy person who plays driving games on a keyboard. I don't like playing with a controller and can't get on with a steering wheel and pedals (despite being able to drive cars in real life).
I find Dirt 4 a joy to play. It's tough, beautiful and unforgiving. The physics are insanely frustrating (in a good way). Just when I've mastered a gravel track, the game throws a tarmac road at me or a snow covered lane and I suddenly can't drive again and am snaking all over the place. I've not mastered left foot braking - because doing that on a keyboard is HARD. But that doesn't matter because I'll practice, practice, practice on those insane bends, jumps and twists until I perfect it and come in first, second or third place.
There are things I love about Dirt 4 that I also loved about Dirt Rally - how you can make hash of one stage, then batter the next few and come out on top. How you can have rubbish splits, but make up for it in the next few and come in the top three. How you can be doing really well, right until the end, then miss-hear a co-driver call and totally balls it up and lose then have to start all over again.
There's no rewind system. There's no handbrake slides into corners. I've seen far worse arcade driving sims (GRID 2 for example). And I, for one, am glad Dirt moved away from the days of DIRT Showdown and the hooning nonsense of Ken Block.
When I first started playing, I nearly cried when I heard a female co-drive voice, but a few more levels and I was happy.
There's loads and loads of content and it just keeps coming. I get stuck, then I come back and try again. I'll probably never complete it but I love every minute.

Overall a great rally game imo so long as you're not looking for something sim-ish.

A great blend of chess and WH40k. On the surface it appears very simple, but you will quickly realise there is a varied amount of tactics to use in Regicide mode with all the unlockable abilities. The normal chess mode is great, because the animations, sounds and voices bring it to life in a way that cannot be achieved IRL.

A very well done mashup of chess and warhammer.   The game plays like chess, but there is an extra phase where units can also shoot and slash at each other.  It might sound goofy, but it works well, and changes up some of the typical chess strategies.
The production values are also top notch.  The game is easy to navigate and understand, there is polish throughout.  With luck there will be future expansions that include more races from Warhammer 40K.

Warhammer 40k: Regicide is chess with a few twists. The twist being the game having an action phase where you have a couple turns to do a multitude of actions. These actions can range from damaging enemy peices to increasing the defences of your own piece as well as other things.
Like chess, This game will test your mind and it feels great. The gameplay is simple. Pick a piece, move it and begin action phase. If an enemy piece is within kill distance, you can instant kill that piece like in real chess. Overall, very well done mechanics and adds interesting things to a board game that I used to play as a child.
Speaking of the old board game, There is a classic mode in Regicide as well. It's classic chess with a brutal look at taking pieces. The animation on the kills are nice and violent. Each kill is satisfying.
As far as graphics go, The game looks pretty nice. The boards are interesting and of course, the armor on the characters looks amazing. This goes for the Space marines and the Orks. Overall, a nice game to look at as well as play.
When it comes to sound, I'm a tad iffy on it. I've had a couple sounds cut out consistantly. The sound of Rook's Gattling gun seems to have an odd cutout. Music is nice but in the heat of the moment, I don't really notice the music and just want to focus on the game at hand.
Overall, This game is brilliant. If you want to test your mind or just have fun playing a strategy game, get this one.

-Party/Group options, where groups of 5-20 people can come together for big battles (temporary, able to disband, but share kills, XP and Loot)
-Messaging/Chat options, OMG please some kind of chat system that allows people within groups, clans, parties, or even just friends, to have separate, PRIVATE conversations. A friend and I were trying to make a plan of attack and someone else kept butting in.
-Options from clicking on a person. As it is, you have to go to the top of the screen and click on their name, in LOTRO I could just right click their avatar in front of me.
-A map that shows you where you are, where quests are or what direction to go in.
-A slightly longer respawn time. The creatures respawn so fast that sometimes they gang up on you.
I'm sure these are all things the Devs are planning to get to anyway, but this is my two cents. These are the improvements I'd like to see.

Introduction
Warhammer 40,000 Regicide is published and developed by Hammerfall Publishing.
Regicide appears to be their only title at the time of this review.
Regicide has recently left early access and is currently available to purchase.
The game is a part of the well known and well developed Warhammer 40k universe,
How does the game hold up to the other multitudes of Warhammer games? read on and find out!
Plot/Storyline
"Set in the Segmentum Obscurus, the story begins with the death-rattle of a proud Imperial world and the victorious warcry of its alien conquerors.
The Orks live only to wage unending war, and know it is only a matter of time before the Imperial war machine responds to their invasion."
You begin as a commander of a group of Space Marines battling against Ork hordes.
I like the story personally, it's similar to many of the older titles developed
by other companies but it still feels like a part of the universe
GAMEPLAY
Gameplay is obviously influenced heavily by Chess, You have weak pawn units and
strong but weak King/Queen units. If the King is taken it's a victory/checkmate.
Each campaign mission can feature varied side objectives and main objectives,
such as "capture all enemy pawns" or "Have your knight reach the objective".
I found myself getting bored of the repetitive gameplay after a while but stayed
for the great story and dialogue between missions. Each turn you can move
one unit (piece) or if an enemy is close enough you can also instantly kill the enemy
during the movement phase then comes the initiative phase, where you
can choose which unit abilities to use, for example, the Librarian unit
can use life leech to steal health from an enemy unit to replenish his own.
Even tho it seems nearly identical to chess you can play it as if it were a turn based game.
When you move onto an enemy occupied title it will activate a "Killcam" a fancy cutscene showing your unit slaughtering
(or being slaughtered by) an enemy unit.
I found the tutorial extremely helpful and managed to pick up the gameplay
really easily.
GRAPHICS/TECHNICAL DETAILS
The graphics are similar to most of the 40K games but aren't bad by any means.
Textures appear sharp and clear, environments are somewhat bland as to keep the chessboard
appearance. I noticed the occasional missing special effects, such as when certain units fire their weapon,
the muzzle flash fails to appear. I kept a constant framerate and didn't notice any slow downs,
even during action sequences. Load times appear to be nearly instantaneous.
SOUND
Overall sound quality is fantastic, the developers really put a lot of work into the sound effects,
voice acting is top notch and really give the marines and Ork their well-known personalities.
Weapon effects are great and you can hear iconic weapon sounds from many forms of 40K media,
characters speak and react to their actions and the actions of the enemy.
The game features full English audio with subtitle & interface support for the following languages.
English
French
Italian
German
Spanish
MULTIPLAYER
Regicide features Multiplayer, Local Co-op and Cross-Platform Multiplayer
CONCLUSION
My final verdict is, it's worth the asking price for the amount of content you are getting,
the game is frequently updated, you can buy the game on steam for £10.99.
If you are a fan of Warhammer 40,000 you won't be disappointed.
PROS/CONS
+ Great CGI intro sets the mood
+ Good voice acting and music
+ Good graphics
+ Informative Tutorial
+ Dialogue scenes for each campaign mission
+ Well written campaign
+ Fantastic Killcams
+ Great environmental audio
- Repetitive gameplay

In the past, Wakfu was a terrible F2P MMO. All the business model cared for was money money money. Players weren't able to get in-game currency and you weren't able to leave the newbie area unless you were a subscriber to the game.
Now everything has changed. F2P players can go to the zones that subscribers were able to go to, and monsters drop in-game currency (in the past, the only way you were able to get money as a subscriber was by minting it.)
The only downside to this is that the in-game currency minting machines are almost obsolete now unless they revamp that system somehow to make money-minting more profitable than grinding. But in the past items were much more cheaper than they were due to the fact that money HAD to be minted to order to get money. Now everything is a lot more expensive.
Overall if you like games that play like FF Tactics or FF Tactics Advance for fighting, as well as games that have job professions, and a Havest Moon like open world where you are able to plant things that grow (even monsters,) try this game out.

Or the upper hand in a trinket wars, which is mutated team death match (great maps in this mode! trap ridden aztec temples, nordic strongholds etc). But, what really makes PVKII a must try, are the unique melee combat mechanics. You can block in 4 different directions, attack in 4 different directions and accumulate hitting power by holding down the attack button. Then there are class based special abilities, which can be used after dealing enough damage. Such as a two handed whirlwind attack, a bomb firing blunderbuss, or just berserker rage.
Adding the overall humorous scenario and custom made radio messages (they are just a blast!), PVK II is a great ride of fun. You like melee combat, or combating melee classes (no one likes archers though, especially with friendly fire on)?

This is the single / coop PVE version of AirMech Strike. The split came after developers realized it was becoming increasingly difficult to balance both PVE and the PVP. This oil and water division allows for both to grow separately in their own ecosystems without disturbing the other, offering a much more pure experience.
While still very early in its development, it's clear this is going to have a lot of content. Already there are a multitude of missions, survival maps, and four difficulties that be selected on the fly (after clearing the previous).
For the uninitiated, the game follows a small group of resistance fighters in a post-apocalyptic environment using huge transforming mechs, and a number of tanks and bots to help them. Currently, there are nine different 'AirMechs' to choose from, each filling a different battlefield role.
Gameplay currently revolves around two kinds of missions: destroy the fort and survival in a blend of RTS and MOBA that is both and neither. Creeps will regularly come from your base (the fortress) to capture nearby Outposts, but you must build units to help them. Capturing Outposts grants more upkeep, and you can make your way toward the end of the map and destroy the enemy fort. The enemy has their own mech and units that will try to stop your progress, and recapture lost Outposts.
Survival missions, as one might imagine, requires the player to defend their fort from a number of waves. Some don't allow you to build units to help with defenses, and you'll have to make do with limited resources.
In order to tackle higher difficulties, you'll need to level up your individual mechs and find parts that drop on the battlefield. Parts are a central part of mech progression. They can grant higher Airmech weapon DPS, armor, as well as unit build speeds and damage resistance. Every incremental bonus you acquire will help you clear harder missions.
The game is meant to be played online, so you'll need an internet connection. You'll see fellow Wastelands players flying around the overworld map and a global chat that is always active. Still, if you would rather play by your lonesome, there is a 'Do Not Disturb' button preventing others from inviting you to games.
One last feature worth mentioning is that inventories are shared between the two sister games. The unlocks you acquire in Wastelands will be there when you open Strike, and vice-versa. Items that do not apply to that game will be hidden. For example, Airmech parts have no use in the PVP-only Strike, and so are hidden in your inventory when you open Strike. Likewise, if you have a Drop Boost Cube, which increases the quality and frequency of after-game drops, have no use in Wastelands, and will be hidden when you open Wastelands.
In closing, yes it's early and there's a number of issues and features not yet implemented, but what is here is already a lot of fun, and I look forward to what this game will look like in another year.

Story 8.5: The Rook Islands are a great place to spend a vacation. It's beautiful, it's tropical, the beaches are nice, tons of murder...wait a second...dear God! That's not good at all! Well, Jason Brody and his friends did not hear take note of how terrifying this place is as they go on a skydiving trip only to be caught by a ♥♥♥♥ing amazing villain named Vaas Montenegro and his pirate crew. As the first one to escape, your job is to save your friends and take over the island. It's a great story with flawed and well developed characters. It even goes into some pretty uncomfortable territory later in the game. And Vaas. Oh my God Vaas! He's insane, he's diabolical, he's one of the best villains ever put in a video game! "Did I ever tell you the definition of insanity?" The only flaw I have with the story is its endings. There are 2 of them yet none of them left a good impression for me.
Visuals 9: The world of Far Cry 3 is beautiful! It's huge and is insanely detailed. From its lush vegetation to said vegetation getting caught on fire to the animals attacking each other! It all looks best at max settings. Though it's pretty demanding for a 2012 game and it does require a damn good card to render everything.
Audio 9.5: The music sets the mood for each scene and the characters are highlighted by outstanding performances. Michael Mando kills the show as Vaas!
Gameplay 9: The Far Cry games have always been about giving a large set of options for you to approach combat. Whether you go in guns blazing or choose the stealthier path (which it rewards you more for), the ways in which you encounter these situations is varied. The more mentally unstable Jason is, the more fun it is to play. Even more rewarding is exploration. There are numerous relics to collect, wildlife to hunt, and outposts to takeover.
Verdict: Far Cry 3 is one of the best games Ubisoft has ever released. Great Villain, great story, great everything! Even after the 20-30 hour story, I still have lots of stuff to do!

-Varied Combat
-Beautiful World
-Great Story
-Vaas. Just Vaas.

I have been playing this game for years, and played Dofus before it. My review will be based on how I think it will be for new players, and in light comparison to their previous installment to the franchise. It should be noted however I played during their subscribtion fee era and have recently returned. For those of you who don't know this game takes place many years after Dofus, another similar turn based strategy MMORPG by Ankama.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
First off, it's free-to-play. They removed their subscribtion fee half a year ago. Great business decision if I do say so myself. This should be stressed to veteran players! Come back and check the game out again, the reason why you left is no longer existent!
(There isn't many pay-to-win elements. There are certain spiritual weapons you can buy if I recall that level up with you and the more they level up the stronger they get. Think heirlooms from World of Warcraft, but you can sell them. And weapons you get along the way can compare relatively closely to it, and end game even surpass them. You can also buy booster packs to boost your XP gain and such. But there's no obnoxious sets of gear that you can buy to trample over other players with. No, none of that. Just a bunch of cosmetics!)
We'll start with appearance. Graphically speaking this game emphasizes their anime style. If you don't like anime, you probably won't like how this game looks. Luckily, it handles on just about any potatoe laptop on the lowest of settings, so unless you're rocking a 1GB of RAM notebook, you should be able to run it.
The UI is very easy to learn, they have a great 10-15 minute tutorial (which you actually get free levels from, so I'd do it anyway) which teaches you everything about the UI. Not many games do this, they generally throw you to the wolves. AND THE TUTORIAL IS -OPTIONAL-! YES, YOU HEARD ME, -OPTIONAL TUTORIAL-.
In terms of actual gameplay you have various strategy elements from the economy, ecosystem to their turn based combat. The combat doesn't pick up until later levels however; expect a bit of a grind to get to the good stuff as per any MMORPG. I personally love the gameplay over Dofus' as the world of Wakfu feels much more alive and interactable. It's definitely good fun with a group of friends. I mean, there are 16 unique and quirky classes to choose from. -16-! Though they have a lack of races to choose from (your race depends on the class you pick) and character customization, you're sure to find something you like. Only one class is gender specific, but... it's not exactly a gender at all.
The other side of the gameplay is the political aspect. You can literally be elected to lead your nation of players and make executive decisions and create your government. Or you can take a step back and just place your valuable vote in!
So if the graphics catch your eye and the gameplay piques your interest this is definitely something to check out. Wakfu is very friendly to the casual players just as they are the hardcore players. They often give out free gifts to enlighten your experience if they make a mistake or something. I highly recommend joining a guild or playing with friends however; the world isn't as flourishing as it once was (which is why I'm making this review) and it can be pretty lonely leveling up without company!
If you really get into the game and immerse yourself you might find  some of these other few activities interesting; they have their own anime series that takes place in Wakfu, I mean, it's called Wakfu. (I believe there's 2 seasons? Maybe 3 now? It's really good even if you don't play Wakfu) and not only IN-GAME but in real life they have their Krosmaster board game which you can play. A bit pricey in real life, but, in-game throughout your adventures you will loot characters for it which you can collect, sell, trade, and play with!
Overall rating; 7/10. I would rate it higher if there were as many players as their used to be, the points are deducted because it took them that long to realize they couldn't do a subscribtion fee. And their UI changes bug me but that's my own personal preference and shouldn't effect the new player.
A  lot of bugs, a lot of unfinished features and content, a lot of grind. Still a good game.

Not really sure why there are so many negative reviews towards this game. I own both DiRT Rally and Dirt 4 and love  them both. There are many things about DiRT Rally that could be better that were improved on in DiRT 4 but DiRT 4 is obviously not perfect. Yes there could be more locations, and the physics do feel a bit different than DiRT Rally. It is almost impossible to judge what feels realistic unless you've actually driven one of these race cars IRL. They had actual rally drivers play the game to help make the gameplay as authentic as possible. It also depends on what peripherals and settings you are using that can drastically change the gameplay, for better or worse, depening on your knowledge and skill. The game is not perfect but it is a step forward to creating the perfect racing simulation game. I have confidence in codemasters to keep improving on what they got right and whay they didn't.
Positives:
+ Gameplay/Physics
+ Character development
+ Driving tutorials and Challenges
+ Team Creation & Customization
+ Free roam course
+ Stage customization
+ Branding Suite (car and sponsor design and settings)
+ Huge selection of modern and historic rally cars
+ Gorgeous graphics
+ Informational videos (how WRC, WRX, Landrush works)
Negatives & Suggestions:
+ Free roam course gets boring, would like to see more courses or customizable ones in the future
+ Hard to find multiplayer games
+ Driving physics could be improved to feel even more realistic (even in simulation mode)
+ More locations to race
+ More car customization

Verdict: 5.5 out of 10  Buy only when on sale, if your a newb to sim racers, or already have DiRT Rally and DiRT 3, if not, buy DiRT Rally first. It may look like there is plenty to do in this game, but Codemasters have pretty much abandonded it, and mystage luls after the first few playthroughs. Rallycross is solid, just it could've been an update to DiRT Rally instead of a whole new game.
There's so much this game does right, and a lot it does wrong. The rally sections, while on the surface, look and feel similar to DiRT Rally's efforts, they don't quite deliver on their promises. Yes, you still have the fantastic co-driver audio, yes it is still way more challenging than DiRT 3, but even with a few subtle positive improvements to handling, the cars just feel off. My stage is an interesting but poorly executed idea. The RallyCross is the only mode that feels fully developed, but there are so few changes there it literally could have just been an update for the rallycross in DiRT Rally.
I will give it to Codemasters, the tarmac physics is improved, but the gravel physics is just bland now. The cars feel heavier, but feeling of weight transfer is no longer there. It won't accidentally fling you 20ft in the air because of a miniscule bump in the road like in DR, but any attempts at throwing the weight of the car to help in a corner is nearly fruitless. Scandinavian flicks are nearly useless in this game, which is frustrating because it's one of the few techniques you could reliably use to fight understeer prone handling in DiRT Rally. On the topic of understeer, there is a lot of it. The FWD cars actually behave like you'd expect, but the AWD cars are more understeer prone than the FWD cars. The only exception to this is the Rallycross cars, R5 rally class, the N4 Sub when tuned for almost no rear grip and insane diff settings, and a few RWD cars. Group A cars were so lovely and easy to understand in DiRT Rally, in DiRT 4 they are bland, dull, and lifeless. Yes DiRT Rally may have not been 100% realistic, but it's sad when I can't power oversteer a purpose built rally machine with a 70% rear bias and locked diff in this game, but I can power oversteer my 240hp front biased AWD sedan on gravel IRL. For Pete's sake, I can do scandinavian flicks in my front biased AWD sedan easier than in DiRT 4. Forget using lateral forces to help through corners, just use a basic racing lines for everything except hairpins and the occasional 1 or 2.
On to MyStage, I commend their efforts, and it's an interesting practicing tool, but it doesn't make fresh stages. After one medium length stage, you've experienced everything each location has to offer. Anything from that point forward is a random shuffled copy paste of what came before. It wouldn't be so bad if they just added more tiles/environments to the stage creator, but at this point Codies have nearly abandoned the game one month after release. All this leaves me thinking that this could have just worked better as a DLC for DiRT Rally. There are only two stages I really think are great from here are Sweden and Spain. Even at that, though, Monaco from DR was a significantly more interesting location than Spain, the tarmac physics just needed tweaks. Mystage just feels like an unfinished concept that was pushed out way too early. I would've been fine waiting a little longer for an improved stage creator.
And spurring off from mystage is singleplayer AI, which is probably one of the most broken things about this game. It swings from completely incompetent, in impossibly fast depending on what level of engineers you have in your team in SP and how straight of a section mystage decided to create. With the highest AI difficulty on most sectors I could stomp the AI, until I hit flat out straights, to which the AI would inexplicably gain anywhere from 3-20 seconds out of nowhere. In the corners I would then proceed to beat the ai by 3-10 seconds a sector. You can win all but the last sector by several seconds and lose for no reason becasue the AI decides to just gain 20 seconds on a 35 second sector, putting the average pace of the AI car beyond the car class' top speed. The math on these is completely broken. Your stage times don't matter in SP, just don't crash and take whatever broken mess mystage hands you. There is no incentive to push, you either beat the AI or magically lose for no reason. If you want a consistent metric of how your stage times are, just play the community events.
Community events are the only area where mystage does give an advantage to this game over DiRT Rally. At least you can't practice the exact stages ahead of time. They still give much more of a challenge and thrill over the singleplayer simply because you can't restart and the pressure is on. The best moments I've had with the rally sections were just doing the Daily/Weekly events. There is nothing like the feeling of pushing the car right to the edge and almost bailing, only to pull it back in the last second and still put in a fast time. When you do well here, it feels so rewarding, and when you crash you learn a lot about staying cool under pressure.
I will say, I did like the Joyride mode even with sim handling and a wheel and pedals setup. It is nice to have someplace to practice and just goof off with the cars, and smash attack and time attack actually are closer to real Gymkhana events than the previous Gymkhana attempts in DiRT 3. Even though I put more time into the rally stages, I do appreciate this mode.
Last and certainly least... landrush... It's the same as with DiRT 3, but with slightly different vehicles, and slighlty more challenging handling. Although Codies improved the AI in rallycross from DR (the AI doesn't go all kamikaze on everyone when it takes a joker now) the crazy lack of situational awareness from DR's rallycross AI has been transplanted into landrush. The cars are fun to hoon around the track alone, but the AI would rather flip your car then actually win the race. That may be fine with closed wheel trucks, but with open wheel vehicles, bumping is bad news.
Overall verdict:
Is there a lot of stuff to entertain a racing fan for a while in this game? Yes.
Is it an improvement from DiRT 3? yes.
Is it an improvement from DiRT Rally? Maybe on a few small things, but in most areas this is a significant step backwards from DR.
If DiRT Rally didn't exist would I think higher of this game than I do? Absolutely. I know they claimed it would mix DiRT Rally and DiRT 3, but honestly they marketed this more as an improvement to DiRT Rally, but this game is nowhere near as well executed. DiRT Rally wasn't perfect, there were still some weird quirks, but it did so much right. The core rally experience was brutal, thrilling, unforgiving, yet totally justifiable in it's difficulty. DiRT 4 is just, stubborn, boring, frustrating (from an AI standpoint), and blandly predictable. Yes, the core gameplay that made DiRT Rally so fun and challenging exists to an extent in DiRT 4, it just doesn't have the staying power that DiRT Rally did.
Honestly put, DiRT 4 doesn't scare me like DiRT Rally did, it may have a million "unique stages" but everystage is made up of the handful of corners you've already seen thousands of times. The order is different, but you are never surprised, nervous, or scared to go fast. If you play with gamer handling, you probably won't notice the difference enought to care. If you've never played DiRT Rally, you probably won't notice the difference enough to care. But, if you loved DiRT Rally and just wanted some more, this is it, just not as good. With that, I leave you with two random stages in DiRT Rally, that no stage I've played in DiRT 4 comes close to even being near as fun, interesting, or challenging.
