UPDATE November 2017, version 1.09:
A lot has happened in the last two years of my original review (see below). But superficial only.
- All maps are way way better than before! So much better!
- More gear (field medics) and vehicles (planes, cars, tanks) round up the "tech"tree.
- More individualization options (uniforms, helmets, skins), but still not very far in this regards although many other companies have learned that cosmetic upgrades make money without interfering with the balance.
- Constant Terrible Balance! Due to an overpopulated faction (AXIS) the designers decided to hammer all weapons and equipment of said faction into the ground, hoping to achieve that players switch to /start with factions which offer superior gear.
But as a consequence the by far most number of players are constantly annoyed and feel bullied by the Devs. Great thinking...
- The General part is completly redundant unless one plays the most underpopulated faction (Russia), which benefits from superior gear and insane bonuses (based on population difference).
- Devs don't found any ways to master their own creation, compare with my review from over 2 years ago below!
ORIGINAL review:
Now some patches after introducing the Sowjet faction! (this is a pre-Walker, July 2015, build review, I edit when I notice considerable changes from what I pointed out below)
A game set in WW2 that appears to be as a dynamic, gamebalance-first, capture the point mission, fast-paced Arcade game, with sufficient historic assemblage (>Heroes). On top, there is real time strategy part, where you move your troops on the map and then zoom into the FPS battles (> Generals).
Sounds nice so far, that's why it attracted me in the first place.
There is a bit of overdramatizing following, but more than just the essence is true:
But the developer, despite claiming otherwise, extremly favors 1 hit kill Infantry camping play style, making the game a spawncamp game. No matter if you have a non-sniper class, just grab the >sniper< Bolt Action rifle and camp, preferably at the opponent spawnpoints.
The developer appears helpless of his own creation, finds no other way to balance his game towards his aim to have defenders win about 60% of the matches, resulting in frustrating gameplay.
Enemies kill you at sight (although there is an Arcade lifepoint system) and your own men prefer to sit in the woods as well, believe they are heavenly snipers and don't care about defending the cap points, taking or retaking them; mission objectives are failed. Not so dynamic... It's not the players' fault, they just accept what the designer offers.
To play it on some decent level at least you need to grind and the grind/farm factor for key items is ... well, let's say you have to spend a lot of money (€, $, etc.) instead.
The strategy part is out of balance due to the issue of an underpopulated faction, making the whole Generals part for the most populated faction a pain in the ***: German troops can easily stay 1-2 days (!) in the waiting queue while Soviet faction immediately deploys...

Pre-face:
I received this game for having silver status in the original airmech, meaning that I bought some packs for that. So I didn't functually got this game for free, and thus I will not mark this review as such.
Ok.
It looks and plays like an indie game from 2012 because it essentially is.
Originally Airmech was supposed to end up as fully featured game containing both singleplayer story-driven campaign and multiplayer PvP mode.
Except it only had PvP mode for years. I played it for a bit, but left because I just don't play arena games. I can't even say if it was good or bad.
Fast forward 5 years promised singleplayer content is finally released as a stand alone game, which is also given to all who has silver or higher status in the PvP version. Which I think is good decision for both new and veteran players.
Game itself is a spiritual successor to Sega Mega Drive/Genesis action-RTS hybrid called "Herzog Zwei".
You control a humanoid mech that can transform into air craft and carry your units around the place. You can give your units order and directions, but you only have total control over your own commander mech.
This particular game adds RPG elements to the formula so you can find better gear for your mech and upgrade it.
There are different mechs with different abilities.
There A LOT of different units too.
Game is not open world, it is played on mission-by-mission basis, but you can also replay previous missions for extra grinding if you want it.
There are microtransactions, but from what I understand they are purely cosmetic or only affect Airmech Strike, which is a separate game.
So far gameplay is exactly the same as Airmech, meaning good if a bit simplistic, but is a positive thing for me.
Graphics are undoubtedly dated, which they try to hide with cartoony art style. I don't care much about visuals, but its age shows. It's really a game from 2012.
I say play Strike to feel the controls and see visuals, as it can serve as decent demo for what Wastelands provide.

It's Left 4 Dead with an actual progression system and customizable loadout that works. You feel rewarded doing tougher missions, and getting a super-powerful item is a heavenly feeling, especially after a really tough run.
PROS-
1. 5 classes that function differently, but no group feels especially weak for lacking a certain teammate. While the Bright Wizard is certainly helpful against hordes and high-armor targets, I never felt like the team was screwed by their absence.
2. Weapons that actually feel good. Hammers make excellent, meaty crunches, imploding skaven skulls, while a Zweihander cuts the ratmen in half, letting the legs stumble about before falling. I'd say there's a character and loadout for everyone, and each person plays it differently.
3. The loot roll system's got its good points and its bad points, but the fun of rolling a big♥♥♥♥♥handful of hard earned dice feels awesome, and watching them all come up sixes feels even better. Do you risk losing the mission by reducing everyone's max health, for higher rewards should you succeed? Or should you play it safe, and risk getting worse loot for your success?
4. The skaven come in excellent waves, much like the zombies in left 4 dead, but ever-so-slightly smarter. The skaven specialists all feel different, and each one feels almost like a mini-boss rather than a run-of-the-mill skaven with a fancy hat. You will learn to fear Stormvermin, and the sound of their march.
CONS-
1. There's no way to get a specific weapon, no matter how much you want it. You can pray to the altar to try to create one, but the random factor is high, and you also have to melt down a significant number of other items to get the chunks necessary for the prayer. Everything's randomized, and even a high loot roll can be dissapointing when you end up getting YET ANOTHER mace and shield for the Sargeant, instead of a bow for your Waywatcher. Even when you get items you want, the perks the rare items have are also randomized, meaning that you could end up with extra zoom on your shotgun, or extra-strength block on your two-handed axe. Joy.
2. The game's quite lonely without friends. If you aren't chatting away with your teammates, you'll notice the difference because the bots are incredibly stupid, and easily tricked by the skaven. Bots will always run and hide at the sound of a Ratling Gunner, even when you're bleeding out on the floor and easily picked back up without getting into harm's way.
3. The player-search is a little weak. Nothing that I found experience-ruining, but I often found myself waiting 5-10 minutes trying to find players for my game. Since there's no real lobby system, you just have to pray the matchmaking finds you teammates to join up with.
TL;DR: This game is everything I wanted from Left 4 Dead. Strong replayability, great progression, good map layout, varied misisons, cool skaven mini-bosses, and more. All the game's best aspects shine even brighter when playing with friends, so grab a buddy before you get the game, or share a copy if you're rich as hell. Any problems I've had with the game are either really minor, or easily fixed in the future by Fatshark.
Have fun skavenslaying, and remember, you're together to the end.

Hydrophobia is a puzzle/action/platformer akin to games like Tomb Raider, Prince of Persia, Legacy of Kain and countless other titles that we have probably played at one point or another. It's extremely atmospheric and it's got great visualizations (particularly the water effect- no kidding, right?) and sound. Here's the break down:
THE GOOD: Stuff I liked.
1. The Water
The water is, as the name implies, the cornerstone of this game. It is the reason for the game's interesting atmosphere and environment based puzzles. The physics, graphics and visualizations (movement of waves, transition from surface to underwater, water on camera, etc) are superb. Best water effects I've seen in a game. Period.
2. The Environment Interaction/ Movement
I really enjoyed the layout of the levels and their design in general. There was a decent mix of swimming and climbing, giving each zone a level of depth that I don't often notice in other games (save for some of the ones I mentioned previously). Or maybe it's just because I was actually able to interact with it to such a high degree that made it interesting. This includes shooting out glass doors, blasting through bulkheads and raising the ambient water level. Very cool experience.
3. NAVI Mechanic
I really enjoyed the NAVI mechanic. The protagonist comes equipped with a transparent PDA gadget that acts as your GUI in the game, keeping all your notes, grants access to your in game menus, highlights secret messages in the game and enables you to do all your non-combat trickery (hacking, opening doors, etc).
4. PRICE!!! $$$!!
I think I bought the game on sale for $0.50? So in the end it was money well spent. ^_^
The BAD: Stuff that was 'Meh.'
1, Clunky Movement
So, while you can do all this neat stuff like roll, climb, swim and cling to cover... the controls felt somewhat unresponsive. Often I'd lose the ability to shoot around cover and have to back off and re-cling to get it working again. Likewise, occasionally the game would ignore a command to dive, roll, or jump. The fact that it occurred sporadically made it that much more of an aggravation when these missed commands would pop up... particularly in a heated, combat situation!
2. *Occasional* Camera Angles from Hell
Again, these didn't happen very often but when they did it was really difficult to get out of them. It most often happened while swimming and most usually in tight corridors. Of course, this is typically a problem of any game with a high degree of mobility in a given environment.
3. Backtracking
I don't mind a whole lot of backtracking personally. Given the NAVI's ability to help you perceive new things in the environment and the changing level of water, I'd rank this game about equal with such games as Legacy of Kain and Chrono Trigger. OF COURSE, there's backtracking... the designers want to show you how a place has changed. So I don't think it's a problem, but a lot of other reviews did.
4. 'Easy' Combat...?
I played the game on Normal mode and died a total of 2 (maybe 3?) times while in combat. The badguy AI is fairly responsive in my opinion: when you don't shoot at it, they sneak closer to you. When you do, they scramble for cover. They try to flank you, etc, etc. They don't do any of this quickly, but they do it. They also deal enough damage that you can't go barreling in guns blazing very often either.
But, if you're like me and you rock the sneaky/cautious/clever game style, you'll probably breeze through the game since there's ample opportunity for you to use environmental hazards to your advantage. This is NOT Call of Duty, Counterstrike, or anything resembling a "real" shooter. It just happens you can shoot things.
5. Voice Acting
I've seen a lot of bad reviews because of voice acting... but honestly, I've heard a LOT worse (none come to mind this instant, but we've all heard worse). Plus, there's not a whole lot of it. I actually think the worst voice acting comes mainly from the protagonist (which is unfortunate) because I thought the acting of the antagonist and your plucky tech support ally were decent enough (if not reading from a very unimaginative script).
THE UGLY: Stuff that's unforgivable (imho).
In order,
1. Repetitive game play and goals.
The whole game is about finding keys to locked doors, almost without exception. This sucks. I'm just glad the environment was fun to navigate to make me forget that this was all I was doing. Blah.
2. Very few upgrades/collectables/etc.
You pick up about 3 'new' abilities that you use sporadically throughout the game. There was also about 6 different types of ammo you could collect... but you really never needed it until the end of the game. This is one extremely crucial difference between this game and the likes Legacy of Kain and Prince of Persia (also games like Metroid, Castlevania and Megaman)… you never really feel like your power level advances.
3. INCREDIBLY SHORT GAME!
Overall, if you can snag this game for less than the price of a bottle soda at the gas station AND have a few hours to kill, you may as well pry what fleeting joy you can from it’s very beautiful, if somewhat flawed and arthritic fingers.

Boson X is a 3D endless-runner. You have to go through 18 levels (3 worlds, 6 levels in each) with 3 different characters (only for the skin, you do not have different skills). In order to win, you have to discover particles by running and jumping (left, ahead or right) on blue tiles and reach 100%. The more you stay on a blue tile, the faster you increase your %. It does not matter how long it takes you, as long as you stay alive and reach 100% without dying.
About dying, it is going to happen a lot : you have to die again and again to get better and finally complete a level. Do not be afraid, this is how this game works. You will get an achievement for each completed level, but the difficulty is increasing after each level, and it becomes quite challenging quickly (I must confess that this is my first endless-runner).
To conclude, this is a pretty good and fun game, plus a challenging one ! If you like this kind of game, do not hesitate, at the current price (2,99€), you should buy it :)

DiRT 4 a game with an extremely divided fanbase, a fanbase that doesn't know what it wants and criticizes a perfectly coherent and well made product.
DiRT 4 is a rally racing game that comes from a line of triple A, top quality predecessors and this game is no different. I am ashamed of the sheer amount of negative reviews for DiRT 4 knowing that Codemasters delivered exactly what they promised. Just to be clear,
This game is in a sweet-spot between arcade racing and hardcore rally simulation. It's a perfect start for players that are new to the series and a very respectful nod to us older, more experienced players.
The cars handle beautifully and each one feels different in a good way, it shows the level of detail and effort Codemasters put in to the game. The sound design is phenomenal, the developers always manage to have the perfect audio both inside and outside of the vehicle. You can hear the turbos whistle, the Anti-Lag systems explode, the terrain rumble underneath your car, etc. you hear everything as if you were actually there. The physics in DiRT 4 are in that sweet-spot I mentioned earlier. The user interface is gorgeous and the soundtrack is unmatched (in the racing genre).This game is best played at higher difficulties to really get the most out of your rallying experience, but be aware that there is a learning curve.
The graphics are marvelous and it doesn't take a high-end PC to get good levels of detail and FPS.
DiRT 4 plays well for both singleplayer and multiplayer and it's up to the community to maintain the multiplayer aspect (regarding playercount) by playing the game and supporting Codemasters.

As someone who has spent many hours with both MMO's and Tactical RPG's, this was a pleasant find.
I spent many years playing WoW, Star Wars:TOR, and DCU, but I had come to find myself tired of the formula that MMO's had fallen into. I had basically given up on the genre, as there is very little variation beyond setting. When I saw Wakfu on Steam for the first time, I overlooked it. The artwork was not my favorite, and the name of the game itself didn't draw me in at all. It wasn't until a few days later that I was looking through the games again that I decided to look closer.
What I saw reminded me of when I'd spend hours at a time playing one of my favorite games of all time, Final Fantasy Tactics. Most Tactical RPG's do that to me, as their style is so distinct in comparison to other genres. The grid on the floor is a dead give away to any one remotely familiar with the genre. Armed with some nostalgic goggles, I dove deeper in to the game Wakfu.
Wakfu is a mix of Tactical RPG combat, with MMORPG sprinkles to top things off while you're not in battle. You'll find your usual culprits; Proffessions split into gathering and crafting, Taxi locations for fast travel, an Auction House in the form of a "market", and Mounts and Costumes to show off how cool you are, just to name a few of the things you'll recognize from the MMO genre. Most of the activities within the game are easily recognized standards that even people who have only played something like Minecraft should be able to pick up quickly. It also tries to do it's own things, like a completely player run government, and an eco system than can give bonuses if its in a good shape.
The battle system is also pretty standard as far as Tactical RPG's go. Veterans will be able to pick up the battle system quickly, as soon as they understand the some times confusing tool tips for their spells. Combat takes place on a field created when you start the fight with monsters in the world. Each participant is put in order based off their "Initiative" stat. The batle then goes by in turns. Each combatant is restricted by how many tiles on the grid they can move, how far their spells can hit, and how much those spells cost. Of course this sounds simple, but like any great Tactical RPG, there is a lot of depth in this simplistic system, than can only be found out the longer you play. The classes range from simple to complex. RPG veterans will be able to pick up classes like Cra, Osamodas, and Sram, and easily identify them as your typical Archer, Summoner, Assassin. Then they will look at classes like Feca and Foggernaut, and scratch their head a bit. What you'll find seems to be missing is the quests. After storming through the opening area-Astrub-you'll be left to your own devices. Sure there are quests you can do, but they can be hard to find, since there is no mini map, and no indication of who gives you these quests. This can make leveling very unfocused until you learn how to recognize where these quests will be.
Wakfu has a very light hearted atmosphere. Jokes are common in dialogue and most of them worth a chuckle, especially once you start to understand the games lore. Enemies have idle animations and will use in game emotes, that allow them to be their own characters rather than just another random creature for you to mow down. The artistic design fits well, its very animated and colorful, adding more life to the world they've created. For those really enjoying the Wakfu setting, theres even an Anime now, allowing you to see the world in a more cinematic presentation.
Unfortunately, the Music and Sound is lacking here. The sounds can get downright repetitive and annoying. You'll know what I'm talking about when you experience being stuck loading up your character select screen and you hear those cogs for 10 minutes straight, or someone is spamming emotes near you. The music on the other hand, is just all together forgetable. I couldn't tell you what one song on this game sounds like, because none of them are memorable at all.
The other strike against this game, is how much is locked behind a paywall. The game itself is free, but there is a lot that you have to pay for, that I don't think you should. For one, the mounts. You can get a mount in game for free, but its terrible. If you want a good one, you gotta pay. The other thing, is many costumes and emotes are up for purchase. Costumes I might understand, Vanity items are often sold in free games, but why emotes? Most games let you have all emotes from the start, but this one forces you to unlock them. Or in some cases, buying them is the only way to get them. Its not all bad, some of the things offered in the shop are very good, and I understand why you must pay for things like Nation Changes, or Class changes, even if they are over priced in my opinion.
While I recognize this game wont be for everyone, it is for me. The blend of an MMO and Tactical RPG is right up my alley, but I'd say you probably have to enjoy Tactical RPG's more than MMORPG's. I could easily see fans of Ogre Tactics, Disgea and Final Fantasy Tactics enjoying this, but if you find yourself more of a WoW, Rift, or Old Republic fan, you might find this is an overly simplified version. If you're relatively new to either genre, this is a great place to start.

I wanted to like this game. Sadly it's something that probably looks good on paper but is not as fun as you'd hope for. Regicide mode makes the game of chess so much slower than it has to be through initially fun though eventually slow animations. The UI is buggy with a particularly large number of problems with cursor raytracing. I've seen my king attempt a melee attack but miss with 100% hit-chance. The regicide abilities make winning a game almost more chance than skill. There is a mode to play conventional chess though you'll soon be wishing you had a simplistic chess game minus the unskippable animations and without cluttered/confusing view of the game. So the conventional chess mode is more annoying than a free online chess alternatives, and Regicide will only ever annoy you with its chance-based ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The raw-chess mode might be more fin if devs can patch up some of the more annoying bugs, optimise code that causes the obscene loading times, and make gameplay much more fast-paced. The regicide-mode could only be improved my making all chances to miss <5% and drastically lowering the damage being dealt by all units.

Honestly I was very disapointed in the game overall.  The death animations are cool for a bit, but they grow tiresome quickly as there aren't all that many, with most of them just being shooting bullets till the enemy falls or explodes.  The graphics are alright, but not particularly impressive, especially considering how feel animations they seem to have.  The animations are also painfully slow.  Luckily you can skip watching the devistator trooper lumber along for 30 seconds to get from one side of the map to the other, but the fact that you would need to skip it in the first place is a telling sign.
The abilities are an interesting twist on the classic chess, but ultimately most people like chess because it is a game of absolute strategy, no luck involved, and the abilities throw in a massive dose of luck.  Kudos for shaking up the normal strategies by adding abilities, but less props for doing it by introducing random luck into the game.
Perhaps one of the biggest downfalls of the game is how terrible some of the UI and general information on the game is.  Finding out exactly what an ability does, how likely it is to work, how far you can use it from, and so on is nearly impossible.  You can't even see what an ability does or how to use it, unless you can actually use it.  Want to know how far your troopers can shoot before you move them into position?  Hope you've memorized it.  Want to take a quick glance at what an ability does? Hope you're in range to use it, because the ability won't even show its name unless it is available, in range, and use conditions are met.
Similarly, there is virtually no documentation on what any of the stats mean.  Strength seems to mean how much damage a unit does, and might somehow be reduced by toughness, but I'm not entirely sure, as no where in the game or the 'manuel' (which only lists half the units, and is poorly laid out where there isn't simply a void of information) is any sort of explanation given as to what the stats do.  In one fight for example, my armor kept getting ignored by the enemy shootas.  No idea why.  Nothing in the manual indicated it should be happening unless they were using psychic attacks.  I don't think ork bullets are psychic weapons, but I could be wrong.  I have no way to check anything after all, since getting information from the game is like prying teeth.
These last bits give the game a very 'lets rush out something with Warhammer 40k slapped on it for some quick cash' feel.  I think it recently got out of early access, and it seems like it could have used another week or two there to do some polishing on little things like a manual and proper UI.
Overall I don't think it is a game that chess people will like, because the animations are slow, the additions are luck based (though there is a classic option that removes them), and the space marines theme isn't likely to appeal to them.  I don't think it's something Warhammer 40k people will like because it is chess with fancy figures.  If you happen to like both, it might be a decent buy, but I'm very fond of both, and feel there are much better places to get my dose of 40k and of chess.  I don't need to get them together.

This game has recieved a lot of flack recently. There are those who say it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized what made Adventure 1 great, those who say all the playstyles that aren't Sonic are trash and so forth. I believe that this is one of the best Sonic games out there, and I didn't even play this game as a kid. I STARTED with Generations
First off, the story might seem cheesy these days but for the time it was quite unique and impressive for a 3D platformer to have. Adventure 1 technically beat it with getting that achievement first, but Adventure 2 improves on the now horribly dated cutscenes from the original. The audio mixing is pretty bad, however, and makes it hard to hear the characters a lot of the time. It's a minor nitpick, but the sound mixing is probably the worst part of this game.
As you all probably know the game is split into three playstyles; Speed, Treasure Hunting and Mech Shooting. I won't go in deep analyzing these but to summarize: All speed stages are great except for maybe Final Chase if you're not careful, most of the Treasure Hunting stages are open or small enough to let you explore them quickly and makes the nerfed radar from SA1 a minor issue with the exception of Death Chamber and Mad Space, both of which are simply too confusing for their own right. Finally, almost every single Mech Shooting level with Tails is awful while the Eggman levels are simply mindless fun most of the time, except for Sand Ocean which is a bit heavy on careful platforming and can be hard since you don't have the hover yet.
Finally, what really sells this game for me is the replayability. Let's list off the things you can do in the game, shall we?
-Beat the Hero story
-Beat the Dark story
-Beat the Last story
-Replay the stages to get better times
-Play 5 missions on every single one of the 32 stages and get the highest ranks on all of them
-Raise your chao into either a hero or dark chao and pit them in combat or races against other chao
-Play the multiplayer with all three+Cars playstyles, including online play if you use mods (Requires Hamachi!)
-Check up on the online global leaderboard (mostly hackers and modders) or your local leaderboard of friends who own the game as well
-Write a way to olong review of the game you probably love after doing most of the above features.
That, and the game is just insanely fun. As someone who first played this game in 2016 and has heard nothing but negative reviews about it, I can say that it is one of my favorite Sonic games ever made.

While I used to love this game, I can't say the same after coming back to it several times. I don't write many serious reviews, but here are some reason you shouldn't play this game.
-Heavily focused on buying things with real money. While you are able to get some clothes / other accessories for free, its very limited and few cash items can be earned.
-Community is very small and limited. As this is a partly social game, it should be easy to socialize and make friends! However, this is not the case. If you are an english only speaker, this game is not for you. Many of the users don't speak English. As I mentioned, the community is small, and the very few people that do still play are AFK or in locked rooms, talking to friends. Very little "newbie welcoming" environments.
- Competition isn't nearly as fun anymore. This game used to be very focused on "fam battles", which are kind of like guilds fighting to those who are new to this genre. Fam battles were fun and an interesting way to get new members involved with bigger activities and meeting&making new friends.
-This game has had a problem from the beginning that to my knowledge, is still not resolved. Horrible, awful, people with no measurements being taken against them. The filter in this game is subpar and trolling is very easy to do. But that's not the issue, the issue is harrassment. Very often in this game are people (even creepos) harassing  other users, and no action is taken against them. This was the reason I quit the game several times, each time coming back hoping that the issue was resolved. You'd think, "Oh I'll just block that person and they can't do anything lol". That's not the case at all. iirc, blocking just prevents them from private messaging you and being on their friendlist. However, they can still view the rooms your in and follow you around. The community in this game used to be horrible, and hopefully it is different now.
I wanted to like this game, as I am a huge fan of the genre, but there's nothing but toxicity floating around this mess.

It's Left 4 Dead with an actual progression system and customizable loadout that works. You feel rewarded doing tougher missions, and getting a super-powerful item is a heavenly feeling, especially after a really tough run.
PROS-
1. 5 classes that function differently, but no group feels especially weak for lacking a certain teammate. While the Bright Wizard is certainly helpful against hordes and high-armor targets, I never felt like the team was screwed by their absence.
2. Weapons that actually feel good. Hammers make excellent, meaty crunches, imploding skaven skulls, while a Zweihander cuts the ratmen in half, letting the legs stumble about before falling. I'd say there's a character and loadout for everyone, and each person plays it differently.
3. The loot roll system's got its good points and its bad points, but the fun of rolling a big♥♥♥♥♥handful of hard earned dice feels awesome, and watching them all come up sixes feels even better. Do you risk losing the mission by reducing everyone's max health, for higher rewards should you succeed? Or should you play it safe, and risk getting worse loot for your success?
4. The skaven come in excellent waves, much like the zombies in left 4 dead, but ever-so-slightly smarter. The skaven specialists all feel different, and each one feels almost like a mini-boss rather than a run-of-the-mill skaven with a fancy hat. You will learn to fear Stormvermin, and the sound of their march.
CONS-
1. There's no way to get a specific weapon, no matter how much you want it. You can pray to the altar to try to create one, but the random factor is high, and you also have to melt down a significant number of other items to get the chunks necessary for the prayer. Everything's randomized, and even a high loot roll can be dissapointing when you end up getting YET ANOTHER mace and shield for the Sargeant, instead of a bow for your Waywatcher. Even when you get items you want, the perks the rare items have are also randomized, meaning that you could end up with extra zoom on your shotgun, or extra-strength block on your two-handed axe. Joy.
2. The game's quite lonely without friends. If you aren't chatting away with your teammates, you'll notice the difference because the bots are incredibly stupid, and easily tricked by the skaven. Bots will always run and hide at the sound of a Ratling Gunner, even when you're bleeding out on the floor and easily picked back up without getting into harm's way.
3. The player-search is a little weak. Nothing that I found experience-ruining, but I often found myself waiting 5-10 minutes trying to find players for my game. Since there's no real lobby system, you just have to pray the matchmaking finds you teammates to join up with.
TL;DR: This game is everything I wanted from Left 4 Dead. Strong replayability, great progression, good map layout, varied misisons, cool skaven mini-bosses, and more. All the game's best aspects shine even brighter when playing with friends, so grab a buddy before you get the game, or share a copy if you're rich as hell. Any problems I've had with the game are either really minor, or easily fixed in the future by Fatshark.
Have fun skavenslaying, and remember, you're together to the end.

With the 1980 release of Ace of Spades, Motörhead had their anthem of anthems -- that is, the title track -- the one trademark song that would summarize everything that made this early incarnation of the band so legendary, a song that would be blasted by legions of metalheads for generations on end. It's a legendary song, for sure, all two minutes and 49 bracing seconds of it. And the album of the same name is legendary as well, among Motörhead's all-time best, often considered their single best, in fact, along with Overkill. Ace of Spades was Motörhead's third great album in a row, following the 1979 releases of Overkill and Bomber, respectively. Those two albums have a lot in common with Ace of Spaces. The classic lineup -- Lemmy (bass and vocals), "Fast" Eddie Clarke (guitar), and "Philthy Animal" Taylor (drums) -- is still in place and sounding as alive and crazed as ever. The album is still rock-solid, boasting several superlative standouts. Actually, besides the especially high number of standouts on Ace of Spades -- at least relative to Bomber, which wasn't quite as strong overall as Overkill had been -- the only key difference between this 1980 album and its two 1979 predecessors is the producer, in this case Vic Maile. The result of his work isn't all that different from that of Jimmy Miller, the longtime Rolling Stones producer who had worked on Overkill and Bomber, but it's enough to give Ace of Spades a feeling distinct from its two very similar-sounding predecessors. This singular sound (still loud and in your face, rest assured), along with the exceptionally strong songwriting and the legendary stature of the title track, makes Ace of Spades the ideal Motörhead album if one were to choose one and only one studio album. It's highly debatable whether Ace of Spades is tops over the breakthrough Overkill, as the latter is more landmark because of its earlier release, and is somewhat rougher around the edges, too. Either way, Ace of Spades rightly deserves its legacy as a classic. There's no debating that.

Guess I should balance out my one review (positive, for Trails in the Sky) from the ~80 games Steam says I own with a negative counterpart.  Sadly.
On paper I liked the idea of this.  Basically, chess, with a shooting phase after moving a piece.  A chess-style capture is an automatic OHKO, while attacks gradually deplete HP on a unit (or multiple units with AOE abilities).  You have three initiative points per turn (which can roll over to later turns) to have units attack or use various unique abilities.  Terminators, which stand in for rooks, can generate a protective shield, tactical marines (pawns) have grenades, Librarians (queens) can heal themselves by stealing enemy HP, etc.  There are also global player abilities.
The dealbreaker for me here is that most attacks and abilities have a chance to hit, and the RNG is a steaming pile of AI-biased bantha poodoo.  Now, if you're about to tell me to "git gud" and "learn2turnbasedtactics", my response is that that is generally my line, so you KNOW it's bad.
Now, I COULD soldier on regardless, but I had no real motivation to:
Twenty missions into the 50-mission campaign, I have killed a lot of orks, including a weirdboy, and seized a communications relay.  I fought a warboss, but he got away, and the scout squad that got to the relay before us is dead.  There we go, summed up, by the numbers, 2/5 of the story for you. My squad is not persistent or customizable, no character has a personality, and although I'm supposedly the Blood Angels, there is nothing distinguishing me from generic space marines but one mention of the Red Thirst and the paint job.  Perhaps there's a shocking twist lurking.  I doubt it.
You might say this is irrelevant, since the real draw should be multiplayer.  Maybe, but I can't find any matches, literally zero.  Now, I freely admit this may be an issue on my end.  On any computer I've owned, some games just can't seem to do this.  The problem is, most DO, and I can't be bothered to search forums and forward ports and make firewall exceptions and a lot of other stuff that generally, speaking from experience, doesn't actually help when I could instead just play something that works out of the box.
Speaking of which, the last few other turn-based tactics games I played and liked that coincidentally address something I complained about above:
Invisible, Inc -- no chance-to-hit whatsoever, your agents and the enemy guards are perfect shots.  All about cover and thinking ahead.
The Banner Saga -- has a free, separate multiplayer mode, Factions, which has at the moment an extremely small community (probably will go up whenever TBS 2 releases and there's a new surge in interest) but at least, if there's a game to be found, it will be found.
Fire Emblem (pretty much the whole franchise) -- the Random Number Goddess reappears and smirks deviously at me, but I shall know no fear, for I am fear incarnate...or perhaps because here, unit stats change over time, weapons can be switched, and different terrain exists, meaning it's actually pretty easy to get a 100% or 0% that even she wouldn't lie about.  ALSO, there's actually characters and plot worth caring about even when I want to tableflip my emulator.
Hey, at least the animations are pretty cool, and from what I can tell the devs are too.  In fact, apparently they're considering removing the RNG.  Perhaps in time this review will become anachronistic.  Until then, if you want strategy play chess or something above; if you want to watch space marines stomping xenos skulls into the dirt, Dawn of War I & II and Space Marine exist.  I miss Relic...

This game includes two modes of chess: regicide & classic.
The regicide mode of chess is classic chess with a twist, and that twist is a complex of RNG (after moving, you're given the option to use abilities to damage opponent pieces or bolster your own), game board physical barriers (a wall or giant spikey fence on a square), 40k story elements (to arms, brothers!), and limited starting pieces (e.g., a game begins with three knights instead of the entire chess compliment). Chess classic is, well, the classic mode of chess.
I bought this game to play chess classic with neat looking 40k chess pieces, and I think it's a good game to play if you like chess. The AI is actually difficult to play against on higher difficulty settings. Most new to chess can probably start at intermediate. Regicide chess is an entertaining (and sometimes a RNG infuriating) bonus.
If you don't like chess, then you've not got any business buying this game. If you want a cheaper chess classic game without the bells and whistles Regicide provides, there's a free chess game on steam and a pretty good Amazon app called ChessGenius. So largely buy this if you enjoy 40k or want to play chess with a twist.

The Codemasters have been and are still the kings when it comes to the feeling and handling of your car. I've had a couple hours of fun with this game. What have stopped me playing however is the following:
The new random built level system is a good idea, but after you have played a while, it feels unnatural and you start to recognize sections that may even repeat several times throughout a single level.
The campaign is lacking in interesting content. You basically just choose a difficulty and you play through predetermined levels that which seems to have been created, even them, with the random level generator in the first place.
I like that they have tried adding a competitive mode to the game. However, it's executed poorly and feels rushed. They should try to get inspiration from other successful games (not racing games) how to make an interesting ranking system that keeps the player motivated to rank up. Seeing your division doesn't say anything and it's not motivating enough. They also should increase the number of players that can play simultaneously. The game starts before the lobby is full and players leaving mid game leaves you often with only you and someone else competing against eachother.
The navigation in the menus could be improved a lot.
For the next Dirt game, which I really hope will come out eventually, I hope they fix and improve all of the above and for good measure, add a level editor tool, so you can create tracks yourself and share with your friends.
It's a hard choice if I should recommend this game or not. I'd say if it's in the 30 eur range or below and you're into racing games, go for it!

It's almost like they developed this game way before Dirt Rally and released it after.  All of the things that make Dirt Rally great are tragically gone from this game.
After painstakingly perfecting my driving techniques in Dirt Rally, which felt completely natural with the physics engine behaving the way you would expect a real rally car to behave, I was expecting Dirt to continue my education and progression toward becoming a true rally car racer. To provide a little background.. I began playing Dirt Rally with Nvidia 3d Vision glasses and found the 3d immersion very helpful in getting a good feel for the road and the physics.  Then when I bought an HTC Vive and started playing it in VR (with the help of ReVive) my game was taken up several pegs and the experience was truly lifelike and thrilling.  Still the best VR game to this day.
Dirt 4 has NONE of those things.  Physics engine is broken with cars either being way too grippy on surfaces, or difficult to control with FFB not providing any useful information to the driver and the physics just way off.  Nvidia 3D vision is also severely broken in most of the stages with crazy artifacts or game crashes making it unplayable using it.  And NO VR support is there or being discussed by devs.
In summary all the things that made Dirt Rally feel real to drive are either absent or totally broken in Dirt 4.
To me it seems like Codemasters has turned there backs on the game and the community with this one and released a game that is a huge step backwards instead of being part of a progression toward perfection.  Truly a shame.

Dirt 4 is very good game, but it seems an ambitious project run out of time/budget to fulfill wath it takes to make a great rally game.
It will be a very long review because a lot of things need to be said and clarified; I've spent over 140 hours on it; I've played Dirt Rally and I’ve just had a brief test drive of WRC 7.
If you do not want to read the extended part, here is the bottom-line:
- If you want a basic driving experience with a good selection of tracks and
beautiful locations, but bad FFB  then get WRC7, it is also fairly priced
- If you want a full driving experience with very challenging tracks, amazing locations, great FFB and very good physics, but an awful career mode, then get Dirt Rally; it is still quite expensive but for good reasons
- If you want a full driving experience with an infinite selection of tracks, bad to good locations, great career mode, great FFB and excellent physics, but you are prepared to accept some flaws, then get Dirt 4; beware, at the current price tag (55 euros) is overpriced
Now the detailed review coming from a full sim experience with no assists.
Physics Engine
The physics engine is amazing. The level of detail of how suspensions reacts to even minimal surface variations if wonderful, accurate and consistent. The way wheels get and lose traction on the road is a fulfilling experience; breaking is believable and the traction model is wonderful (you feel the car getting gradual traction as you push the throttle pedal and you risk spinning if you push too hard) but can be very punitive. Weight management is finally here; cars have weight, meaning the bumps are realistic (cars do not fly as in DR) with credible tilt, and thre is inertia. The mai isue I see is the lack of slip at the back and too slippery tracks which makes harder to drift.
Force Feedback
Great. Combined with physic engine, the FFB provides every little nuance coming from the traction, the suspensions and the wheels. On the downside, in the FFB there are a couple of settings which I’m not sure they do what they are supposed to do.
Graphics
Graphic engine is excellent. The road has incredible detail, the effects (puddles, rain, fog, snow, dust) are amazing and lighting is the best in class. Despite that, the textures and the polygonal models of the trees are a bit too simplified and the colour palette is a bit too saturated, leading to an overall experience which is still very good but slightly below Dirt Rally level.
Sound
Sound is wonderful. Overall is on par with Dirt Rally with some additional fineness. Also, on the positive side, the soundtrack is great. Not that much to add, you cannot be disappointed.
Tracks
This is tricky area. The track generator (Your Stage) is an amazing piece of software. It works flawlessly and produce different and consistent tracks; you can decide the challenge level, the length, the weather conditions and the time of day. Pretty awesome. Unfortunately, the selection of corners and curves is not that hege as it should be to achieve the desired effect; random generated tracks can have multiple repetitions not only of curves but also of sequence of curves. Overall, the track generator does not deliver the experience you are looking in an occasional stage (also considering the limited attractiveness of the locations design). Despite its limitations, it is a great tool if you want to setup a personal championship or to participate to an online event featuring stages unknown to all the competing players.
Locations
Definitely the downside part. In first instance, 5 locations are not enough. The design of the locations (in terms of variety and detail of environment) is not adequate. Michigan and Australia are fair to good, Wales is very good, Sweden is not bad but too flat. Spain is very bad and deserves a special mention; tracks are of pure flat asphalt (with no variations, aside from when you cross a village) and provide a very boring experience; also, the grip is way too slippery.
Cars
Selection is limited but I believe in line with Dirt Rally and the design is very detailed. The car configuration menu is clear and well organized and every change made in setup reflects consistently in the actual behaviour on road. All cars have different handling and this is nice. Pretty much in line with Dirt Rally. Unfortunately, some cars come with a weird default setup, and you should spend some time in putting it in order. Most of them are fun to drive but it must be noted that some specific cars have a bad handling; namely, most of the 2000cc cars and some RWDs (aside from Fiat 131 Abarth which is great already at default settings).
Damage System
Simply great. Every damage is reflected accurately, aesthetically and functionally. Also, while driving, you can have occasional downgrade of car performances, which is nice. Minor remark: the repair times are too forgiving for my taste.
Weather System
Wonderful. 13 different weather choices that combined with 108 possible choices of the time of day allows you to set-up 130 possible situation for the same stage. But where the system stands-out is in the way it dynamically affects not only visually but also functionally (in combination with the physics engine) the race. Really, no other rally game compares in this regard.
Gameplay
Career mode is outstanding. It features 4 sections: contemporary rally, rally cross, land rush and historic rally. Land rush is not my cup of tea (to be noted that in land rush the drifting works very nicely). Rally Cross is nice. The contemporary and historic rally are very nice and long (can take easily 200 hrs) and you’ll never face the same track twice. You can setup and manage your team, design you own livery, and with the credits you gain you can buy structures and cars.
Personal championship is the area where D4 stands out compared to any other games; it is where the track engine really delivers its best. You can setup an event where the stages follow a consistent sequence in the time of the day and in the progression of the weather.
Online events. Pretty much as Dirt Rally (daily, weekly and monthly challenges), with the plus of random tracks. Sadly, the online championship is almost desert now; the same goes for multiplayer.
I can just hope the situation changes, but do not buy this game if multiplayer is your primary drive.
Replay System
Good. Similar to Dirt Rally (including the limitation of not being able to save the replay) with some additional features (choice of selecting/muting background music, enabling/disabling co-pilot voice, helicopter view).
Conclusions
In conclusion the fundamentals of this game are great. I kept away from D4 until recently due to bad reviews; then I purchased it and realized that, along with some legitimate criticism, most of harsh reactions were coming from incomptent people, or gamers (like me) disappointed for not having a DR2.
My suggestion to you is to stay away from reviews with less than 40hrs of gameplay. What really should drive your choice of purchase, is how you want to play a rally game.
If your priority is the full rally experience (championships/events with multiple stages always different) then D4 is the best rally game to date.
Vice versa, if your priority is to pick up a predesigned stage and improve your time record in a challenging track (of which you know may already every corner and the copilot is just a useful reminder), while driving in a wonderful location, Dirt Rally wins hands down. D4 will disappoint you.

Mount & Blade: Warband, is an open world, medieval themed game in which you can take on the role of who ever you aspire to be. The game contains several factions, who have control over many villages, castles, and towns. The game is kind of like a mix between Skyrim, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, and the Total War games. Your able to march around the giant land of Calradia, in an army as small as just you, or as big as, well I don't think there is a limit to how big your army can be; however, you can only have up to one hundred and fifty NPC's in a battle, without mods. Your able to command your men on these giant battlefields, while also partaking in the fighting yourself, either in first-person or third-person. There's so much to see and do in this game, it's almost endless. The game has a very in depth troop tree, and plenty of mods both in the workshop, and online to suit your other needs; some of those great mods are things like "A Clash of Kings", and "Brytenwalda". Besides the default game being absolutely stunning, there is also grea DLC, including Napoleonic Wars, and the new Viking Conquest.  I'd recommend this game without hesitation, it's worth the full price without a doubt, and if you see it on a sale I'd recommend swifty grabbing it.

The soundtrack is much better than the first Hotline Miami, the story fleshes out into a great story, and it's fun, but this game is just too hard.  The mechanics for weapons are also sometimes clunky; the doors are still buggy and it's hard to hit dogs around corners.  The gameplay has turned from fun and a bit challenging in the first game, to insanely hard (even in normal mode).  It feels like many levels are built for the sole purpose of making it nearly impossible to beat them.  It takes the fun out of the game for me when I have to plan every move I make to beat a level, and often get shot by an enemy that isn't even visible.
That being said, the game has a lot of levels, a great story, and many weapons to choose from.  If you loved the first Hotline Miami and are ready for a tough challenge you'll probably like it a lot.

A frustrating experience. I love the first Hotline Miami, but there are just too many added flaws to its next installment for me to give it a recommendation. It has the same core gameplay, but with an added twist where you take control of different characters with different abilities. This would be a great way to vary up the gameplay if they were all fun characters to play, but alot of them in my opinion are not. I love the freedom that the first game provides in how you can approach a situation, but Hotline Miami 2 makes you do what it wants you to do, when it wants you to do it. The areas you conquer are way overly long making it very frustrating when having to repeat a area upon death. The added lore and backstories are interesting, but take alot of  the mystery of the original game away. They are some great surreal moments, but the characters are not very interesting on their own. Overall the game is fun at times, but frustrating at others. It grants you freedom in your approach just to take it away. I've had a decent time playing it, but its definantly a step down from the first.
A true sequel in terms of upping the ante and taking you out of your comfort zone. The split second thrills, hair pulling frustration, hypnotic music and angry violence are all cranked up to 11.

Where do i start...
Hotline Miami 2 is well, a sequel to Hotline Miami.
How surprising.
The gameplay is very similar aside from a few things such as stupidly large maps, which in some cases, result in cheap deaths, and the multiple characters.
Some of the most unique ones of these characters is the soldier who is given a knife and one gun which you can get more ammo for, and Alex and Ash, siblings with a chainsaw and a pistol.
It's significantly more story based than the first one, tying up a lot of loose ends, even if the ending is VERY abrupt.
The soundtrack is just amazing.
If you want a extra challenge upon beating this already difficult game, another difficulty is available, which is significanty harder, due to a few things. More enemies, guns have less ammo, and no lock on, for example.
Pardo was born with thick skin.
All and all, I prefer it over Hotline Miami 1, but it boils down to a matter of opinion.

Codemasters phoned it in with Dirt 4. The generated tracks are a good idea and can throw up some really good runs but mostly come across as generic with generic scenery. If some more variety was mixed in it could have been excellent. An idea that doesn't need to be thrown away but needs work.
The team management aspect doesn't really work other than to create a bunch of hurdles to access upgrades and car settings. Graphics are typical Codemasters which means on the high side of decent but again let down by a lack of care about the details. Why, for example, does your car throw up black dust clouds on red Australian roads? The first time I saw it I thought my car was blowing smoke.
The camera views are very restricting and I can't for the life of me find something I like. There is no look to apex and the camera is fixed straight ahead which means on a single screen (which I guess most are using) you need a wide FOV set. The trouble here is this makes the in-car view like trying to drive while looking out a mail box. The dash cam has a narrow fixed FOV and the dash top (that's it, no panel at all) obstructs half the screen. The bonnet cam is fixed and can't be offset to the drivers side and the full screen view is about six inches off the road. If that isn't enough to annoy Codemasters have encrypted the files to prevent modding. Camera shake is abysmal and doesn't reflect reality so is best turned off.
Performance is ordinary at best. A 1080ti struggles for 4K@60hz with everything turned down to near rock bottom. SLI isn't supported and I can't find a halfway usable profile.
Codemasters must have needed to top up the bank balance while they worked on F1 2017.

I usually don't review games let alone thumbs them down, but Dirt 4 has really let me down.
Codemasters gave me a lot of trust after the Dirt Rally EA I was a part of from day 1.  I was promised "Dirt Rally but with improved physics and limitless stages" and I was sold, I pre-ordered at full price trusting they would deliver after my experience with Dirt Rally.  Man, was I wrong.  Rally physics are horrible.  You cannot slide the cars on gravel at all, as soon as you break the rear end loose to take a hairpin or fast drift through a corner, LIKE REAL RALLY CARS DRIVE, they instantly correct themselves and point straight ahead forcing you to not counter steer but then steer into the corner immediately like some hand of god is stopping you from any kind of momentum.  It's the most unsatisfying rally "sim" I have ever played.  AWD's and RWD's drive more like FWD's with 150% traction control on, and this is on "sim" mode.
Dirt 4 is the epitomy of an overhyped and underdelivered type game, up there with No Mans Sky for me but at least those guys have improved their game.  Almost 3 months later and other than minor bugfixes here and there, NO word on addressing the horrible rally physics at all, NO word on improvements to the extremely repetitive and bland Your Stage or adding locations, nothing!!  The devs were always answering questions on the CM boards and making improvements during Dirt Rally EA, but this seems to be deemed a failure and abandoned.  Maybe they'll prove me wrong, I've spent 17 hours trying my hardest to find something to like about this game, but I can't.  Horrible physics on rally, terrible FFB, repetitive generic stages with too many repeating sections in a single stage.
The tech is there, Your Stage could be incredible if they worked on it and added a lot more variation with no repeating sections.  And the Rally Cross physics are amazing, so the physics engine is good but they completely F'd it on the Rally side which is why most people buy it.  3 months down the road, with the community outcry about the physics and stages so bad from day 1 with zero response is why I have to leave a negative review.  I hope I can change it in the future, that's up to Codemasters to actually try and improve their game and deliver what they promised.

I recently picked up this game with my group of friends about 4 days ago.
It was exactly the type of low-key goofy fun we were looking for and in the beginning everything was looking up (we even made ourselves a fam!) but...
This game has a lot of issues.
The biggest one being that if you don't play absolutely perfectly, %100 of the time, your experience will be severely lacking.
I've seen many other players complain about the 'spacebar issue' and it's as true as ever.
The spacebar has become mine and my group of friend's mortal enemy; every time we see one the group goes into a panic-- we are all DESPERATE for the seemingly random timing of the spacebar to finally go in our favor-- and only about %25 of the time will it.
We've tried all kinds of fixes-- cleaning our keyboards, plugging in a controller (there's no support for it) changing window sizes, turning on and off settings-- none of it works.
Even with practice, our spacebar hits don't get any better. It's insanity.
This becomes an issue when almost literally every aspect of the game is about getting your combos PERFECT.
(Which sucks because we all do really great with the arrow keys and get %80 and %90 on spacebars but…%100’s are like a far off dream...)
If the spacebar had even a second more of leniency on it-- a lot of problems would be fixed. We would be able to do Beat PangPang, WOW parties, and finally beat that boss Lamb we all hate so much.
This game allows NO re-mapping (apparently for the sake of fairness?) and has a very limited range of customizable options in those terms.
Speaking of customize-- the other big issue is the horrid buying system for cosmetic items.
For those of you who haven't played-- you can buy an item for 1 day, 7 days, 30 days, or permanently.
Some items you can buy with in game money, some with real money-- and this isn't what bothers me.
I think micro-transactions have a place if you know what you're getting and the prices are reasonable; most of the items are cosmetic and most of them are pretty cute.
Plus, I don't mind throwing money at a developer that I like who makes a good product. It costs money to make a game, and I understand this!
BUT: Permanent outfits range from $10-$20 dollars AT LEAST-- and this isn't even for a FULL SET.
One shirt could be $15, a hairstyle could be $7, and so on and so forth.
The fact that it's so unobtainable for new players to get any kind of permanent gear makes the game feel like an experience you are meant to leave after a few days-- it doesn't MAKE me want to stick around.
It makes me feel like my account is throwaway and I think this is a big issue.
Seeing higher level players with amazing outfits and gear, none of us can understand how they do it; how they afford it?
We don't understand how it is ANYONE gets any kind of enough beat for clothing or how ANYONE can consistently get spacebars %100.
(I've searched all over google and so many other people have this same problem.)
It sucks because I LOVE THIS GAME and I love the potential. It's got a lot of great and super fun elements-- it's so fun to play in a lobby with 7 other people and really just BE A SQUAD and it's got a TON of fun and interesting songs with a lot of variety and the emotes are GREAT!!!
There's so much I love about this game and WANT to love but these two big things really keep me from wanting to become a long time player...I just never feel rewarded; I always feel like I'm throwing myself against a brick wall...
Overall;
Is this game perfect? Absolutely not. Does this game need a lot of work? Absolutely yes.
Would I recommend this game to a group of friends as a good goof?
In a heartbeat!

Mount & Blade... where do I start? It is essentially a crime against PC gaming and humanity as a whole if you don't own this game. Yes, I'm exaggerating a bit, but this is honestly one of the best, yet most underrated, PC games I've ever played. It's a medieval RPG with kings, kingdoms, bandits, and almost anything else that has to do with medieval times.
PROS:
- There is no set plot. The story is very open-ended. It basically drops you into the game, allowing you to complete quests and fight battles whenever you want. You can fight for one of six kingdoms, rob villages and caravans, be a merchant, and even become king of your own kingdom at some point if you make it far enough.
- The swordplay in this game is amazing. It's pretty realistic, taking the direction of your swing and your speed both into account. You can also use bows and arrows, crossbows, lances, or spears.
- There are a bunch of quests you can complete, ranging from training poor villagers to capturing lords.
- You can make friends or enemies with lords, ladies, and kings, which allows them to support you in your adventures. You can also make friends and enemies with kingdoms.
- Graphics are decent but don't need a very powerful PC to run.
- You can recieve fiefs, which basically means you can get villages, towns, and castles.
- You can marry.
- You can raise an army.
- The music is pretty good and sounds medieval.
- There is multiplayer. I haven't played it yet, but I've heard good things about it. You can only do battles instead of full campaigns like singleplayer, though.
- In-depth character customization. You can make his/her face look however you want.
CONS:
- After a while, the game can actually get a bit boring.
- This game isn't that friendly to new players. It pretty much has a tutorial just for combat and nothing else. Most things can be learned with a simple Google search, though.
- Even though the graphics are decent, that's only on medium or high settings. Compared to most games newer than 2008 or so, the game looks kinda bad. I'd say it's probably Wii quality graphics. This is pretty easy to look over in the heat of battle, though.
- The side quests can get a bit repetitive.
- Even though it's realistic, I'm not a fan of the morale system. No matter how many soldiers you have, their morale will be low unless you fight a large battle or do something else to raise their morale. Winning a battle where you're outnumbered greatly helps. (I actually defeated King Yargolek's army of around 250 with only around 70 men of my own, which obviously helped. But I digress...) Morale lower than 30 will make some of your soldiers leave your party, which is probably what makes me dislike this system.
Overall, even with it's flaws that are mostly minor compared to the pros, Mount & Blade: Warband is an amazing game. If you're a fan of RPG's, medieval games, or are just looking for a challenging, but fun, experience, I highly recommend this game. If you're unsure about buying it, there is a free demo that you can try out.

It's an enormous tug of war for me here to choose between whether this game's pros dominate it's cons or vice versa. In the beginning, you really can't just select a server to play on and then immediately get the hang of the combat mechanics. It takes weeks if not months to completely master the controls (especially the keyboard if one decides to use keys as directional attacks/blocks) in the melee combat aspect of the game. Studying your opponents is especially important in this game, you have to know when someone lands an attack on you (e.g. upper directional attack), there's a very short time within that strike that he will have the opportunity to switch to defensive, and then strike at you in a completely different direction. Because all of this can happen so very quickly, the average "newbie" is extremely vulnerable and confused and really doesn't learn a single thing from this scenario. This is precisely why I think there should be a rank system to the game (hopefully if Taleworlds even decides to make another game after VC), because in the beginning it's easy to find yourself outmatched by people who have played the game for years.
The aspect of the experienced vs. the inexperienced and the vast complexity of hand-to-hand combat in this game is most certainly a major issue, but if you can find yourself playing the singleplayer "campaign", trainers around Calradia and local tournaments will certainly help the player get a better grasp of how the combat system works. Even though there really is no gain in playing this game, other than steam achievements and everything in singleplayer, the multiplayer is still quite exhilarating when you notice your opponent miss a block and then stab him in the face. For all the people who buy this game, as mentioned above, I'd seriously recommend learning about the combat mechanics of the game and practice it in singleplayer before doing anything in multiplayer. I cannot possibly regret all the hours I've spent playing this game, so on that note I'd recommend this game.

This game is basically Left 4 Dead: Exterminator Edition.
Pros:
Cons
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed L4D, or is interested in a co-op game that will have you at the edge of your seat cheering (or cursing) your friends as you wade through a sea of bipedal rodents with medieval weaponry against all odds.

If you like Left 4 Dead style survival FPS gameplay in a fantasy setting this may hold your interest, its very simplistic (with the exception of a simple crafting system), overall I lost interest with its repetitive gameplay after the second day. Might be worth $10.00 if it goes on sale.

You'll see many comparisons to Left4Dead, and it's true for the most part. But where a lot of clones have tried and failed with a medieval/fantasy style Left4Dead co-op this game is much smoother and better built. You choose between 5 characters in a 4-player level run, wielding different weapons for each character as well as which playstyle you prefer.
The difficulty is higher than most games. Do not feel bad if you have to crank it down to easy to get the hang of it, but each succesful run feels like an accomplishment due to that. Combine that with how the game prioritizes skill over loot grinding and you have a great challenge to look forward to that's never impossible but never easy either.
Now, with the praise out of the way I'll get to the cons. The chance based rolls on items as well as their effects means you can get a very Diablo-esq feeling of loot grinding. After you beat the campaign on easy/normal, most players will tend to replay the first level or a quicker run numerous times. And while the levels differ based on what enemies spawn where, it can get repetitive very quickly. Especially if rolls don't go your way. On top of that, the overall narrative is very intriguing but sparse at best, leaving you with very little to do aside from getting better items to do more runs to get better items, etc etc etc.
All in all, the price is worth it for a single person solely because of the challenge and generally solid fun. Playing with friends however makes the whole experience exponentially better, and I would even go as far as to say don't buy it until you have a friend or friends to run this with. Simply because the game is so much better with good coordination and equally great celebration at the end.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Genre
While the first game was a fast and intense experience that rewarded risk-taking and aggressive play, with tight, well-designed levels and challenging but fair gameplay, its sequel is the opposite.  Massive, open levels where you get gunned down from any angle the moment you stick your head out of cover, enemies that detect you instantly with aimbot gun accuracy, regardless of if you're behind them or if they're out of your field of vision, forcing you to hide behind corners and stick your head out to lure enemies closer, and an overreliance on gunplay in a game that truly shines in its melee combat turn Hotline Miami's second outing into an exercise in patience rather than the challenging and rewarding trip that was the first game.
If you don't mind being forced to play it like a stealth game, then feel free to purchase, I'm sure you'll enjoy it, but if you loved the first game for its speed and aggresion, then avoid this like the plague.
Tough as nails, a fitting end to the series

Wakfu is a tactical MMORPG unlike any other MMO except for its prequel, Dofus.  It has play style similar to Final Fantasy Tactics where combat takes place in a grid.

The character classes (15 of them) in Wakfu (and Dofus) have unique play styles and the classes themselves can be played many different ways.
The spells have a variety of rules, and positioning makes a big factor in damage dealt/recieved.
The art in this game is very charming.  It's very pleasing to just look at the content in the game.
The music is very pleasing as well.  All from playful, cheery music to serious, blood-pumping music.
There is a lot of humor in this game and a lot of funny parodies.  A lot of naughty references are in the game too, but are subtle enough that kids wouldn't (or shouldn't) understand.
Of course, playing in a team with others is a lot of fun (and often necessary for tackling dungeons of your lvl).  Being in a guild & the in-game group finder tool helps with playing with others to enjoy the game better.
Players can also make an impact on the environment.  Most mobs can be planted to have them spawn, and they can also be killed enough to have very little to no population in the area (sometimes ghost forms appear when that happens). Flowers, Trees, and crops can also be planted in the world and are shared with others, and they can also be completely harvested with none left for others.  Making certain plant/mob population too high or too low or just right can affect area bonuses and nation bonuses.  One nation (Riktus) benefits from other nations having their bonuses ruined.
The environment, plus nation laws and wars set by a governor voted by its citizens (who then can appoint other people to different positions in government), makes for interesting experiences in the world.
I've been playing this game for a long time (since open beta Jan 2012).  It's enjoyable and I recommend it.

Thoroughly disappointed by this game. There are only two preset difficulty settings; boringly easy, and impossibly difficult for players with keyboard or controllers. If you fall somewhere in between, you are left with a ton of settings to tweak around until you find a playable setting.
But still, there is not a hint of a sense of progression, I re-tried the very first track with settings I found good toward the end of the game, and was surprised to be unable to make it to the top 3, despite the best of my abilities.
So basically the game forces you to turn up or down the game's difficulty settings as you go, completely destroying a sense of accomplishment in the process, because it simply doesn't bother figuring out difficulty on it's own.
Add on top the fact that all racetracks are proc-gen out of a limited number of tiles. It means that there is never and never will be a fun wow moment. Everything is bland and cookie cutter.
TL;DR: Don't bother playing this unless you are hard-core with a legit driving game setup, this game simply doesn't care about making itself entertaining.

I stumbled on this game while browsing the free to play section.  I loved Dance Dance Revolution back when it came out, so I thought I'd give this a try and see how it worked out.
First, you make a character.  You select a gender (do know you can't change this after you've created the character).  You then select from a few basic hair styles and clothing and give your avatar a name.
The lobby screen is a bit confusing at first and there is no mouseover hover for things like the small icons at the top.  If you play around with it a little you'll figure it out quickly, though.
There doesn't seem to be many players active and the ones that are active are very high level and set their game mode to a very high difficulty which can be off-putting for brand new players.
You can create your own room and password protect it (max 5 characters, if I recall), which is what I did for the first while trying to practice the game to see if it was something I would continue to play.
The controls are a bit strange as you use the arrow keys, and the play bar is one bar with the directions displayed.  As the timer comes up to the 'decision line' you hit the keys, not exactly in rhythm as is with most games, but before the timer runs out.  The space bar key is another that is in the game and is the one you must hit exactly on the beat.
Another confusing aspect is that sometimes there will be two or even three direction keys in the same box.  During the tutorial, it shows you basic play and doesn't include those keys.   It's not like DDR where you hit them at the same time, think of them more like 8th or 16th notes where you have to press them both in succession quickly before the timer passes the decision line.
There is a cash shop, and two types of currency.  Cash (as always) and "Beats".  You get beats as rewards for passing milestones or in boxes as you play.  You can buy new hair styles or clothing with beats and the price is determined by how 'permanent' you want the item to be.
you can buy a cosmetic item for 1 day, a week, 30 days or permanent.  Depending on the level you choose, the cost of beats goes up considerably.   At the time of writing this, I've played about 6 hours here and there and have been able to unlock two permanent items.
They also randomly will give you cosmetic items you can put on that will last for 24 hours.
There's different game modes, one which you can play to earn beats by getting perfect scores and playing during a beat timer.  The more people playing with you at that time, the more beats you earn.
The game is cute and the music is interesting enough to make me keep playing.
It's free, I say give it a try and see if you like it.  Just have some patience to figure out the lobby and navigation and also be ready for a slightly difficult learning curve when trying to get used to the arrow keys and UI of the gameplay.
I'm definitely going to keep playing, it's a fun game once you start to get the hang of it.  And so far the community I've come across has been very kind and encouraging.
There are a few "R U girl? be my gf??" I ran across in full rooms, but that's bound to happen with any online game.  Especially one like this that has a 'couples' package you can buy for two avatars.
Give it a try, it's free.  The only thing you'll waste is bandwith and time if you don't like it :)
It's really a stress-free game.
