A Fair Review.
Wondering if you should grab this? Well heres a nice summary to help you decide if you want to or not.
What is this game? In a nutshell this game is chess with warhammer figures (but you can turn on the standard chess piece icon above their heads if you get confused) AND a chess LIKE game called regicide, but each piece has stats and abilities (which let you shoot, throw grenades,heal, shields, etc.) after youve made a standard chess move, (letting you alter the chess part greatly by killing pieces without making chess moves) which is cool to some and some hate it. I personally prefer standard chess, however regicide mode is fun and im glad they chose it for the single player campaign.
So this game is Chess with warhammer skins and an alternate chess-like game mode.
Overall the game has some pros and cons.
The pros
are that its chess with a warhammer skin and it looks very pretty both graphic and animation wise the sync kills are amazing when you take an enemy piece. It has a nice online community with match making, lobbies, ways to check stats, leveling up your army, the look of your soldiers, and even battle abilties to unlock for the regicide mode and entire army chapters for space marines, and clans for orks (so basically a different color scheme).
So the game works an runs very pretty and if you like chess its great. However...
The cons
are that there are some VERY infuriating bugs and even a design flaw or two. So the way you unlock stuff that was ALREADY IN THE GAME ready to go on release is done by either two ways, with real money cash shop (calm your p2w alarms) or you can unlock points per campaign mission, skirmish vs the ai, and mp matches. Sounds cool right? The problem is that right now you can easliy complete a mission and its secondary objectives and not get any points at all or credit, there have been MULTIPLE TIMES I have WON a mission and did not get credit for a the PRIMARY objective (aka winning the match!) or done the secondary objective MANY MANY MANY times and not gotten credit, since these points for completeing said things are used to purchase things that are also purchaseable with REAL money its like your being stolen from, and it happens WAY too often for them to not have noticed it. That does two things, leaves a REALLY bad taste in your mouth (unless you like seeing $ taken from you after you have earned it) and forces you to replay mission OVER AND OVER until you get credit which is annoying to say the least. Another HUGE gripe I have with this game and even consider a design flaw as other game give xp for hotseat matches, is that hotseat matches with friends gets you nothing! No cosmetic army experience or anything, this game was gifted to me because they new hotseat games were a HUGE thing at my house, and because of a few losers who might exploit it, we are being penalized and the only way to level up and make your army look cooler is to be forced to play against the AI or random people on the internet, call me crazy but I like social interation with the people I actually INTERACT with in real life, since this game doesn't seem to support that our hotseat game of choice will remain RISK II, or HOM&M # over this ANY DAY.
If you already know what regicide ( the game mode) is and its rules and like it's spin on chess and like playing chess vs ai oppenents or random people on the internet this game is for you and has potential, however if you had any hope of playing and earning rewards IN A GAME DESIGNED to be played by two people in chairs together (aka hotseat on a computer) you can't enjoy it with friends sadly as while the match may be fun, but the fact you didn't progress anything together instantly removes all fun in quite a demoralizing way. The game was gifted to me and I'm greatful for that, however I could not recommend this purchase until they fix the currency bugs, or enable cosmetics to be earned in hotseat.
Final Verdict:
All in all I'd wait for a discounted sale unless your friends list is packed with friends that own the game and youd want to play with because any form of chess against an AI is just really boring, and (to me) playing chess against random people is no where near as fun as friends on skype or heaven forbid in person.
If you plan on playing this by yourself and never hot-seat with anyone, the game is good and i'd normally recommend it, but I still won't recommend it until they fix the in-game currency bugs/ issues as they happen WAY too often, especially for content that was in the game at release. Once they fix those bugs I will change from negative to positive.

This is an excellent submarine simulator, but being an excellent simulator is always a two-edged sword.
Combat is fun and wel modelled, and the graphics are pretty. Wreaking havoc amongst enemy convoys is incredibly satisying, but getting to the battle in the first place is a very tedious process. The game does include a time dilation feature, but the autopilot will have serious difficulty navigating at higher speeds, unless you're in deep open water. This game will appeal to hardcore simulator buffs, but if you're turned off by the idea of spending hours just finding something to shoot, this is not the game for you.
Also, this game requires a internet connection and the Ubisoft online launcher to play. When I buy a game through Steam, I already have a layer of internet DRM. I don't appreciate it when a title requires me to install a second internet DRM launcher to play it.

Contagion is a brilliant, hardcore zombie survival/horror/whatevertheexperienceyouwantittobe in the sort of realistic standpoint.   I'll make it pretty crystal clear: the game leans towards the undead more than anything else than to hold your hand every step of the way.  There's not going to be enough ammo to kill every single zombie ♥♥♥♥er, there's not going to be pointers to where exactly you need to be going other than the text messages you recieve on your phone (in game, not literal), which is pretty clever if you asked me.
so you start off in whatever game mode you chose with your friends and you all help each other tackle the many objectives without getting eaten or killed for whatever reason, and when that happens, you'll either join the undead or will have to sit there and watch your friends in spectator mode depending on the server settings.   You do not want to fight player controlled zombies, especially if they're pretty good at dodging your shots so once your ammunition runs dry, you're good as ♥♥♥♥ed as a fresh batch of mince meat.
It's a bloody mystery how a game like this isn't doing so well with the player population, and might I add, "No More Room In Hell" is a free to play zombie survival game just like this (Except this game's more polished), but I think i can come up with some reasons why this game is so dead....(no puns intended)
There hasn't been an update to this game since 2015 when you get to the main menu, something about a "flatline" update.   I think that looks pretty bad on the game already.  Either erase that or whatever the case---I'm no game developer in any means but come on...
I also think there's not that many maps to play on, and something like Left4Dead 2 is constantly recieving all kinds of workshop content.
also, We live in a generation of video gaming where there's lots of hand holding, and games that don't do that are bound to be dead in months.  It's a shame that something so simple can kill games such as this.  really is.
Don't take this all personal or whatever.  It can be a fun game but when there's no players online, only thing you can do is either play by yourself or get friends that own this game for a few runs and that's pretty much it.   I also think the hunted mode is pretty stupid for the most part, it fuctions like a free for all mode and you only have one life so if you die for any reason, you will become a zombie and its all until the last player standing, whom will die anyway because...well, zombie players are smarter than the regular ones.   Escape is all I really play and it's a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play by yourself since there wont always be enough ammo or supplies you might scavange around the level and I think the game really expects couple of players to die in the party before the whole level is completed, kind of like in those zombie films where that one huge boobed chick dies expectably for instance.
I'll give you a few pointers. aim for the head, Look everywhere for weapons, ammunition and other important items, pay attention to your messages on your phone in the game, save your ammo when you can, and don't fight entire crowds of zombies like an idiot...just like I did.  you'll be sorry later on when you're out of bullets.  And if you happen to die and turn into the undead?  Oh well.  hunt your friends down.  And above everything else?  maintain situational awareness at all times...like don't space out or whatever or else a zombie might grab you from behind and kill you.

Hydrophobia: Prophecy is a science fiction where a group of radicals called “The New Malthusians” are plotting on reducing the overpopulation in a dramatic way.
The atmosphere is great, the game is short, there is a number of interesting gameplay ideas, and enjoyed it a lot. And the phrase “Save the world, kill yourself” really gets in your head.
The water looks amazing, the name of this game is wrong, this is clearly water sim 2011 The person walking around is clearly just a side-game

Hydrophobia Prophecy isn't very good. But before I get into why, it's not completely awful. Considering it's a 2010 game, the graphics aren't bad, though not amazing. But it's the water physics that is this game's shining crown and glory. The water flows, pours and ripples naturally, not too clear and not too murky. When you open doors or break glass with varying water levels, the water flows from one area to another in waves and levels out. Dark Energy Digital have produced a very good water physics simulator in their HydroEngine. It's just a pity they didn't put as much effort into the game itself.
Why did I think this game was bad? Hydrophobia Prophecy aims to be a cover-based, stealth shooter, similar vein to Deus Ex but without the RPG elements. But the stealth elements are absolutely horrible as cover is the only real element that provides stealth. Because the stealth is so bad, the game becomes a generic, watered-down, cover-based shooter. You have 1 weapon with 5 different ammo (i.e. stun, single shot, auto-fire, remote detonation grenade and remote detonation shock grenade). Majority of encounters involved me shooting a guy enough times in the face before he killed me, waiting for my health to regenerate before moving onto the next guy.
Hydrophobia Prophecy is only worth having a go if you're interested in water physics in games. Otherwise the game is not very well done due to many flaws and bugs, only being about 3 hours long, poor design and poor mechanics. Dark Energy Digital went under after low sales of this game, which is unfortunately what happens when you produce a sub-par game. More unfortunately is their response to some negative reviews which can be read about in this article. Looking at the title image below, don't get fooled into thinking this is an action game where you use your magical water power to defeat the bad guys. It certainly needs improvements and more content.
However it's exactly what I expect from a DiRT game, a nice mix between casual and sim, but tends to lean a little more towards casual, a fun soundtrack, a good selection of cars both modern and oldschool, solid gameplay and great presentation. but it has a few major flaws...
Pros -
DiRT 4 has two gameplay types to choose from, a casual leaning type and a sim leaning type. (I've only used the casual, so i cant comment on the sim. But the casual feels how you'd expect a DiRT game to feel) I just like that they give players the option.
They finally added the custom racing team aspect from the Grid series, where you have your own paint designs, colours, sponsors etc. And it's more in-depth with staff management as well as general upgrades and perks.
It looks great, if you've played any other DiRT game, you should expect this.
Gameplay is solid and fun.
An interesting and varied soundtrack.
Game's UI and menus are well designed, an overall nice presentation.
Doesn't pester you with dlc and passes like previous DiRT games. (yet)
Cons -
Career is too short. The events can be too longwinded and there isn't enough variety (I'll go into that)
Variety is limited. Although i'm satisfied with the amount of cars, the location variety is pretty bad and the randomly generated stages can be very repetative. There isn't enough event variety in the career mode, it's very standard feeling, it makes me miss the event variety from DiRT 2 and 3. As a result of the lack in variety, the events are extended in length, making some championships feel never-ending. Also the team customization is laughable when compared to the Grid series.
Overall It feels unfinished. It's a very nice and shiny, well performing unfinished game, I expected a longer career with way more variety in events, challenges and especially locations. It's a well thought-out game, there are lots of neat things and for the most part I really, really enjoy playing it. But it just needs more, and some tweaks here and there.
(Also those who compare this to DiRT Rally, clearly don't understand that DiRT Rally is a spin-off much like Showdown, and although it might spawn it's own sub-series of DiRT games, it's silly for it to be compared with the main series as they're different beasts)

I rarely post negative reviews because I know that, behind all this, stand passionate people who have devoted hours into providing us with their game, and even if it doesn't live up to the expectations, it's still something they have worked on hard and don't deserve to be bashed about it. But with Dirt 4 I feel like I have been tricked, cheated, so this mindset of mine didn't apply here; thus the negative review.
Unfortunately, what ruins everything is the heart of the game. Off-road racing. Dirt 4 is an off-road racing game, it's not a rally game, it's not a rallycross game, it's off-road racing in general. And while I respect that this has been Codemasters' plan with all
games, it didn't work for Dirt 4. Either due to lack of developers or time, the end result is an unfinished game. Sure, we managed to get Rally, Rallycross, crosskarts and landrush trucks. However Rally has nothing
about it, neither does landrush, nor crosskarts, nor Rallycross. Codemasters tried to focus on so many things that the result is a stale experience.
The game gives you an option to choose between Arcade and Simulation physics.
"Simulation" physics are wrong, especially at mid to low speeds. Despite being marketed as "Better than Dirt Rally", all cars are stuck to the ground and you can't carry a slide around a corner no matter how hard you try. I have never driven a rally car in real life, however when I compare in-game replays to real-life ones, they bear no resemblance, especially when it comes to how much they slide.
Rallycross has, by far, the best physics. The car behaviour is nearly identicall, if not the same as in real-life. But none of this matters because the FIA World Rallycross championship only has 5 tracks, 3 of which were in Dirt Rally. Worst of all however, the AI which is extremely slow on the straights and doesn't change its line in the corners, meaning if an AI car is slightly faster than you in 1 corner, it hits you and sends you off the track. There is no racing unless you go Online, where there are rarely any lobbies even with the Region set to England, Eastern, or Southern Europe.
Landrush only has 2 stages and no real championship, while Crosskarts, which are quite popular in certain countries, don't have any tracks of their own. You must drive them in landrush tracks, or RallyX tracks, none of which suit them well.
The Career is by no means immersive. It's basically a series of Championships starting from extremely short ones with 1 event, to bigger ones with multiple events. It may sound interesting but it really isn't, especially when the game forces you to complete similar events in order to unluck the next tier of events, with better Cars. Why should you have to slowly "unlock" events and cars, when you could simply go straight to the World Championship because you are good and have the money? While this helps newbies a lot, they could've easily made 2 seperate Careers to choose from; a realistic and a not-so-realistic. But they didn't.
Now most people will go ahead and call out YourStage  a♥♥♥♥♥♥feature and while I do admit it could have been better, every new technology has to start from somewhere. Codemasters surely learned a lot from the making of YourStage and hopefully we will sea it again in future dirt games and even in other Rally games by other developers (WRC etc.)
EDIT: As of 20th September, the game has not received any updates feature wise since release. Do not buy it in hopes of future updates, unless you are interested in the
state of the game.

It's a fantastically fun game. The game is basically Left 4 Dead outfitted for medieval style hack 'n slash.
Of course, the game itself is unbearable at times.
The AI is an absolute mess. If they're not busy teleporting across the level to help another bot/player, they're standing with their mouths open, looking at the sky while rats are busily clawing at their health. If you're down, don't depend on them EVER getting you back up. Again, it's like their main directive is to stand around and watch you do all the work.
The spawning system for Skaven is terrible. In L4D, you normally had a chance to react to the horde of zombies, since they spawned off screen/map. In this, you're brown bread. The Skaven literally pop in front of you, and surround you in seconds. Sometimes they'll properly spawn in with animations through scripted points. Other times, there's just instant spawning from said points, and don't stop until X units are in the area.
Some of the mechanics for attacking make fighting harder than it has to be. Sometimes the animations don't even play when the rats start to attack. It'll literally just be them sliding towards you, and you taking damage from an attack they supposedly did. If it's not the attack, it's the hitbox. It's insane how even just a slash in your general direction, half way across the world, will STILL hit you. The worst of it is when they happen to be within melee distance, and their model is inside yours, so while they can still attack and hit you with a hitbox the size of a horse, you can't even hit them with normal attacks.
There's a lot of collision issues on top of the aforementioned enemy-inside-you thing. Holes in the level, getting stuck on geometry that's not even apparent until you get stuck in it,
The looting system needs A LOT of work. Don't get me wrong, I know it's supposed to be all luck when it comes to a looting system in general, but when you've played through hours of levels, literally grinding for better gear, it's a smack to the face when you get nothing but the lowest of low rolls. It might just be me, but I've other friends who've complained about it, as well.
Optimization is a big thing, as well. Running a GTX 970 and an AMD FX6300 3.5GHz processor, I get low frames during hordes, and certain maps. Even turning down the settings, studdering, and fps drops affect the game. With the amount of spawning that comes with hordes, you could end up dying just because the delay from what's being processed is overpowering.
Bottom line-- The game is really fun, but there's A LOT of problems with it right now. Some make the game harder than it does, other times make the game nigh impossible to play.

My favority part is I can login and play on here when at a pc and I can login with my tablet at any time without any issues, and the same account, same friends, def true cross platform.
Right now its in open beta, so that means lots of stuff will be added, including but not limited to at least 100 total player levels, tons of new classes (a lot from Adventure Quest Worlds even), trading, group/party system, minimum level requirement for specific instances(keep those lowbies from ruining the raids), housing system, item fusion(keeping the look of an item but stats of another), raid events/dungeons etc.
It is free 2 play and they are keeping to the idea that the only thing the paid for currency Dragon Coins can be used for is for convenience such as buying a craftable item without grinding for the materials for it, xp potions and some aesthetics.
So far however there is one class (Guardian) that is only available as a purchase, its great tank class and has its own quests and what not associated with it as well and as far as inforation is available is the only class that will require payment for, like a dlc.  I thought it was worth it to support the devs, and if you do not have it you are not really losing out as it does not provide the best gear in the game it just provides some awesome looking gear.  And if I remember correctlyl there will be dozens of classes anyways, so 1 that you have to buy to support the devs in my opinion is fair (and worth buying and supporting them for).
The best part for me, it works very well on our crappy computers at work, rather it actually works on them lol, and it works fluidly on my tablet, so something I can enjoy playing without technical limitations or control/mechanics limitations.
If you love traditional mmorpgs, you love hats, you love awesome armor and weapons, or just want to be able to get your mmo fix on the go, this is the game for you.  Plus I will be there so what's more to love?

I really like this game! It's a great mixture of strategy and... well... Chess! Yes, yes I know Chess is a strategy game, but the added abilities of your 'pieces' AFTER moving really add another layer on top of this classic strategy format.
For example:
In one of the earlier missions I had to get 1 of my 3 Assault Marines (Knights) to 'Point A' , with the secondary objective to achieve this within 5 turns. 2 Turns in I was in position to do this with a turn to spare, however, an Ork Loota (Bishop) had positioned themselves so that if I moved to the point from which I would leap to victory, the Loota would move and take me, like in normal Chess. So I was forced to re-evaluate my strategy and my life, meaning I would achieve the Primary but not the Secondary Objective of the mission.
But then, during the enemy's turn, the Loota moved into the square I was planning to eventually get to! I smiled deviously, smugly moving my Assault Marine to destroy the Ork Scum, "Stupid AI", I chuckled to myself. Ending the turn after healing (an ability) and presenting this pinnacle of human achievement an Iron Halo (a shield ability) I ended the turn, preparing myself a triumphant Nutella Sandwich. I then proceeded to watch a Storm Boy (Knight) move next to me, and I, like a plum, watched with triumph as the Loota shot at me futiley, taking out my shield. "I'm still alliiiive" suddenly stopped in my throat as the chant turned to an anguished groan, as the Storm Boy, the Knight, then used his Orkish brute strength in Assault to take the exact amount of health I had left, away, with a single denying swipe.
Curses.
Campaign is good, the Skirmish function is also good, as you can play against AI OR Human, and you can play Space Marine v Ork, Ork v Ork or Space Marine v Space Marine. Plus it's Warhammer 40K! I haven't tried multiplayer yet...
It is true that you have to pay for skins other than White Scars, Blood Angels or Raven Guard on Space Marines, and vice versa but for 3 clans for the Orks, but it doesn't really matter to me.. those skins/Chapters are cool enough and the skins don't change the gameplay.

This seems to be an attempt at blending Chess and Warhammer 40k, two great games, but in reality, it falls apart. The tutorial, which you can't skip, just points you to a bunch of confusing on-screen icons without explaining what they mean or what they do. When you finally get to play a game, you find that the rules of chess sometimes apply, but sometimes not - one of the biggest flaws is that putting the enemy leader into checkmate doesn't actually do anything - the Warboss, despite being in checkmate by a Terminator, was perfectly content to sit there, gunning down my Librarian and Assault Marine until I finally felled him with a sustained barrage of bolter fire.
Yes, the cathartic joy of perforating Orks with rocket-propelled rounds is obtainable here, and the graphics are excellent. But the voice acting is minimal - I think they have two, maybe three people doing all the voices. And since the actual rules of chess seem to be applied randomly here, anyone looking for that aforementioned cathartic joy is much better off with the many older 40k games available.

This game is often on sale for $0.99 or less, and at that price, I think it is definitely worth it.
There are a lot of negative reviews for this game, and they aren't entirely wrong, but I don't think it's a terrible game. It has its ups and its downs and a full load of meh. So, let's break it down. Warning: Minor spoilers, but nothing that really gives away the story.
Positives:
- The water physics: they are definitely cool and a major positive. I wish more games would make such use of flowing water physics to affect the characters and environment. It is fun to use water flooding to disorient your enemies and sweep them off their feet, it's neat how the intensity, direction, and depth of the water flow affect your own movement and so on. In some cases, you can see flooded compartements behind glass barriers, and if you shoot out the glass, that water floods into an area to have several effects. Similarly, some destructable leaky bulkheads can be shot out for similar effects, in some areas even completely filling the corridors and compartments you are in, which can be a danger but finding an air-pocket is usually not too hard.
- Use of the environment as weapons: not just the water, but leaky gas pipes, explosive panels and barrels, electrical panels and wires... all can be used strategically to trap and take out groups of bad guys.
- The "Mavi" device: I found the way you can use it to scan and control somethings in the environment as well as see invisible messages and such pretty nifty. Not awesome, mind you, but cool enough.
Negatives:
- The voice acting: it's very weak, and I'll be surprised if you don't find the main character's voice to be whiny and annoying.
- The keyboard and mouse controls: if you play this game, you'll definitely want to do it with a controller. Controlling with a keyboard and mouse is just really wonky. It's not perfect with a gamepad but it is much better and will save you a lot of frustration, especially later in the game when it comes to controlling water.
- The final boss battle is pretty terrible and frustrating until you figure out what to do. It's darned near impossible with keyboard/mouse controls.
The meh:
- The story is really weak. It wanted to be something good, but the writers didn't pull it off well.
- The gameplay in general. It's not terrible but it isn't very good either. It tries to combine a lot of things: cover-based shooting, tomb-raider style climbing and platforming, and a bit of "magic" in the form of a nanobot infection giving you the ability to somewhat control the water. But it doesn't do any of these these things particularly well.
- The challenge room is pretty dull (unlocked upon completing the game), and the gameplay is not good enough to make it much fun. Only worth playing if you must go for 100% achievements.
This game doesn't do a lot, so don't expect a lot. It wanted to be something amazing and utterly failed at that, but there is fun to be had.  I think you can easily get several hours of enjoyment out of it for $0.99 when it's on sale, but don't go in with high expectations and you won't find yourself being too disappointed. Again, playing it with a controller is pretty much a must.

CM made a mess of this game. It constantly reminds you that the developer didn't have enough time/money/skill to finish this properly.
It has lot of improvements in terms of team management, car damage and immersion, but at the same time lacks what was so great about Dirt Rally: the high quality stages and the excitement of driving a rally car.
Cars now have weight and better suspension so you're no longer taking huge jumps and bouncing the car of the ground. You can loose control when braking, so you need to be careful. This is great, but... throttle oversteer seems to be almost gone. You can smash the gas pedal on corner exit and the car will have almost perfect grip. If you want to power through the corner, counter steering and controlling the car with throttle, then this game isn't for you. If what you enjoy the most about Dirt Rally is taming historic RWD cars, then save yourself the disappointment and don't waste your time and money on Dirt 4.
Your Stage was supposed to be a revolutionary technology that can produce an infinite amount of stages. At least that's what CM claimed it is. What you get are generic looking stages that too often give the impression your doing laps on a racing track. There's not enough variety and 5 locations is too little. Furthermore, the co-driver calls sometimes are too late and will result in a crash. Unfortunately, you can't trust your co-driver.
What's the worst is that it's been almost two an a half month since release and the developer still hasn't commited to fixing the major problems.

It's a fantastically fun game. The game is basically Left 4 Dead outfitted for medieval style hack 'n slash.
Of course, the game itself is unbearable at times.
The AI is an absolute mess. If they're not busy teleporting across the level to help another bot/player, they're standing with their mouths open, looking at the sky while rats are busily clawing at their health. If you're down, don't depend on them EVER getting you back up. Again, it's like their main directive is to stand around and watch you do all the work.
The spawning system for Skaven is terrible. In L4D, you normally had a chance to react to the horde of zombies, since they spawned off screen/map. In this, you're brown bread. The Skaven literally pop in front of you, and surround you in seconds. Sometimes they'll properly spawn in with animations through scripted points. Other times, there's just instant spawning from said points, and don't stop until X units are in the area.
Some of the mechanics for attacking make fighting harder than it has to be. Sometimes the animations don't even play when the rats start to attack. It'll literally just be them sliding towards you, and you taking damage from an attack they supposedly did. If it's not the attack, it's the hitbox. It's insane how even just a slash in your general direction, half way across the world, will STILL hit you. The worst of it is when they happen to be within melee distance, and their model is inside yours, so while they can still attack and hit you with a hitbox the size of a horse, you can't even hit them with normal attacks.
There's a lot of collision issues on top of the aforementioned enemy-inside-you thing. Holes in the level, getting stuck on geometry that's not even apparent until you get stuck in it,
The looting system needs A LOT of work. Don't get me wrong, I know it's supposed to be all luck when it comes to a looting system in general, but when you've played through hours of levels, literally grinding for better gear, it's a smack to the face when you get nothing but the lowest of low rolls. It might just be me, but I've other friends who've complained about it, as well.
Optimization is a big thing, as well. Running a GTX 970 and an AMD FX6300 3.5GHz processor, I get low frames during hordes, and certain maps. Even turning down the settings, studdering, and fps drops affect the game. With the amount of spawning that comes with hordes, you could end up dying just because the delay from what's being processed is overpowering.
Bottom line-- The game is really fun, but there's A LOT of problems with it right now. Some make the game harder than it does, other times make the game nigh impossible to play.

Warhammer 40,000.... and Chess? An unlikely duo but oh my goodness, so beautifully brutal. Its very similar to Battle Chess where the rules have been modified to allow units to fight in a variety of ways rather than just regular chess movements. All your standard chess pieces are here, Space Marines and Shoota Boyz as pawns, Terminators and Nobz as Rooks etc etc. Every differing unit comes equipped with special abilities (such as frag grenades, snap shot, only in death, etc etc) and comes with multiple visceral executions that literally make you giggle with bloody joy. The first time you watch a Librarian turn a Shoota Boy into a giant pile of organs and blood, you'll probably feel the same way. Furthermore, the graphics are quite beautiful and there is some considerable detail in every model and the maps. From my time spent so far, I do wish there were more maps, though.
Unfortunately, the game can get sort of repetitive unless you are a diehard Chess player. But the campaign definitely breaks up the monotony of just playing chess with modified rules. All in all, for only 14.99 (12.74 right now) this game is great value and I definitely recommend it to my Chess/Warhammer 40,000 fans out there.

If you're looking for a hardcore rally sim, this isn't it. If you're looking for a casual racing game, this isn't it either. What this is is a game placing itself in the difficult middle ground; targeting itself towards gamers searching for a moderate challenge (but not a hardcore simulation), and those wanting to have fun. It's incredibly difficult to achieve both, and a lot of racing games fail at this. The handling needs to be approachable, yet challenging; "easy to learn, hard to master" as they say.
DiRT 4 attempts to straddle this particular issue by sitting on the fence; offering players a choice between a Simulation and a Gamer mode for handling. While this is effective in providing a choice which will no doubt please many people, I find myself (as ever) in the middle ground of difficulty settings in terms of my driving ability. I am by no means a driving expert but I have played a fair few racing games at this point: I want realism, but not too much of a challenge - in short, I want to have fun, and I want a challenge - but often I feel like DiRT 4 is making me choose between the two. The Gamer handling is a little too easy in some ways and the Simulation a little too hard - I feel like I'm in the middleground between these two difficulty settings. So often the problem with me and racing games, I'm caught between two difficulty settings where one is too hard and one is too easy, and I can't quite enjoy myself all the time.
As a result, I'm forced to challenge myself a bit more and sacrifice a bit of the fun. I'm enjoying this game, though; for me it's easily the best game in the series, though DiRT Rally may scratch that itch for some looking for more of a challenge. This is a great game, I just wish it would let me enjoy it a bit more.

Since I already decided that no Steam game and genre is out of reach, I have finally turned my attention towards a title which combines more than one review novelty as far as my previously published articles are concerned: LoveBeat mixes quite efficiently the F2P (free-to-play) formula with arcade dancing, an established community of fans and last but not least, a cute anime visual style. It is the Steam debut of CRAZYDIAMOND and so far, their only game. Even if my experience with rhythm games is mostly related to the mini sections from titles which implemented them on occasion (Sleeping Dogs comes to mind), I kept an open mind and agreed that this genre has its merits. Video games can’t be only about digital violence in fantasy worlds, right?
Instead of being presented with a cheesy pre-rendered storyline, players are encouraged to create an avatar of their liking, from the gender (which you can’t switch once you opted for one already) to clothing and moods or something similar. MMOs in general, were never my specialty. Alas, I shall do my best to write in my own words and thoughts, the exact experience I had in LoveBeat. For a casual title, the tutorial is complex and intuitive. You can fail it but managing to pass, players receive their first rewards in the game.
As with most F2P games, LoveBeat can also be made much easier or allow for faster avatar customization through the purchase of specific currency (which you buy with real money, naturally). I’m not a fan of this formula but the game has a second medium of exchange, called “Beats”. So you won’t be disappointed by the reward system, even if you don’t wish to invest cash in the game. Keep in mind that the dev team keeps supporting the game and deserve a minimum amount of gratitude from its player base.
The biggest issue I have with LoveBeat is that I couldn’t change the resolution at all. I can’t recall playing a PC game at 1024x768 in the past decade. Even my “gaming” laptop had a native setting of 1366x768. On a 4K monitor, the game looks worse than some of the smartphone “games” I tried in desperate times (I try to avoid them whenever possible). Since graphics aren’t everything and especially since not every gamer out there will mind it, I shall turn a blind eye this time. I did in fact and managed to play quite a bit since the gameplay evens out the underwhelming looks.
The sound effects may be limited and there's no voice acting whatsoever, yet LoveBeat’s soundtrack is its saving grace. Superb selection of songs, not related only to K-Pop even if that’s the predominant genre. From what I’ve seen and heard so far, new songs get added on a steady basis and for a game about dancing, I think that most players won’t care about voice actors or misc effects. It’s an acquired taste, but the songs are pleasant and foreing languages never stopped me from enjoying music in which I couldn’t understand the lyrics at all.
As expected from this genre, you’ll need quick reflexes, a good keyboard and lots of patience if you wish to climb that leaderboard to LoveBeat stardom status. It sounds more difficult than it really is. With a moderate amount of practice, I didn’t find the game to be as challenging as some describe it. Of course, I didn’t play a lot and definitely haven’t reached the top players in order to compete against them. Grinding is a sad reality, but come to think of it, there must be a way to separate the new players from veterans which quite literally kept the servers going through their monetary support.
I wouldn’t go as far as to call it Pay-to-win either. Your level of experience and eye–hand coordination can’t be bought afterall. Just as the AI (aptly named Tesha) suggests, the key to in-game success is never to overexert yourself. Both failure and repetition are crucial elements of any learning process. What value would wins even have, if loses wouldn’t constantly remind us that improvement is the only motivation to go further ahead?
LoveBeat literally bombards players with brightly-colored screens detailing what current events they should try, what rewards they can unlock and so forth. It takes some time getting used to it, but the design is meant to be like this. I’ll never call too much information as being a “flaw”. Barebones interfaces though, are a video game sin. So stop complaining and read it all. Let the information sink in and have fun. It’s the type of MMO which you pick up and play, not dig through online encyclopedias in search of a winning strategy.
I’m certain that higher resolution settings could be implemented at some point. It would be a pity if such an entertaining game gets dragged down by something so superficial. Do give it a try, it’s not like it’ll require you to spend cash to enjoy it. Some Steam Achievements would be welcome as well, but first of all that ghastly 1024x768 needs to stuff the dustbin of technology long past its prime. If you can overlook that, LoveBeat won’t disappoint.

Mount & Blade... where do I start? It is essentially a crime against PC gaming and humanity as a whole if you don't own this game. Yes, I'm exaggerating a bit, but this is honestly one of the best, yet most underrated, PC games I've ever played. It's a medieval RPG with kings, kingdoms, bandits, and almost anything else that has to do with medieval times.
PROS:
- There is no set plot. The story is very open-ended. It basically drops you into the game, allowing you to complete quests and fight battles whenever you want. You can fight for one of six kingdoms, rob villages and caravans, be a merchant, and even become king of your own kingdom at some point if you make it far enough.
- The swordplay in this game is amazing. It's pretty realistic, taking the direction of your swing and your speed both into account. You can also use bows and arrows, crossbows, lances, or spears.
- There are a bunch of quests you can complete, ranging from training poor villagers to capturing lords.
- You can make friends or enemies with lords, ladies, and kings, which allows them to support you in your adventures. You can also make friends and enemies with kingdoms.
- Graphics are decent but don't need a very powerful PC to run.
- You can recieve fiefs, which basically means you can get villages, towns, and castles.
- You can marry.
- You can raise an army.
- The music is pretty good and sounds medieval.
- There is multiplayer. I haven't played it yet, but I've heard good things about it. You can only do battles instead of full campaigns like singleplayer, though.
- In-depth character customization. You can make his/her face look however you want.
CONS:
- After a while, the game can actually get a bit boring.
- This game isn't that friendly to new players. It pretty much has a tutorial just for combat and nothing else. Most things can be learned with a simple Google search, though.
- Even though the graphics are decent, that's only on medium or high settings. Compared to most games newer than 2008 or so, the game looks kinda bad. I'd say it's probably Wii quality graphics. This is pretty easy to look over in the heat of battle, though.
- The side quests can get a bit repetitive.
- Even though it's realistic, I'm not a fan of the morale system. No matter how many soldiers you have, their morale will be low unless you fight a large battle or do something else to raise their morale. Winning a battle where you're outnumbered greatly helps. (I actually defeated King Yargolek's army of around 250 with only around 70 men of my own, which obviously helped. But I digress...) Morale lower than 30 will make some of your soldiers leave your party, which is probably what makes me dislike this system.
Overall, even with it's flaws that are mostly minor compared to the pros, Mount & Blade: Warband is an amazing game. If you're a fan of RPG's, medieval games, or are just looking for a challenging, but fun, experience, I highly recommend this game. If you're unsure about buying it, there is a free demo that you can try out.

: Fantastically meaty co-op melee action, that can cater for multiple playstyles depending on class/loadout, offers a good range of difficulty, and has brilliant attention to detail, though the loot system (improved from initial release!), a few bugs, and occassional crashes may still annoy some.  Read below for a (much) more in depth explanation of features/issues.
Vermintide inevitably draws comparisons to Left 4 Dead because of its similarities; four person teams move through linear levels, accomplishing objective tasks and dealing with interspersed enemies, while random horde events lead to on-the-fly adaption, and special enemy types will incapacitate team members separated from the group/use AoE attacks. You even have a similar inventory system; slot for healing items, slot for buff items, and a slot for a bomb.  All very familiar.
However, upon closer inspection, Vermintide offers a significantly different experience.  The L4D similarities seem to be there to make the game accessible; you can jump in and understand the basics, since almost everyone has played L4D.  Mechnically, however, it's a whole different story.  Melee combat, the meat of the game, has four main components; light attacks, charged attacks, parries, and dodging.
These four components, working in tandem, make for a thrilling melee experience.  Learning that the greatsword has wide, multi-target swipes, but only small knockbacks, encourages a style of play built for well timed charges and backsteps.  Faster dual daggers can slash and parry almost instantly; switching between light attacks on single targets, to wider charged swipes for larger groups.  Positioning and reading enemy attacks is vital; regular Skaven do telegraph significantly, so kiting and parrying, then going on the counter attack, feels satisfying.
The game feels entirely possible to play without taking damage, and that's fantastic.  Every hit to your front is usually a strategic mistake; punished for overreaching and not being able to parry in time, pressing too aggressively without backstepping between swings.  Even special enemies have counter-strategies; Gutter Runners/hunters can be avoided with well timed sidesteps, and Rat Ogres/tanks can be parried and dodged with deft footwork and parries. Indeed, once you get into Catacylsm difficulty, no-damage starts becoming an expectation when a single clan rat is wiping 30% off your health.
Combine the precision with a wonderfully visceral dismemberment system (literally cutting rats in half/decaptitations with charged attacks) and you have a melee system that gives constant satisfaction.  You feel in control of your movement at all times, and the feedback from big swings and parries is excellent.  Spot on.
Lots of customisation avaialable.  Every character has at least three melee and three ranged weapons to choose from, covering single target damage to wider attacks.  There's some crossover weapons between classes, but everyone has at least something distinct on the table.  Being able to choose your own loadout for missions allows a level of specialisation L4D doesn't have; at higher difficulties, people take on damage and support roles (Tank, DPS, etc), forming a more cohesive fantasy party, and a greater level of cooperation, and allowing for a lot more playstyles than its comparison game.
This feels like a game put together by pre-Age of Sigmar Warhammer fanboys/girls, and that's fantastic.  Characterisation is done wonderfully; all the characters have biographies on the official website which are worth reading, but in-game dialogue still gives plenty away.
You have your zealous Witch Hunter who occassionaly lets his humanity slip through, a dwarf filled with stories, songs and numerous references to the seemingly endless feats of his cousin, the sharp wit and oft-times manic enthusiasm of a bright wizard, an elf who babies the entire party, and the straightman Empire Soldier to the bunch of misfits surrounding him.
Incidental dialogue has them play off each other; typically throwaway lines of dialogue, such as the Witch Hunter telling the Bright Wizard to "take my hand, and we'll speak no more of it" during a revival, will make you smile and start liking the characters.  Fatshark does a great job with the little lines like this that make you like the characters, rather than just playing them as entirely one-dimensional (which, in a game like this, they could have easily gotten away with).
The Skaven deserve credit too; L4D zombies weren't smart enough to talk smack during a fight, but these guys certainly are.  Clan Rats will mock you if they get behind you for a backstab, Gutter Rats taunt from the shadows as they ready to strike, Packmasters sort of just scream at you, and a lot of these lines, particularly from the basic enemies, all have character specific variants.  Skaven will, outside of horde events, wait for friends to join them before attacking, cower in place if they see you charging an attack, and generally act in a way that makes them believable and improves the immersion.  You feel, at times, like you're fighting cunning ratmen, not mindless mobs.
Every character also has their own personalised room in the hub, with specific items and decorations that you'd expect from them.  Again, fantastic.  The devs love the lore, and it shines through perfectly.
Controversial, to put it lightly. Playing on higher difficulties makes rarer items appear in your potential post-mission loot table; picking up side items give better dice to roll at the end to decide what item you get.
On the positive side, this has made me experiment with multiple classes and discover my love for two handed swords, but on the downside, it keeps me from getting some weapons I really want (my kingdom for an epic rapier).  You can, at least, fuse items from the same tier to produce one item of the tier above it, or scrap weapons you don't want and use the resources to 'pray' for a ranged or melee weapon at the same tier.  Even so, RNG features heavily no matter how you look at it, and while this increases game longevity and encourages experimentation, it can also be a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  Your mileage may vary; as other reviews show, some people love it, some people hate it.
The only area the game is let down.  One of the lessons you quickly learn in Vermintide is to avoid standing next to walls when you know enemies are on the other side of it, because they *will* attack and damage you through them.  Packmaster thing-catchers are able to travel through solid surfaces, and then bestow the same property to the hero they grab, carrying you through a wall and away from your team before you can do anything about it.
These situations are rare; I've been attacked through a wall maybe five times, and the afformentioned Packmaster only happened once (but it was on Nightmare difficulty, so I'm still salty).  But the whole game has a slightly beta feel to it.  Some enemy animations get hung up, such as rats rolling in place, or subtitles remaining in place for the entire mission.  However, most are minor annoyances at worst, but can drag you out of the otherwise well crafted world.
Crashes are also rare, but extremely annoying.  Had it happen four times over my playtime, which I can cope with, but would rather it didn't happen at all.
I've had a blast with Vermintide, despite a short campaign.  The loot system is built to encourage multiple playthroughs, learning the combat inticracies has been great, and I've enjoyed the characters a lot.  The devs are constantly asking for feedback/new ideas on Reddit, so I can only expect the game to improve over time.  Lizardman hero DLC pls.
Strongly recommended.

The player can set on missions with other players to play along as five characters, each with their own specialties. This game can be seen as heavily influenced by Valve's Left 4 Dead games, as the players have two weapon slots, one melee, and one ranged, along side one utility item, one, grenade item, and one healing item, totalling out to five carriable items.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide would be identical to the Left 4 Dead series, but there is loot and progression in this one. At the end of each mission, if successful, the players may roll for loot, using die, and having a chance at white, green, and blue rarity items; with white being the lowest and blue being the highest. Unlike Left 4 Dead, the player also has a level to keep up with, like a normal account level. The higher the level, the more features may be unlocked in the inn.
Like Left 4 Dead, this game has special types of rats, as in the Left 4 Dead series. There are a few: the Rat Ogre, portraying the tank in Left 4 Dead, the Pack Master portraying the Smoker, the Assassin Rat, portraying the Hunter, and last but not least, the Ratling Gunner, portraying... well... it's a gunner, so I wouldn't know.
There may not be much to this game in the long run, as it does get repetitive, but it does offer a lot of fun times if played with friends.

As it says, this is an Early Access Review. In other words, the game will improve over time. If you don't wish to play the game when it's incomplete, you aren't suitable for Beta Testing or any testing for that matter. Stay away from this currently incomplete game. (You have been warned).
Just like every other AE game, this has the same concept. Farming. It's extremely grindy, like seriously. If you hate any form of grinding or TOO MUCH grinding, then stay away as well.
There are new features such as crafting and now even the Pumpkin Lord Armour is farmable. Which is a great step forward for non-p2p players. In other words, it is more farmy and less cashy. Just like how an AE game should be.
For anyone that complained that the PumpkinLord armour is too hard to farm due to low levels joining in the dungeon, they have capped it and is now much more easy.
A new area has been released and guess what? More farming! Before anyone starts complaining that the hard area is too hard, it's probably because you're too low level. (Basically a newbie. NOT AN INSULT HERE.)
I take back my previous statement about levels being less important though. They are super important because the best armour currently available in game is level 15.
If you're new to AE games, I really don't recommend this because the story DOES NOT FLOW. Yes. AE games are made in such a way that if you never played any other games made by them, the story will feel very weird and rushed. As a long time player of ALL their games, I can say that their lore is extremely deep. For example, the plot twist about Artix and Gravelyn actually makes sense. If you looked back at their past storyline, you'll actually see why. Sepulchure's backstory is personally my favourite (And the way he died T^T)
Basically, if you want to start on this game, PLAY ALL OF ITS PREQUELS.
If you wish to just jump into this game without any knowledge of how AE games work, you will have a 50% chance of either loving it, or hating it.

Make sure that you know that how cool this game looks, it is CHESS. I did not know that and i bought it out of hype. Later i figured out that yes it is just chess with abilities. It's not really a game for people who just want to play a turn based stategy game, considering there is not that much stuff to do. Besides playing chess.

WH40k and Chess, if you love these games then this is a no brainer IMO. You can play Regicide, which is their version of chess or you can play normal chess with just the WH40k characters as chess pieces. The Regicide game play is actually very challenging once you learn the special abilities and traits of each race. I still think there are a few balancing issues, as Space marines in my opinion die too easily against Orcs. They could have addressed this by making the space marines more powerful but limiting their numbers. The whole feel just doesn’t seem right IMO, but this is still in early access stage, so I expect a lot to change.
The UI was a bit confusing to start with, but I managed to find the exit button for it. There is no unit customisation or modding option for this game, which I think is a shame as it would be great to see units that have been customised by each player when you go on MP.
I haven't played MP yet, as I prefer SP games and modding my own maps or missions, so I can't really day anything about that aspect of this game.
At the time of writing there are only two Race’s, the Orc’s and the Space marines. They do however have some selection within these Race’s, but I am not sure if they have any impact on the gameplay or are just purely cosmetic? What would be good to see, is if you choose to field, let’s say the White Scar’s Chapter, then you will be allowed to field fast attack units etc. The different chapters need to reflect their different fighting styles and abilities.
Would I recommend this game? Sure if you are a fan of the WH40k universe and like challenging tactical games that are turned based. This is as close as you’ll get to the table-top version of the game. The graphics aren’t out of this world, it’s more in keeping with the DOW series rather than cutting edge, but I think that this is a small development team so their resources are going to be tight. I am hoping that this game is developed further and they make available some customisation or editing tools for the community. Out of 10 I would give this a solid 7.5 with plenty of scope for improvement, but its slowly getting there.

Story? Yeah, there is a surprising and quirky story in there. And it isn't half bad. I am interested in how it's all going to tie up in the end. (No spoilers.)
Fun? YES. It is so satisfying to destroy space aliens.
Conclusion: This game is worth so much more than $10. Highly reccommend this title for gamers of all skill levels and backgrounds. In the words of a famous infomercial host "Make like N'Sync and BUY BUY BUY!"

I enjoy it, Ive seen a lot of negative response to this game but personally I dont think there is anything wrong with it. I think a lot of people were going into this game with the mindset that it was a dirt rally 2.

If you're looking for a robust rally racer, go for DiRT Rally instead which is miles better! You can truely feel the G-forces with the camera shaking and compressing while going over bumps and landing jumps (which is immensely satisfying, exhilarating or whatever word suits you, it feels like a f*****g rollercoaster ride) whereas this feature got completely removed with now a static cam. This game is a joke... gravel physics are off (cars don't drift), rwd physics are a complete step backward and you feel like driving over the same road tiles again and again with the procedural track generating flat roads all over the place. The graphics are also much more realistic in DiRT Rally whereas here, the graphics looks dated, uninspired (especially Michigan), the grass cartoonish and tracks surfaces way less detailed.
I could continue on and on as to why this game is a huge letdown, but basically everything Codemasters promised us was all lie because the end product feel exactly like the opposite.
(Please take note though the asphalt physics have greatly improved and although the rallycross content still falls pretty short compared to it's real life counterpart, it feels much better.)
Overall, it feels like they've released this game in the wild quickly as an easy cashgrab as it's apparent this game could have benefited from an extra year of work. It's like, hey, just add an extra 2 rallycross tracks here, that feature there and we're good to go. There is only 5 rally locations which is ridiculous. The devs even admitted themself (I applaud such honesty and transparency) that they've only tweaked the rallycross cars physics and R5 rally cars without barely touching the rest. During DiRT Rally development, they said they could have tweaked the aero of the cars but it would have impacted the driving negatively and now guess what? this is exactly what they've done just to say this time ''hey, we've tweaked the aero'' as press marketing without telling us the existence of all the issues it introduced under the hood, issues they knew about but didn't gave a dam to fix, which is truely a backstab to their fans. I have nothing against the devteam, it's more about how Codemasters handled the situation. And supposedly they're now working on leagues implementation, like why on hell such a massive feature had to be postponed after launch? Oh and still no VR support.
If the physics ever get patched (which I barely think so), this game will still suck because of the track generator ruining the dynamic handling. DiRT Rally have maybe less rally locations, but the fact they're all handcrafted with little attention to details everywhere is spot-on, very immersive and makes it a truly authentic rally experience. There was also hillclimb which got removed from DiRT4 sadly.
I don't recommend this game.

The negative reviews of this game come from people who dropped a few hundred on a realistic racing set up for Dirt Rally. Dirt 4 is definitely more of a game than a sim (even on Sim mode), but its still fun as hell. Its challenging enough without being anger inducing like Rally can be. Rally had handcrafted stages, Dirt 4 has randomly generated ones. They lack that natural feel that Rally captured so well, but honestly these stages are still freaking fun to race on. Also, driving on pavement doesnt feel like driving through super glue like it did in Rally, which is great. This also makes Rally X actually fun. Land Rush (buggies and trucks) takes a race or two to get used to, but holy crap is it fun. I also like how they split up the modern rally cars from the classic ones unlike how Rally lumped the two together. It sucked starting Rally with a slow a$$ old a$$ mini cooper. Dirt 4 puts you in an easy to use Fiesta right from the get go. IMPORTANT POINT!!! The very first track you do, the game feels like its on rails and I laughed out loud, ready to refund it. Be careful. Once you join the world of Wakfu you will find yourself very addicted and you will only be talking to your in-game friends. For those who have lives....BEWARE!

The system is now just an annoying hassle and the support team for this game barely try to assist you if anything happens. The game is buggy and constantly changing for better and worse. I regret spending so much time on this game only for them to ruin it for me.
The ECOSYSTEM in this game.
What do I mean? Wakfu is unique in the sense that the players control the ecosystem of the world which also applies to the shops. If someone chops down all the trees they will be gone from an area forever until someone plants them back. This causes a lot of annoying problems especially because a lot of people just go to an area to "ecoterrorize" it because they are from the enemy nation. Having to plant things back takes a very long time and it is very boring. Things HAVE become close to impossible to find in this game. One of those things are beans...yes, beans. In the NA server Nox you can't find them anywhere and it is only a matter of time before more in-game resources become extinct and you won't be able to craft important items.
That player influence also pollutes the in-game MARKET. In Wakfu there are no npcs that sell you items, everything is sold by other players. You can imagine how this influences the prices of things you need in the game especially if you are new.
From levels 120-145 (I believe) there is nothing to do but grind. Grind the same 3 or so dungeons over and over until you make it to 145. I've spent hours grinding and by the time I quit the game my character was level 134. It just didn't feel worth it to me. Beyond level grinding is the relic grinding. You need to do the same 2-3 hour dungeon to MAYBE get a relic about every 5 runs just to get a good item. It's ridiculous especially in my personal experience where the game glitched and all my relics disappeared (I had like 30) and when I sent in a support ticket they just gave me a rare costume and an emote as conpensation...but all my time grinding was for nothing.
CONCLUSION:This game feels really good in the beginning but late-game it just seriously becomes a head ache especially when you notice all your in-game friends have quit. All the new updates just make the game feel even worse because Ankama only adds things and never fixes what already exists in the game. You're honestly better off watching the series on Netflix but even that is decent at best.

After having played for a good month or so, I have to say, this is a rare find among rpgs. Albeit starting the game is mildly difficult, it's a fun and interesting game to play! For what it's worth, I love this game mostly because it's all about the player.
The economy is not run based on a setup from the developers, it's completely player-based, meaning you can set up shop in the little customizable bag you are given at the beginning of the main part of the game. Not only that, but there are a bunch of balanced, customizable classes you can jump into depending on your play style! Couple that with spells you have to use to improve, gear you can craft/find/buy from others, and all sorts of bonuses like Clan Member bonuses and Guild bonuses, you can increase your stats and quickly find a build for yourself! If that wasn't enough of a hook for the gameplay, you have several opportunities to "Restat", or change up all your spells and ability bonuses!
There are a few major downsides to the game: There are NO NPC characters that are useful. By this, I mean there are no shopkeepers or helpful questline helpers, it's all based on you and your groups. This might be bad for some people, but this means you can literally cut through all the crap with hirelings and stuff, and just find like-minded players to work alongside!
+ The game is simple to work with, using mostly the right and left mouse buttons to control your character and your surroundings.
+ You control the environment! You can decide what crops to take and what all is removed from the area, like herbs, trees, and even the monsters!
+ The economy is easy to understand, you sell anything at whatever price you want! It's up to the player that wants what you have to pay the price.
+ The graphics are good, as well as the sprites and animations!
- There are bugs, as with every game. If you spot something, report it, please, the devs will want to know what is going wrong.
- Guilds are at a downside, as there are what are called Haven Worlds, or a World for your guild members to use. Others can slip in and steal stuff from it if you aren't careful, and you'll want to realize you probably WON'T be getting one for a long time if you're a new or semi-poor guild.
- PvP is included, so those of you who are low-lvl with high professions, beware other players! Some will want to steal all your crops and leave you nothing in return!
- You have to reintroduce anything missing into the environment. If there are no more Ash Trees, to name something important, then if you have the seedlings for it, you'll be forced to replant.
There are ways around all the farming/environment stuff, but until you get enough money to buy the Haven Gems needed, it's a bit much to go after. Alot of the players love to help one another out, so ask questions if you want to know something. That said, enjoy playing Wakfu, and hope to see you in the World of Twelve!
P.S. if you steal my crops, I'll shoot you. It's as simple as that. D:<

Boson X provides a simple and clean endless runner experience with a mixture of randomization. While the characters that you chose only make a difference visually, the game attempts and succeeds in providing a unique set of levels that you will definitely find challenging without some practice. The controls are simple yet may feel difficult if you try to jump like a traditional platformer would.
The only reason I picked up Boson X was to complete the achievements and try out something that I usually do not play. I'm one of those observers that looks at the running genre and wants to run with it but ends up saying no because of price, mechanics, or fear that the product will fall short of my expectations. Boson X  not only met my expectations but blew my mind with some of the crazy levels that were thrown at me.
The objective of the game is very simple: keep on the platforms and try to run on the blue ones. While there are several hazards to look out for, that is the essence of the game. Running on blue platforms will get you closer to completing the level and make you run faster and faster building up tension and excitement when your beat your highscore. Leaderboards are offered and can be fun to push yourself further up the leaderboards after you have completed a level.
The level variety and difficulty is reasonable and able to be mastered to a certain extent. Randomization helps break up monotony and adds to the mystery of what your going to run through next. Levels that I thought were impossible were beatable in a few days of learning the level (and a lot of failing).
During my time of playing Boson X, I have not found any game breaking bugs... or actually any bugs at all.  I can confirm that it works on the Xbox 360 controller as advertised. The game performed exceptionally well and had options to play in window and fullscreen modes. This was especially useful as I was able to practice and play Boson X while watching Youtube or Twitch.
I highly recommend this for anyone who think they might be into runners.

TL;DR: This is a great vareint of chess, with a seemingly small change that affects the tactics of the game. However, it needs a few more features to make it worth 13$.
*my personal bias*
I was in chess club as a kid, and always was excited for my churches chess nights. I have grown up around chess. Recently I have fallen in love with the Warhammer 40k universe, although I cannot play the table top game as my friends are gold fish that are terrified of anything more complex than monopoly. 40k would just spend them into a spasm.
*Gameplay*
Basically this is chess. The units are the same as in chess, and the movements are all the exact same as chess. And any chess captures(like moving a knight on top of a pawn) are always insta kills. HOWEVER, what sets this game apart is the second phase of your turn. There is the movement phase, and then the cool second phase. In this phase your units can do various different abilitys, like shooting, throwing frag granades, and other ablilitys. Although these are not insta kills, they do damage to a unit and overtime the health reaches 0 and that unit is as dead as any captured peice. I think I have killed more orcs by just shooting them then actually capturing them. Also, this is where the sides differ, The pawns of the Space marines have different range, health, armor, and so on than the orcs. TLDNR: If you like chess, 40k and/or liked Battlechess, maybe give this a go if you can play with others.
What's on offer here is a chess based game (including a pure chess game version) set in the 40k universe with a (currently) 10 stage story mission set, multiplayer and vs AI modes.
PROS:
+ Animations and graphics are nice - if you remember and liked Battlechess, you'll enjoy this.
+ Its 40k - always a plus.
+ You do get (limited - like skins) rewards for levelling up as you play.
+ It's not an AAA price tag.
+ The Regicide game mechanic element adds a "twist in the works" to normal chess strategy.
CONS:
- The AI is just really really bad - I'm no chess master but when the AI throws it's queen to be taken by my pawn for no reason, or I can beat the AI moving only 3 pieces, I know it needs work.
EDIT:  Found the AI difficulty setting after writing this review - moved it from "novice" to max difficulty and it handed me my♥♥♥♥♥pretty quickly so ignore the CON referring to the AI!
- Although it is multiplayer, I coundnt get a single game - this may be because I live in the UK however?
- The Regicide game mechanic is pretty much pointless in the games I have played - when you can "take" a piece with a normal chess move that takes 2+ rounds of "regicide" moves to kill otherwise, its just much easier to play chess in a game with Regicide rules and win - however this may be because I have only had the option to play against the AI.
SUMMARY:
I had a fun evening playing this -  I would probably recommend it to any chess fans for fun with online friends.  If multiplayer actually found me a match I'd also be more enthusiastic and perhaps have a more positive take on the Regicide gameplay spin.  However, as it stands from my experience of the game, 6/10 (perhaps 8/10 if multiplayer worked), so yes I'd recommend but with a but!

It's an enormous tug of war for me here to choose between whether this game's pros dominate it's cons or vice versa. In the beginning, you really can't just select a server to play on and then immediately get the hang of the combat mechanics. It takes weeks if not months to completely master the controls (especially the keyboard if one decides to use keys as directional attacks/blocks) in the melee combat aspect of the game. Studying your opponents is especially important in this game, you have to know when someone lands an attack on you (e.g. upper directional attack), there's a very short time within that strike that he will have the opportunity to switch to defensive, and then strike at you in a completely different direction. Because all of this can happen so very quickly, the average "newbie" is extremely vulnerable and confused and really doesn't learn a single thing from this scenario. This is precisely why I think there should be a rank system to the game (hopefully if Taleworlds even decides to make another game after VC), because in the beginning it's easy to find yourself outmatched by people who have played the game for years.
The aspect of the experienced vs. the inexperienced and the vast complexity of hand-to-hand combat in this game is most certainly a major issue, but if you can find yourself playing the singleplayer "campaign", trainers around Calradia and local tournaments will certainly help the player get a better grasp of how the combat system works. Even though there really is no gain in playing this game, other than steam achievements and everything in singleplayer, the multiplayer is still quite exhilarating when you notice your opponent miss a block and then stab him in the face. For all the people who buy this game, as mentioned above, I'd seriously recommend learning about the combat mechanics of the game and practice it in singleplayer before doing anything in multiplayer. I cannot possibly regret all the hours I've spent playing this game, so on that note I'd recommend this game.

To avoid the impression that I see nothing good in Hotline Miami 2 let's go through the good things first:
+New masks!
+New weapons!
+Good soundtrack! (by saying good soundtrack, I mean there were few good tracks tossed in there)
+Alex and Ash! Oh.. okay - this one needs some more details. Alex and Ash is a mask choice that lets you play as 2 serial killers at once. One of them - Ash - has a chainsaw and another has a ranged weapon - any ranged weapon you can find on the ground or the standart pistol that Alex gets at the start of the level. Very fun character despite buggy A.I.. Sad thing is that you can't choose any mask for any level you want now - there are different timelines and different roles you must take, so no - you can't go Fists of Fury every single level. And oh yeah - some masks are very unique, but the total number of masks reduced when compared with the first game.
Now let's get to the truth which is difficult to accept - Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is very hard to recommend. Don't get me wrong - this game is not absolutely bad, but it's a sequel to the Hotline: Miami, and as such it's not very fun. Actually it's far from the original Hotline Miami. Developers tried to make this game more realistic and that created a lot of problems. Let's talk about them. Before I start ranting on the combat system, let me tell that this game isn't as fast as the first one. And pacing really kills that mad blood lust of running without any fear of death from the HM1, because sometimes you have to play boring characters in long cover based shootouts (levels with a detective character are especially guilty of this). Other thing I didn't like was the story. It's forgettable and quite frankly, very generic when compared to HM1's "Acid-Hallucination-Trip with a talking rooster who knows more about what's going on here than you do".
Okay, let's get down to the combat and level design:
-Melee system is now almost useless, because weapon throws aren't as powerful (half of your thrown weapons will drop 10 centimeters away from you and will not reach their target), so you can't stun or kill enemies without firearms as reliably as you could in the original HM. What makes melee even worse is level design. levels are now huge. You can only see very small part of the floor without endangering yourself. You easilly die by the shots that were fired from across the map, where you couldn't even see. Needless to say, levels are now unnecessarily difficult. In the first game every time you died, you died because you made a mistake, made a risky play or just had a bad luck with A.I. (A.I. likes to react to those gunshots that they want to react to). Now you will die much much more and not because of your mistakes - no. You will die as much as it takes for you to remember every single enemy on the map that is 2-3 times bigger than in the previous game. Small rooms and corridors were changed to big open halls and open large rooms full of regular enemies and the larger ones that take ~4 seconds to kill. I know, they were in the first game too, but this time some of them carry automatic rifles and are followed by several soldiers. Also, that room is surrounded by 3 other rooms full of enemies. If you try to kill them all carefully - you will fail. There is little careful planning in this game. That aspect of the game, just like fun melee system, was swapped with running with your gun (or knife if you run out of ammo) from room to room trying to clear them out before you die, so you could catch your breath and thin out enemy numbers as much as possible by luring them to the doorways. Sounds fun? It isn't. It just is not fun, because as soon as you feel that you cleared all the enemies except 1 or 2 that are standing in the room across the corridor you will run there only to get shot in the head by the guy, who was standing under some object that made him almost invisible. You may say that it used to happen in the first Hotline Miami and dying is the part of the game. And you would be correct. You could die by someone you couldn't clearly see and dying was a part of experience - but you have to remember that due to bigger levels, autosaves are now very rare, making you curse this game for killing your character in the cheapest way possible.
When I played the first Hotline Miami, I never raged. For me it was adrenaline fueled run, where every kill was satisfying - especially when going into the room with Fists of fury. In Hotline Miami 2 and its open, large levels it's rarely possible, so prepare to cower behind the corner, fearing for your life when you know the level is about to end, but you must go through the last corridor. And you know that if you slip up just a little bit - click one button a moment too late - you will die and you will have to go through the entire same floor that is big enough to fit 4 floors from HM1. Believe me - at that point no amount of good retro themed soundtracks will help you. Prepare for the endless grinding and a new type of story telling that doesn't really fit the mood of the first game. If you never played Hotline Miami - go buy the first one. If you are not sure if you want buy this game after playing the original - don't bother.
