Tried a bunch of these with 6 people. OVerall a great pack. I really really wish you could alter the round lengths for some of the games like Fibbage and Quiplash. Lots of the games have the option to make them more "family friendly" by removing some questions or, for Earwax, sound effects. The game is perfectly acceptable for young teens though. Its more like normal Telestrations, and definitely not Telestrations: After Dark.
There are streaming features but I have no experience with those.
Fibbage
A classic and great fun. Answer a silly trivia question and try to get others to vote for YOUR answer while you try to pick the real answer. This game needs more rounds. We'd usually play 3-4 in a row.
Quiplash
A fun version of "would you rather A or B?" where individuals answer silly (non-trivia) questions the group votes on their favourite answers. Very much a classic of the series and great to play in groups.
Bomb Corp
An okay "Keep Talking..." knockoff. Each player has a different clue for how to defuse a bomb and you need to work together to defuse it. We only played two rounds before we wanted to try something else but we've all been spoiled by the real deal. Might be better for more casual players. A little too much talking
Earwax
A surprise winner for my group. You're given a situation, and you need to choose a pair of sound effects to go with it. A judge chooses the best. We were all in pain from laughing so hard at some of the answers. Some of the situations were linked to a player, ie. "The only way *player* can wake up in the morning." There are some VERY risqué sound effects without the family filter on. "Sexual Moaning" is.... yeah.
Bidiots
An interesting one. Draw pictures for a very vague clue given, then you have to try to buy other's drawings based on vague clues and drawing values. Its no Drawful but still really fun. A hard game to explain to people but surprisingly fun and difficult.

It still needs some work. The procedural track generation is made up of preset tiles rather than drawing a road and putting an environment around it, so you'll often see the same segments of track repeatedly through various courses, and sometimes within the same track. Pace note delivery can be a little slow with too much emphasis on inconsequential things like negligible bumps and dips. There are a lot of options to be desired as far as multiplayer options go. Headlights don't seem to work on non-nighttime stages in multiplayer (if you have shadows on High or Ultra, the headlights will not illuminate them. Turning shadows to Low or Ultra Low makes the track visible again.) And some other issues.
But on the whole, I'm greatly satisfied with Dirt 4 so far. Dirt Rally felt good at the time, but the vehicles were distinctly floaty, like your were piloting a pat of butter on a hot skillet. Dirt 4 now features realistic aerodynamics and improved weight modeling, the result being that the cars tend to feel grippier than in Dirt Rally -- and this is main dividing factor of the community. Many long-time DR fans feel like D4's handling is far too unrealistic and arcady. An opinion I disagree with.
But I'm having a great time with the game. A friend and I have been playing a ton of multiplayer events, including rally stages, Land Rush with stadium trucks and buggies (the karts are a little too finicky for our liking), and rallycross races. We keep our games Public when we play and almost always have half a dozen random players racing with us. The Pro Tour mode (which is like a matchmaking ranked ladder mode, pitting you against racers of similar skill as you progress through 3 Divisions consisting of 7 Tiers each) is a lot of fun, although this mode is often lacking players to get the best experience from it. I'll often sit for a minute waiting for the minimum number of racers to show up only to reach it (4 players), then people quit when it doesn't launch within 10 seconds and we're left to wait more... It's rather disappointing.
I play with a game pad, and my friend with a FFB wheel and pedal setup, both on full simulation with all HUD settings off. We both fare pretty well, but there are definitely some incredibly skilled racers out there who really put us both to shame.
All told I think it's a fantastic game and I stand by my recommendation.
EDIT: Just felt like I had to state this again after reading multiple negative reviews in a row all claiming the same thing: "I CAN'T MAKE MY CAR DRIFT! IT'S IMPOSSIBLE!" These people clearly have not tried tuning their cars, or they have but don't understand how the variouis settings impact the handling of the cars. If you want to make a 4WD car "drift" around corners, you need to set the torque bias to the rear (putting more power to the rear wheels rather than a 50/50 front-rear split). Then set the center viscous differential to loose. This will allow the front and rear wheels to spin at different speeds (for instance when the front wheels have grip, the rear wheels will still be able to spin at high speed.) These changes alone will tend to allow you to slide the back end of the car around corners with heavy throttle.
If you want to exaggerate this effect, you can stiffen the rear anti-roll bars (making the rear of the chassis more rigid, which will allow the inside wheel to lift off the ground during hard cornering, reducing grip and allowing the back to slide more), making the rear differential stronger (forcing the rear wheels to both spin regardless of differences in grip), reducing negative camber on the rear wheels (negative camber  angles the bottom of the wheels outward so that when the car leans during hard cornering, it actually increases grip... setting camber to 0 or even positive will reduce this effect, again, allowing the rear of the car to drift out.)
There are still more things you can do to make the cars more "drifty" than their  default tunings. Don't listen to the negative reviews claiming the physics are garbage and cars are glued to the ground. They obviously don't know what they're talking about!
After another 40 hours from my initial review, I still conclude that the Your Stage system lacks true variety. Don't misunderstand, there are thousands of possible track combinations, from fast, simple sprints taking a minute or less to complete, to (relatively) long, technical courses that take upwards of 8 minutes to complete, with tons of 1- and hairpin/acute turns. But if they could add more variation in the types of turns, and more variety in the scenery, it would be fantastic. The game could also use longer stages (the longest I've seen is 8.4 km), because it would be great to do some 20 km stages that take 15-30 minutes to complete. And it would be nice to see some transitions between tarmac and offroad sections within each stage. The game is good now, but this added variety could greatly increase the longevity of the game!
And regarding the poor pace note timing: This really only applies to sections of the track with very long straightaways, mainly just Australia. If you tune your 6th gear to be really long so you can reach a higher top speed on these sections, you have to be prepared for the eventual sudden turn at the end. Your codriver will actually give you approximate distances remaining on the straight, and it works well most of the time. The problem comes when there's a blind crest at the top of a climb. You can't see the upcoming corner, and for some reason he deems it necessary to call out the crest... which delays the call for the turn by the half a second you could have used to begin braking. That tiny misstep can ruin your whole race. After a while you learn to watch for it, but early in your time with the game, it can be very frustrating, especially if one of your sponsor targets requires you to play with no restarts or vehicle recoveries. Not to mention the time lost can cost you a first place finish!
Still worth a buy unless you're a delusional armchair rally master who preferred the unreleastic low gravity greased pigs on ice physics of Dirt Rally. (Don't misunderstand me, I ♥♥♥♥ing love Dirt Rally still as well, but it's far from realistic.)

This game looks promising, and could have potential, but ends up wasting what it has with clunky controls and with just how short the game is.
First off, the good points. The graphics are very good, especially the water and the way it flows between rooms. The near-future sci-fi setting is above-average and shows quite a bit of promise.
Unfortunately, the bad points significantly outweight the good for this game. The controls need quite a bit of work. For simply walking around they're fine, but the jumping controls are extremely spotty. I died far too many times because the character wouldn't jump or would jump the wrong direction. Also, the cover system doesn't work consistenly (won't always go into cover when you need it, randomly can't shoot around corners, sometimes randomly jumps out of cover) which makes some of the firefights later in the game quite frustrating.
The sci-fi setting, as interesting as it is, is woefully underutilized. The game supposedly takes place on a floating city, but you never actually see it (the quick glimpse out the window at the beginning notwithstanding). For all I know this could be in a secret underwater base or in tunnels deep below a conventional city.
The water powers are a cool concept, but the clunky controls combined with the fact that you don't actually get them until almost the end of the game and that there is only really one power was a big letdown since it was one of the selling points of the game for me.
Finally, the biggest weakness of this game is just how short it is. I blew through it in 4 hours without a walkthrough and with dying a significant number of times due to the controls. There is no closure on the story (unless it's in a hidden video after the credits). Sure, you stop the bad guys, but what happens to the city?
I feel like the concepts behind this game are solid, the setting and the basic gameplay ideas are spot on, but the poor execution and lack of content really hurts this game.
Unfortunately this game is from 2011 and it's been a long time since the last update so I'm not confident that there will be any further improvements. Not recommended.

I don't normally post reviews, but the experience of this game really left me wanting to say something about  it.
First of all, I strictly recommend this game based on the environments and narrative, and as something to experience and analyse. I wouldn't say it's a good game at all, given how every interactive portion has its bugbears and in some of the standards of games (glitchiness, depth and/or satisfaction of interactivity, voiceacting and character performance) it's lacking. However, if it were a graphic novel or something of that nature it would be very solid, as far as games go.
The game is divided into three acts, roughly associated with gameplay aspects of the game. Act One is almost entirely "platforming," hacking, and learning about the lore of the game. I found the flavour, especially subtle parts interwoven with the gameplay like the horror-esque sounds you hear when near and submerged in water, to be intriguing. Act Two is when you get a gun and start engaging in combat. I never, aside from the end where other rounds are required, used anything but sonic rounds for the gun so maybe I didn't get the full perspective on the combat. What combat I did partake in was fairly entertaining, concussing enemies and utilizing environmental hazards, but dragged on for too long to remain interesting. Near the end of Act Three you get the fabled water powers. After becoming inured to the gun combat, I enjoyed using the water powers to throw objects and disorient enemies. Once I adjusted to the essentially one-note power it seemed as though the buildup throughout the rest of the game hadn't had enough payoff. I felt like the designers didn't allow enough time to figure out exactly how the water powers, simple as they are, affected enemies and the dynamic environment and it would have been nice to gain a power more complex than "use water to lift and move/throw things/people". Even being able to throw the water itself at enemies for a more reliable stun or kill would have been good enough for me.
In short, the game feels like a long demo. At no point in the game do hints on what to do and how to do it stop appearing (by default, anyway), and each of the sections acquainting players with the interactive elements could have been made much shorter to allow more/better-implemented narrative elements, variations in gameplay, or just a more solid version of what it currently is. Like a good demo, what this game leaves me feeling is unfulfilled and wanting more. Maybe that's what the developers intended, and kudos to them for making something that's at least intriguing, but I will be very disappointed if this game is a one-off that they don't build upon or follow up with in any way.

Oh boy, where do I begin...
Back in 2009 when I discovered Mount&Blade, it was pretty fun. The combat system was, at that time, immersive and 'realistic' (for the lack of a better word). I spent countless hours in the arena, enjoying these simple clickfests a.k.a melee fights, day after day (in the demo btw).
Sooo...
The game had its obvious downsides and issues, but as far as I can see, they are  still oblivious to the devs. First and foremost, Mount&Blade franchise suffers from severe gluteus maximus trauma: IT STILL IS HALF-ARSED. Very much indeed, in my humble opinion. The models, the animations, the textures, the sounds, the landscapes: all of it can be improved by an army of great modding community and the mods it produced since the original M&B and Warband were released. Secondly, it doesn't apply only to graphics and audio, oh no. The very basic gameplay mechanisms implemented in M&B, like party and kingdom management, quests, sieges, huge AI battles seem all but finished. When you take a look at how the community managed to improve the 'final' product of them devs, you begin to realise how lackluster and barebones the starting, Native product was -- and you never want to come back. This is sad, very sad. Finally, the DLCs. Heheh. Hehehhehahahhhuahuah...
Oh my, they are sure a treat. Buggy, unfinished, riddled with performance issues, memory leaks, random fps drops... But hey, you get to support devs! The devs that didn't care to improve their product, cause that's what the mods did, and still do as a matter of fact.
Now, don't get me wrong. I really enjoy this game. Maybe not as much as in 2009, but still, I find it really good, and well worth its price, even without discounts. I'd say: buy it, but you probably did already...

To avoid the impression that I see nothing good in Hotline Miami 2 let's go through the good things first:
+New masks!
+New weapons!
+Good soundtrack! (by saying good soundtrack, I mean there were few good tracks tossed in there)
+Alex and Ash! Oh.. okay - this one needs some more details. Alex and Ash is a mask choice that lets you play as 2 serial killers at once. One of them - Ash - has a chainsaw and another has a ranged weapon - any ranged weapon you can find on the ground or the standart pistol that Alex gets at the start of the level. Very fun character despite buggy A.I.. Sad thing is that you can't choose any mask for any level you want now - there are different timelines and different roles you must take, so no - you can't go Fists of Fury every single level. And oh yeah - some masks are very unique, but the total number of masks reduced when compared with the first game.
Now let's get to the truth which is difficult to accept - Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is very hard to recommend. Don't get me wrong - this game is not absolutely bad, but it's a sequel to the Hotline: Miami, and as such it's not very fun. Actually it's far from the original Hotline Miami. Developers tried to make this game more realistic and that created a lot of problems. Let's talk about them. Before I start ranting on the combat system, let me tell that this game isn't as fast as the first one. And pacing really kills that mad blood lust of running without any fear of death from the HM1, because sometimes you have to play boring characters in long cover based shootouts (levels with a detective character are especially guilty of this). Other thing I didn't like was the story. It's forgettable and quite frankly, very generic when compared to HM1's "Acid-Hallucination-Trip with a talking rooster who knows more about what's going on here than you do".
Okay, let's get down to the combat and level design:
-Melee system is now almost useless, because weapon throws aren't as powerful (half of your thrown weapons will drop 10 centimeters away from you and will not reach their target), so you can't stun or kill enemies without firearms as reliably as you could in the original HM. What makes melee even worse is level design. levels are now huge. You can only see very small part of the floor without endangering yourself. You easilly die by the shots that were fired from across the map, where you couldn't even see. Needless to say, levels are now unnecessarily difficult. In the first game every time you died, you died because you made a mistake, made a risky play or just had a bad luck with A.I. (A.I. likes to react to those gunshots that they want to react to). Now you will die much much more and not because of your mistakes - no. You will die as much as it takes for you to remember every single enemy on the map that is 2-3 times bigger than in the previous game. Small rooms and corridors were changed to big open halls and open large rooms full of regular enemies and the larger ones that take ~4 seconds to kill. I know, they were in the first game too, but this time some of them carry automatic rifles and are followed by several soldiers. Also, that room is surrounded by 3 other rooms full of enemies. If you try to kill them all carefully - you will fail. There is little careful planning in this game. That aspect of the game, just like fun melee system, was swapped with running with your gun (or knife if you run out of ammo) from room to room trying to clear them out before you die, so you could catch your breath and thin out enemy numbers as much as possible by luring them to the doorways. Sounds fun? It isn't. It just is not fun, because as soon as you feel that you cleared all the enemies except 1 or 2 that are standing in the room across the corridor you will run there only to get shot in the head by the guy, who was standing under some object that made him almost invisible. You may say that it used to happen in the first Hotline Miami and dying is the part of the game. And you would be correct. You could die by someone you couldn't clearly see and dying was a part of experience - but you have to remember that due to bigger levels, autosaves are now very rare, making you curse this game for killing your character in the cheapest way possible.
When I played the first Hotline Miami, I never raged. For me it was adrenaline fueled run, where every kill was satisfying - especially when going into the room with Fists of fury. In Hotline Miami 2 and its open, large levels it's rarely possible, so prepare to cower behind the corner, fearing for your life when you know the level is about to end, but you must go through the last corridor. And you know that if you slip up just a little bit - click one button a moment too late - you will die and you will have to go through the entire same floor that is big enough to fit 4 floors from HM1. Believe me - at that point no amount of good retro themed soundtracks will help you. Prepare for the endless grinding and a new type of story telling that doesn't really fit the mood of the first game. If you never played Hotline Miami - go buy the first one. If you are not sure if you want buy this game after playing the original - don't bother.

Since I discovered Doorkickers three years after its release, I'll keep this short because there are already a plethora of good reviews out there. I'm always impressed by games that do more with less. Doorkickers is a testament to the fact that good gameplay doesn't require that a game be a 3D AAA title. Of the top-down/issuing-orders games I've played, this one plays the best. If you like turn-based games, you can play in orders mode which allows you to pause the game and give orders to each unit to execute simultaneously. If you want more action, you can control the team in real time (though it's more difficult and you lose some tactical control). Or you can do a mix, issuing orders to some units while controling others. And the amount of missions is very impressive, with more than 80 standalone missions, six campaigns, and an editor you can use to create your own. So if you like top-down shooters, I highly recommend this one, and I eagerly await Doorkickers 2.
The only thing I'd change is the equipment unlocks. New items are purchased by earning stars, so I just saved enough stars to get the best items and I now have little interest in unlocking the rest. To give players more to strive for, I think a "Call of Duty" style of earning gear would be better, i.e., at squad level X unlock gun Y. I think the desire to unlock new gear would give people more incentive to play when they finally complete all the single missions and campaigns.

This isn't exactly easy for me to write, and it sure as hell isn't going to be easy for the fans to read, so I'll start by listing what I love about PVKII. Its Chivalry-like combat system is novel and sometimes quite rewarding. It has a good sense of humor and a sense of place that adds to that humor, to the point where occasionally I found myself giggling while playing.
The whole game is not only generally designed well, but looks and feels great, and it has a purity of form that you don't see often these days (rolling, kicking and certain achievements notwithstanding) - although it remains to be seen how the slow but steady updates will affect this going forward. The dedicated dev team who craft updates in their free time is yet another positive aspect. Community contributions to the game have been usually positive. At the very least, the mechanics of the game generally aren't stagnating somewhere they really shouldn't be. Player titles and parrot customization are both really cool. Basically, the game can be really fun at times.
However, after more than a hundred hours of direct play over several years, and having gotten a number of friends into the game? I started to not only become increasingly frustrated, but I started seeing problems. Problems that aren't exactly fixable by developer manhours, problems which eventually turned me off the game, and they'll more than likely keep me away until or unless the game becomes wildly more popular than it is. It won't, and that is an honest damn shame, because PVKII has had - and continues to have - real passion and work put into it.
I hate to say it, but a lot of those problems stem from the game's playerbase. The central issue is something called the
. Since there are three teams that can all attack each other, it's possible for the two losing teams to fight each other instead of the winning team. Players often indiscriminately hunt and fight each other instead of ganging up on or even paying any attention to the winning team.
Why? It's no real fault of the devs. This is a competitive multiplayer first-person mod with a not-insignificant difficulty curve made with an engine that's 12+ years old at this point. A small community and to a lesser extent players who ignore objectives are problems for ANY competitive multiplayer game, but here the situation is especially bad: a decent chunk of this game's small community seems hellbent on being deathmatchers and killfarmers who play into either the prisoner's dilemma or the apparently unacknowledged need for there to be an official and officially supported deathmatch version of bt_island, which is the de_dust2 of this game. A good helping of toxic gamer culture doesn't improve things.
The problem with being decently skilled in this game is that the aforementioned decent chunk of the playerbase is still plain better than you on average, and you have a much steeper climb in front of you to hold your own against them. Teamwork is important in doing so, and it
happen sometimes! It's still not coordinated often due to the reasons in the above paragraph.
Meanwhile, you're usually facerolling new players so hard I'd wager a good number of them would be roughed up enough to give the game a pass. This is a problem in every game with a small community, as I mentioned before, but here it's compounded by a number of factors. If this game could grab and
a critical mass of players, this wouldn't be nearly as much of an issue, but I cannot say it has the visibility or indeed the gameplay base to do so. It is a real shame.
The achievements are both the icing on the cake and the red flag for me personally. Some of the more recent ones are frankly ridiculous in their difficulty, especially going up against the usual crop of veterans, to the point where they're seemingly
for them. One of them is literally named 'Fifty Shades of Gestir', earned for using all of the Gestir's weapons to kill an opponent and unlocking the title of "The Fetishist", which I find utterly ridiculous yet strangely representative of the toxicity present in the community. A friend of mine outright told me that "the PVKII community has become so inbred that it's eating itself alive", and I'm sadly forced to agree!
I want to like this game, and I want to recommend it, because it can definitely be fun. Unfortunately though, PVKII just proved more frustrating than I wanted to put up with, and for reasons that seemingly cannot be fixed anytime soon. I'm sorry, folks.

What hurts this title in comparison to the broad array of FPS Zombie Survival games is that it offers very little to differentiate itself from other great titles the genre is known for. I guess the big draw is that, at any point in time in a level, you can become a zombie in an effort to infect the other survivors that are attempting to flee the level. This would be fine if it weren't for the fact that zombie combat is so underpowered. And you don't have unlimited lives either. You just become a cockroach until the end of the game. This would be better if there were more players on, but I just don't think it's worth it anymore.
Compounding on top of that sweet new gimmick were zombies not so nerfed, environments are stale. Weapons all feel the same, and there is plenty of ammo. Melee combat feels rigid and beyond janky. While the presentation of mission objectives is sweet, the escort missions feel like they'll never end because of how repetitive the environments and goals are.
At the end of the day, I do have to commend the game for not charging a price for DLC, and the sale price makes it worth giving it a go if you're a fan of these types of games and this is the only title you haven't played.

This is the rally game of my dreams, from the rally school to the best career mode I've seen in a racing game; from the driver and car customization to the classifieds and upgrades; and all the immersive details of rally atmosphere—changing conditions over the running order, stopgap repairs, stopped competitors, driving to the marshal—that contribute to the feeling of taking part in actual events. I’m enjoying the procedurally generated stages, even if I'm intimately familiar with Michigan's left-4-left-3, and left-5-watersplash, I don't know when they're going to come up. Plus the wider diversity in stage lengths over Dirt Rally’s sprint/long options, and the white-knuckle 6th gear straights Dirt 4 can throw up, make up for the repetition in the stages. Of course it'd be great to see even more variety in the tiles, or getting the corner call at the end of a straight earlier, but those improvements should come in future games. I understand others’ concerns about this first go at procedural generation, and the sim handling compared to Dirt Rally (even if those issues haven’t bothered me), but show me a rally game with better random stages—along with the career mode, weather and times of day, and everything else this game offers for the fantasy of being a professional rally driver. As a complete package, Dirt 4 is unrivalled.

I feel kind of bad that this game has a mixed review rating. To be fair, it is not what they advertised it as, which was a successor to DiRT Rally. The game is a lot less of a pure sim than Rally was. That said, it can still be challenging if you want it to be and it also offers a more arcade style of play for those who like to experience rally racing for fun. I personally find myself in the middle. My first DiRT experience was Rally and I purchased it to get away from the never ending derp show that is Need 4 Speed and with how crappy Xbone is, Forza wasn't a real option.
So here we are now, 80 hours later, and I have completed all of the Rally and Rally Cross events and really liked them. It seems like there aren't a ton of vehicles because of how many different racing groups there are. The reality is, though, there are a LOT of different cars. From 80's Group B super cars to modern Ford Focus R5 to Stadium Trucks, there are a lot of very unique feeling vehicles in a lot of very different types of racing. I will go ahead and stop this essay here and just throw out a Pro's/Con's for those considering getting it.
Pros:
Amazing DiRT franchise sound effects
Runs super well (getting 180 FPS @144hz on my 1080)
Courses are well detailed from laser scanned replicas to randomly generated
Cars genuinely handle differently and you NEED to tune them
Good soundtrack
Solid multiplayer experience
Grind is long but enjoyable for solid crew, sponsors, and facilities
play how you want to play with a lot of customisation to game mechanics
Cons:
Not a pure sim, and a LOT of people expected that
NOT a sequel to DiRT Rally
DiRT isn't super big on adding tons of new cars/tracks
Once you beat all the events it's repetitive
They spent a lot of work diversifying rather than making one discipline super expansive
"Feeling" of a car is not as good as Rally if you are playing as a sim
So all in all this game doesn't really deserve the hate it is getting. Sure, if you wanted DiRT Rally 2 you are going to be really disappointed. I understand that, Rally pretty much saved the franchise and people paid full price for an experience promised to be even better. All that said, it's still a great game. It probably reached out to a wider audience than Rally, but it slightly alienated their core fans.
It's a good game. I would 100% suggest getting it when it comes up on sale, then there is no way that it's not worth every penny.

Far Cry 3 was a pleasant surprise for me. I’m not a big FPS fan, and I only buy them rarely. For me this sits with the first Modern Warfare game in terms of quality.

Instead there was an incredible character arc as the Jason Brody escapes a slavery ring and while rescuing his friends, inadvertently starts a revolution that sees the islands put back in the hands of the local tribe. While this is going on he slowly loses his connection to his home you get a real sense of what is going through his mind. Has he become a monster himself? After every person he’s killed does he deserve to go home? Can he go home? Beware when hunting monsters etc.
The only weak point is the boss fights. Too much QTE and I felt suddenly jarred out of the flow of gameplay. That's it.

Ever wanted to play chess but instead of the classic black vs white scenario, you wanted to face off your army of post-human genetically engineered bad-asses against a mob of dumb but relentless orks? Then this is the game for you! This game is essentially chess, and if you don't know what that is then you really need to get out more. The attraction to this pc version of the game however is the fact that the theme is warhammer 40k (which is fricken fantastic) and it also has its own twist on the rules. "Regicide" mode is classic chess but after a movement has been completed you are given an additional phase. In this phase you use initiative points to activate different abilities (snapshot for concentrated damage, krak grenade to lower a pieces armor value, etc) and this completely changes the strategy you need to employ, because pieces can be removed from play without being taken by other pieces. In other words, this is no longer an average game of chess. In conclusion, with the amount of time I've spent with the game I can easily recommend this to any pc gamer looking for a game with a high difficulty, or a solid version of chess.

Dirt4 is a bitter-sweet affair in my opinion.  It built upon Dirt Rally and Dirt 3 in many ways but there are a few things that leave me wanting.
Pros:
+ Visually stunning and runs well.
+ Changable weather in stage adds extra challenge (duststorms in Australia are murder!).
+ Small touches such as random stage events are a nice extra boost to immersion.
+ A good selection of vehicles and a team management (more on this in a bit).
+ Choosing between handling modes is great to attract more people to the game.
Cons:
- The live stage feature that was inspired by Grid 2's similar course generating system leaves uninspiring courses that you can count where various sections have been reused within stage (I counted 3 significant course elements repeated 3 times during a 10 mile stage).  I don't think this feature was particularly outstanding in many people's mind when Grid 2 launched originally.
- Sponser objectives are not varied enough to actually change up the way you drive to meet them (e.g. x number of clean stages or x number of fastest splits seem to continously come up.
- Pro stage matchmaking has only ever matched me twice despite logging in repeatedly almost daily.
Suggestions:
Dirt4 still is really a new game and I'm sure that Codies are still working on it.  Most of the con's that I have listed were mainly due to trying to keep working hours down but you still really can't beat blasting through stages like Sweet Lamb where each turn feels unique. The amount of locations have been brought up time and time again across the threads with people saying that Michigan is a cheap replacement for Finland is something that I agree with.  In Dirt 3, Michigan had a totally different feel to Dirt4's interpretation and I would have felt that the former's direction would have been a better choice.  I am expecting that Codies probably has the idea of adding locations from Dirt Rally and even Dirt 2 into the game and I feel that it would be a good move.  Events such Malaysia and LA would provide a different spin and challenges on what is currently on offer.
The absence of Trailblazer events and Hillclimb (mainly due to the licensing issue with Pikes Peaks) also leaves a hole that can be filled.  Trailblazer events in previous games used combined rally stages to form the tracks, surely the engine improvements here can do the same thing as we already have stages over 10 miles long?  Maybe a return to Japan should be on the cards as an alternative to Pikes Peaks. We have seen touge in the Grid series so could it be a too larger leap to incorporate it here?  We also see many hillclimb events in Europe too so maybe that can be an alternative to the classic american location?
Overall:
Dirt 4 like Grid 2 was a sequel that was excellent in many ways but flawed in others.  It is still an enjoyable thrash into the world of offroad racing but this is not Dirt 2 or the original CMR series reimagined.  Codemasters have done an excellent job so far with the game and I'm sure we will hear news about what is in the pipeline for the future soon, but I think we should take a step back and look at it's main competitors which used Early Access (like Dirt Rally) and Betas to actually produce a game where it felt more complete.  Maybe closer working with the community for the next Dirt which doesn't have the same time constraints that the F1 series would be beneficial for all.  I see Dirt4 has a lot of potential so currently recommending it but please Codemasters, don't let this title grow stale.

Driving physics from Codemasters is my favorite.  Race historic cars, stadium dirt tracks, and try out some new rally cross cars to unlock the triple crown.  Multiplayer with your friends is super fun.  But the only time i am able to get rally pro tour matches is on the weekend.  I guess that's when everyone has time to log on.

I was trying to like it, but everytime I play, I could not complete a full race because I was getting annoyed by the handling.  The handling is very poor compared to Dirt Rally. An average sim racer with a good set of FFB wheels and pedals will definitely not appreciate the driving physics and handling of Dirt 4, especially Dirt Rally sim racers.  For players using the keyboard or a joystick, they may probably like this game because it is very easy to control, all they need to do is press those buttons, unlike hard core sim racers who use skills and most part of their body to play the game.   I liked Dirt Rally more than Dirt 4 because it is more intense and having a good set of wheels and pedals makes it more realistic and I felt like I was really driving a rally car.  Each turn  in Dirt Rally requires skills and eventhough I have played a particular race track hundreds of times, they are still very challenging, and one single mistake can make you crash and lose seconds.  Dirt 4 did not impress me like Dirt Rally using my FFB wheels and pedals, that is why I cannot recommend this game to Sim racers.

Coming from Dirt Rally (and only having played in simulation mode), i've got to say i'm dissapointed. This game is made for the masses, not for the Dirt Rally fans.
Simulation mode is very different from Dirt Rally. Where DR feels light and predictable when it comes to oversteer/understeer, Dirt 4 feels heavy and has loads of grip. The difference is when you do find some oversteer, you're going to hit whatever the car's heading for, no matter what you do. In DR i was able to control the oversteer in almost all cases. Hopefully some of this can be "fixed" with updates.
There are also some improvements. The menus look better, loading times are looking good, and the time penalties department has been in improved. So does that make up for the dissapointing driving expererience? Not for me.
Do i recommend this game? If you're coming from Dirt Rally, no (or not at this point). If you coming from Dirt 3 or pretty much any (non-sim) racing game, yes.
EDIT: This game has been out for almost three months now, and nothing has been done to inprove the points i mentioned above. So it goes from recommended to not recommended. Sloppy play, Codemasters.

Ive seen alot of bad reviews for H&G.
I agree with some, disagree with others. Its still Beta so tkae that with a grain of salt.
The Devs do take into consideration what the community likes and dislikes.
For starters I play the Russian faction so my opinion is a bit biased, I feel that like most gamers though... I am a glutton for punishment. What kills me the first 5 times teaches me not to do the same ol crap when attacking a new obj.
Some things are lopsided from time to time, more often than not the Russians are WAY outmatched. But theres good reason for it.
The game has two options to play, one not readily accessible at the time of Download unless your willing to pay, or grind a soldier up to a high enough level.
Heroes- 1st person shooter
Generals- Strategic European map overview.
Having not played the strategic side yet, I've no opinion one way or the other, but from what I've seen on youtube and after playing the FPS side of the game I can't wait until I get to that point.
People complain about having to pay to be a general... I find this pointless since you earn "war-funds" to deploy assault-teams on the strategic map by playing the Hero aspect of the game. You can buy these warfunds... but after leveling up a soldier through the ranks to become General, one should have enough war funds to have fun in the strategic aspect of the game. In other words, learn the ropes of the game first by playing the FPS side of the game, pile up some resources and use them according with what you've learned through playing boots-on-the-ground war.
Alot of folks say the starting-out weapons suck... I'm no FPS pro, I have a day-time job and not too much free time, but I was able to keep a 1.5 Kill-Death ratio throughout all my time playing even with those starter weapons. And after you've grinded through a couple levels/ribbons, it is VERY gratifying to add an upgrade to your weapon of choice.
Folks also complain about not being able to change loadouts during game, this is only true to an extent. You can change by exiting the match, picking your new loadout and rejoining. It kinda sucks but theres a reason I don't mind it too much.
You earn badges in the game that give you slight buffs in a wide variety. Some add more stamina, one allows you to take a bit less damage, another allows you to carry more explosives, while another (my favorite) allows you to move silently.
If I join a match and your loadout is set up to kill infantry with a badge that gives me more stamina, but the opposing side has a ton of tanks, Ill exit out and grab a badge that allows me to carry more anti-tank grenades and change my loadout accordingly. The matches range from 10 minutes to maybe an hour and a half.
As I've said, the game is still beta, its being fine-tuned, but its free and totally worth a try if you like FPS's.

Boson X is a minimalistic runner with very simple gameplay. However, that's all it needs; the execution is almost flawless and the game is very fun, challenging, and addicting.
Boson X is based around one main mechanic that involves rotating the world as you jump, allowing you to leap to either side of you or straight ahead. By running on glowing blue platforms, your score (and speed) will increase; victory is achieved by scoring 100%. As mentioned above, while the premise is very simple, each level is distinctly different from one another and some even include special hazards.
$3 gives you 18 levels with huge replay value. The price is exceptional for what the game offers, but if you aren't convinced, there is a free version on the
with 6 levels (and one less character skin).
Overall, Boson X is a great game and I definitely recommend it.

Updating This Review from formerly Nov 7, 2014
Wakfu is a unique game like most have already told you, it mixes MMO with turn-based battling ALA Final Fantasy Tactics and to a lesser extent, things like X-com, though the visuals may seem cartoony the game is still very complex in my opinion and you need awareness and quick-thinking to fight some higher level enemies with specific mechanics and priorities in battle. The sad thing about Wakfu is that it has changed several times in the past years, some for good and some for bad. I still stick with my original belief that this is a fun game with the potential for enjoyment for a lot of people.
The Good :
Character builds and customization are great, although the last change to the system limited potential, I still am able to make builds that are to my flavor and effective in combat past level 150+ where I currently am.I use the heroes system they have to play my myriad of characters who usually complement each other in some way. The Heroes system was in beta for some time, and essentially just allows you to play three characters on your account for a fee. (Booster + Heroes System costs around the same amount as a standard MMO sub).
The Challenge system in this game adds much needed variety to farming, though some challenges are left better suited to particular characters in the game. Being turn based, you're able to effectively "backstab" enemies for more damage on your turn by being behind them. Some challenges require all enemies be killed this way for a bonus to exp and drop rate. Sometimes its worth it, sometimes its not, choose how to spend your time and you may cut your grinding in half.
Dungeon System in this game is interesting, and it is good for the most part, being able to set dungeons to an easier difficulty for less rewards or making them extra hard for potentially double the rewards is great for people who need to learn a boss mechanic or feel up to overpowering a boss/groups and getting a better chance at those rare/unique items they seek so desperately.
The community in Wakfu has always been an interesting one, somewhere between hospitable to passionate individuals who try their best to work with Ankama and revive this dying game. They love the game, and so do I, and I wish to see it thrive. It shows when I login and people are hanging out, talking about strategies, calling for dungeon runs, selling their stuff, and generally just wanting to have fun together.
The Bad :
Wakfu is a hard game to get into past a certain point, while being visually welcoming to those of a young age, you will quickly understand the elemental system and either learn to memorized enemies weakness/strength or grow frustrated as your damage is abyssmal because you forgot X monster was strong against X element.
The customization for the game as far as battles has become a little more limited since the changes, and you will see optimized builds (like any other game) are almost necessary with the lack of choice. Though you can skimp on one or two skills, always having the core ones assures near maximum potential for damage/survivability especially against enemies who may have strong resistances against two of your three elements which each character has access to spells for.
Grinding can be pretty bad unless you have friends to run dungeons with, and the shame is that the heroes system while making it fun for soloers, makes going in with randoms more unnecessary as well. With just yourself and a single other friend paying a premium subscription you can practically do all dungeons in the game, or six box accounts like some have in the past.
They somewhat recently changed how gear in the game drops, claiming it was for more "unique builds" with elements being rolled out randomly with gear but this has just made rerolling stones more valuable and frustrating. Now you can't simply get a set and use it, you have to get the elements for your build correct as well. Just a chore, really, along a lot of other systems in the game unless you nibble at the grinding of mats, tokens, and crafting a bite at a time.
Ankama mostly puts out cosmetics while delivering small trickles of actual content, changing the game seemingly with no input from the community (Though you see when Flat responds in the forums all the time) and its moreso they can't seem to filter the "bad" suggestions from the "good". Bugs still exist in the game for 3+ years ago. Oddly enough its their birthday for this game as of writing this and I feel like the cake is a little stale.
The Overall TL;DR Version
Wakfu is a game I love, and this review is probably biased as hell, but I am aware of it. In saying that, would I recommend this game to new people? Yes, for a while, levels 1-50 might be fun to dabble in but once you get 80+-100+ is when the game "starts" and thats when it will either make you or break you. Do I think its worth playing right now? Maybe? Depends on how much you can tolerate. Bugs, graphical issues, optimization problems, class balances, promises both delivered poorly or well, or not at all plague this game. It has its faults. THIS GAME IS NICHE AS **** AND YOU SHOULD KNOW THAT GOING IN! Besides that, I enjoy it, I put away my 13 dollars a month for it, even when I don't play, because some days its just fun to hop in, say hello to my guild, kill a few things, bake a couple of loaves of bread, and then go on about my day.
The game features 17 unique classes, all with strengths and weaknesses, healing or tank, positioning or dps, and mixtures of both. Not gender locked, lots of cosmetics to buy, emotes to find, places to explore, and all set in an open-world environment (For grinding mobs). There are a handfull of big "Quests" to do at certain levels such as 50, 100, 110, etc that will boost you a few levels.
Heroes system allowing to play 3 classes/combos at once. Guild level up system, pvp (Haha don't), and a few other things you'd come to expect quality of life wise like teleports and lore. While the game is not pay to win, the premium sub makes this "easier" to deal with. The typical 30% "faster" for premium sub, but if you don't want to invest, you can still eventually get there...albeit in a car with one flat tire.

Having played through and beaten this game (non-Steam version) before the Rebirth update, I wanted to see what the changes were. What I found were more detailed in battle character sprites, new music tracks, smoother gameplay, better dialogue, and now I get to have achievements and trading cards with the Steam version. It's a solid RPG. With a great story, challenging bosses, good combat, really good music, and memorable characters (especially Xiria) you can't go wrong.

The developers tell me it's a limitation of RPGMaker but this game won't run properly on large monitors. It's fine at a lower resolution though, and a resolution screen pops up every time before the game launches, so it isn't a hassle. Still, be prepared to play in windowed mode for the entire game.
Perhaps this is another RPGMaker problem but there's no "objective" screen. At least, I can't find one. So if you miss what a character says (or forget) then you'll be looking for a guide or wandering aimlessly until you figure it out.
Aside from the technical difficulties, the game is good. Not as good as a professionally made RPG but still solid. The enemies lack variety, you'll see the same creatures over and over, a some of them spam annoying poison attacks, but at least you've got a healer in your party who can cure you for a small amount of MP.
You'll run into challenging monsters who are levelled just right so they're not unbeatable. Grinding feels effective but very tedious after a while.

It's, uh...not good.
This is an RPG-Maker game, which is a bad sign. In the right hands, RPG-Maker is a powerful tool that can be used to make a low-budget game that's actually worth playing. This isn't one of them.
It does a few somewhat interesting things: random battles can be seen ahead of time, thanks to a handy bar at the top of the screen on the world map; the characters will talk breifly after a battle is over; and the story is completely unorthodox - but despite these few redeeming traits, it's clear the author of the game has no idea how to really /make/ a game.
Yeah, you can move around and do things and fight things, but from the get-go the main character is extremely unlikable and we're given no reason to care whether he lives or dies. The story is also bizarre; when the game first started up, I thought it was going to be a reversal of the typical RPG hero story - y'know, where you play as the good hero from humble beginnings and gain strength and beat the bad guys. I was actually kind of excited to play through an evil overlord's rise to power. Then the game time-skips past all of that to when the empire is already formed. ...And that's about where I stopped playing.
I could go on, but I don't think I have to. It's really, really not worth your time. I'm sorry, game creator, but brush up on basic storytelling before trying anything like this.

I think I'm getting sick of RPG Maker games.
The outdated graphics, battle system, and overused stock items, characters avatars, etc. gets to be quite boring over time.
It's also worth nothing that the majority of RPG Maker games do NOT support Steam Overlay, so you can't even SEE the achievements you earn as you earn them, and you need to alt tab to see any messages. This is worth skipping games in the engine for that reason alone unless your not very social or don't care about Achievements, but I found this to be a negative.
I generally only play these games for the battle system, so I'm not really going to say much about the story, but the battle system is rather generic.
The problem I have with this game is that all you do in battles is use special moves and heal. As your team levels up, you will begin to do insane amounts of damage in the 1000s which means any weak attacks is a waste of time.
The flow of the game is basically going from one town/dungeon combo to another, fighting about three of the same enemies in boring dungeons using your most powerful specials, and buying ether to keep the MP up.
You will get a flock of similar characters (almost all female) to join you as you progress, but you will eventually find that only some of them are strong enough to invest your time in.
I did read a lot of the story, but I found it to be rather boring. The music and sound effects are nothing special either.
I never once considered this game to be fun, exciting, or creative.
There are better RPGs to play, using better more updated game engines. Don't waste your time or money here like I did.

Just My Opinion that Dirt 4 is the best Rally game yet for sure. Ive played many of them and dont really write reviews, but after putting in a few hours i have to say im really enjoying it.  Im actually pretty surprised the reviews are 'Mixed' instead of mostly positive.
Instead of going into detail (because i dont have time) i would just like to say i agree with most of the positive reviews here. Just wish more people would get buying it because the Competative Matchmaking just take forever. Not had one race because i cant sit in a que for more than 15mins, but the single player career mode is awesome.

Graphics
- There is a lot of people saying the graphics are a huge downgrade from previous titles which is not entirely true. Lighting and textures are a lot better than before. The only thing that looks bad to me is the foliage, especially on Michigan tracks.
- At current time, optimization is still really bad. The game barely runs at 60fps for me while dirt rally had steady 140fps. Knowing how Codemasters supported previous titles, I strongly believe that this will be improved in future patches.
- Car damage is better than before but it still is long way from realistic. You can still hit a tree ending up with barely a scratch.
Sounds and Music
- Car sounds are literally the best I've heard in any other racing game. It's a pure masterpiece, simply nothing to complain about here.
- Music is also awesome, easily the best soundtrack we had in dirt serial so far.
Physics
- People that say this is not dirt rally 2 and therefore we shouldn't expect it to be one are wrong. It's a worthy successor to both dirt 3 and dirt rally and Codemasters advertised is as one. As most of you already know, there are 2 handling models to choose from "Gamer (similar to dirt 3)" and "Simulation (similar to dirt rally)". I am mostly going to talk about the Simulation one, cause that's what I played with for most of the time.
- Simulation handling model is really an improved version of dirt rally handling model with some bugs to it. Overall it feels more realistic to me which is exactly what they aimed for. Braking is improved, cars feel heavier, tarmac physics is much better now.
- The biggest problem I see here is with the RWD cars as they feel way too stable now but it seems to be more of a car setup problem. Messing with car setups I was able to make them drive better (similar to dirt rally) so saying that this handling model is fully arcade and has nothing to do with dirt rally is a total lie. I also strongly believe that Codemasters will work on this in future patches as Paul Coleman already confirmed.
- Gamer handling model is for all of people that enjoyed dirt 3 but thought dirt rally was too hard although it feels slightly harder than the one from dirt 3.
Career mode
- It is a blast. There is much more stuff to do now. You can take part in championships in these 4 disciplines: Rally, Rallycross (short circuit races with rally cars), Land rush (races with trucks and buggies) and Historic rally (rally with older cars).
- There is also joyride mode which includes some of the elements from dirt 3 gymkhana, it's a great mode when you just want to have fun.
- Team management is also greatly improved. You can customize your team name, livery, sponsors and even buy facilities that allow you to hire more engineers, have more cars etc. I really like the new staff hiring system which not only allows you to hire engineers but even co-drivers and spotters. I think we might see new co-drivers added in future updates or dlcs.
- Another new thing is vehicle upgrades. This time you can choose to buy different parts for your car with grade scale (worst E to best A) which will affect the overall durability. For example, gearbox with grade A will break harder than gearbox with grade C.
- AI needs to be fixed. At times I would beat the AI by 20 seconds and at times even with a perfect run would lose by 20 seconds.
Gameplay
- Rally and Historic rally. There are 5 locations for rally driving (Spain, Australia, Michigan, Wales, Sweden). All of the tracks are now generated with this new thing called "Your Stage" which really adds a new feel. You really need to listen to your co-driver now in order to complete a stage. The only flaw I see here is that some of the stages can have 2 or more identical corners. It still feels better than having limited amount of stages which you can learn after some time.
- Rallycross. It is way more fun than in dirt rally. Tarmac physics is vastly improved which is best seen during rallycross. There is more tracks than before (these are all real life tracks, not generated).
- Land Rush. I found it more annoying than fun on simulation mode but it still adds more variety to the game. Not too much tracks here.
- Pacenotes can get really weird at times. Sometimes you get them way too late and sometimes right 5 would feel more like right 3 etc.
- There is so many little details added. While rallying you will occur other drivers wrecked cars parked next to a track, drones flying over you, co-driver radio signal jamming, gearbox making weird sounds when damaged, brakes squeal sound when damaged etc. It really adds up to overall immersiveness.
Multiplayer
- Daily, weekly and monthly challenges are the same as in dirt rally with one big difference. As I mentioned before, all of the tracks are generated meaning you can't practice and learn the track before driving the online event.
- There is also a jam session that allows you to drive rally, rallycross and landrush against other people online.
- They also added "pro tour" where you race against other people with similar rank in order to rank-up/down. Something like matchmaking from csgo.

If I had to sum up Hydrophobia in three words it would be "two-thirds awesome".  What I mean by that is that the first two acts of the game are really quite good, mixing together something that is a blend of parkour, exploration, and wonderfully detailed water physics.  It's only in the third act that things go a bit pearshaped.
First though, let's talk about the good.  The most obvious is, of course, the water physics.  Oh man does this game spend a lot of time on water physics.  It flows, moves, cascades, splashes, washes over things, shows visible eddies and flows, and pushes things around as it is manipulated.  Most importantly though, your character reacts to it believably.  At no time did I feel like I was witnessing some badly out of place animation or hacky changeover from walking to swimming physics.  That also helped with the game's immersion greatly, which is good because the world presented in Hydrophobia is fairly interesting.  Though it doesn't go into much detail about the history and backround of the world, the game's areas are rich with ambiance and little touches that make it feel well designed and deep.
Another tally in the good category are the game's "puzzles", such as they are.  While less a matter of clever puzzling and more a matter of "find the thing you need to shoot, push, or interact with", there's a lot of creativity involved in getting to those things sometimes. There's a clever little hacking minigame that comes up where you basically match a waveform, which is delightfully satisfying without being too easy.  More often than not it winds up being some mix of water trickery or environment climbing a la Prince of Persia, which brings me to my next good thing: your character's parkour moves.  Much like the interaction with water, at no point did I feel like I was watching some crap animations play out while my character progressed along the game's expected linear path.  Movement felt smooth, limber, agile.  The controls for all this climbing could have been explained better, but once I figured them out it was easy enough.  It's satisfying to watch too.
Okay, so on to the other stuff: the bad stuff.  What's bad in this game?  The combat, mostly.  To be fair, in the first two acts it's not bad so much as just there, enemies serving more as other obstacles to get around.  The interior of the ship is littered with environmental hazards you can use to trip up enemies, which is amusing, and if you have to shoot it out with them the single gun you get is decent enough.  Where it becomes a problem though is the third act, because the third act is focused almost exclusively around combat rather than all the exploration and water puzzles you'd been getting good at.  If combat was a bit snappier and less, well, repetitive and tedious then it wouldn't be so bad.  As it is the transition makes you feel like you wandered into the wrong game by accident.
With that going badly for it, the third act makes things worse by committing a few of the big no-nos of game design.  Probably the worst example I can think of is spawning more enemies in areas you just cleared as you get closer to them.  One area in particular was utterly maddening, as I would clean out the area before proceeding across a rather narrow exterior walkway, only to come around and find a guy popping into existence just in time to shotgun me in the face.  I don't mean he came out of a nearby door (there weren't any) I mean he literally appeared in a formely empty space and started shooting me.  In previous acts the additions of new waves of enemies was justified by your actions activating alarms, with said enemies coming from nearby doors.  In the third act all pretense is dropped, and the game suffers greatly for it.
I can't comment on the final boss, other than to say that unlike virtually everyone else I found it ridiculously easy (water powers, throw barrel, repeat).  I do think it was a bit out of place given the rest of the game at least.  The ending is a bit abrupt - you can tell they were trying to sell this as being episodic or needing a sequel - but it at least has some resolution to it.
The only other thing I can say gameplay wise is that the game's "water powers" are squandered in the most tragic of ways.  Though the controls are a little counterintuitive, the biggest problem is that you get them for an incredibly brief time.  While they aren't amazing, they are at least impressive, and yet I had maybe a half hour of gameplay to use them before I'd reached the end.
With all of that said, I still had fun playing Hydrophobia. The core of the gameplay is fun, the story is a bit simplistic but engaging all the same, and the characters are memorable and easily likeable/hateable as appropriate.  As I said, I love the ambiance of the game, and I would enjoy seeing more content set in the same world, be it a sequel or something else.  I think I got my money's worth out of the game, but I hope that if there is a sequel the developers keep the puzzle-exploration to combat ratio a bit more consistent throughout it.

I liked the fact that there were objects that could be blown up to kill enemies, which left some room for creativity. There is a mechanic for hiding behind walls, which is pretty useful and effective. The mechanic for hacking is pretty standard, just matching sine waves together.
The real star of the show was the water, as it was beautiful and the physics were amazing. Unwater challenges were difficult, as the physics changed when you fought underwater, and certain areas were hard to get past without running out of breath. Left 4 Rats 3 - The Vermining; A lot of people compare this game to L4D, and rightly so. It's almost a perfect clone. I know this because I've read nearly every review on Steam for it. Consumer research folks. I don't say the former in a negative light though. Left 4 Dead was / still is one of my favorite games, and one of the few online multiplayers I've sank any time into. Instead of making vermin jokes and talking about the similarities of the two titles, I'll leave some footnotes;
Pros:
+ It's fun with all one other person I know who plays it. (if you're reading this, add me, I'm not total trash at it) We beat the story mode, and all the side missions and had a ball. Even when we died horribly.
+ The learning curve isn't so steep that new players are handicapped at the start screen. (Smite...).  Kill stuff, beat the mission, and get a new (sometimes dupe) weapon, or Trinket. Revel in glory, and repeat.
+ The random encouters make each run feel different, as with the random item spawns. It makes you have to adapt to the situation, and adds some excitement. Nothing makes you crap harder to burn all your ammo on trash enemies for fun, only to be met with a Rat-Ogre around the corner.
+ The sound design is great. The enemies feel 'alive' right before you turn them into paste with a hammer. Their little squeeks and insults are darling. It's worth mentioning that the enviromental effects are also very good. Lightning sounds like lightning. The steel sword clinks when it his armor. It's all very well done.
+ Level load times are quick, considering the size of the maps. Im sure they load mostly on the fly, but it doesn't hiccup when the map is being generated. I'd take one big map over 5-6 little grinder maps. Keeps me engaged in the game more, I think. 2-3 of the maps feel similar, but aren't purposed the same. i/e One may be a straight run, while another is a objective (protect / destroy target), and another may be an item collection mission.
Neut:
= I run a potato, so I have no idea what the game 'should' look like.
= The 360 controls, while better for dodging attacks, feel sloppy. KB controls just fine.
= It's Left 4 Dead with rats. Special / Boss enemies are entirely transparent to that extent. It works though. [oops]
= The end-game loot system / character progression doesnt break anything, balance wise.
= The in-game 'Tomes' and 'Grims' you can collect is hard to do with less than 3 human players. You can manipulate the bots into carrying one, but it's a chore making sure they dont dump it for a medki- Health potion. So your end game rewards often suffer as a result.
= Has hats... At least there's no pay to win B/S. Item crafting works well enough, despite the grind it takes to get anything worth while. It's slow, but atleast it's all in-game, and not credit card dependant.
Cons:
- The game does not feel finished, not to the point of a gold code release (1.0+). I dont have a top-end machine, I have a morgage. I have all the settings down to potato, and there are times when the game dips to 10-15 fps. I can only deduce that there is some engine problems, that I HOPE get fixed / patched / what have you.
---->  If I can run Fallout 4 on 'med' at [read; playable] 45+ fps, than antything else should run at atleast 30+ on low. And Fo4 is optimized like pure♥♥♥♥♥♥
- Often times, you will run right into a random enemy pack spawn, and as a player, really breaks the flow of things. It looks like a blackhole is giving birth to 100 Jimmy Falons'. SOME GAMES are much better at enemy spawns, you know, like L4- nevermind. Either way, that shouldn't happen. It just looks / plays gross.
- The bots. Period. I know it's meant to be played online with people. But still, there's no excuse for how dumb they are. If I want to be a socio, and not play on a team, I shouldn't witness death, after defeat, after death, because the bots thought transversing the map to kill a Gas-Rat was Delta-Level 5 Mission Priority.
Overall;
I feel like this could, and should be a household name like it's older, uglier brother 'Lefty'. It's fun, addictive, and has tons of replay value. I know I personally have to upgrade my setup, but despite that I have a good time playing. Maybe I'll wet my feet into an actual 4 man game. Until then, pardon me while I go scoure the wasteland for glue...

This game is EXTREMELY overrated. Most of the appeal for this game stems from nostalgia, and if you don't have any such nostalgia, then, like me, you won't view this game to be God's gift to 3D platforming like all the fanboys would lead you to believe.
Now, the following is from the view of an outsider looking in; I never played this in the time it came out, so I'm looking at the aspects of the game compared to more contemporary games I've played.
So, what's BAD about this game?
Well, for starters, the voice acting. 95% of the time, it sounds like the voice actors are reading off of teleprompters. Special mention goes to Rouge. I find my hand rapidly connecting with my face almost every time she opens her badly animated mouth.
Which leads us to another problem: inconsistent lip-syncing. Sometimes the characters' words match up with the movement of the mouth no problem. But, most of the time, their mouth movements are
out of sync.
Now, on to actual gameplay.
Sonic and Shadow's stages are okay. You get to blaze through the level at high speed (most of the time) like one should when taking control of these speed demons. However, enemy placement is NOT one of the strengths of these levels. you have been warned.
Tails and Eggman's stages aren't that bad, but one logical issue that really bugs me is, when they hold onto those rope lifts, how do they stay in their mechs without their arms getting ripped out of their sockets? I'm sorry if this seems trivial,  but I can only suspend my disbelief so far.
Now, onto the WORST stages: Knuckles and Rouge's. I wish the aforementioned bad voice acting was the only problem here, but no, there's worse. The biggest problem I've seen thus far is the dig mechanic. As many of you probably know, when you're close to the emerald piece (or whatever random item the game wants you to find), you hear a beeping noise and see an indicator of how close you are. When you're EXTREMELY close, an exclamation point appears above the character's head. The problem is, it does so within a certain radius. In the event that the piece is w/ an enemy, in a box, or out in the open, this works just fine. However, in the event that it's buried in the ground or in a wall, your job is made INFINITELY more difficult, as the game is very anal about the digging hitboxes. If you're even a MILLIMETER off, then you aren't getting that item, pal. This is made worse by the fact that except for the first stage for both Rouge and Knuckles,
has at least one item buried somewhere. Happy hunting, sucker!
One final note: boss battles.
The boss battles are shamefully terrible for a Sonic game. That's all.
So, not factoring in nostalgic appeal, this game is "Meh" quality at best, and "Oh god, someone pour me a glass of Clorox!" quality at worst. It may have been mindblowing back in the day, but it has NOT aged well.
Put simply, if you aren't considering buying it due to nostalgia, you're better off spending the cash elsewhere.

Back when I was eight, I was obsessed with Sonic Adventure 2 Battle on the Gamecube, and it remained one of my favourite games during my childhood. Now moving on to this release, I am completely baffled why it was promoted in some areas as a "HD" release, as besides from being able to switch to HD resolutions, the game's graphics are practically the same res as they were on the original release. Besides this minor complaint, the game runs excellently, although it has aged a bit in a few ways, particularly the graphics (it was released in 2002, though!) and some of the dialogue is cringeworthy at times.
Although the game is generally enjoyable, it sadly suffers from a number of flaws, the most apparent being the utterly dire camera design which can lead to you missing platforms and falling to your death. And the level designs, whilst quite good in some places, begin to turn grind-heavy towards the end of the game, and whilst this does make it more challenging, the rail jumping mechanism is very unreliable making jumping from rail to rail quite difficult.
Musically, the game sounds amazing - unlike most games of its time Sonic Adventure 2's soundtrack is almost fully orchestrated, with real instrumentation rather than MIDI ones. If I had one complaint, it would be that the rapping in Knuckles' level music is a bit cheesy, but it manages to make up for it by being relatively subdued and not completely in your face.
As a whole, f you're looking for an introduction into 3D sonic games, I'd highly recommend SA2 along with SA1, as they're both great games if you can overlook their numerous flaws. However, if you're willing to acquire SA1 I recommend looking into installing BetterSADX for the Steam version as it fixes so many issues that are present in the Steam release.

VERY basic game for a 3d mmo. While AE does 2d games great, this is their first 3d attempt.. So yea, has almost none of the features you'd expect from a 3D mmo these days eg:
- Forming parties.
- Trading.
- Really just interacting with other players in ANY WAY AT ALL.
- It's really that basic, I mean may as well be a single player game. The only multiplayer functionality is 100% bare bones: You can see other ppl (sometimes, its randomly instanced), and attack the same monster.
Interface:
- No rebinds. Essentially zero control options.
- Not even mouse invert.. Makes the game completely unplayable for me, luckily for AE, I loved there 2d games enough to put in the time to fix this myself, with a complex autohotkey script. It's not at all ideal, but it's somewhat superior to the default mouse camera control tho, since I set it up to hide the mouse cursor (game does not do that).
- Barely any options. You get sfx/mus sliders, rez and a the default built in unity quality slider (which barely does anything).
What it does have:
Quirky artix humor. A few somewhat cool dialog cutscenes (no voice acting). A few zones with bare bones grindy mmo quests (kill x, click a thing an arrow points you to). A few dungeons with monsters with stupidly high health to force you to play with 2 other completely random players (no you cant take your friends) to take them out, but no real challenge or strategy to them.
VERY frequently updates. Artix ent puts an insane amount of dedication into their games and never abandons them. They updated the original adventure quest like a billion times over the last 14+ years, literally every single week. You can expect the same dedication to this game, thus while today it's pretty boring, someday it may get quite fun, so maybe check back if you like the core concept.

DONT, if you dont want to wasit your time, play the original. It has 13 years of work. The company, Artix clearly doesnt know how to run this game too good. With it's cross platform this game is limited, so dont expect too much from it.
Again, if you want to play this game and dont like it, go to the original and then see.
